We report early James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) observations of a unique sample of 11 galaxies at redshifts $z\sim 3-10$ that are optically faint or undetectable but exhibit bright mid-infrared (IR) emission. These objects represent a previously elusive population, with 8 confirmed through NIRCam imaging and 3 via NIRSpec spectroscopy. Their average stellar mass is approximately $10^{10} M_{\odot}$, and they are characterized by high infrared luminosity ($L_{\rm IR}$), low stellar masses, and significant dust extinction. The mean extinction value of $A_{V}\sim 2.5$ aligns with theoretical predictions for galaxies at these early cosmic epochs. These galaxies are predominantly detected in the infrared luminosity function rather than the stellar mass function, indicating that they represent a major source of obscured stellar birth rates in the early Universe. Furthermore, they are likely progenitors of the bright galaxies observed in the local Universe. Notably, the most massive galaxy in our sample, a $z\sim 7$ super starburst with a star formation rate of $\sim 1000 M_{\odot}$ yr$^{-1}$, was previously undetectable in Hubble Space Telescope imaging. This study demonstrates that JWST is capable of identifying a previously hidden population of high-redshift galaxies that are heavily obscured by dust. Consequently, future surveys must prioritize infrared follow-up of optically undetected sources to uncover the true nature of high-redshift galaxies. Finally, we discuss the implications of these findings for the early evolution of galaxies. Finally, the data are accessible at https://doi.org/10.1093/mnras/stad1008. We examine seven-dimensional gravity extended with geometrical terms constructed from Riemann curvature tensors. This approach allows us to derive a family of hadronic seven-dimensional ghosts from the Lagrangian, where the equations of motion for these ghosts generate an infinite hierarchy of constraints on the metric. As a result, the metric acquires the characteristics of a confined, fluctuating structure. We identify specific members of this family that can serve as effective hadronic actions. Notably, this method allows us to bypass the challenges associated with non-uniqueness and combinatorial explosion typically found in multibody gravity theories. We demonstrate that seven-dimensional Einstein-Cartan theory and a two-term generalization of the Born-Inflield theory belong to this family. Furthermore, we show that the lowest-lying hadronic ghosts correspond to the lowest and second-lowest mass spin states in four dimensions. Finally, we establish that the geometrical ghosts are automatically unitarized and analyze the analytic structure of the resulting hadronic S-matrix. Our findings indicate that only a few residues dominate the poles near the second-sheeted cut in the physical region, suggesting that seven-dimensional gravity may serve as a viable non-GRN effective hadronic action. In this context, the gravity ghosts function as confined, fluctuating structures with an infinite hierarchy of mass and spin states. We also examine seven-dimensional gravity coupled to a Yang-Mills field, showing that the Yang-Mills field possesses a massive spectrum. The seven-dimensional ghost retains an infinite hierarchy of mass and spin states, with its polarizations influenced by the Yang-Mills background. We observe that the Yang-Mills field and its associated gauge bosons can be interpreted as excitations of the seven-dimensional ghost within a specific background. Additionally, we investigate the analytic structure of the S-matrix for this coupled theory, finding that the Yang-Mills bosons receive corrections from gravitational interactions, and their residues are dominated by a few poles. Finally, we discuss the implications of these findings for M-theory and M(atrix) theory. We also address the issue of non-uniqueness in matrix theory and explore the implications of our findings for string theory, the AdS/CFT correspondence, and the membrane paradigm. This paper presents a formula for enumerating alternating sequences of disks with two sizes and weights within a channel, offering an extension to the formula for general sequences of disks without weights by one specific component. Furthermore, the authors demonstrate that their formula serves as a bridge between the general enumeration of sequences and the enumeration of balanced sequences. The study employs two distinct counting methods: molecular partition functions and generating functions. The latter method yields a system of recurrence relations, which are solved using the former method. The resulting formula is valid under a specific condition. Additionally, the authors propose an open conjecture. Finally, the paper concludes with an outline of potential applications. These applications involve enumerating sequences of polymeric chains of two lengths that are linked at specific points, such as the $\beta$-turns found in amyloid fibrils. In this context, the $\beta$-sheets within the fibrils can be modeled as a series of blocked disks. The authors intend to address the enumeration of such sequences in future work. They also note that molecular models for other types of fibrils can be adapted in a similar manner. Finally, the paper suggests that future research could explore the enumeration of weighted sequences of blocked disks. This approach would provide a more refined description of the molecular structure of amyloid fibrils, as well as other fibrils, by distinguishing between disks of various sizes. The molecular basis for this refinement lies in the fact that some amino acids are larger than others. Enumerating general sequences of disks with three sizes and weights is expected to offer a more refined description of the molecular structure of amyloid fibrils. The molecular basis for this further refinement is that certain amino acids are larger than those with three possible sizes. The authors propose that the enumeration of blocked disks with three sizes and weights can be viewed as a stepping stone toward the enumeration of blocked disks with more than three sizes and weights. This progression represents a natural evolution in the field. Finally, the authors suggest that future work could explore the enumeration of blocked disks with three sizes and various weights. This approach would provide a more refined description of the molecular structure of amyloid fibrils. The blocked disks in these sequences would have three possible sizes and a variable number of monomers, with the number of monomers in each disk determined by the amino acid it represents. The enumeration of blocked disks with three sizes and a variable number of monomers can also be seen as a stepping stone toward the enumeration of blocked disks with five sizes and weights. This progression is also a natural evolution in the field.

This study examines the joint probability distributions of seasonal precipitation extremes across various global regions, with a specific emphasis on how distinct El Niño flavors influence these patterns. By analyzing 20th-century observational data and simulations from the CMIP5/CMIP6 models, we identify distinct precipitation regimes characterized by either very low or very high seasonal totals. We observe that the differential impacts of unique El Niño flavors on precipitation in the Amazon basin, southeastern Africa, Australia, and northern South America are notably weaker in the CMIP5/CMIP6 simulations compared to observations. These findings underscore the need for enhanced understanding of the land-ocean precipitation connection and its response to the specific flavors of ENSO. Furthermore, they suggest that Earth system models may require improved representation of the atmospheric circulation mechanisms driving precipitation extremes in these areas. This study presents findings from experiments measuring the non-affine growth factor of disordered, non-linear elastic materials through scattered light. By applying nonlocal linearized theory to interpret photonic data, we reveal the underlying physics governing the material's microstructure and its connection to macroscopic elasticity. Our results demonstrate that this growth factor increases with both temperature and probe wavelength, a phenomenon that can be quantitatively explained by the interplay between thermal fluctuations and the material's yield stress. Furthermore, we quantify the scattering contribution from near-surface regions, which becomes significant at larger probe wavelengths. These insights are crucial for future investigations into disordered elastic materials using photonic techniques. Ultimately, the methods developed here establish a quantitative framework for exploring disordered elastic materials, enabling the examination of their complex microstructure, aperiodicity, and nonlinearity. This approach is expected to facilitate the discovery of new materials with tailored mechanical and sensing capabilities. Finally, this research is supported by the recent establishment of the Center for Nonlinear and Nonlocal Optics at the University of Michigan.

This paper introduces a single-population single-age structured population dynamics model that incorporates the impacts of pollution and biological behaviors. The study first examines the existence and uniqueness of the solution to the linear system under polynomial growth conditions. Subsequently, utilizing the Lyapunov function method, the author establishes the polynomial stability of this unique solution. The remainder of the work focuses on the qualitative analysis of the nonlinear system. The polynomial growth solution is shown to exist globally and is proven to be locally asymptotically stable. Through the construction of a suitable Lyapunov function, the paper demonstrates that the globally asymptotically stable solution represents an extinction state. Furthermore, it is established that the population age structure remains invariant over time. Finally, extensive numerical simulations are conducted to illustrate the theoretical findings. These results indicate that the model accurately reflects reality and holds significant practical value. Additionally, the analysis reveals that the impact of the carrying capacity on the pollution parameter is more pronounced than the effect of the pollution parameter itself. This conclusion is supported by the observation that in a polluted environment, the population's carrying capacity is lower than in a non-polluted one. Consequently, the model suggests that controlling pollution is more effective than merely expanding the habitat to increase the carrying capacity. These insights could assist in formulating more rational policies for sustainable development. This paper introduces a number-theoretic method for calculating the proof complexity of hypersequent substructural logics that permit structural rules of weakening and contraction. We demonstrate that the proof complexity problem is undecidable for this broad category of logics, a result achieved by establishing the soundness and completeness of a labeled calculus and its corresponding number-theoretic model. Specifically, we generalize an earlier decidability result regarding contraction-only substructural logics to the case of weakening, revealing that relaxing contraction constraints causes the proof complexity problem to transition from undecidable to decidable. Notably, we identify a precise boundary within the hierarchy of weakening hypersequent substructural logics where this shift in decidability occurs. These findings are deeply intertwined with recent advancements in number-theoretic methods for analyzing contraction rules in substructural logics. Furthermore, we establish the soundness and completeness of a labeled calculus for specific weakly structuring logics—extensions of linear logic featuring contraction on the succint of sequents—and explore the connections between our findings and the behavior of the rank function in these systems. Finally, we conclude by discussing potential future research directions inspired by these results. This work extends the arXiv preprint arXiv:2101.01301.

Although taxonomies are highly suited to the intrinsic geometry of hyperbolic space, manually expanding them is both labor-intensive and costly. This paper introduces HyperExpan, a taxonomy growth framework that learns representations within a hyperbolic embedding space. By leveraging the geometry of hyperbolic neural networks, HyperExpan effectively expands taxonomies by automatically discovering and integrating new concepts based on user interactions with existing ones. We evaluated this approach on two hyperbolic feature spaces derived from the Sylvester and Ball projections, trained on a taxonomy learned from 1,000 user interactions. Our results demonstrate that HyperExpan successfully uncovers concepts in subsequent training batches that were absent from the initial taxonomy, maintaining the structural relationships of the original embedding while incorporating novel concepts. Furthermore, when compared against state-of-the-art methods, HyperExpan exhibits greater resilience to variations in initial taxonomy quality and size. This study examines S66, a benchmark dataset for non-covalent interactions between molecular pairs, within external electric fields. The dataset comprises 110 molecules and 3,580 molecular pairs, including both parallel and antiparallel configurations subjected to electric fields ranging from 0 to ±0.05 a.u. The analysis focuses on the electric field-induced enhancement of van der Waals and charge-transfer interactions. To achieve this, the study employs the Coupled-Pair Natural Orbital-Coupled-Cluster (CPNO-CC) method, which offers high computational efficiency. The findings indicate that van der Waals interactions are significantly amplified by external electric fields, with the most substantial increases occurring in pairs featuring weaker van der Waals forces in the absence of the field. Non-deterministic scheduling incorporates various types of uncertainty, such as stochastic data and non-deterministic information. The latter refers to incomplete knowledge regarding future events, where uncertainty exists but is not random. This form of uncertainty is prevalent in real-world settings and is typically modeled using possibility theory. Consequently, the resulting optimization challenge is defined as a possibility of feasibility problem, which is generally NP-hard. This study introduces a novel heuristic approach designed to address general possibility scheduling problems and validate its effectiveness through extensive testing on a specific instance: the possibility job shop scheduling problem (PJSP). In this context, uncertainty affects operation processing times, and the objective is to minimize makespan. The proposed method combines a genetic algorithm with a decoding technique derived from a polynomial-time heuristic. To enhance solution quality, the optimization process employs custom operators and strategies, including a novel heuristic operator. Additionally, the study integrates robustness into the genetic algorithm to prevent premature convergence. Results indicate that the approach is highly effective, achieving an average improvement of 10% in performance metrics compared to existing methods in the literature. Furthermore, a computational study demonstrates that the robustness strategy significantly boosts performance, increasing the average improvement to 13%. Finally, the robustness mechanism is shown to enhance both convergence speed and the diversity of the solution set. The paper concludes with several recommendations for future research. Keywords: Non-deterministic; Possibility; Robustness; Robust genetic algorithm; Robustness; Heuristics; Scheduling.

The efficacy of traditional control strategies, which prioritize system performance while assuming a stable cyber infrastructure, is compromised when subjected to cyber attacks. To overcome this limitation, we introduce a new STL-based framework designed to ensure the resilience of cyber-physical systems (CPS) against such attacks, thereby guaranteeing that specific high-level performance requirements are met even during malicious intrusions. This approach entails developing a high-level temporal logic specification and subsequently deriving a corresponding low-level control policy capable of satisfying the logic constraints despite cyber threats. We demonstrate the practical utility of this proposed resilience framework through a simulation case study. The results confirm that the resulting control policy successfully enforces temporal constraints, thereby achieving the desired resilience objectives. Furthermore, we establish that the associated optimization problem is convex, ensuring that the proposed control policy can be efficiently computed online. Finally, we present a real-world implementation of the resilience framework, which has been deployed to enhance attack resilience in a hardware testbed featuring a quadrotor vehicle. This implementation successfully illustrates the framework's applicability to complex, real-world scenarios. Our work represents the first step toward realizing resilience in practical CPS, with future research focused on extending this framework to address more sophisticated and intricate real-life systems. Additionally, we have made the simulation code and models for this work publicly available. Our code repository includes a demonstration where the resilience framework is implemented to protect a quadrotor vehicle from a real cyber attack, thereby validating the framework's utility for real-world systems. This study examines the potential for detecting dark matter candidates with masses ranging from $10^{-14}$ eV to $10^{-2}$ eV/$c^2$ by analyzing data from existing acceleration sensor networks. To maximize sensitivity across the entire mass spectrum, we propose an analysis strategy that leverages both spatial and temporal correlations inherent in such datasets. Our findings indicate that current accelerometer networks can already explore approximately 10% of the parameter space, with future upgrades and new instruments capable of covering an additional 1% to 2%. We also outline key requirements for upcoming high-quality acceleration sensors and existing platforms, including those for the LISA Pathfinder mission, to enable definitive conclusions. Furthermore, we estimate that a cost-effective global acceleration sensor network, achieving performance levels of $10^{-9}$ g or better, could conclusively detect these dark matter candidates within the next decade. This initiative would require an investment of around $100 million and the participation of approximately 100 scientists. We conclude that exploring these dark matter parameter spaces using accelerometer networks offers a promising avenue for future research. Additionally, we identify the next generation of accelerometer networks as a vital field for scientific advancement. We also discuss how these networks could contribute to other areas of fundamental physics, such as searches for stochastic gravitational wave backgrounds and tests of gravity. Finally, we address the challenges associated with calibrating accelerometers and developing data analysis methods. To facilitate this, we have created a new open-access repository for acceleration sensor data, which we believe will be valuable for future research. This repository includes datasets from various sources, such as the LISA Pathfinder mission, the Gravity Probe B mission, and the GRACE satellite mission. We also provide a suite of open-source software tools to assist researchers in conducting their own analyses. Our goal is to make this research accessible to the entire community, thereby fostering new collaborations and accelerating discoveries. We hope that our work will serve as a catalyst for new initiatives in the field of acceleration sensing. We believe that investing in this area is essential for advancing our understanding of dark matter and other fundamental physics phenomena. Ultimately, we are confident that a global acceleration sensor network will play a pivotal role in the future of scientific research. We look forward to the day when this network is fully operational and can begin to uncover the secrets of the universe. We believe that this is an exciting and promising time for acceleration sensing, and we are excited to be part of this journey. We are confident that this field will continue to grow and make significant contributions

The source of radio emission from galaxy clusters has been a subject of debate for many years. While the intracluster medium (ICM) is considered the primary emission region, its magnetic field strength remains a critical, yet unmeasured, parameter. This study aims to determine the magnetic field strength within the ICM by analyzing the ratio of ICM emission to the magnetic power spectrum, a value that depends on the angular dimensions of compact radio sources. We examine a sample of 1,000 compact radio sources with a magnetic power spectrum index of -2.8 and a magnetic-to-ICM emission ratio of 0.015. Using the magnetic power spectrum index as a function of angular dimensions, we establish the angular dimensions of these compact sources. Our results indicate that these sources are not point-like, with dimensions ranging from 0.01 to 0.1 arcseconds. Consequently, the magnetic-to-ICM emission ratio is determined to be between 0.01 and 0.02. These findings suggest that the ICM is not the sole region responsible for radio emission in galaxy clusters. Furthermore, the derived magnetic power spectrum index of -2.8 aligns with the theoretical prediction of -3 proposed by Schure et al. (2009). Finally, we estimate the magnetic field strength within the ICM to be approximately 1 microGauss. These outcomes support the hypothesis that radio emission originates from jet-ICM interactions. The paper concludes with several recommendations for future research. We recommend that readers utilize the provided data and code to replicate our analysis and explore the properties of compact radio sources in greater detail. Additionally, we encourage readers to examine the distribution of magnetic power spectrum indices and their relationship with angular dimensions to gain deeper insights into the magnetic properties of galaxy clusters. Finally, we suggest that readers analyze the data using different stacking methods to investigate other aspects of compact radio sources. Hidden Markov Models (HMMs) are a fundamental tool in quantitative information flow, used to measure the leakage of sensitive data from high-level programs. This paper introduces A-HMMs, a generalized variant of HMMs that can represent any non-deterministic, higher-order probabilistic program. We demonstrate that, unlike standard HMMs, A-HMMs offer a concise and exact characterization of information flow in high-level languages. Specifically, we show that information flow in high-level languages can be modeled as a natural transformation from the power set monad to a new monad defined by A-HMMs. This result provides a unified framework for describing various information flow metrics, including min-entropy, max-entropy, and expected max-entropy. Finally, we extend the definition of A-HMMs to support asymptotic information flow metrics. Our work builds upon recent research in category theory applied to high-level synthesis and probabilistic programming. By leveraging the category theoretic definition of HMMs, we generalize the model to create A-HMMs. The definition of information flow metrics relies on the concept of observation channels, which are the image of high-level programs under the natural transformation representing information flow. We believe the structures defined in this paper hold significant promise for program analysis. Our definition of A-HMMs rectifies this by providing a practical method to compute the necessary distributions for analyzing observation channels. This enables the development of algorithms to calculate entropy-based information flow metrics for high-level programs. This direction is pursued in our companion paper, where we introduce a type-directed approach to compute these metrics. This approach is derived from the definition of A-HMMs presented in this paper. Additionally, our framework facilitates the definition of asymptotic information flow metrics, a capability that extends beyond the reach of existing techniques. We provide a phenomenological analysis of the flexible scattering amplitudes for $2\to2$ and $4\to4$ processes within the massless limit, incorporating constraints from analyticity, unitarity, and unitary irreducible representations of the Poincaré group. Our findings reveal that in the high-energy, large-momentum transfer regime, these amplitudes exhibit nontrivial angular dependencies. Furthermore, we establish that all such amplitudes adhere to generalized soft-winding asymptotics, thereby extending this behavior to a broader class of processes. Additionally, we derive explicit expressions for the imaginary components of these amplitudes, demonstrating their alignment with the optical theorem for the $2\to4$ process and the Mandelstam double-commutator theorem for $4\to4$ processes. Finally, we examine the implications of these amplitudes regarding differential cross sections, BSM search strategies, and the testing of causality in high-energy colliders. These amplitudes may become accessible through multi-particle final states in the future, such as those observed in $pp\to Z_{(1,2,3)}Z_{(1,2,3)}$ and $pp\to ZZtt$ events at the HL-LHC and FCC-ee. Our findings suggest that incorporating angular information into flexible scattering observables could significantly enhance the sensitivity of searches for new physics. This approach offers a comprehensive framework for final-state analysis, capable of fully utilizing experimental data and maximizing the potential for discovering physics beyond the Standard Model. Consequently, this methodology is expected to be applicable to various flexible scattering processes in the near future. This work introduces a novel privacy framework for location tracking that employs conditional probability distributions to forecast the movement of anonymous data subjects. The method is broadly applicable to various fine-grained location privacy systems that depend on prior distributions to derive posterior probabilities regarding user movements. We demonstrate that utilizing conditional priors yields either superior or more interpretable outcomes compared to standard priors across three specific scenarios. A fourth scenario highlights the method's capacity to address specific domain-related challenges. Ultimately, we conclude that conditional priors offer distinct advantages when designing location privacy mechanisms that integrate user-specific contextual elements, such as demographic data or health status. The proposed framework is designed to ensure privacy by enforcing prior distributions that limit the potential information leakage from location traces, regardless of the specific mechanism being evaluated. Furthermore, to facilitate the adoption of this approach, we have developed an open-source Python library that implements the framework and includes various utility functions for assessing the privacy guarantees of different mechanisms. This library is made available to the research community. The code can be accessed at: https://github.com/epiclab/conditional-prior. The Normal Distribution Transform (NDT) has long been a preferred method for solving the 3D global localization problem due to its rapid and reliable performance. However, applying NDT to increasingly complex and large-scale environments remains difficult, primarily because of the high computational cost associated with calculating multivariate Gaussian probability density functions across numerous grid cells. This study introduces NDT-Transformer, a novel approach that leverages Transformer architectures to efficiently model NDT. By utilizing self-attention mechanisms, the model captures long-range dependencies between grid cells, thereby enhancing both solution accuracy and convergence speed. Furthermore, by approximating the NDT objective function with Transformers, the need to compute Gaussian probabilities is eliminated, resulting in substantial computational savings. The method is demonstrated using the widely adopted nuScenes dataset. Experimental results indicate that NDT-Transformer achieves a mean absolute error of 0.75 meters, surpassing the 1.02 meters achieved by the nCDT algorithm. Additionally, the NDT-Transformer model is lightweight, consuming only 1.5 milliseconds on an NVIDIA RTX 2080 GPU, compared to the 11.5 milliseconds required by nCDT. Source code is available at https://github.com/Chenchen99/NDT-Transformer. Keywords: 3D Localization, Normal Distribution Transform (NDT), Transformer Representation.

Resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging (rs-fMRI) connectivity is extensively employed in neuroscience to investigate brain organization and investigate links with behavioral and clinical variables. However, the reproducibility of connectivity metrics derived from short-duration scans remains a significant challenge. This study introduces a statistical framework designed to assess the signal-to-noise ratio in rs-fMRI data and evaluate the influence of critical acquisition parameters on both reproducibility and the accuracy of predicting external targets. By synthesizing data from the Human Connectome Project (HCP) and the Multi-Modal Multi-Site fMRI (MaMuS) database, we analyzed 1,000 participants scanned under diverse conditions. Our findings indicate that while task engagement and physiological noise during rest are the primary determinants of functional connectivity, the impact of temporal filtering and spatial resolution is contingent upon the specific connectivity metric used. Furthermore, we quantified how variations in recording duration, temporal filtering, and spatial resolution influence the statistical strength and accuracy of node-level features in predicting resting-state cognitive performance. Ultimately, we established optimal acquisition and analysis parameters that enhance the statistical power of node-level feature prediction without compromising functional network topology. These insights aim to guide future rs-fMRI research toward more robust and reproducible outcomes. Furthermore, the proposed framework offers a generalizable approach for designing multisite neuroimaging studies and can be readily adapted to other contexts. This study examines the naming problem within beeping networks, specifically targeting single-hop systems where nodes lack prior knowledge of their identifiers. In this context, nodes must determine their correct IDs through message exchange via beeps, adhering to specific constraints: no node may know more than two identifiers (its own and one neighbor's) at any moment, and total beep count must remain minimal. We introduce a straightforward, deterministic algorithm capable of resolving naming for all nodes within $O(n)$ iterations. Subsequently, we enhance this approach to ensure energy efficiency by minimizing total beep consumption. Our refined method achieves energy-conserving status for every node, requiring each to execute no more than two beeps. Extensive simulations demonstrate that our proposed solution outperforms existing state-of-the-art alternatives. Furthermore, we apply this energy-conserving algorithm to address distributed coloration in single-hop networks, successfully generating proper colorings. Finally, our findings regarding distributed coloration are evaluated through simulation-based comparisons. Notably, our algorithm surpasses current methods in both maximizing the count of properly colored vertices and reducing total beep usage. Additionally, the algorithm operates without any pre-existing knowledge of network parameters. To our knowledge, this represents the first instance of an energy-conserving, deterministic naming algorithm for single-hop networks that is entirely independent of network size or specific node identities. Consequently, our solution is particularly well-suited for deployment in resource-constrained environments. This paper serves as a preliminary report, and a more comprehensive version will be published in *IEEE Transactions on Parallel and Distributed Systems*. A detailed comparison with existing solutions will be presented in that full publication. Given the problem's inherent complexity, we anticipate that our proposed algorithms will advance the state of the art by a significant margin. Finally, our work addresses a critical gap in current research by offering the first energy-conserving, deterministic naming solution for single-hop networks that does not rely on prior knowledge of network parameters. This capability is essential for addressing challenges in distributed networks. To the best of our knowledge, no other deterministic algorithm exists that can name all nodes in a single-hop network without pre-known parameters. While randomized algorithms do offer such a solution, they are not energy-conserving, meaning some nodes may consume excessive energy. Our work thus establishes a new state-of-the-art for single-hop naming, achieving energy conservation for all nodes without prerequisite knowledge of network parameters. This study addresses the challenge of generating spatial restrictions for motion planning within dynamic environments. The primary goal is to create spatial constraints that limit the set of possible actions for dynamic objects, thereby increasing the efficiency of motion planning algorithms. To achieve this, we introduce a sampling-based algorithm designed to produce non-redundant, feasible restrictions. Visual relocalization serves as a fundamental component for enabling autonomous robots to explore and map environments. Surfel maps, which represent 3D scenes as collections of local patches, are highly effective for this purpose because they are compact, robust, and facilitate accurate local estimation. However, the similarity between surfel patches and 3D point clouds makes their descriptors particularly vulnerable to perturbations caused by lighting changes, dust, and other environmental factors. To address descriptor robustness, we introduce PNet, a neural network that learns global image features. Additionally, we develop a novel descriptor learning approach that integrates geometric information into neural networks, allowing them to adapt to the dynamic nature of our data. Our results demonstrate that combining PNet with informed neural descriptor learning yields superior performance compared to utilizing either component alone. Experimental evaluations confirm that this enhanced surfel-based relocalization pipeline surpasses state-of-the-art methods. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/ashwinbhat/3dSurfelNet.

This study investigates particle self-assembly by concurrently evoking both particle properties and simulation protocols. To accelerate this process, we introduce a sparse neuroevolutionary method where both particles and strategies are Membranes, featuring internal structures that facilitate multi-level selection. Results demonstrate that this approach efficiently generates self-assembly protocols for specified target particles. Furthermore, applying multi-level selection to both particles and strategies enables the rapid discovery of self-assembly protocols for a diverse range of particle types. This rapid evolution is attributed to a novel way of mapping self-assembly tasks onto abstract computational problems, thereby preventing premature convergence. The resulting particle strategies offer profound insights into self-assembly, including multi-step protocols, entropic design, and the manipulation of inter-particle interactions. Ultimately, this work establishes a powerful framework for accelerating the design of self-assembly protocols and particles for advanced materials science. We demonstrate that magnon-squeezing can be observed in antiferromagnetic thin films at temperatures exceeding 100 millikelvin. This thermal squeezing arises from the antiferromagnetic spin structure and is predicted to reach approximately 50% near room temperature. These findings are supported by recent experiments conducted at four-terminal magnon detectors in yttrium-iron-garnet and by numerical simulations. Furthermore, we predict a thermal nonlinear spectral shift in yig samples, which is expected to be on the order of a gigahertz at temperatures above 100 millikelvin. This shift stems from the thermal dispersion of magnons and can be detected using narrow-band magnons and high-precision frequency measurement devices. Our results indicate that thermal squeezing is universally present in antiferromagnetic materials, potentially opening avenues for detecting and manipulating them. Additionally, these phenomena may have significant implications for developing magnon-based quantum devices and circuits operating at room temperature. We introduce two modifications to Loidreau's code-based cryptosystem. The first variant preserves the original public key structure but substitutes McEliece's syndrome decoding problem with the weighted minimum set cover problem. The second version employs a public key composed of two matrices, thereby increasing the key's dimension. For both versions, we analyze the public key size, computation requirements for key generation and verification, and encryption/decryption speeds. Our results indicate that this system offers better efficiency than McEliece while maintaining comparable security levels. Furthermore, the public key size is smaller than that of the original McEliece scheme or the Ding-Kazymyuk variant, and it rivals the efficiency of the digital signature algorithm NTRU. We present an exhaustive attack on both versions using integer linear programming, which successfully recovers the secret key in a feasible timeframe. Additionally, we examine potential improvements to enhance resistance against such attacks. Finally, we demonstrate that the minimum set cover problem serves as a viable replacement for the subset sum problem in McEliece schemes, and our proposed public key matrices exhibit a higher search-to-decision complexity ratio than those used in Hermitian or triangular matrices. This ratio acts as a metric for estimating public key security in code-based schemes that utilize support set decoding attacks. We conclude by discussing how this ratio can guide the selection of appropriate matrices for constructing secure code-based cryptosystems. Notably, this work marks the first instance of an exhaustive attack utilizing integer linear programming for any code-based cryptosystem. A language model's efficacy in downstream tasks relies heavily on the richness of its learned word representations. While current pre-training approaches utilize massive corpora to capture intricate lexical and semantic relationships, they often fail to fully represent nuanced word connections, particularly regarding synonyms and related terms. To address this shortcoming, we introduce Dict-BERT, a new pre-training model that integrates THACOM, a large Turkish-Turkish THAC (Term Alignment and Comparison) dataset, to provide explicit guidance on words and phrases with clear semantic links. We employ two pre-training strategies to model these semantic relations: Cross-Encoder Pre-training (CE-PT) and Cross-Encoder Fine-tuning (CE-Ft). CE-PT leverages the extensive Dict-BERT dataset to learn local semantic structures, whereas CE-Ft utilizes a smaller version of the same data to refine BERT's pre-trained knowledge. We evaluate Dict-BERT across various Turkish Natural Language Understanding (NLU) tasks, including sentiment analysis, question answering, and natural language inference. Our experimental results demonstrate that Dict-BERT consistently outperforms BERT and RoBERTa, achieving an average performance improvement of 1.6% over BERT and 2.1% over RoBERTa. The dataset and the pre-trained models are accessible at https://github.com/THACOM/DictBERT. Furthermore, our code for CE-PT and CE-Ft can be found at https://github.com/THACOM/DictBERT. We establish tight asymptotic bounds for minimal spanning acycycles within random simplicial complexes, specifically addressing random geometric complexes and models featuring long-range interactions. These results yield tight bounds for the extremal values of persistence diagrams generated by random balls and Euclidean distance transforms. Additionally, our methodology enables the derivation of tight bounds for both the mass and the number of faces in minimal spanning acycycles. Finally, we demonstrate tight bounds for the convergence rates of minimal spanning acycles, persistograms, and extreme statistics to their deterministic limit counterparts. This comprehensive set of findings offers a thorough understanding of the behavior of these minimal structures and extreme statistics in high-dimensional contexts, a domain where data often exhibits local clustering despite being drawn from a global distribution. Our work introduces novel techniques and concepts that may prove beneficial for other convergence problems involving high-dimensional point clouds. Notably, we prove tight bounds for the convergence rates of persistograms to a deterministic limit, a result that was previously unknown. Furthermore, we show that the speed of convergence for persistograms is strictly slower than that of minimal spanning acycles, thereby resolving an open question posed by Cohen-Steiner, Chazal, and Sabourou in 2012. We also provide a tight upper bound for the quantile convergence rate of persistograms to a deterministic limit, which is optimal up to logarithmic factors for the median convergence rate. These results are derived through the application of concentration inequalities, which are also presented as independent contributions. Finally, we propose a general framework for defining random complexes and develop a unified approach to analyzing extreme geometric random complexes. Vertical Federated Learning (VFL) represents a privacy-preserving framework where multiple parties collaboratively train machine learning models by combining complementary features. While VFL offers privacy and security benefits, it remains susceptible to various attacks that compromise model integrity and user privacy. This paper presents three novel VFL attacks: (1) a new reconstruction attack utilizing information-theoretic principles, (2) a novel membership inference attack leveraging optimal transport theory, and (3) a successful reconstruction attack against Differential Privacy (DP) models based on the concept of approximate counting. We demonstrate the efficacy of these proposed attacks. Our findings indicate that the proposed reconstruction attacks substantially enhance the accuracy of models such as logistic regression and random forest compared to previous state-of-the-art methods. Furthermore, our novel membership inference attack achieves significantly higher accuracy compared to existing approaches. Crucially, these attack vectors effectively bypass current VFL privacy preservation mechanisms, including Secure Aggregation and DP. Ultimately, our work underscores the necessity for enhanced VFL privacy protection strategies to safeguard sensitive user data. To our knowledge, this represents the first study to integrate information-theoretic and optimal transport theory into the contexts of reconstruction and membership inference attacks within VFL, respectively. We analyze the decay $B\to p+D$ within the framework of the $q\to n$ dark sector dark matter model, where the $B$-meson transitions into the dark sector via an effective four-fermion operator. Our findings indicate that the decay width $\Gamma_{B\to pD}$ is proportional to the fourth power of the dark baryon mass, $m_D^4$, and the effective coupling constant, $|F|^2$. Furthermore, the decay rate is highly sensitive to the light-cone distribution amplitudes of the dark baryons. For the $B$-meson mass, the predicted decay width falls within the range $10^{-63}\sim 10^{-57}~{\rm GeV}$. Additionally, we examine the constraints imposed by the dark baryon number conservation law on this decay process. Finally, we discuss potential experimental detection methods for this decay channel. These results suggest that the proposed decay is feasible to detect in the near future at facilities such as LHCb, PANDA, or the proposed P2 experiment. Additionally, our findings provide a stringent constraint on the parameter space of the $q\to n$ dark sector dark matter model. Future experiments will offer a complementary search for dark matter, with the ultimate goal of measuring the branching ratio for this decay. This measurement could potentially determine the Wilson coefficient of the effective operator, $F$, and the dark fermion mass, $m_f$, thereby identifying $q\to n$ dark sector dark matter as a viable candidate. Consequently, the $B$-meson decay $B\to p+D$ offers a promising avenue for detecting dark matter. This paper introduces the Intelligent City Defense game, a real-time, turn-based strategy title featuring a unique asymmetric multiplayer setup. Designed to explore the challenges of defending intelligent cities against cyberattacks, the game requires players to allocate defensive resources to safeguard critical city assets. The core loop involves players simultaneously launching cyberattacks and managing their own defenses, with resource decisions made under conditions of imperfect information and incomplete knowledge regarding an opponent's capabilities. The authors discuss how the game's design elements influence player decisions, present a mathematical model of the gameplay, and analyze the associated decision problems. Furthermore, they examine the use of machine learning techniques for both automated play and the analysis of resource allocation strategies. This work represents an initial step toward a new category of domain-specific games. The authors demonstrate that the game's structure fosters strategic thinking, while its integration of physical, cyber, and decision-making layers offers players and researchers deeper insights into the complexities of resource allocation within smart city defense. Additionally, the application of machine learning in this context opens avenues for further research into the application of these technologies in defense systems. The Intelligent City Defense game is available on Steam (https://store.steampowered.com/app/1180040/Intelligent_City_Defense/). This study examines the Hawking–Page phase transitions of Schwarzschild black holes within an anti-de Sitter background and within a cavity to analyze the thermodynamic phase behavior of black holes confined in a container. Our findings indicate that within the anti-de Sitter spacetime, a Schwarzschild black hole remains stable across the entire temperature spectrum. In contrast, a Schwarzschild black hole within a cavity exhibits an unstable radius range of $(0, 2r_c/3)$ and a phase shift occurring at the critical radius $r_{cr} = \left[\frac{27\pi r_c^3 T^2}{2}\right]^{1/3}$, where $r_c$ denotes the cavity's radius and $T$ represents the temperature. Additionally, the transition type for Schwarzschild black holes in a cavity is identified as either Hawking–Page or limit transition, contingent upon the specific values of $r_c$ and $T$. These results offer a theoretical basis for comprehending the thermal properties of black holes. Furthermore, the methodology employed is applicable to investigating other black hole systems under similar cavity constraints. This paper introduces a straightforward yet effective strategy for training deep learning models under noisy labels. The approach partitions the training data into groups based on labels, utilizing bag-level sampling to train individual models within each group. Subsequently, a group-level loss function is optimized to train the final model. Experiments conducted on the RCV1 and OHSUMED datasets demonstrate that this method yields more consistent results compared to existing state-of-the-art techniques. Furthermore, the method exhibits superior performance in high-noise scenarios and maintains robustness when trained on multiple groups with varying sample sizes. Finally, the proposed approach is applied to a large-scale noisy dataset, highlighting its potential for noise mitigation in extensive real-world data collections. Semantic tag generation is a cost-effective strategy for training models with limited labeled data, as tags can be readily generated using large language models. This paper introduces a pseudo-tagging algorithm designed to filter out uninformative tags and retain only those with high semantic value. Our method employs a two-stage approach: first, it utilizes pseudo-labels to calculate confidence scores for each tag; second, it selects tags with the highest confidence scores as pseudo-tags. We applied our proposed InfoP2T algorithm to node semantic tag generation, where it significantly surpassed baseline models in both the number of unique tags and F1 scores. Additionally, experiments on graph classification demonstrate that InfoP2T effectively improves the sample efficiency of Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs). Finally, we release the Node-Tags-Knowledge-Graph dataset to support future research in node semantic tag generation. The code and dataset are available at: https://github.com/Chenchenchenchenchen/InfoP2T. This work was presented at the 18th Workshop on Neural Symbolic Learning and Reasoning (NSLR-2023). This paper examines simulations of betatron radiation generated by the 400 GeV/proton beam-beam interaction studied in the AWAKE Run 2 experiment. We analyze the spectral and angular characteristics of this radiation, which could pose significant challenges to detector systems. Additionally, we explore potential mitigation strategies, including the use of small elliptical beams. Our findings indicate that while reducing the number of interacting beam particles is one option, it may not be feasible due to the need to maintain sufficient luminosity for the AWAKE program. Instead, we demonstrate that an elliptical beam profile can effectively suppress betatron radiation in specific directions. We also address various technical obstacles associated with simulating these interactions and present proposed solutions. Ultimately, we outline key questions regarding the implementation of such simulations within the PRIMO framework. These issues are not only pertinent to AWAKE but also extend to other laser-plasma accelerator projects, such as the European XFEL upgrade and the CLFEL proposal. Furthermore, we emphasize the necessity of conducting realistic simulations that incorporate radiation reaction effects and space charge forces to accurately capture the physics of beam-beam interactions. This approach will facilitate the design of appropriate detectors and shielding systems to protect them from intense betatron radiation. The analysis code employed in this study is now available to the community under the name AWAKEBeamBeam. This open-source tool is built upon the PRIMO framework and is designed to be easily adaptable to future projects. It is accessible at https://github.com/AwakeTeam/AWAKEBeamBeam. Additionally, we have published a comprehensive tutorial on simulating beam-beam interactions, beginning with a simple scenario and progressing to an investigation of betatron radiation, which can be found at https://github.com/AwakeTeam/AwakeBeamBeam/blob/master/BeamBeamTutorial.ipynb. We anticipate that this framework and tutorial will be valuable for AWAKE simulations and will also aid other communities, such as XFEL and CLFEL, in understanding the complexities of beam-beam interactions. Furthermore, the tutorial will be updated regularly to reflect new features added to AWAKEBeamBeam. This study addresses a critical challenge in distributed machine learning: training decision trees while maintaining differential privacy. We introduce a private decision tree algorithm based on the scalable and efficient Gradient Tree Boosting framework, ensuring both privacy and performance. Our approach employs two distinct methods to safeguard data during distribution. The first utilizes a novel application of the randomized response mechanism within the distributed setting, achieving $d$-differential privacy for any privacy parameter $d \ge 1$; this method is highly accurate and delivers private training that closely approximates public training. The second method relies on the secure two-party computation model, offering stronger privacy guarantees. Both strategies substantially outperform existing state-of-the-art techniques in both privacy protection and training efficiency. Furthermore, we systematically examine the trade-offs between privacy levels and accuracy, providing comprehensive insights to guide practitioners in selecting optimal privacy parameters. Finally, we demonstrate that our methods support the generation of differentially private decision tree ensembles, a functionality that has not been previously explored. Extensive experiments across various datasets and scenarios highlight the versatility and effectiveness of our proposed solutions. This paper introduces the use of Bregman proximal gradient algorithms to regularize the Rényi divergence between probability distributions. Rényi divergence serves as a family of generalized divergence measures encompassing well-known metrics such as Kullback-Leibler divergence, Hellinger distance, and Total variation distance, with the specific member selected based on the particular properties desired. Unlike Total variation distance, Rényi divergence is defined only when the underlying distributions are absolutely continuous with respect to one another; specifically, it is undefined if their supports do not fully overlap. This study examines the optimization of Rényi divergence under various constraints, utilizing Bregman proximal gradient methods. These approaches leverage the information-geometric structure inherent in these problems, where Rényi divergence acts as a measure of dispersion among probability distributions and serves as the foundation for defining the Bregman proximal gradient algorithm. The research analyzes the convergence characteristics of this algorithm and illustrates its application in optimizing both the type 1 and type 2 Rényi divergences. Furthermore, the study explores how the parameter $\alpha$ influences the optimization outcomes and reports numerical results demonstrating the algorithm's performance. The methodology is applied in a binary classification setting, where Rényi divergence regularizers are shown to enhance classifier performance, particularly when prior information regarding class distributions is available. This prior information can manifest as known distributional properties, constraints on the distributions, or prior estimates, with the objective being the minimization of Rényi divergence relative to these known values. Finally, the paper addresses the optimization of Rényi divergence when both distributions require estimation, addressing the challenge of estimating distributions with differing dimensions by employing dimensionality reduction techniques. The efficacy of these proposed methods is validated through numerical experiments. The approach is also pertinent to other domains, such as clustering, where estimating distributions with varying dimensions poses a similar challenge. Furthermore, Rényi divergence is valuable in information bottleneck theory, a framework for learning data representations that balance information retention about the target variable against compression, a topic that remains an active area of research. Additionally, in hypothesis testing, Rényi divergence quantifies the ability to distinguish between two distributions, with different $\alpha$ values yielding different hypotheses; for instance, $\alpha=1$ recovers the Neyman-Pearson hypothesis, while $\alpha \to 0$ and $\alpha \to 1$ converge to the likelihood ratio. Consequently, Rényi divergence is applicable in estimating the distribution of sums of random variables, where the distributions of individual random variables may differ. Chain event graph models extend the capabilities of discrete Markov models and offer a potent framework for analyzing sequential data. Nevertheless, their application remains constrained because there are no established statistical tools for estimating these models or selecting between different chain event graph representations. This work introduces a method for model choice that extends the standard marginal likelihood approach to accommodate chain event graphs. By enabling comparison of various models, this method facilitates the analysis of complex data and a broader range of scientific inquiries. We demonstrate the proposed method through an example of disease progression analysis. Furthermore, we evaluate the method's performance via an extensive simulation study covering both favorable and challenging scenarios. Finally, the paper discusses potential extensions of the method. Key contributions include an open-source R package, the application of chain event graphs to disease progression analysis, and a systematic assessment of Bayesian model choice performance across diverse settings. Additionally, we examine how the method handles difficult situations, such as when the true model is not available within the candidate set. The results indicate that the method performs well when the true model is included in the candidate set and remains viable even when it is excluded. However, when the true model is absent from the candidate set, a more complex mechanism is required to analyze chain event graph data. We conclude that the proposed method is a valuable tool for researchers working with chain event graphs. This result extends recent findings by Attouch, Cabot, and Zhou (2021) and contrasts with the behavior of the inertial proximal point method with non-viscous limits, which exhibits oscillations. Furthermore, we establish convergence to the minimum norm solution for a generalized gradient flow arising from a non-viscous limit, offering a significant improvement over prior results. Finally, we demonstrate local convergence with a rate for a Kurdyka-Lojasiewicz type inclusion, which encompasses finding the minimum of a convex function or solving a variational inequality involving a maximally monotone operator. These continuous findings are complemented by corresponding theorems for their discretized inertial proximal point method with non-viscous limits and Tikhonov regularization, including a sufficient condition for strong convergence to the minimum norm solution. Numerical experiments illustrate the behavior of these dynamics and their finite-dimensional approximations. Wall-following robots are essential for autonomous navigation along corridors, but how do they handle decision-making when encountering dead ends, dead robots, and obstacles? This paper investigates the disorderly dynamics inherent in such systems by introducing a minimal continuous dynamical system that models key decision-making aspects. We demonstrate that these decisions follow a simple linear form, revealing that common heuristics—such as staying close to walls and avoiding obstacles—are mathematically linked through a single parameter. Furthermore, we show that the resulting system can exhibit disorderly transitions, a phenomenon we explore across various parameter regimes. Our findings indicate that slight variations in decision-making parameters can trigger diverse transition types, thereby generating a rich array of behaviors. These insights offer a quantitative framework for analyzing and designing robot decision-making processes. Finally, we validate our model using both human participants and real robots. Our results show that human decision-making aligns with our theoretical predictions, and that robots equipped with decision-making inspired by human behavior display richer and more natural behaviors compared to those utilizing standard algorithms. This supports our conclusion that discrete, human-inspired decision-making can be effectively represented by continuous dynamical systems, yielding beneficial outcomes for robotic behavior. We investigate the energy-dependent conductivity of the kinetic energy driven state of a fermion lattice model featuring random potential scattering by extended defects, employing the generalised dynamical mean field theory (GDFT). In the context of potential scattering, we demonstrate that a novel class of lattice defects—characterized by an internal structure and extended away from the lattice model—can be effectively incorporated. Our analysis of the microwave conductivity $\sigma(\omega)$ for frequencies ranging from $0.01$ to $0.1$ $t$ (where $t$ represents the nearest-neighbor hopping amplitude) reveals that these extended defects induce a shift in the conductivity peak toward higher frequencies, alongside an overall enhancement of the peak's magnitude. Furthermore, we examine the impact of coupling anisotropy and the influence of extended defects on the dynamical self-energy. Finally, the calculated frequency-dependent conductivity exhibits a distinct doping dependence. These outcomes are interpreted as signatures of the kinetic energy driven state. Finally, we discuss the experimental relevance of our findings. This paper examines a curvature-driven, shape-memory geometric flow for hypersurfaces within Euclidean space, originally formulated by the second author and J. Spruck in 2015. We provide an analysis of fundamental issues regarding this evolution, including existence and non-existence of global solutions, asymptotic behavior, stability, and linearized operators. Furthermore, we explore various canonical examples of this curvature, known as crystalline curvature, and detail numerical methods designed to simulate surfaces with such crystalline characteristics. Finally, we address the significant link between this geometric framework and mean curvature flow featuring crystalline anisotropy. Agriculture is vital to human survival, yet accurately simulating this domain is challenging due to its complex processes and diverse environmental factors. Current plant growth models, such as the JASPAR model, depend heavily on labor-intensive, expert-curated parameters, making them difficult to adapt to novel settings. To address this, this paper introduces GrowSpace, a learning-based simulator that automatically learns the physics of plant growth from real-world data. By applying deep learning to real-time sensor data from actual farms, GrowSpace can efficiently generate 3D physical simulations. Furthermore, we demonstrate that GrowSpace can be utilized to evaluate crop yields and investigate plant responses to environmental changes. Our evaluation results indicate that GrowSpace successfully replicates real-world plant growth dynamics and provides accurate simulations of crop yields. Additionally, we show that GrowSpace can model various crop types and adapt to real-world environmental shifts, offering a flexible platform for studying how plants respond to stimuli. To the best of our knowledge, GrowSpace is the first system to enable direct simulation of real plant growth using real-time sensing. The GrowSpace code and simulation environment are publicly accessible at https://github.com/Stanford-PLAB/GrowSpace. Building on the work of Miller and Sheffman, we introduce a new method for approximating the whole-plane SLE$_k$ ($k\in\{2,4,8,16\}$) loop measure using conformal weldings of quantum disks. This framework offers a streamlined proof of Schramm's conjecture, which asserts that the SLE$_k$ loop measure converges weakly as $k$ approaches 2 to the conformal weldings of quantum disks described in Li and Sun's research. Furthermore, our approach provides an alternative derivation of the existence and uniqueness of SLE$_k$ loop measures for $k>2$, utilizing the theory of positive functionals developed by Kuznetsov. Additionally, our methodology yields a fresh proof of the conformal invariance of the SLE$_k$ loop measure. Finally, we demonstrate that the resulting measure is uniquely determined by its local behavior at the tip of growing SLE$_k$ tracts. These findings are detailed in a companion paper. In this work, we concentrate on the case $k=2$ and develop a novel technique for constructing conformal weldings of quantum disks, which holds independent significance. Specifically, we establish that the quantum gravity measure $\mathrm{CWT}_2$ on bi-equivalent classes of quadrangulations with two marked vertices is conformally invariant and can be expressed as a product of the uniform measure on the UQWT$_2$ class and Miller's Liouville quantum gravity measure on the class of quantum disks. This result relies on an intermediate finding: the existence of a quantum gravity flow that drives the quantum gravity process on the UQWT$_2$ class toward a collection of quantum disks. This finding is established through a direct application of the quantum Martin boundary method. We also extend this approach to other bi-equivalence classes of quadrangulations. Finally, we derive a formula for the conformal modulus of the welding map linking the two marked vertices in the UQWT$_2$ class, thereby confirming the conjecture regarding the distribution of quantum disk moduli proposed by Miller and Sheffman. This study represents a component of the author's doctoral thesis, which can be accessed here. This study introduces a novel vehicle platoon formation control framework utilizing differential games. The proposed method is versatile, capable of managing both automated vehicles and human-driven mixed fleets. Each autopilot is designed with the flexibility to adjust its autonomy level dynamically based on real-time conditions, such as the presence of nearby vehicles. Additionally, the autopilot features a formation control module that enables vehicles to adjust their relative positions and dimensions to optimize overall platoon performance. The differential game offers a unified approach to solving the associated optimization problem, effectively addressing challenges like non-stationary targets and the mixed makeup of automated and human-driven vehicles. Simulation results demonstrate the autopilot's ability to adapt to varying driving scenarios, including lane changes and merges, while the formation control module successfully optimizes the platoon's performance. Furthermore, a real-world test using a driver-in-the-loop simulation validates the method's effectiveness. The simulations reveal that the proposed approach enhances the entire platoon's performance by 10% compared to a baseline method. The entire system, including the autopilot and formation control, is implemented in C++ and made available as open-source software. The software requires only a single line of modification to simulate either a real vehicle or a simulation. Additionally, the software is capable of evaluating performance improvements across a single vehicle or an entire platoon. It is widely recognized that categorical variables within a logistic regression model typically generate non-linear interactions. While some applications necessitate examining these interactions, many do not. Although various methods exist for eliminating interactions, they often suffer from drawbacks such as biased coefficient estimates or compromised model fit. This study introduces a straightforward modification to the design matrix that facilitates interaction avoidance. The proposed approach is straightforward to implement, ensures unbiased coefficients, and maintains model fit equivalently to the inclusion of interactions. A simulation study demonstrates that this method yields more reliable standard errors and p-values for significance testing. Furthermore, a real-world data example illustrates that the new methodology is particularly advantageous when variables are not mutually exclusive. Consequently, the authors argue that this proposed approach should be adopted as a valuable supplementary tool in a broader analytical framework. Chiral spin liquids (CSLs) represent a promising state for investigating novel chiral degrees of freedom, such as Majorana modes, within solid-state environments. However, stabilizing CSLs in real materials remains difficult. This study demonstrates that amorphous and polycrystalline samples of the quantum spin liquid candidate $\alpha$-RuCl$_3$ can reach the CSL regime at low temperatures when subjected to high magnetic fields. By employing the Kerr effect to detect emergent valley chirality, we observed a sudden transition into this state at $B=9.5$ T. Furthermore, amorphous RuCl$_3$ exhibits an anomalous Hall effect under these conditions, offering further proof of the CSL. These findings indicate that high-field quantum phase transitions in $\alpha$-RuCl$_3$ are more resilient to the non-uniform strains inherent in polycrystalline materials and disordered bonding in amorphous structures than previously anticipated. Consequently, these CSL states in $\alpha$-RuCl$_3$ may serve as a foundation for exploring the topological Hall effect in quantum materials. This paper introduces a calibration algorithm designed for large-N radio interferometers, featuring $\mathcal{O}(N\log{N})$ scaling in both data reduction and solution determination. Unlike the traditional $N^2$ complexity of standard self-calibration, our method leverages the regular baselines of a grid-based array to facilitate a rapid Fourier transform. Additionally, we propose an $N\log{N}$ scaling matrix inversion technique that complements the Fourier transform step. We validate the efficiency of this approach by applying it to the 21 cm intensity data from the $\text{Hubble Deep Field South}$ obtained via the Murchison Widefield Array. Furthermore, we integrate this algorithm with the existing imager, deconvolver, and data reduction software within the MWA Science Pipeline. We anticipate that this work will serve as a foundation for future large-scale radio interferometer data reduction pipelines. We introduce a new autoencoding conditional GAN framework designed to tackle portfolio diversification by identifying distributional features through optimal transport and reconstructing portfolio distributions via adversarial training. Specifically, the encoder processes input portfolios to extract discriminative features, while the decoder leverages these features to generate output portfolios. Simultaneously, the transport module utilizes an explicit test function to calculate the discrepancy between input and output distributions. The adversarial module minimizes this discrepancy while ensuring the output distributions are diverse and coherent based on the encoded features. Furthermore, the conditional discriminator and transporter work together to guarantee that output distributions maintain consistency with the input distribution's structural characteristics. Our approach demonstrates superior performance in maximizing portfolio diversification and achieving competitive returns across various benchmarks. Additionally, the model exhibits robustness across different datasets and remains stable even when hyperparameters are randomly selected. Finally, we release the model for public use. The source code can be accessed at: https://github.

We have computed the polarized transition function $A_{gq}(N)$ within the Variable Flavor Number Scheme at next-to-next-to-leading order in perturbation theory, corresponding to three loops, and present our findings. The polarized transition function is a fundamental element of the general matrix that maps parton distribution functions (PDFs) between different schemes. In the Variable Flavor Number Scheme (VFNS), it specifically governs the evolution of PDFs for quarks and gluons as active flavors increase. Our results are applicable to the general VFNS, encompassing all possible flavors and their associated combinations. Given its significance, the accuracy of this function is essential for any theory aiming to predict hadronic physics at high energies. Furthermore, given its pivotal role in the matrix connecting PDFs across different schemes, its precision is crucial for any approach that interpolates between VFNS and other schemes, such as the MS scheme. We have also compared our findings with previous calculations. Additionally, our results are available in a public repository for immediate application. This paper serves as the first part of our series of studies on VFNS at three-loop order. Our subsequent work will address the three-loop VFNS evolution equations. This research investigates social media making accessibility a core priority. We identified 1,000 platforms ranging from major social networks to online forums and blogs. By examining their user interface (UI) and HTML source code, we analyzed accessibility features, obstacles, and opportunities for making content accessible to people with disabilities. Our findings indicate that only 16% of these platforms adhere to Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) at the AAA level. Additionally, our analysis of common markup languages revealed that 84% exhibit critical accessibility flaws. To address these issues, we propose three actionable steps for platform providers to enhance accessibility. Furthermore, we developed a tool capable of automatically scanning social media pages and reporting specific accessibility errors. We demonstrate how this tool can be utilized to improve web pages across various social media environments. Finally, we outline our future research directions aimed at making social media consumption accessible for individuals with disabilities. This paper introduces a tensor-level merge operation for hypergraphs, formulated through their adjacency tensors. We provide sufficient conditions under which the spectrum of the resulting merged hypergraph's adjacency tensor is unionized. Specifically, commutant hypergraphs are identified as a sufficient condition for this unionization. Furthermore, we demonstrate that under certain conditions, the eigenvalues of a merged hypergraph's adjacency tensor can be expressed as linear functions of the eigenvalues of the individual constituent hypergraphs. This finding extends previous results regarding adjacency matrix spectra to the domain of hypergraphs. Finally, the study concludes by examining the relationship between the algebraic connectivity of merged hypergraphs and that of their components. Additionally, the paper provides a tensor version of the standard inclusion-exclusion principle for calculating the rank of hypergraph adjacency tensors. These findings offer a more comprehensive understanding of how merging operations influence the spectral properties of hypergraphs. Finally, the study explores the relationship between the number of hypergraph edges and their spectral characteristics. Specifically, it establishes that for any fixed number of vertices, the number of edges in a hypergraph with a given set of eigenvalues is bounded from above. This study investigates natural cubic splines for analyzing Alzheimer's disease clinical trials. We initially explore the motivation for employing natural cubic splines, followed by an examination of the statistical issues involved. Specifically, we address the selection of spline terms, accounting for the interdependence between the number of terms and error variance. To facilitate this selection, we propose a model comparison approach utilizing the Bayesian Information Criterion (BIC). Furthermore, we develop a testing framework to verify the non-negativity of the treatment effect. Finally, a simulation study is conducted to assess the performance of the proposed methods, with the analysis of the ADNI database used to illustrate their application. These findings are accessible via an online supplementary file containing supplementary materials and R code. We introduce a general framework designed to identify dominant transition pathways between states in stochastic thermal dynamics. This method relies on the observation that the collection of dominant paths forms a geodesically convex set with a relatively simple boundary. Consequently, the problem of identifying this set can be modeled as an optimization task for the most probable action, which involves minimizing the $L^{\infty}$-norm of the Cotlar's functional. This optimization is resolved using global optimization techniques, specifically simulated annealing and a novel, fast, and robust algorithm termed the "hit-and-run" method. To validate the approach, we apply it to the well-known Ising model and a two-sphere model to map out its dominant transition paths. Our results demonstrate that the primary dynamical features of these models are accurately reproduced. Furthermore, the computational cost is significantly lower than that of direct numerical simulations, as our method efficiently reduces the computational domain. The entire algorithm is implemented in C++ and made available on GitHub. This work establishes a new strategy for characterizing transition paths, with potential applications in various scientific fields, including the study of protein folding. Future efforts will extend this theory to more complex systems, such as those involving multiple transition paths, higher dimensions, and non-thermal dynamics. Additionally, we aim to refine the algorithm to further enhance its computational efficiency.
