This paper aims to establish robust estimates for parabolic complex Monge-Ampère and Gaussian equations. Specifically, we derive sharp $L^{\infty}$ estimates for the Monge-Ampère exponent $\nu$ and the gradient $|\nabla\varphi|$ regarding the boundary values, as well as "mixed type" estimates concerning the initial values. These findings significantly sharpen the "mixed type" bounds previously established by Dinew and Kolodziej in [Dinew-Kolodziej, *Ann. Inst. H. Poincaré Anal. Non Linéaire* 2011, 28, 601-617]. Furthermore, the methods developed here yield explicit constants and substantially improve the a priori $L^{\infty}$ estimates. As an application, we derive an explicit bound for the Laplacian $\Delta\varphi$ that depends on the initial value of $\varphi$, thereby enhancing the result obtained by Dinew and Kolodziej in [Dinew-Kolodziej, *Ann. Inst. H. Poincaré Anal. Non Linéaire* 2011, 28, 601-617]. Additionally, we prove a parabolic version of the Skoda-Bourinay estimate, which serves as a crucial tool in our approach. This parabolic estimate is also applicable to the $\partial$-equation. Our results have broad applications in parabolic complex geometry, particularly in addressing problems related to Kähler-Einstein metrics with negative scalar curvature. We demonstrate this by solving homogeneous parabolic complex Monge-Ampère and $\partial$-equations with Laplacian operators, obtaining explicit $L^{\infty}$ estimates with explicit constants. These findings represent a substantial advancement over the work of Dinew and Kolodziej [Dinew-Kolodziej, *Ann. Inst. H. Poincaré Anal. Non Linéaire* 2011, 28, 601-617]. Finally, we apply these techniques to address a parabolic version of Demailly's open problem. In this context, we derive sharp $L^{\infty}$ estimates for the Laplacian $\Delta\varphi$, the mixed type estimate, and the scalar curvature $S_{g_t}$ of the parabolic Kähler-Einstein metric with negative scalar curvature, all based on the initial data. Standard functions, originally introduced by Bezem and Coquand and later formalized in the proof assistant Isabelle/HOL by Nipkow and Wobus, offer a straightforward method for representing complex function behaviors. Their primary advantage lies in the ability to express both pre- and postconditions within a single type, thereby eliminating the need for separate lemmas to establish correctness. Despite their utility, these functions possess limitations. In this paper, we introduce extensions to the typed lambda-calculus that incorporate superclasses of standard functions. We demonstrate that the type system remains strongly normalising and provides type-assignment decidability by utilizing translation into the calculus with inductive types. Furthermore, we illustrate how these extended functions can model behavior that standard functions cannot, such as exceptions and non-termination. Finally, we present examples that illustrate the practical benefits of using standard-calculi with superclass functions. Additionally, we have developed a prototype compiler that translates programs written with superclass functions into programs utilizing standard functions, and we provide evidence of this prototype's effectiveness through various examples. This work serves as a foundational step toward enhancing lambda-calculi with classes to more accurately represent function behavior in programming languages. Specifically, it addresses the limitation where lambda-calculi with classes are not generally strongly normalising. Our proposed solution involves modifying the subtyping relation to allow a superclass to be more general than a direct function and adapting the calibration argument to support non-terminating programs. This mechanism enables the representation of exceptions and other behaviors and is not overly restrictive, as it maintains the desirable property of strong normalization. The paper is structured as follows: Section 2 reviews standard functions and their connection to lambda-calculi with classes; Section 3 introduces superclasses of standard functions and establishes the calculus's type-assignment decidability; Section 4 connects this calculus to the calculus of inductive types; Section 5 presents an example program and its translation into the calculus of inductive types; Section 6 provides a practical example; and Section 7 concludes the paper. This research investigates numerical methods for solving stochastic differential equations (SDEs) that utilize conditional measure flow to represent conditional measure density within their stochastic terms. These equations serve as computational tools for simulating experimental data processing in fields such as physics, chemistry, and biology. The study demonstrates the equivalence between the Stratonovich and Itô formulations of an SDE where the stochastic component depends on a functional of a conditional measure flow. These forms correspond to numerical algorithms employing either the Euler or Milstein methods, respectively, with the Itô version offering superior numerical stability. Furthermore, the paper provides criteria ensuring the existence and uniqueness of an SDE solution and validates these theoretical findings through specific examples. Initially, these spaces are built using the lattice of all subgroups of G. We present specific examples, such as the space corresponding to the free group on two generators, and investigate various topological and dynamical properties. Furthermore, we analyze the lattice of subspaces within the structure space and establish connections between this space and the geometry of non-amenability. We establish an upper limit for the dimension of the space associated with any discrete group and demonstrate that this dimension can be infinite for specific groups. Additionally, we outline an approach to generating structure spaces from the lattice of subgroups of G, which allows for the construction of spaces possessing arbitrary prescribed dimensions. A key feature of these spaces is the presence of a minimal dense subset consisting solely of subgroups that are either conjugate or inversely conjugate to simple groups. We conclude by proposing several directions for future research. This work is situated within the field of topological dynamics. This study addresses safe navigation within multi-robot systems operating under uncertain conditions. We introduce a data-driven, risk-aware model predictive control (MPC) framework designed to ensure collision-free navigation and prevent entry into unsafe zones. This approach utilizes a black-box representation of multi-robot dynamics alongside a data-driven probability model for process noise. By employing data-driven hypothesis generation, the method accommodates various distribution types, including Gaussian, non-Gaussian, and correlated noise. Furthermore, it integrates recent advancements in risk-averse optimization to satisfy probabilistic safety constraints during MPC optimization. The proposed framework was tested using digital twin simulations of multi-robot systems subject to correlated, non-Gaussian noise, with results demonstrating its ability to achieve safe navigation while maintaining high path efficiency. Additionally, simulation results for outdoor autonomous vehicle navigation were presented to validate the approach's applicability in real-world scenarios. The MPC formulation ensures recursive feasibility and stability by leveraging the contractivity of the underlying discrete-time dynamical system. Simulation studies confirm that the MPC strategy achieves safe navigation with minimal path length and low control input usage. The MPC controller was implemented in MATLAB, utilizing the YALMIP modeling toolbox and solved via branch-and-bound methods within the Gurobi solver. This paper serves as an extension of our prior work on risk-aware navigation for multi-robot systems. Specifically, it expands our previous research by enabling the handling of correlated process noise and by providing a rigorous stability analysis for the MPC scheme. The proposed methodology is applicable to diverse robotics challenges, such as multi-robot coordination and collision avoidance for autonomous vehicles and robots in real-world environments. The MPC scheme is formulated as a finite-horizon optimal control problem, solved at each time step using a nonlinear MPC (nMPC) approach. To enhance computational efficiency, the nMPC problem was converted into a convex quadratic programming problem through linearization and approximation techniques. Furthermore, the study incorporates a novel safety constraint based on the concept of tube-based model predictive control (T-MPC), which guarantees collision-free navigation under bounded process noise. The MPC controller was developed in MATLAB, modeled using YALMIP, and solved using YALMIP-Gurobi with a branch-and-bound algorithm. The paper also provides an in-depth analysis of the computational complexity associated with the proposed MPC scheme. Finally, the work includes a comparison of the performance of different MPC formulations and an analysis of their respective computational complexities. We report the discovery of Andromeda XXV, a new ultrafaint dwarf galaxy situated approximately 770 kiloparsecs from the Milky Way. This galaxy contains 10 confirmed member stars, with 7 of them exhibiting low metallicity. By combining these new observations with existing data, we derive a mean metallicity of $[Fe/H] = -1.7 \pm 0.2$ dex. Our analysis reveals that Andromeda XXV possesses a low concentration of dark matter in its center, characterized by a core logarithmic slope of $\gamma_0 = 0.3 \pm 0.3$ and a logarithmic slope at 100 parsecs of $\gamma_{100} = 1.1 \pm 0.3$. This low central concentration is statistically significant at the 95% confidence level. Additionally, we observe that Andromeda XXV lacks a resolved stellar population extending to the main sequence turn-off, suggesting it may have been tidally disrupted. Its properties, including a low surface brightness, low stellar mass, and low stellar velocity dispersion, align with those of other recently discovered ultrafaint dwarfs. The presence of XXV within the Andromeda group strengthens the hypothesis that Andromeda hosts an extensive halo of dwarf galaxies. Furthermore, the low central dark matter concentration of Andromeda XXV is consistent with theoretical predictions regarding the internal structure of ultrafaint dwarfs. Finally, Andromeda XXV exhibits a low specific star formation rate, which may indicate that it was quenched during its initial infall into the Andromeda halo. These findings contribute to our understanding of dwarf galaxy formation and evolution. The catalog of Andromeda satellites now includes 29 dwarfs, accounting for approximately 10% of the total satellite population around Andromeda. This supports the hypothesis that the majority of Andromeda's dwarfs reside in the outer regions of its halo, beyond 100 kiloparsecs. The complete catalog of Andromeda satellites is available at https://www.astro.uva.nl/~josef/AndromedaSatellites/. Non-orthogonal sequence design is essential for grant-free massive connectivity, aiming to optimize system performance by balancing sequence orthogonality and distinguishability. This paper introduces a two-stage genetic algorithm to generate new sequences for the complex design space of non-orthogonal sets. The process begins with low-resolution sequences generated via a novel hybrid search method, which are then refined into high-resolution sequences through a standard genetic algorithm. The primary advantage of this two-stage approach is its ability to efficiently explore a vast design space. Numerical results confirm that the proposed method outperforms existing state-of-the-art techniques. Furthermore, this proposed method surpasses low-resolution designs by achieving a 10% to 20% reduction in the minimum mean squared error distance, demonstrating that resolution enhancement is critical for optimal design. Additionally, numerical comparisons show that the proposed method achieves a 10% to 20% improvement in maximum mutual information distance compared to high-resolution designs, indicating that while resolution is vital for optimization, it is less critical than maximizing mutual information. Finally, the proposed method achieves a 10% to 20% increase in the average number of edges in the optimal graph relative to other state-of-the-art methods, highlighting the essential role of non-orthogonality in grant-free massive connectivity. These findings underscore the necessity of developing non-orthogonal sequences that maximize mutual information to achieve optimal grant-free massive connectivity. Consequently, the proposed two-stage genetic approach is highly effective for designing non-orthogonal sequences in such systems. The algorithm's computational complexity is $\mathcal{O}(N_{iter} N_{pop} L \log L)$, where $N_{iter}$ represents the number of generations, $N_{pop}$ is the population size, and $L$ denotes sequence length. This represents a significant advantage over brute-force methods, which suffer from exponential complexity relative to sequence length. Experimental results indicate that the proposed algorithm converges within approximately 10 generations, resulting in a complexity of $\mathcal{O}(N_{pop} L \log L)$, a substantial reduction compared to traditional approaches. In summary, the proposed method is highly effective for grant-free massive connectivity, particularly in MIMO OFDM environments. However, it is important to note that this algorithm is not space-invariant; its performance depends on the initial population, meaning the search space is not invariant with respect to the population. Accurate atmospheric modeling of moist air relies on three primary components: approximations for moist thermodynamic properties, moist thermodynamic and transport equations, and numerical discretization schemes. While sophisticated models employ complex, thermodynamically consistent property calculations, operational weather and climate systems often utilize simpler, piecewise-linear look-up tables to enhance computational efficiency. However, these simplified properties may not align with the approximate thermodynamic equations, creating a discrepancy where model outputs are derived using one set of moist properties while internal consistency is maintained through three-dimensional, physically based thermodynamic equations. This paper introduces thermodynamically coherent alternatives to existing approximations, specifically targeting the representation of liquid water saturation and tropical moist convection. The study examines various liquid water saturation formulations and their associated thermodynamic equations, evaluating them based on consistency with the Makkonen cloud droplet activation model. Furthermore, the Makkonen model is implemented in a thermodynamically coherent manner. Although the analysis concentrates on convection modeling, the proposed thermodynamic relations are of general applicability and can be utilized in other contexts, such as weather or climate modeling, provided the corresponding look-up tables are constructed consistently. The paper concludes by outlining potential future extensions. Although word-level confidence scores (WCS) from automatic speech recognition have proven effective for various dialogue systems, they remain underutilized during system execution. This study investigates using WCs to detect and mitigate the impacts of ASR errors in dialogue state monitoring. We introduce a Bayesian method for jointly modeling transcription errors and recognition ambiguities, alongside a new algorithm for labeling WCs with semantic confidence (SC) for specific slots and values. This SC-based approach for monitoring (SCAM) demonstrates superior performance compared to label-based WCs and standard state-of-the-art methods. Additionally, we present findings on the effects of different ASR engines, systems, and features on WCs and SC, along with insights regarding training data requirements for SCAM. Finally, we outline potential extensions of SCAM, such as its application in multi-turn dialogue contexts. Our results indicate that SCAM can achieve a 2–3% absolute increase in F1 scores for state tracking. The code is accessible at https://github.com/abhishekkumar1997/SCAM. In universal access structures involving $n$ users, each user may or may not request participation in a session alongside up to $r-1$ other users. A universal access structure is defined as the collection of all feasible sessions. The intricacy of a universal access structure represents the count of these feasible sessions. This paper investigates the properties of universal intricacy. We establish upper and lower bounds for the universal intricacy and examine the conditions under which these bounds are achieved. Additionally, we analyze the universal analogue of the minimum size problem and provide a universal counterpart to a conjecture regarding the maximum size. We provide a partial resolution to this conjecture and highlight an open question. Finally, we present a universal two-level design and a universal universal design, bringing these concepts closer together. We conclude by outlining several directions for future research. Our methodology relies on elementary combinatorics. Our findings may also find application in information-theoretic and graph-theoretic contexts. This work is based on the study by N. S. Tikhonov and A. A. Pashkova, "Intricacy of universal access structures," which appeared in the Journal of the ACM Research in Reports (JACM:R), Volume 1, Issue 1, March 2021, Article 2, 10 pages.

We derive the general formula for the minimum number of copies of a generic pure two-qubit state needed to optimally assess their entanglement. This requirement is determined by the dimensions of specific irreducible representations of the SU(2) group, into which the copies are decomposed. We apply this optimization to various scenarios involving different types of entangled states. Furthermore, we extend these findings to the case of N-qubit pure states. Our results demonstrate that, compared to classical states, entangled states can be optimally verified with significantly fewer copies. These findings hold significant relevance for experimental quantum information processing. Additionally, our findings improve upon earlier estimates regarding the minimum number of copies required for optimal entanglement verification. Finally, we explore the application of these results to continuous-variable entanglement verification. Prolonged H-mode discharges at the JET tokamak, utilizing deuterium and tritium mixtures, reveal a unique feature in fast ion diagnostics: a persistent and robust oscillatory signal at the natural frequency of the beam emission spectroscopy (BES) sightline. This phenomenon, termed "palm tree modes" due to the shape of the mode amplitude profile, was previously observed in TCV and recently in DIII-D. While earlier studies suggested a link to toroidal mode number $m=0$ neoclassical tearing modes (NTMs), no such NTMs are detected in the current palm tree mode cases. This study employs a combined analysis of JET BES data and fast-ion diagnostics to investigate the origin and characteristics of these palm tree modes. We report on a specific palm tree mode event featuring a well-developed profile and significant amplitude, which was accompanied by both D-alpha and neutron oscillations. The palm tree mode exhibits a narrow radial profile, high amplitude, and low poloidal mode numbers ($|n| \leq 1$). Furthermore, the mode displays a toroidal mode number $m$ that varies with the poloidal direction, shifting from $m=+1$ to $m=-1$ as the mode number increases. These findings suggest that palm tree modes are likely intrinsically related to NTMs. Additionally, the palm tree mode demonstrates a strong correlation with neutron fluctuations, indicating that it may represent the low-mode-number counterpart to NTMs. Consequently, the palm tree mode is hypothesized to be an NTM with low poloidal and toroidal mode numbers. This conclusion is supported by the mode's radial profile, which aligns with the typical radial structure of NTMs. Finally, the paper discusses the potential impact of palm tree modes on fusion reactor operations. Given their association with NTMs, these modes could be detrimental to plasma performance and wall loading. However, their low poloidal and toroidal mode numbers might also render them less harmful compared to conventional NTMs. Therefore, further research is necessary to fully understand their effects on fusion reactors. This study aims to contribute to that ongoing investigation. Keywords: tokamak, beam emission spectroscopy, neoclassical tearing modes, edge localized modes. Continual learning (CL) involves training a model sequentially on new tasks while retaining knowledge of previous ones to prevent catastrophic forgetting. Although numerous CL techniques exist, selecting the most suitable one for a given scenario remains difficult. This paper introduces the concept of a "CL-Scenario," which categorizes CL challenges into two types: (1) CL-Perm, where task orders are variable, and (2) CL-Seq, where task orders are fixed. We demonstrate that simple, lightweight baselines utilizing weight initialization and fine-tuning can effectively address CL-Scenarios. Specifically, we propose the Repeat & Fine-tune (R&F) algorithm, which employs replica networks and dynamic fine-tuning to mitigate CL-Perm and CL-Seq issues, respectively. Notably, R&F outperforms numerous state-of-the-art CL methods that depend on extensive pretrained models and memory for classification CL. Additionally, we observe that CL-Scenarios stem from dataset bias rather than true sequential learning, and that CL-Perm represents a more significant challenge than CL-Seq. These findings offer valuable guidance for selecting CL-methods and underscore the necessity of developing solutions that function without relying on heavy pretrained models. Social media has become a primary platform for expressing thoughts and emotions, often giving rise to abusive language. Although various social media corporations have introduced numerous methods to detect such language, these solutions often produce false positives. To address this limitation, we introduce a multi-modal deep learning approach designed to identify abusive content. Our method utilizes a multi-encoder framework that integrates both textual and image data, employing a global attention mechanism to merge features from both sources. Furthermore, we propose an interpretable framework that integrates established explainable AI techniques to pinpoint the specific features responsible for classification decisions. This capability enhances the reliability of the classification process. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods in accuracy while offering valuable insights into the reasoning behind those classifications. This study examines heterogeneous networks linking excitatory and inhibitory neurons, where connection probabilities vary based on cell type and degree, regardless of spatial arrangement. We analyze two models: conductance-based integrate-and-fire neurons governed by conductance plasticity and mean-field type-I firing rate neurons. Using analytical and numerical methods, we assess how degree-dependent connectivity influences network dynamics and stability. Our approach involves analyzing the self-consistent degree distributions of these two neuron types to determine how connectivity patterns affect both the mean and variability of these distributions. Furthermore, we investigate how network connectivity impacts the synchronization of type-I firing rate neurons. Our findings indicate that, in both frameworks, increasing the average degree of excitatory neurons—while holding the total number of such neurons constant—produces two key effects: a broadening of the stationary distribution of membrane potentials or firing rates, and the emergence of a unique stable synchronous state. Consequently, high average degrees of excitatory neurons facilitate the generation of gamma oscillations. These results underscore the critical role of network connectivity in the dynamics of inhibitory neural systems. Finally, we address the stability of synchronous states and the existence of stationary solutions within both models by deriving the characteristic equation from the Jacobian matrix of the reduced system. This analysis also enables the examination of the stability of non-synchronous stationary solutions. To achieve this, we first determine the stationary solutions and their existence conditions, then analyze their stability through the eigenvalues of the Jacobian matrix. Our findings reveal that synchronous states with gamma oscillations can arise via a Hopf bifurcation, while oscillatory states emerge through a Hopf bifurcation or a limit cycle bifurcation. Additionally, we observe that synchronous stationary states exist when the network size is sufficiently large. These insights provide a foundation for future research into the dynamics of neural networks. To conclude, we compare the dynamics of the type-I firing rate and conductance-based neurons, demonstrating that the conclusions drawn for type-I neurons also apply to conductance-based neurons. This suggests that our conclusions are robust and not limited to the type-I firing rate neuron framework. Ultimately, the dynamics of neural networks are profoundly influenced by connectivity, a factor that should be considered in future studies. Our conclusions are also supported by the work of other researchers. Furthermore, the dynamics of neural networks can be significantly affected by the initial conditions of neurons. Therefore, future research should also explore the dynamics of neural networks under varying initial conditions. In this paper, we have examined the dynamics of two distinct models of type-I excitatory and inhibitory neural networks

Automatic Program Repair (APR) has gained significant research interest in recent years. While mask-based techniques represent a prominent APR approach, they rely on mask-guided selection and recombination of existing code fragments to synthesize repair patches. However, these methods often fail to generate patches that can successfully resolve bugs. To address this, we propose an adversarial mask generation strategy to enhance the quality of generated repair patches. Specifically, the mask generator and success predictor engage in an adversarial game to learn optimal masks that produce patches capable of fixing bugs. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method improves upon existing APR techniques regarding bug resolution rates and patch effectiveness. Additionally, we observe that the adversarial framework exhibits strong robustness, consistently outperforming current APR methods in the absence of test cases. Our source code is available at: https://github.

The GIFC (Gaussian interference channel with common messages) represents a significant model in wireless communications, serving as the foundation for broadcast channels with side information and as a critical component in network information theory. While El Gamal and Shah established the outer bounds (ElGamal-Shah bounds) for the GIFC capacity region, subsequent research has focused on determining the exact capacity region, with successful results achieved only for specific parameter configurations. This paper advances the analysis of the GIFC capacity region by adapting Han-Koetter's superposition coding combined with Marton's coding scheme, utilizing a modified version of Wyner-Zell binning. Our proposed scheme yields an expanded outer bound, termed the MKWY bound, which effectively integrates the ElGamal-Shah and Han-Koetter bounds. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this bound is tight (exact) for the GIFC symmetry region. Additionally, by employing Gelfand-Pinsker coding, we illustrate that a time-sharing mechanism exists between the two rate bounds within the symmetry region, thereby successfully characterizing the exact capacity region for the GIFC common message scenario. Notably, the symmetry region functions as an inner region for the general GIFC capacity region; consequently, our proposed outer bound becomes the exact capacity region when considering generic GIFC scenarios. Finally, our approach achieves the ElGamal-Shah single-point bound, a result that was previously unattainable. These findings are supported by rigorous mathematical proofs. The paper concludes by outlining several open problems for future research. This work was partially presented at the 2021 IEEE International Symposium on Information Theory (ISIT). The geometric characteristics of the interaction zone in high-energy nuclear collisions are analyzed through 3-dimensional flow coefficients, derived from the 3-dimensional momentum ($p_x$, $p_y$, $p_z$) of final-state particles. This approach offers fresh perspectives on the collision geometry and constraints regarding the Equation-of-State (EoS). The method is grounded in a 2+1-dimensional hydrodynamic model, which is computationally efficient for exploring EoS-dependent phenomena in heavy-ion collisions. Simulations of central Au+Au collisions at various energies were conducted to examine the collision geometry and the sensitivity of flow coefficients to the EoS. Results indicate that 3D flow coefficients provide a detailed and comprehensive depiction of the collision geometry, revealing that the EoS significantly influences both the initial and final spatial distributions of the fluid. Furthermore, this study demonstrates that 3D flow coefficients offer valuable insights into the EoS, a factor that is often overlooked in experimental research. Consequently, 3D flow measurements can serve as an effective tool to investigate the EoS of hot and dense nuclear matter. Finally, the 3D momentum space is visualized using isobaric surfaces, revealing intriguing geometric structures that offer new perspectives on 3D flow. These findings are expected to advance the understanding of 3D flow and its potential applications in experimental studies. Detecting COVID-19 early is crucial for mitigating its severe health impacts. Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have recently demonstrated exceptional efficacy in analyzing wireless networks, yet their traditional centralized training and inference require all data to be sent to a central server, creating latency and privacy risks. This paper introduces a fully decentralized framework for both training and inference. Specifically, we propose Decentralized Information-Theoretic GNN (DIT-GNN), which enables decentralized inference for graph classification tasks. In this approach, nodes exchange only minimal information with neighbors, such as the probability distributions of local features, rather than raw features themselves. We theoretically analyze the convergence properties of DIT-GNN and validate its performance through simulations on both synthetic and real-world datasets. Furthermore, we extend this inference methodology to wireless transmission systems, applying it to real-world trace data to minimize interference in millimeter-wave networks. Our results demonstrate that the performance of Decentralized GNN inference is comparable to that of centralized GNN inference. Additionally, our findings indicate that decentralized inference in millimeter-wave networks achieves higher performance than centralized inference when utilizing graph convolutional networks. Finally, our DIT-GNN framework offers superior performance compared to existing decentralized learning approaches for graph classification. Overall, this research paves the way for decentralized machine learning-driven solutions in wireless systems, addressing challenges like privacy, scalability, and resource constraints. Homicide rates have risen steadily over recent decades, prompting researchers to employ various statistical approaches to identify the underlying causes. This study utilizes spatial statistical techniques to detect variations in homicide rates across Brazil's municipalities. By applying a spatially lagged regression model, the analysis identifies spatial dependencies within the homicide time series. The data were gathered from the State of Goiás, a region known for high homicide levels. Spatial clustering methods revealed distinct groups of municipalities with varying homicide trends between 2002 and 2014. Furthermore, the spatially lagged model indicates that the average number of homicides in a given municipality is influenced by the activity levels of its neighbors. The findings suggest the existence of spatial "hotspots" linked to social determinants such as social exclusion, inequality, and the presence of organized criminal groups. These results could inform public health strategies aimed at reducing violence. Additionally, a new spatial clustering technique is introduced, designed to handle observations with different temporal trajectories. This represents a methodological advancement with potential applications in other fields. The study concludes by discussing implications for public health policy regarding the reduction of homicides. The dataset used in this analysis is accessible at http://www.scielo.br/scielo.php?script=arttext&pid=S1980-220X2018000100001&lng=pt&ng=0. Supplementary materials, including maps and tables, can be found at https://doi.org/10.1016/j.socscimed.2018.01.038. The source code is available at https://github.com/fernandoalmeida1980/ClusterexaminationofHomicideRatesinBrazil. Finally, this research demonstrates the value of integrating spatial and temporal methods to enhance the understanding of the complex dynamics driving the rise in homicides.

This study introduces a novel adaptive gradient method designed to overcome the limitations of current techniques, which are primarily tailored for either biased or unbiased stochastic gradient descent (SGD). Our approach enables adaptive learning rates for unbiased SGD under both strong and vanishing noise conditions, while simultaneously supporting accelerated convergence even in the strong noise regime. Although unbiased SGD is typically incompatible with acceleration due to noise, we demonstrate that a specific variant of stochastic covariance scaling can render it acceleration-compatible by effectively treating the algorithm as regular (full) gradient descent. Furthermore, we establish that stochastic covariance scaling functions as a tunable bias mechanism, allowing it to bridge the gap between biased and unbiased algorithms to address their respective challenges. Finally, we propose a new algorithm that adaptively manages both step-size and stochastic covariance scaling based on historical loss values. This solution addresses the trade-off between exploration and exploitation inherent in stochastic covariance scaling, thereby enhancing robustness to hyperparameter selection. Experimental results confirm that this adaptive method surpasses existing state-of-the-art approaches. The implementation is publicly accessible at https://github.com/ChenchenLi2017/Adaptive-SPSA. Additionally, we have released a new library, AdaptSPSA, which implements a hyperparameter-adaptive algorithm based on stochastic parameter space averaging. This method achieves an asymptotic convergence rate comparable to constant methods while exhibiting superior robustness to hyperparameters. The source code is available at https://github.com/ChenchenLi2017/AdaptSPSA. The accompanying code includes implementations of various existing algorithms for direct comparison. IAXO stands for International Axion Observatory, a next-generation solar axion detector designed to observe the Sun's core over decades, thereby directly probing core physics. While current Solar Neutrino experiments like Borexino primarily analyze the Sun's equilibrium state, BabyIAXO will begin operations before reaching this state, allowing it to detect time-dependent signals. This capability enables the investigation of the convection zone's evolution and, potentially, the rotação diferencial of the core. However, signals from the Sun's radiative zone are expected to be too weak for BabyIAXO to identify. This study demonstrates that, given a 5-signal-to-background ratio, BabyIAXO could detect axial flow resulting from the convection zone's evolution approximately 10 years after launch. Furthermore, if axion production occurs due to the mismatch between the actual rotation rate and the rotation rate predicted by standard solar models, BabyIAXO could detect this signal within 10 years of operations. This detection would provide constraints on the age of the convective zone and the rotation rate of the radiative zone, offering insights into the Sun's internal structure. Additionally, a signal from the Sun's core could be detected roughly 100 years after BabyIAXO operations begin, though this detection is not guaranteed. Such a finding would reveal the inhomogeneity of the Sun's core, including its density, temperature, and composition. Conversely, a non-detection of axion signals from the radiative zone within 10 years of BabyIAXO operations could impose constraints on the mixing between the convective and radiative zones, as well as the rotation rate of the core. Ultimately, BabyIAXO offers a unique opportunity to study the Sun's internal structure through axil signals. Future IAXO operations are expected to achieve even greater sensitivity, allowing for the detection of even fainter signals. This will enable the investigation of the Sun's age, the mixing of its convective and radiative zones, and the rotation rates of both the convection zone and the radiative zone. This work introduces and investigates self-oscillating systems of any order $n$ that arise as perturbations, up to third order, of autonomous canonical systems defined by the equation $\dot{y} = \{y, H\}$, where $H$ denotes an arbitrary Hamiltonian and the bracket $\{\cdot, \cdot\}$ represents the Poisson bracket for variables $(q, p)$. Notably, this perturbative scheme enables the construction of self-oscillating systems that defy standard classification. Specifically, these new systems oscillate around a fixed point with a period $T$ determined by the parameters of the autonomous system and the perturbations, yet they lack a conserved quantity and do not conform to either Van der Pol-type or Josephson-type models. Additionally, the study examines perturbations of order $k$ where $k > 3$. Furthermore, an analytical model of a new class of self-oscillators is proposed, utilizing the principle of "inverse design" to derive an autonomous equation (unperturbed) and subsequent perturbations (up to fifth order) specifically so that the resulting self-oscillators possess a period matching that of the Van der Pol oscillator. The paper concludes with several unresolved questions. Finally, several models are presented as illustrations of this novel class of self-oscillators. Keywords: self-oscillating systems, Van der Pol oscillator, Josephson junction, self-oscillators with prescribed period.

**Background:** The integration of free-breathing acquisition with advanced motion correction in 4D (3D+respiration) T2-weighted turbo spin-echo (T2-SE) MRI offers the potential for high-quality lung and liver imaging.

**Aims:** This study sought to assess the efficacy of a 4D T2-SE sequence combining free-breathing data acquisition with motion correction for visualizing both healthy volunteers and patients.

**Methods:** Four free-breathing 4D T2-SE scans were performed on six healthy volunteers and 14 patients (five lung, five liver, four kidney, and four breast) using a 1.5T scanner. Each 4D scan was reconstructed into a 3D+retrospective motion correction (3D+MC) image, a 3D image without motion correction (3D), and two 3D+MC images featuring different motion correction levels (strong and weak). These 3D+MC variants were generated by applying strong or weak motion correction to the 3D+MC data following a 2D+MC step. All three image types were evaluated for 2D slice cross-sections.

**Results:** The 3D+MC images demonstrated superior motion correction compared to the 3D images. Among the 3D+MC images, the strong correction level yielded better results than the weak level. The 3D+MC images exhibited better anatomical correspondence with the 3D images than the 3D images alone.

**Conclusion:** The 4D T2-SE sequence effectively combines free-breathing acquisition with motion correction, producing 3D+MC images that outperform 3D images in terms of motion correction quality.

**Key words:** MRI, free-breathing, 4D, respiration, motion correction, T2-weighted, turbo spin-echo.

Compressive modeling has attracted significant interest due to its ability to match the performance of state-of-the-art models on standard benchmarks. However, existing approaches primarily optimize the parameters of small models independently, often disregarding the internal structure and information flow of their corresponding large models. This paper presents InDistill, a new framework designed to enhance compression quality by maintaining the information flow of the large source model. Specifically, InDistill proposes an information flow-preserving knowledge extraction method that refines knowledge within small models using gradient information derived from the large model. By leveraging first-order information from the large model, small models can effectively distinguish between important and irrelevant knowledge, thereby accelerating the learning process of neural network parameters. Extensive experiments demonstrate that InDistill yields substantial improvements in compression quality across various vision tasks, including image classification, object detection, and semantic segmentation. The code is accessible at https://github.com/ChenYixing1993/InDistill. Furthermore, our results reveal that InDistill outperforms competing methods by 1.0% to 2.5% in top-1 accuracy while utilizing 30% less FLOPs on CIFAR100, and it achieves gains of up to 3.0% in mAP and 3.5% in mIoU on the COCO and Cityscapes datasets, respectively, under the same FLOPs constraints. Consider a real-valued function $f$ defined on $\mathbb{R}^2$ that possesses a singular set consisting of a single point and exhibits superlinear growth at infinity. Under these conditions, the level sets of $f$ form a non-degenerate foliation outside the point at infinity. The shape of these level curves is described by the submersion function $f$. We demonstrate that the topological structure of $f$ can be represented graphically using a topological equivalence matrix (TEM). This matrix encodes the topological types of the foliation's leaves and their mutual relationships. Furthermore, we establish that the TEM is an invariant under topological transformations of $f$ and provide a criterion based on the TEM for determining whether the foliations of two such functions are topologically equivalent. The analysis specifically addresses functions with a singular set comprising a single point and a non-degenerate foliation (excluding focal leaves) at the point at infinity. These results are derived through the application of the blow-up technique. The findings are supported by numerical examples generated with the software TEM-Web. The methodology presented extends to a broader context: functions whose singular sets are one-dimensional submanifolds of $\mathbb{R}^2$, provided their level curves do not intersect at any finite point. This paper serves as the first installment in a series; the subsequent article will focus on the generic case. The approaches utilized are also applicable to other areas, including the study of real algebraic curves, the classification of real analytic surfaces, and the analysis of level sets of functions arising from the mean curvature flow. Additionally, the concepts introduced can be extended to real-valued functions defined on $\mathbb{R}^n$. Non-local grazing, where animals move between distinct vegetation patches, can significantly alter dry-land vegetation dynamics. This paper investigates such systems by extending spatially distributed models to include grazing kernels that generate non-local effects. We demonstrate that these nonlinearly rescaled kernels can trigger critical transitions and reshape stability regions within spatially homogeneous systems. Furthermore, spatial analysis reveals that traveling pulses and localized aggregations of livestock can further influence plant-herbivore interactions. Our findings indicate that these nonlinear feedback loops can either mitigate or exacerbate the impacts of grazing on vegetation biomass. Our results provide insights into the mechanisms driving vegetation pattern formation in semi-arid environments and highlight how nonlinearly enhanced grazing pressure can shrink the parameter ranges supporting vegetation persistence. Ultimately, our study offers a comprehensive understanding of the mechanisms underlying complex dry-land vegetation patterns. CountSketch is a widely used dimensionality reduction method that projects vectors into a lower-dimensional space, enabling the recovery of $k$-order moments such as the mean and frequency. Although numerous theoretical guarantees exist for this technique, they largely assume that input vectors are fixed and independent of the random counting vectors. This paper introduces theoretically backed algorithms that maintain strong resilience against adaptive inputs. Our results demonstrate that for both deterministic and randomized adaptive vectors, these algorithms can still accurately estimate the $\ell_2$ norm, as well as the mean and co-occurrence terms, potentially with a marginally larger sketch size. Furthermore, our findings are robust whether the adaptive vectors are independent or dependent on prior outputs. Finally, we validate these theoretical insights through experimental validation. We introduce ipie, a Python-based auxiliary-field quantum Monte Carlo (AFQMC) code designed for extensive, high-precision quantum simulations on workstations featuring multi-core CPUs or GPUs. The primary objective of AFQMC is to determine the uncorrelated ground state of quantum systems; however, achieving this goal requires overcoming significant challenges, including the sign problem, the measurement of diverse observables, and the accurate calculation of two-body correlation functions. To address these issues, we propose a series of strategies, including the development of a Python-based, parallelized framework, a novel configuration-biased approximation technique, a tunable optimization method for the variational ground state, and a new approach for computing two-body correlation functions. High-frequency trading (HFT) serves as the backbone of the global stock market, with transaction volumes reaching hundreds of thousands per day. A quantum HFT platform leverages quantum networks to execute transactions and run quantum games, such as the famous Prisoner's Dilemma, within the network. This research examines an economy characterized by intermediaries who facilitate transactions between producers and consumers. It introduces a novel mechanism that generates higher revenues than direct, non-intermediated deals. The study analyzes the producer-side auction designed to maximize total income, alongside an exploration of the associated equilibrium dynamics. Furthermore, it investigates the dynamics of a linear best-response learning process among intermediaries, who act as price setters, and the evolution of consumer participation. The findings indicate that the auction generates sufficient income to cover the costs of intermediaries. The paper also presents numerical simulations of the proposed mechanism, which reveal the emergence of complex periodic behaviors and chaos within certain parameter ranges. Finally, it addresses the issue of mechanism design robustness by considering perturbations in producer and consumer valuations. The resulting robustness analysis demonstrates that the auction's income is stable against such perturbations. Additionally, it is observed that the number of active intermediaries remains constant under small disturbances. However, the study also highlights that the participation of consumers, who are also intermediaries, is sensitive to valuation perturbations. Consequently, the robustness of the producer auction is further analyzed with respect to consumer valuations. The outcomes suggest that, under small perturbations, the total income of the producer auction remains robust. Finally, the paper concludes by examining the robustness of the producer auction under consumer price perturbations. Results indicate that this auction is robust to price perturbations, provided they are sufficiently small. Notably, the number of active consumers is also robust to these price perturbations. Creating a concise abstract for a specific domain requires a deep understanding of the text's inherent structure. To effectively summarize a text, one must first identify and promote key structural elements, such as the most significant topics and the arrangement of sentences. Consequently, we introduce Entity Prompt Planning (EP-Plan), which first plans the acquisition of prompts for entities to facilitate summary generation. This approach involves two main components: (1) planning the sequence of prompt acquisitions for each entity, and (2) producing the summary using the acquired prompts. Our method's planning algorithm utilizes natural language planning techniques, and its efficacy is validated across three different domains. Additionally, we demonstrate that the model can acquire domain-specific knowledge and successfully plan prompt acquisition sequences. These results indicate that EP-Plan can identify domains of interest and their sentence ordering, thereby generating coherent summaries. Furthermore, we show that the model successfully acquires domain-specific knowledge and effectively plans the sequence of acquiring prompts for entities like Event, Person, and Organization. This paper investigates quantum manipulation of information within the quantum circuit framework. We examine a specific category, $\lambda\text{-}S_1$, which serves as a generic model for these operations. This category is constructed using a monad, a comonad, and their natural transformation pair. We demonstrate that an object within this category can function as a generic quantum wire. Furthermore, we establish that the commutativity of a quantum circuit is a direct consequence of the commutativity of these wires. Additionally, we explore a degrading process for quantum operations that preserves unitality and linearity, providing a corresponding categorical model. Finally, we show that an essential property of this model—the existence of duals for 1-morphisms—plays a crucial role in facilitating this degrading process. The study concludes by proposing several directions for future research. Notably, $\lambda\text{-}S_1$ represents a generic model for quantum manipulation that is not constrained by the specific dimensions of qubits. Consequently, this framework offers a valuable foundation for investigating dimension-independent issues in quantum computation and information, such as quantum circuits and degrading processes for operations. We introduce a novel approach to calculate the internal energies of two quasiparticle excitations within fractional quantum Hall effect states, specifically for both particle and particle-hole pairs. Leveraging this method, we derive precise analytical expressions for these energies in the lowest Landau level under a uniform perpendicular magnetic field. Furthermore, we compute the corresponding creation operators for both particle and particle-hole pairs, demonstrating that they yield identical potential energies and internal energies. Finally, we calculate internal energies involving any number of hole excitations. This framework offers a unified explanation for prior findings and resolves several previously unexplained issues. Additionally, our results indicate that particle-hole duality is not exact in this context. Specifically, we find that internal energies for two hole excitations are lower than those for two electron excitations, even though those for $2p-1$ holes exceed the energies for $2p$ electrons. These conclusions are supported by numerical calculations of exchange energies. Our findings suggest that the non-exactness of duality may stem from the inability of trial wave functions to accurately describe internal states, rather than from the bosonization method. Finally, we propose a potential extension of this approach to higher Landau levels. This paper is accompanied by supplementary material, including detailed derivations, as well as trial wave functions and trial creation operators. Furthermore, we outline several intriguing open questions regarding the excitation spectrum of highly filled Landau levels. This study addresses the numerical resolution of a Stokes variational inequality within the context of glaciology. Specifically, it focuses on a "semicoercive" variant of this inequality, characterized by nonhomogeneous Dirichlet boundary conditions on a portion of the domain boundary and a source term governed by a nonlinearity of growth $(2-s)$, where $s>1$. The analysis demonstrates that the associated energy is both noncoercive and noncoercive modulo shifts, with the degree of noncoercivity varying based on the value of $s$. The paper establishes the existence and uniqueness of weak solutions within appropriate function spaces, proving that these solutions possess regularity sufficient to ensure uniqueness across a broader space. Furthermore, these properties facilitate the development of a robust finite element approximation scheme. For the case where $s>2$, a posteriori error estimates are derived relative to the data. Finally, numerical simulations are presented to validate the theoretical findings. The code utilized to generate these results is released under an open-source license. Additionally, this work extends our prior research on approximating Stokes variational inequalities featuring linear $(1)$ and superlinear $(1<s<2)$ source terms, which employed a technique applicable to supercoercive function spaces. This current study represents a significant generalization, as the error analysis methods previously used are no longer directly applicable. Instead, an entirely novel approach is introduced to derive variational stability estimates that yield optimal convergence rates. This new methodology is expected to be applicable to other variational inequalities exhibiting mild noncoercivity. The article is structured into two parts: the first provides an overview of the variational inequality, while the second details the finite element approximation strategy. Given the extensive scope of the proofs, they are omitted from this version but are available in the original manuscript. However, the original paper's error estimates are not sharp; they are subsequently refined in a companion work, where a more direct error analysis is applied. That refined analysis yields identical convergence rates but with a substantially reduced constant, thereby enhancing the practical utility of finite element methods for glaciological simulations. This refined approach is expected to be applicable to a wider range of $s$. While this article concentrates on refining the error analysis, its companion will focus on extending its scope. Together, these two works will enable a substantially more efficient implementation of Stokes variational inequalities in glaciology. We introduce the initial findings of DUVET, a study utilizing high-resolution observations from the Hubble Space Telescope (F814W filter) and the VLT/FLAMES spectrograph to investigate the interplay between star formation and galactic outflows in the nearby starburst disk galaxy NGC 4536. By analyzing the spatial correlation between H$\alpha$ emission and [OIII]5007$\AA$+[]5007$+$[OIII]5660$+ [OIII]5007$+$[OIII]5660$+[NeV]7424$+$[NeV]7744$ emission, we identified a prominent outflow extending from the galaxy's center toward the northeastern periphery. Furthermore, we measured the spatial distribution of H$\alpha$-derived ionization parameters ($\log(\textrm{OIII/H\alpha})$) and compared them against the star formation rate surface density ($\Sigma_{\textrm{SFR}}$) to determine the star formation efficiency (SFE) within the central kiloparsec. Our results indicate that $\log(\textrm{[OIII]5007$+$}$/H$\alpha$) and $\Sigma_{\textrm{SFR}}$ are inversely correlated, confirming that outflowing gas is being expelled from central regions where the SFE exceeds $0.01$ Gyr$^{-1}$. Additionally, we observed a strong correlation between the H$\alpha$-derived SFE and the [OIII]5007$+$[]5007$+[NeV]7424$+$[NeV]7744$-derived SFE, demonstrating that the observed outflow originates from star formation occurring within the disk. These findings support the hypothesis that galactic outflows are driven by the most intense star-forming regions. Finally, we estimated the total mass of outflowing gas to be approximately $1.5 \times 10^8$ M$_\odot$, with a mass outflow rate of roughly $1.5 \times 10^4$ M$_\odot$ Gyr$^{-1}$. These values align with the $\Sigma_{\textrm{SFR}}$-dependent relation established by Veilleux et al. (2013).

This study analyzes the impact of the initial geometry on the generation of the third harmonic ($v_3$) within the context of a multiphase transport model. The research compares Au+Au and Cu+Cu collisions at various center-of-mass energies to explore how the colliding nuclei's size influences $v_3$ as a function of transverse momentum ($p_{T}$) and midrapidity pseudorapidity ($\eta$). The findings indicate that $v_3$ is more pronounced in Cu+Cu collisions than in Au+Au collisions, particularly at low $p_{T}$ values. This observation is attributed to the greater sensitivity of low-$p_{T}$ particles to the precise initial spatial configuration. Conversely, at higher $p_{T}$, the magnitude of $v_3$ becomes comparable between the two systems, as high-$p_{T}$ particles are predominantly determined by binary collisions and are thus less affected by geometric variations. These results provide valuable insights into the initial conditions of non-central heavy-ion collisions. Furthermore, the study examines the effect of varying the equation of state (EoS) on $v_3$, revealing that a stiffer EoS results in a larger $v_3$ magnitude. Finally, the analysis confirms that the model's predictions for $v_3$ align well with experimental data. Consequently, this multiphase transport model serves as an effective tool for investigating the influence of initial conditions on collective flow phenomena. Additionally, the framework can be utilized to study the production of other particles and their correlations. Overall, this research underscores the significance of initial conditions in understanding the dynamics of heavy-ion collisions. The results also suggest that a more detailed understanding of these initial conditions is necessary to fully interpret the complex phenomena observed in heavy-ion collisions. Finally, this study contributes to the broader effort to improve our understanding of the quark-gluon plasma and its properties. By examining the effect of the EoS on $v_3$, the work provides a valuable insight into the thermodynamic properties of the QGP. This is a crucial step toward a more comprehensive understanding of the QGP and its role in the early universe. This paper introduces a new approach for the concurrent control of multiple robots. We define a new framework called a simultaneous robotic system (SRS), which consists of several mobile robots linked by a series of physical connections. Each connection features a controllable actuator on one side to regulate the motion of the adjacent mobile robot and, crucially, a sensor on the other side to observe that side's motion. We propose a unified control framework designed to achieve any desired configuration of an SRS. This framework relies on a novel concept known as the side-aware feedback matrix (SAFM), a new tool for controlling the motion of mobile robots within an SRS. We demonstrate that this control framework is universally applicable to any SRS configuration and provide theoretical proof regarding its convergence. Furthermore, we have implemented the framework in a physical system comprising two differential drive robots connected by an actuated wheel and distance sensor, with experimental results confirming the theoretical findings. Our findings hold significant potential for applications in robotic swarms, where a central controller manages multiple mobile robots through various linkages. We believe our results will inspire future research into simultaneously controlling multiple robots via various connection types. Additionally, we have made our code and experimental data available to the community to facilitate further research and experimentation. Pre-training on large-scale datasets has become a standard approach to enhance deep neural network performance across various vision tasks, typically involving supervised learning. However, practitioners often overlook the specific advantages that certain pre-training tasks confer for particular downstream applications. This paper presents an empirical study that compares the efficacy of two distinct unsupervised pre-training tasks—monocular depth estimation and self-supervised image reconstruction—when applied to semantic segmentation. We demonstrate that the benefits of these pre-training strategies are task-dependent, meaning one approach does not inherently outperform the other in all scenarios. Furthermore, we analyze how network depth and architecture influence these outcomes, offering insights to assist practitioners in selecting suitable unsupervised pre-training methods for specific semantic segmentation tasks. Our findings are supported by experiments conducted on semantic segmentation using the CUB-200-2011, PASCAL VOC-2012, and Cityscapes datasets, as well as semantic and instance segmentation on both 2D and 3D versions of the COCO dataset. All experiments were conducted in a low-data regime, where datasets were split into 1,000 images for training and 2,000 images for testing. The results of these experiments are available at https://github.com/ashishkumar12345/semantic_segmentation_pretraining_analysis. Additionally, we release a new self-supervised pre-trained model, DepthNet, which integrates a depth estimation head with a semantic segmentation head, achieving state-of-the-art performance in low-data semantic segmentation settings. Our code can be accessed at https://github.com/ashishkumar12345/DepthNet. Finally, we provide recommendations for future unsupervised pre-training research, particularly in the fields of semantic segmentation and instance segmentation. This work serves as an initial step toward understanding the effects of self-supervised pre-training across diverse downstream tasks. To our knowledge, this represents the first effort to analyze the impact of self-supervised pre-training strategies specifically on instance segmentation. Kendall's tau serves as a nonparametric metric for correlation, valued for its robustness against outliers and applicability to vector data of any dimension. However, calculating the exact estimate and deriving credible intervals is often computationally demanding. Consequently, researchers frequently rely on approximations that sacrifice accuracy to achieve a balance between performance and precision. This study introduces a rapid method for inferring Kendall's tau, achieving a 1000-fold reduction in inference time with negligible loss in accuracy. Additionally, we present a novel procedure for estimating the minimal mean-squared error of Kendall's tau, a metric that has not previously been readily estimated. We evaluate the performance of our proposed estimator against existing literature and highlight several opportunities for future improvement. Our methodology is implemented in the R package {\tt kendall}. The package also includes utilities for assessing estimator performance, allowing users to replicate the performance evaluations found in this paper. Furthermore, we demonstrate how to apply our approach to real-world, messy datasets, including those with missing values, outliers, missing variables, and incomplete observations. These practical examples can be reproduced using the included tutorials. The source code for both examples and the performance assessments is available in a public repository. We anticipate that our method and the supporting tools in {\tt kendall} will facilitate improved comparisons of estimator performance in the future. Finally, we outline several directions for enhancing the performance of {\tt kendall} in an upcoming extension. The widespread adoption of connected and autonomous vehicles (CVaWs) has spurred significant research into intelligent edge computing for automotive networks. While machine learning (ML) models deployed at the edge can enhance safety and performance, they often demand high computational power that individual vehicles may lack. Although offloading these ML tasks to access point servers offers a solution, it introduces substantial privacy risks regarding data and model integrity. To address this, we propose a privacy-preserving edge intelligence framework utilizing federated learning (FL). This framework incorporates two key security modules: (1) a secure FL framework that safeguards local data and ensures honest model updates, and (2) a trusted access point server that securely offloads heavy ML tasks from the global model, thereby improving ML efficiency. Experimental results demonstrate that our proposed framework not only ensures privacy and security but also achieves superior ML accuracy and runtime performance compared to existing methods. Additionally, we have released an open-source library to support FL, enabling automotive networks to more readily adopt privacy-preserving edge intelligence. This work offers a comprehensive solution for secure, privacy-preserving ML at the automotive edge. The related resources are available at: https://github.com/zhijunzhou1992/SecureFP. We introduce a novel manifold called the Euler characteristic manifold (EC-manifold), designed to encode the combinatorial and differential structures of any given manifold. Our approach relies on two key concepts: the vertex set of a differential manifold and the egraph of a differential or combinatorial manifold. By defining EC-manifolds through vertex sets and graphs, we demonstrate that they retain combinatorial information, thereby enabling the application of graph theory to the computation of these manifolds. A central component of this work is a graph algorithm that calculates the Euler characteristic of a manifold from its associated egraph. This method facilitates a comparison between the manifold-differential and combinatorial structures of any manifold and those of a simplicial complex sharing the same Euler characteristic. Furthermore, this algorithm allows for the determination of whether a manifold's egraph can be constructed from a specific graph (such as one representing a simplicial complex) by utilizing vertex sets and shared combinatorial data. Finally, we illustrate the application of EC-manifolds in data analysis. Specifically, we show that data sets can be modeled as such structures, utilizing vertex sets and egraphs derived from these, which enables a direct comparison between data-set structures and those of associated simplicial complexes that share comparable combinatorial and differential properties. This study introduces a Holling-Tanner predator-prey model featuring a strong Allee effect in the prey population. The proposed framework accounts for both Holling type II and type III functional responses. We establish the global stability of positive equilibria and demonstrate the absence of Allee cycles within the system. Furthermore, by analyzing the model across various parameter values, we identify multiple bifurcation types, including saddle-node, Hopf, and Bogdanov-Takens. Finally, the paper explores the model's potential applications in the context of COVID-19. Notably, our findings indicate that the proposed system can serve as an effective representation of the SIR model for the virus. Additionally, we show that the COVID-19 model exhibits similar bifurcation behaviors to the Holling-Tanner framework, with implications for understanding the pandemic's progression and the impact of control measures. Specifically, we observe that the basic reproduction number ($R_0$) can be reduced below unity through vaccination and other interventions, thereby preventing the emergence of an endemic state. These results underscore the necessity of implementing control strategies to mitigate the spread of COVID-19. However, the current work does not incorporate the impact of natural death rates, a factor that should be addressed in future research. Ultimately, we conclude that the mathematical model presented here offers a viable approach for managing the COVID-19 crisis. This conclusion is supported by the model's ability to capture the epidemic's progression and its sensitivity to different control measures. Our analysis reveals that specific interventions can significantly influence the epidemic's trajectory, thereby reducing the risk of uncontrolled viral transmission. These findings highlight the importance of implementing appropriate control measures to mitigate the spread of COVID-19. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the model is highly sensitive to various control strategies, which can substantially lower infection rates and alleviate the burden on healthcare systems. In summary, the work presented herein provides a valuable tool for policymakers and public health officials to develop effective strategies for containing the COVID-19 outbreak. By utilizing this model, stakeholders can make informed decisions regarding resource allocation, contact tracing, and other mitigation efforts to protect vulnerable populations and prevent further transmission. Ultimately, the model serves as a crucial instrument for guiding public health efforts and ensuring the safe management of the ongoing pandemic. Finally, we emphasize the model's utility in informing public awareness campaigns and educational initiatives, which can play a vital role in fostering individual responsibility and collective action to combat the spread of COVID-19. In the first paper of this series, we demonstrated that the facet rotation simplex method, introduced by Zadeh, constitutes a polynomial-time algorithm for polynomial-time encoded linear programming instances, resulting in a linear iteration bound of $O(m+n)$. In this follow-up work, we demonstrate that the analysis can be extended to handle rational inputs. Specifically, for linear programming problems featuring a feasible region with $m$ facets and $n$ variables, where all data are rational numbers with bit lengths not exceeding $L$, the number of iterations of the facet rotation simplex method is bounded by $O((m + n)L)$. This represents a linear iteration bound in the size of the input. Consequently, when combined with Tarjan's technique for managing rational arithmetic, this yields a polynomial-time algorithm for rational linear programming. Furthermore, we present a novel upper bound on the diameter of the graph representing the polytope defined by randomly generated linear constraints with random coefficients. We also explore connections to the recent findings of Conforti et al. [10] and establish a novel link to the theory of random graphs. Finally, we outline an avenue for extending these results to integer linear programming. This work is partially derived from the author's thesis [24]. Let $\mathcal{A}$ be a graded ring. For any unital connected graded $\mathcal{A}$-module $\mathcal{M}$, we demonstrate that the obstruction to lifting $K_1$-symbols in $\NK_1(\mathcal{M})$ to $K_1(\mathcal{A})$ vanishes. This result holds specifically for modules that are either graded projective or graded free. Additionally, we provide a non-trivial example illustrating a situation where the obstruction does not vanish when considering one-sided modules. Our findings rely on the observation that the functor $\mathcal{A}\otimes_{\mathcal{R}}\cdot$ preserves $K_1$-groups, where $\mathcal{R}$ denotes the direct sum of the diagonal subrings and $\mathcal{A}$ represents the direct sum of the corresponding diagonal subrings of $\mathcal{A}$. This observation is established through an inductive argument that may hold independent interest. Furthermore, we present an example demonstrating that the observation fails without the assumption of a graded structure. These observations form the foundation of our results. As an application, we compute the groups $\NK_1(\mathcal{M})$ for specific cases. The primary reference for this work is Bak's study on units and $K_1$ in the context of unitary collections of unital connected graded $\mathcal{A}$-modules $\mathcal{M}$. Our findings indicate that Bak's original assumption—that the diagonal subring $\mathcal{D}$ of $\mathcal{A}$ must be a product of rings—is unnecessary. We have provided examples where this condition fails, yet the diagonal subring remains a product of rings. We anticipate that our results will find applications in various other settings. This paper is a contribution to the field of algebraic $K$-theory. Our approach is inspired by Bak's work on units and $K_1$ for Bak's unitary collection of unital connected graded $\mathcal{A}$-modules $\mathcal{M}$. In this context, $\mathcal{A}$ serves as a graded ring, which is defined as the direct sum of $\mathcal{D}$-modules, where $\mathcal{D}$ represents a collection of unital connected graded rings. This study investigates the potential impact of off-shell contributions on the top quark mass measurement using LHC data in $t\bar{t}j$ events. To address this, we developed an analytical model for the $\Gamma_{tW}$-dependent total decay width, which incorporates both off-shell and interference effects. This approach offers two key benefits: it simplifies the modeling of off-shell phenomena, and it ensures the resulting cross section strictly adheres to unitarity in the high-energy limit. We determined the mass distribution for the dilepton final state, a primary channel for $t\bar{t}j$ events in $t$-channel kinematics, by fitting this decay width into Monte Carlo simulations. Our findings indicate that off-shell effects leave a negligible impact on the $M_{t\bar{t}}$ distribution, a conclusion that aligns with results from full simulations. Consequently, these findings suggest that off-shell contributions can be neglected when extracting the top quark mass from $t\bar{t}j$ data at the LHC. Furthermore, we observe that the $m_{T2}$ variable serves as an effective alternative to the $M_{t\bar{t}}$ mass for mass extraction purposes. Finally, we note that the $m_{T2}$ distribution remains largely unaffected by off-shell contributions, even when utilizing full simulations. These results are particularly relevant for upcoming LHC analyses aimed at measuring the top quark mass. Our work also provides a practical tool for studying new physics scenarios involving $t\bar{t}j$ events, where off-shell effects are expected to be more pronounced. We anticipate that the proposed formalism will facilitate future research into extracting the top quark mass from $t\bar{t}j$ events. All findings in this paper were validated using the LHCb Monte Carlo 9.0.0 framework. Additionally, we have made our code available to the public to support future research in this area. Specifically, the $m_{T2}$ mass distribution can be easily calculated via an analytic formula, allowing users to avoid the need for full simulations. The increasing prevalence of deep learning techniques has led to the rapid advancement of automated face anti-spoofing (FAS) systems. While recent research indicates that pre-trained vision models can effectively detect live or spoofed faces within short video clips, the scarcity of large-scale public datasets has necessitated the development of open-source alternatives. This paper introduces OpenPrintFinger, a comprehensive open-source FAS dataset featuring a wide array of print attacks, including various paper types, lighting conditions, and individuals. To evaluate the efficacy of pre-trained models, we conducted an extensive comparative study using vision transformers (ViT) across different open-source anti-spoofing datasets. Our findings reveal that high-accuracy ViT models are highly effective for FAS; however, their substantial computational costs and reliance on large training datasets pose significant challenges. Consequently, we propose an efficient ViT architecture that surpasses existing state-of-the-art performance. The code for our method will be made publicly available. The dataset and its associated code can be accessed at https://github.com/ChenYi-chen/OpenPrintFinger. The source code for OpenPrintFinger is hosted at https://github.com/ChenYi-chen/OpenPrintFinger/tree/main/Code. Additionally, our paper is available on arXiv at https://arxiv.org/abs/2209.01014. Finally, our source code is also accessible via our lab's repository at https://github.com/ChenYi-chen/OpenPrintFinger/tree/main/Code. We look forward to your feedback. Thank you. :)

Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) is a machine learning approach that simultaneously handles perception and planning by utilizing learning mechanisms to optimize long-term goals. It has become a significant research focus in recent years, particularly for autonomous driving. This paper introduces a Deep Reinforcement Learning-based Control System for Autonomous Driving, designed to enhance driving comfort and safety. We present our deep Reinforcement Learning for Autonomous Driving (DRL-AD) system, which serves as a cutting-edge solution. Within this framework, we developed a driving simulator to generate complex driving scenarios. To train the driving agent, we implemented a reward function that evaluates various aspects of vehicle behavior. Furthermore, we integrated a GAIL module to ensure smooth and safe driving. For policy learning, we employed the Soft Actor-Critic (SAC) algorithm, which balances exploration and exploitation to maximize long-term rewards. The system was tested across diverse driving scenarios, including highway merging, obstacle avoidance, and roundabout driving. Experimental results demonstrate that our model effectively performs driving tasks while optimizing comfort and safety. The source code is publicly available at: https://github.com/Abdulrahman-Alshammari/Deep-Reinforcement-Learning-Autonomous-Driving. Our paper can be accessed here: https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.11000.
