Parallel evolutionary algorithms (PEAs) leverage parallel computing to accelerate the evolution of solution populations. Among their variants, asynchronous parallel multi-objective evolutionary algorithms (AS-MOEAs) have gained significant attention for their robustness, flexibility, and performance. However, AS-MOEA evaluation times vary due to their asynchronous nature, creating a "time bias" where solutions are often judged based on estimates rather than precise results. This leads to inaccurate evaluations and suboptimal Pareto front approximations. To address this, we introduce a new parent selection mechanism designed to mitigate the impact of time bias on Pareto front approximation. This mechanism incorporates a frequency-based approach that prioritizes solutions with higher evaluation frequencies. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed algorithm significantly outperforms existing AS-MOEA methods in producing more accurate Pareto front approximations. Additionally, an ablation study confirms that the frequency-based selection mechanism is the primary driver of these improvements. Finally, we show that the superior performance of this mechanism stems from its ability to enhance solution diversity, thereby reducing premature convergence. The microlensing event OGLE-2017-BLG-1434 was identified by the Optical Gravitational Lensing Experiment (OGLE) survey as a possible planetary system. Follow-up observations using adaptive optics on the Keck Observatory revealed a microlensing binary system, where the lighter component was hypothesized to host a planet. This study details the analysis of archival KePOI data, which identified a binary light curve consistent with the BKL model, yielding a best-fit mass ratio of $q=0.10^{+0.02}_{-0.01}$ and a primary mass of $M_{\rm primary} = 0.30^{+0.04}_{-0.03} \, M_{\rm J}$. The planet, OGLE-2017-BLG-1434b, orbits at approximately 2.8 AU from a super-Earth ($M_{\rm primary} = 0.30 \, M_{\rm J} \pm 0.04 \, M_{\rm J}$), completing its orbit in roughly 1.5 years. This system represents a promising candidate for future characterization via JWST. Additionally, the work discusses the implications of this discovery for the mass function of low-mass planets. The quantum Langevin equation, a fundamental framework in quantum optics and information science, describes the evolution of open quantum systems. Its generator comprises a dissipative component and a component oscillating at high frequencies. While the traditional average Hamiltonian approach discards the high-frequency term as negligible, this work demonstrates that under specific conditions, such approximations can drastically alter a system's dynamics. Consequently, we develop an alternative expansion in inverse frequency to accurately capture the effect of the highly oscillating part. This derived expansion is applicable not only to the two-level system but also to general Markovian dynamics of open quantum systems. Furthermore, it is shown that retaining the leading-order term enables precise control over quantum states and channels. These findings are validated through applications to a three-level V-type system and a two-qubit system. Ultimately, this research provides a pathway to manipulate quantum dissipation in both fundamental and engineered systems. Additionally, it offers a method to design novel measurement devices by engineering quantum decoherence. Finally, the results suggest that high-frequency techniques hold promise for enhancing quantum sensing and metrology. These outcomes are expected to stimulate further investigation into the manipulation of quantum dissipation. Notably, the high-frequency approach is observed to complement resonant techniques, thereby expanding the range of achievable targets. Finally, off-diagonal terms in the density matrix can be effectively manipulated, a capability that contrasts with the limitations of resonant methods. Finally, the study examines the impact of non-idealities, specifically time-jitter and detuning, on the effectiveness of the expansion. Specifically, it is demonstrated that for high-quality qubits, the proposed method remains effective even in the presence of these imperfections. Finally, the work establishes a foundation for the design of quantum devices and circuits. Specifically, the results suggest that the expansion can be utilized to develop advanced quantum hardware. Furthermore, the study highlights the potential for high-frequency techniques to achieve control over diagonal elements of the density matrix. Specifically, this approach enables the manipulation of populations, a capability distinct from that of resonant methods. Finally, the work examines the influence of non-idealities, such as time-jitter and detuning, on the effectiveness of the expansion. Specifically, it is shown that for high-fidelity qubits, the proposed method remains effective despite these imperfections. The impact of neutron depolarization, caused by the presence of ferromagnetic regions within sample textures, has been assessed. This phenomenon could lead to the underestimation of true nuclear and incoherent scattering signals, as well as the magnetic structure factor, in experiments utilizing a fixed neutron spin direction. The most effective strategy to mitigate this effect involves depolarizing neutrons upon their entry into the sample, thereby ensuring that variations in scattering intensity are not obscured by fluctuations in the magnetic scattering structure factor linked to sample texture. This critical issue is particularly pertinent to CePd$_{1-x}$Rh$_x$ compounds, which exhibit ferromagnetic ordering at high rhodium concentrations ($x \geq 0.25$) and display signatures of spin freezing at low rhodium levels ($x \leq 0.1$). Furthermore, this problem remains relevant for any research involving the measurement of magnetic scattering from materials with ferromagnetic order. To address this, a new approach was implemented during SANS measurements of the CePd$_{1-x}$Rh$_x$ series, incorporating a comprehensive magnetic characterization of these compounds via VSM, MOKE, and XMCD techniques. These studies collectively demonstrate that neutron scattering investigations on ferromagnetic materials must rigorously evaluate the influence of ferromagnetic domains and the associated neutron depolarization effects. The results of this thorough magnetic characterization are presented and discussed. A key finding is that CePd$_{1-x}$Rh$_x$ compounds with $x \leq 0.1$ display a spin-glass-like behavior, evidenced by the absence of ferromagnetic domains and a lack of hysteresis in magnetization curves. Conversely, the influence of ferromagnetic domains on neutron depolarization in the CePd$_{0.75}$Rh$_{0.25}$ compound was quantified by analyzing the time-dependent evolution of the magnetic structure factor. This analysis revealed that the probability of a neutron beam intersecting these domains is substantial, significantly affecting the interpretation of magnetic scattering data. Consequently, the observed time dependence of the magnetic structure factor is attributed to the gradual transition of the sample from a state with a high density of ferromagnetic domains to one with a low density. This transition is linked to the progressive development of long-range correlations between Rh moments, a process that ultimately suppresses the formation of ferromagnetic domains. We conducted a 21-cm neutral hydrogen survey targeting the high-mass star-forming region G176.51+00.20 using the Green Bank Telescope. This area is renowned for hosting G176.51+00.20 IRAS, a luminous infrared object that illuminates the nearby G176.51+00.20 Nebula. Our observations revealed 15 HI narrow-line self-emissions (HINS) within a 100' x 100' field of view, distributed across two clusters. The spatial arrangement of these HINS clusters aligns with the morphology of the G176.51+00.20 Nebula, and their velocity structures exhibit similarities to the nebula's spectral lines. Furthermore, the HI velocity dispersion of these clusters is comparable to that of the nebula. These characteristics suggest that the HINS are ionization-induced narrow-line HI emissions driven by the nebula's photoevaporation. Additionally, the HINS display a velocity asymmetry relative to the surrounding molecular gas, indicating a photoevaporation-driven outflow. We propose that the HINS represent a direct manifestation of the photoevaporation process occurring in high-mass star-forming regions. This study offers a novel perspective on understanding the photoevaporation of high-mass star-forming regions. The GBT HI survey is anticipated to uncover more HINS in high-mass star-forming regions, thereby enhancing our understanding of the photoevaporation-driven star formation process. We demonstrate that an intermediate $\beta$-shift, defined by a specific gap structure, is topologically conjugate to a greedy $\beta$-shift also characterized by that same gap structure. Furthermore, we establish a finiteness condition for the existence of such intermediate $\beta$-shifts and provide the maximum possible size of the gap. These findings extend previous work limited to cases with a single gap. Additionally, we explore the implications of these results regarding the spectra of binary quadratic forms and the $\alpha(\beta)$ function. Finally, we present an explicit example of an intermediate $\beta$-shift with a non-empty interior that does not possess topological Markov structure, thereby generating new open questions. The resulting value is $\phi_\mathrm{s} = -0.035 \pm 0.063 \pm 0.012 \pm 0.035$ rad, where the uncertainties correspond to statistics, the $\phi_\mathrm{s}$ measurement itself, and other sources, respectively. This result aligns with previous findings within their combined uncertainties. Additionally, the study reports a combined measurement of the mixing frequency $\Delta m_s$ derived from both $B_s \to J/\psi K^0_S$ and $B_s \to J/\psi \pi^+ \pi^-$ decays, yielding $\Delta m_s = 17.657 \pm 0.021 \pm 0.007 \pm 0.010$ ps$^{-1}$. Deep neural networks (DNNs) have become a cornerstone of image recognition, yet their significant size and complexity necessitate training on massive datasets. This process is often costly and time-consuming due to the difficulty of gathering sufficient labeled data. To address this, researchers have developed domain adaptation techniques that allow models trained on one dataset of images to perform effectively on others. This paper offers a comprehensive review of these methods, categorizing them into three groups based on their underlying approaches: feature transformation, semi-supervised, and self-training domain adaptation. We evaluate each category using three benchmark image recognition tasks, comparing various algorithms within the context of these specific benchmarks. Finally, we discuss the pros and cons of each category and provide general recommendations for image recognition applications. To our knowledge, this is the first survey to examine existing domain adaptation techniques specifically for image recognition. Our analysis indicates that self-training and semi-supervised approaches are the most promising for future advancements in the field. Additionally, we identify several gaps in current research and propose potential directions for further study. We anticipate that this survey will be valuable to researchers interested in domain adaptation for image recognition. The source code for our evaluation is available at https://github.com/abhishekgupta1998/survey-domain-adaptation-image-recognition.

We determine the number of curves that pass through a specified set of points and do not pass through a different set of points. Our count encompasses arcs, functions, and conics. Specifically, we establish precise formulas for perfect, semi-super, and super affine functions; super points; and affine planes. For geometric objects involving points at infinity, we provide approximate formulas. Our approach relies on counting matrices with distinct rows and columns and by applying the inclusion-exclusion principle. Additionally, as an application of these counting methods, we utilize a newly discovered identity for the permanent of a matrix featuring zeros on its main diagonal to re-implement the inclusion-exclusion principle using a modified matrix. This allows us to efficiently calculate the number of perfect, semi-super, and super affine functions. Furthermore, we present a novel asymptotic formula for geometric objects situated near infinity. Our findings extend previous work by Balister et al. and by Huang and Li. Finally, we outline several open problems. Keywords: Affine plane, M\"{o}bius inversion, Asymptotic behavior, Counting curves, Counting matrices, Distinct rows and columns, Euler identity, Finite geometry, Inclusion-exclusion principle, Matrix permanent, Rational functions. 2020 Mathematics Subject Classification: 05A15, 05A16, 05A18, 05D15, 05D18, 05E05, 05E15, 11B75, 11T71, 14H51.

Consider the tetrahedral grid formed by the points $(x,y,z) \in \mathbb{N}^{3}$. We provide a combinatorial proof for the identity $\displaystyle {n+3 \choose 3} = 4{ n+2 \choose 3} - { n+1 \choose 3}$ by demonstrating that the quantity $4S_{n} - S_{n+1}$ represents the total count of right triangles with legs of equal length situated on the coordinate planes within this grid. Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have gained significant traction for analyzing graph data, yet the intricate inner workings of the GNN parameterization function remain underexplored. This study investigates the representability of that function within the framework of compressed sensing theory. We demonstrate that under specific conditions, the GNN parameterization function can be represented as the solution to an $\ell_1$-minimization problem. Leveraging this representation, we establish recovery guarantees and provide insights into the generalization error of GNNs. Furthermore, we develop an interpretable GNN model based on this parameterization, where the network's intermediate layers correspond to selected features, and the output layer reflects the final prediction. We validate the interpretability of our approach and the effectiveness of the resulting interpretable model through a classification task on a real-world dataset. Additionally, we obtain promising results for a real-world application involving a railway track fault detection system. Finally, we explore potential future research directions and applications for our work. This paper aims to enhance our understanding of GNNs and their parameters, while also advancing the broader field of interpretable machine learning. We report a serendipitous discovery of the galaxy cluster RXCJ0232.2-4420 during a Chandra observation of the dwarf galaxy IC342. This system is a likely merging cluster featuring a 100 kpc diameter X-ray cavity within the intracluster medium, which we propose is caused by the ram pressure of an accreting substructure. The cluster contains two massive galaxy triplets, each comprising two bright red galaxies and one bright blue galaxy. Additionally, we identified a possible substructure at approximately 100 kpc from the cluster center, characterized by a bright galaxy and a blue group. This substructure is associated with a significant radio source, designated RXCJ0232.2-4420A, which exhibits a flat radio spectrum and a radio lobe diameter of roughly 100 kpc. We suggest that RXCJ0232.2-4420A is an Accretion Mode Radio Galaxy (AMRG), representing a newly identified class of galaxy. Furthermore, we detected a radio source at the center of RXCJ0232.2-4420, RXCJ0232.2-4420C, which we classify as a starburst galaxy based on its morphology and spectral characteristics. This study proposes a dynamic modeling approach in which those interacting agents may migrate between communities. Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) have recently demonstrated significant utility for solving partial differential equations (PDEs) by embedding physical laws directly into the model. However, when applied to PDEs with rapidly varying coefficients, PINNs often suffer from spectral bias, leading to suboptimal convergence. This study investigates the impact of momentum on this spectral bias within the context of solving PDEs. We employ a straightforward approach that integrates a momentum term into the training loop of initial-and-initial-value PDEs, observing that this method mitigates spectral bias. Our analysis examines the proposed technique's efficacy across simple test cases and a more intricate scenario involving a turbulent flow governed by the Navier-Stokes equations. Additionally, we provide a theoretical analysis linking spectral bias to the gradient of PINNs. Finally, we validate our findings on a real-world application: reconstructing a 3D human body surface from a limited set of 2D images. The entire codebase is accessible at https://github.com/taehyung-lee/PINNs_with_momentum.

This study examines a coupled wave system featuring mixed Dirichlet-Neumann boundary conditions, where the system is decoupled within an open subset $\Omega$ of the domain $\Omega$. Outside this region, the equations incorporate undamped Kelvin-Voigt terms. We demonstrate that energy decay occurs when $\Omega$ is star-shaped and, alternatively, when the coefficients of the undamped Kelvin-Voigt damping terms are periodic in the $x_1$ direction with a period $T$. Additionally, the periodic case relies on the strong coupling between the equations. Our approach employs the Hilbert Uniqueness Pairing method for the stability analysis of the coupled system with locally disrupted boundary conditions, alongside an energy estimate for the decoupled wave equation, both of which are novel contributions. Furthermore, we derive a polynomial stability rate for the periodic scenario using a multiplier method, and we establish an explicit stability rate for the star-shaped case utilizing the recently developed multiplier method by Burq and Tzvetkov. Our analysis covers coupled systems with locally disrupted mixed Dirichlet-Neumann boundary conditions, offering new results for the previously studied case of globally Dirichlet boundary conditions. Additionally, the paper presents novel findings for systems with mixed Dirichlet-Neumann boundary conditions that are not periodic. Finally, we introduce novel techniques for both equations, such as utilizing the equation satisfied by the error term in the boundary control problem and applying multiplier methods to derive energy estimates. These novel methods hold independent significance for future research. Finally, our methodology is applicable to systems with locally disrupted dissipation, including viscoelastic damping and fractional dissipation. Our findings extend to coupled hyperbolic systems with mixed Dirichlet-Neumann boundary conditions, although the proofs are restricted to a semilinear heat equation due to space limitations. Future research will address the remaining cases for coupled hyperbolic systems and their associated error estimates. The current work serves as a foundation for our subsequent publications. Although model-based reinforcement learning (RL) offers a path to sample-efficient learning through the use of physics-based world models, it often fails in real-world scenarios because these models inevitably contain errors. This study addresses this challenge by introducing a novel hierarchical RL framework utilizing inductive logic programming (CLASP), which serves as a logical reasoning engine. This approach enables the creation of an interpretable, hierarchical representation of the environment, allowing the system to adapt to model inaccuracies by identifying and correcting its assumptions. The efficacy of this method is demonstrated across two simplified physical scenarios. Our findings indicate that the proposed framework achieves an order-of-magnitude improvement in sample efficiency compared to state-of-the-art model-based RL techniques. Furthermore, the method's ability to uncover incorrect environmental assumptions provides a valuable mechanism for incorporating domain knowledge, thereby facilitating more efficient learning. Finally, we demonstrate how this learned representation can be leveraged to discover novel environmental assumptions. Overall, this work paves the way for model-based RL in complex, imperfect real-world settings by offering a means to learn, interpret, and integrate prior knowledge. Asymmetry is a defining characteristic of many complex systems, yet standard light lacks spatial asymmetry. While recent experiments have demonstrated that spin squeezing can induce complex spin-spatial entanglement in light, enabling the generation of asymmetric photons from symmetric initial states via linear optics, the impact of this symmetry breaking on cavity optical systems remains unclear. This study investigates a two-mode squeezed vacuum state, a typical spin-spatial entangled light source, within a nonreciprocal cavity system. Results indicate that quantum squeezing in one spatial mode can drive asymmetric scattering in the output, with the degree of asymmetry contingent upon both the squeezed degree and the nonreciprocity parameter of the cavity. Furthermore, a distinct threshold of quantum squeezing is identified below which no output asymmetry occurs. Finally, the spin-spatial entanglement of the input light is shown to be a necessary condition for achieving asymmetric scattering, with the entanglement degree governing the final output behavior. These findings offer new insights into the interaction between quantum squeezing and nonreciprocity, holding significant potential for applications in nonreciprocal devices and quantum information science. This paper investigates the best uniform approximation of functions $f(x)=x^k+\sum_{j=1}^m a_j x^{k-d_j}$, where $k$ and $d_j$ are non-negative integers, by a sum of translates of $\psi(x)=xe^{-x^2/2}$. Our primary objective is to demonstrate that the infimum of the uniform norm for the difference between $f$ and the translate sum is attained. Furthermore, we provide characterizations of the best uniform approximation for $k=1$ and $k=2$, and for cases involving $q$ translates when $d_j=0$ with $m=1$ or $m=2$. These findings rely on a key lemma that may hold independent significance. Additionally, we explore applications to the uniform approximation of $x^k$ using a linear combination of $N$ Gaussians. This line of inquiry is motivated by the need to construct functions that closely resemble a "tent function" for use in finite element methods. Specifically, we examine the case of approximating a triangle function with two linear functionals using a linear combination of three Gaussians. We establish that a uniform minimax approximation exists and offer a constructive method to determine the coefficients of these Gaussians. We also present a numerical example with $N=3$ and include an appendix containing an $N=5$ example. This work extends our earlier study [10], which addressed the related issue of uniformly approximating functions of the form $x^k+\sum_{j=1}^m a_j x^{k-d_j}$ with $k=1$ and $k=2$ by a linear combination of Gaussians. Additionally, we reference recent work by Chen et al. [3] and provide a comparative analysis.

We introduce a novel direct detection experiment designed to investigate spin-dependent interactions with nucleons within shadow dark matter. This matter consists of dark fermion-antifermonion pairs produced through annihilations within the galactic dark matter halo. The proposed setup utilizes a lithium-6 bolometer, leveraging its unique nuclear structure to provide sensitivity to interactions with protons that other standard targets cannot match. Specifically, we demonstrate that a $\sim 100$ g $\ ^6$Li target can achieve nuclear recoil energy sensitivity down to $\sim 10^{-3}$ MeV, offering orders-of-magnitude improved detection capabilities. Furthermore, we establish that this target can reach spin-dependent cross-section sensitivities that surpass existing limits by up to two orders of magnitude. Finally, we examine how the proposed experiment can constrain the parameter space of spin-dependent shadow dark matter models that are otherwise inaccessible to current direct detection methods. Additionally, we show that a future 1-tonne scale $\ ^6$Li detector could observe a shadow dark matter signal, with the resulting constraints on the model parameter space exceeding those of the NA64 experiment at the SLAC linear accelerator. Nonuniform associative algebras constitute a noncommutative generalization of pseudofree algebras, offering a framework for the construction of integrable lattice models. This work introduces the concept of nonuniform associative Yang-Baxter equations (ASYB), which are satisfied by noncommutative R-matrices associated with these algebras. We demonstrate the existence of solutions to the nonuniform ASYB within specific cases, including cases where the noncommutativity is governed by an abelian solution to the standard Yang-Baxter equation. These R-matrices hold significant utility in integrable lattice models, enabling the derivation of both dynamical and generalized quantum inverse scattering methods. Furthermore, we establish a relationship between nonuniform ASYB and q-associative Yang-Baxter equations. Specifically, we prove that if a noncommutative matrix A satisfies the nonuniform ASYB, then the matrix B, defined as $B = (\exp(q\sigma_2 \Lambda))^{-1}A(\exp(q\sigma_2 \Lambda))$, satisfies the q-associative Yang-Baxter equation. As an application, we derive solutions to the nonuniform ASYB from several solutions of the quantum Yang-Baxter equation. Additionally, we derive solutions to the dynamical noncommutative quantum Yang-Baxter equation by appropriately modifying the noncommutative R-matrices. Finally, we derive solutions to the quantum dynamical Yang-Baxter equation by applying a linear transformation to the noncommutative R-matrices. These findings provide a systematic approach for generating integrable lattice models. Notably, our results extend and complement recent findings by various authors. Specifically, the models derived in this paper include the quantum XXZ model, the quantum principal chiral model, and the quantum affine Toda model. Furthermore, the quantum integrable models obtained herein are novel and have not been previously reported in the literature. This achievement is facilitated by the recent development of the quantum inverse scattering method utilizing the quantum R-matrix. Consequently, our findings offer a new approach to the construction of integrable lattice models. To illustrate this, we present a solution to the quantum affine Toda model based on a solution of the quantum Yang-Baxter equation. Our results thus provide a nonuniform generalization of this solution. This work was partially supported by the National Natural Science Foundation of China (Grant No. 11471161). The first author is currently a Visiting Scholar at the Department of Mathematics, University of California, Los Angeles.

This paper introduces Hoare Logic, an extension of first-order logic designed to validate the correctness of imperative programs. Its primary objective is to bridge the gap between human-readable specifications and machine-checkable proofs, thereby enhancing the rigor of formal verification. By incorporating special logical symbols that function as placeholders for user-defined assertions, we enable the creation of program correctness proofs checked by a theory solver or a proof assistant. Furthermore, we outline a algorithm for automatically generating this formal specification language from the syntactic and semantic constraints of natural language. This approach extends a previously proposed algorithm for translating first-order logic into constrained first-order logic, which serves as the foundation for our proposed language. We demonstrate the practical utility of this methodology through a formal validation of the bank transaction problem. Our findings indicate that the proposed pipeline for validating imperative programs effectively combines techniques from formal verification and computational linguistics. This creates a framework where humans can participate in the verification process by defining assertions in a formal language or even in natural language.

This study employs molecular dynamics simulations to investigate the mechanical characteristics of lipid bilayers containing cholesterol. We developed an efficient algorithm to calculate the flexural modulus by analyzing the root mean square displacement of individual lipids within the bilayer's neutral plane during oscillations, which significantly accelerates convergence compared to conventional methods relying on the height profile of the bilayer. Our findings indicate that the spectral decomposition-based approach for estimating the flexural modulus of thin elastic shells from stochastic fluctuations is highly effective for lipid membranes with a  cholesterol concentration up to 30%. We further observed that the flexural modulus of DPPC bilayers rises from 20.2 to 30.0 kBT as the cholesterol concentration increases from 0% to 30%. Additionally, we examined the impact of head group size on the flexural modulus of DPPC, finding that it increases from 17.8 to 22.6 kBT with a head group concentration of 0% to 40%, respectively. Finally, our results demonstrate that the spectral decomposition method accurately determines the flexural modulus of lipid membranes with varying cholesterol levels, provided the bilayer's thickness remains consistent. However, the method fails to yield accurate results for the flexural modulus of DPPC bilayers with sugar anchors, as this system exhibits substantial deviations from the thin shell approximation. These results align with existing experimental data. This study examines the application of the loop quantum gravity formalism to a simplified cosmological scenario within the ADM framework, specifically involving a single spatial dimension with no dynamical fields. The resulting loop quantum Hamiltonian is compared against formulations derived from the LQG-ADM mapping applied to the standard FRW model. Significant discrepancies are identified between the two approaches. Furthermore, the application of the strong constraint on the loop quantum Hamiltonian—enforcing no-crossing of the singularity—on the loop quantum Hamiltonian yields a more refined astrophysical model. Finally, the loop quantum spectrum of the area associated with the horizon at the Cauchy surface is calculated and compared with the spin structure of the area spectrum predicted by LQG. Notably, while both models predict an infinite number of spin values, the loop quantum spectrum lacks gaps. These findings suggest that quantum gravity effects may influence the area spectrum in distinct and potentially observable ways. Additionally, the implications of these results for black hole thermodynamics are explored. Finally, this work demonstrates that the loop quantum gravity formalism can generate astrophysical models that offer viable alternatives to black holes. Specifically, it is possible to construct a system that avoids the singularity while maintaining the event horizon, thereby producing a complete thermodynamic system. This outcome may contribute to resolving the black hole information paradox. Consequently, this model could serve as a foundation for future research into quantum gravity effects in astrophysical phenomena. To facilitate this, the text includes a comprehensive appendix detailing the thermodynamic properties of the model. These results indicate that the loop quantum gravity formalism holds substantial potential for advancing our understanding of quantum gravity in an astrophysical context. This aligns with the broader objective of developing astrophysical models that allow for the observation of quantum gravity effects. Finally, the methodology employed in this work is expected to inspire further research in this domain. To support these future endeavors, the source code for the numerical calculations is provided in an appendix. We introduce a bicategory of spaces equipped with relations and define a functor from it to a bicategory of grays, extending the Barr-Robson construction for relations to its localized counterpart for bounded maps between complete lattices. This functor is shown to be both fully faithful and grayspherical. Subsequently, we demonstrate that specific composition of relations between lattices, constructed using specific elements within them, yields a bounded map. These findings enable a characterization of coherence lattices as those relations whose composition is determined by such a bounded map, thereby generalizing the concept of coherence to larger classes of lattices. This approach provides a unified framework that resolves minor inconsistencies in the definition of coherence found in the literature and refines the definition itself. Furthermore, our methodology offers a pathway to generalize coherence to $LC_0$ spaces and lattices where the underlying set possesses additional structure. Finally, we establish that every element in a lattice can be represented as a relation, and every bounded map can be realized as the composition of relations. The primary tool facilitating these results is the fact that coherence lattices are precisely those where every element decomposes into a unique sum of disjoint relations. This uniqueness property is closely tied to coherence; notably, it fails in non-coherence lattices, such as the lattice of subspaces of a vector space, where relations and their composition exhibit distinct behaviors. Our methodology also allows us to generalize coherence to $DL_0$ spaces and lattices where every element admits a unique sum of disjoint relations. This study utilizes the Monte Carlo code CRAND to evaluate the radiation environment for Low Earth Orbit (LEO) satellites, specifically modeling particle trapping within the South Atlantic Anomaly (SAA). The simulations cover altitudes from 200 to 1,000 km at 50 km intervals across longitudes from 0° to 360° in 10° steps. The CRAND code calculates the particle flux spectrum as a function of energy, charge, and particle type. Results indicate that for satellites operating above 300 km within the SAA, the particle flux spectrum exceeds Earth's outer radiation belt levels by a factor of approximately 100. This finding is critical for satellite designers, as it demonstrates that the SAA environment is significantly more hazardous than the radiation belt. Consequently, satellites avoiding the SAA may still suffer from radiation damage, whereas those equipped with adequate shielding can effectively mitigate these risks. The study concludes that future LEO satellites should either be positioned outside the SAA or utilize sufficient shielding to ensure radiation tolerance. Additionally, the paper includes a table detailing the energy, charge, and particle type fluxes for a satellite at 350 km within the SAA. Deep Graph Neural Network (DGNN) models have recently gained significant traction for time series forecasting, yet they often fail to capture the dynamic nature of time series data. To address this limitation, we introduce a novel DGNN framework that integrates global pyramid-like skeleton shrinks and local topological link rewiring. The global shrinks component enables the model to learn dynamic shrinks and long-term dependencies, while the local rewiring component captures dynamic local correlations. Experimental results demonstrate that our proposed framework consistently surpasses current state-of-the-art DGNN models across three time series forecasting datasets. Furthermore, ablation studies reveal that the local rewiring mechanism effectively models dynamic correlations, while the shrinks mechanism successfully models long-term dependencies. Additionally, case studies on the S&P500 and Hang Seng indices illustrate that pyramid-like shrinks successfully extract key features from time series data. Finally, we provide comprehensive visualization findings that offer deeper insights into how our framework models dynamic correlations. We introduce a new, unified model for interstellar dust extinction, polarization, and emission, termed the Astrodust+PAH model. This framework incorporates the polarization of large dust grains via aligned electric susceptibility and an extended description of PAH emission. The AsP+PAH model successfully reproduces the far-UV to near-infrared (100–2500 \AA) extinction curve, including the 2175 \AA\ complex, and accurately predicts the mid-infrared (2.5--25 $\mu$m) emission curves derived from PAH emission features. Astrometrically, the model relies on three components: PAH emission, PAH absorption, and extinction by large grains. The PAH emission component is characterized by a single parameter, $Q_{\rm PAH}$, which scales the intensity of all PAH emission features. The large-grain extinction component is defined by two parameters, $R_V$ and $E(B-V)$, which describe the shape of the extinction curve and its magnitude. Astrophysically, the AsP+PAH model is designed to be applied to line-of-sight averaged quantities in the Galactic plane, where the interstellar medium is sparse and dust clumps are separated by large distances. Empirically, we demonstrate that the relationship between the ratio $Q_{\rm PAH}/\sigma_{\rm PAH}$ and the ratio $R_V/E(B-V)$ is nearly universal, where $\sigma_{\rm PAH}$ represents the average energy of the infrared PAH emission band. This relationship holds for the diffuse Galactic plane and is consistent with theoretical models. We further show that the AsP+PAH model can replicate the correlations between Galactic extinction, polarization, and polarization fraction observed in the Galactic plane. This study introduces a new vari-image segmentation framework that integrates three established image recovery techniques: total variation (TV) denoising, deconvolution, and deblurring. The proposed model incorporates an additional data fidelity term to integrate these methods into image segmentation. By utilizing the proximal gradient algorithm, we demonstrate the model's effectiveness across diverse applications, including noisy, blurred, real-world out-of-focus, and synthetic deconvolution images. Experimental outcomes indicate that the model produces segmentation maps that closely resemble human-perceived results. Furthermore, the model demonstrates superior performance compared to the standard total variation model when applied to image recovery tasks. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/ChenYi1993/VIPS. In these applications, we abbreviate the model as "VIPS," standing for "Variational Image Segmentation model," which effectively distinguishes foreground objects from the background. Additionally, the model exhibits robustness against noise, achieving competitive results against state-of-the-art approaches. We anticipate that this model will be highly effective for segmentation in photomicroscopy, microscopy, and medical imaging. The model is also available on GitHub at https://github.com/ChenYi1993/VIPS. Abstract Interpretation (AI) relies on a two-phase framework: abstracting a concrete domain into an approximated version and ensuring the approximation remains sound. Traditionally, these phases are tightly coupled, as the choice of the abstract domain directly dictates the resulting AI algorithm. This paper introduces and examines a novel decoupling strategy that separates abstract domain design from the construction of AI procedures. We establish a unified theoretical foundation for this approach and demonstrate its practical utility by applying it to dataflow analysis. Specifically, we outline a systematic method for constructing abstract domains for dataflow, which facilitates modular design and enables the development of new domains. Furthermore, we outline a generic procedure for deriving AI algorithms from arbitrary abstract domains. By unifying these constructions, our framework offers a consistent theoretical perspective for analyzing and designing dataflow analysis techniques. Empirical results indicate that integrating any of the proposed abstract domains into idiomatic dataflow analysis yields superior outcomes compared to existing techniques. Additionally, our methodology supports cross-domain operator design, allowing for the creation of operators that automatically derive sound approximations from idiomatic solutions in other domains. Extensive experiments confirm that integrating these cross-domain operators enhances dataflow analysis performance. Overall, this work provides a practical and theoretically sound framework for dataflow analysis that outperforms prior art. Our contributions offer a fresh perspective for both the analysis and synthesis of dataflow techniques. Finally, we demonstrate that our approach supports domain-specific optimization, allowing for performance improvements beyond what is achievable with existing methods. These findings illustrate that this framework effectively serves as both a tool for dataflow analysis and a mechanism for dataflow synthesis. Topological materials have recently attracted significant attention due to their unique properties, including the presence of protected gapless states and the topological Hall effect. These characteristics are rooted in the topology of the electronic band structure. However, phonons can also exhibit topological features, and their phonon topology can be manipulated through external stimuli such as strain and electric fields. In this study, we demonstrate that applying light enables the control of topology in both acoustic and optical phonon bands within perovskite oxides. This manipulation is achieved by using light to alter the lattice symmetry and induce modifications in the effective charge of ions. We anticipate that our findings will inspire the further exploration of optically controlled topological phonons in various materials. Additionally, the ability to govern phonon topology holds promise for enhancing thermal management in electronic devices and developing novel topological phononic materials. Our approach introduces two new algorithms: the Nearest Graph Distance (NGD) algorithm and its optimization, the NGD+ algorithm. Extensive experiments across diverse datasets demonstrate that NGD+ outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods in terms of both accuracy and scalability. The interaction between an atom and a thin dielectric mirror, situated at a distance $d$, is investigated by treating the mirror as composed of weakly interacting electric dipoles. This approach yields two primary findings: first, an optical strobe consisting of a short pulse with a width of $4d/c$ can trigger resonant fluorescence in the atom with an efficiency of $\eta = 1/2$; second, the mirror emits electromagnetic radiation, reaching an efficiency of $\eta = 1$ for ultra-thin mirrors. Consequently, this method provides a novel pathway for stimulating atomic transitions and generates new phenomena. Furthermore, the study offers a solution to a longstanding problem regarding energy conservation in quantum optics. These outcomes are achieved by shifting focus from the conventional focus on atom-mirror energy exchange to the broader distribution within the entire system. The proposed framework holds potential for extension to more complex scenarios, including multi-atom and multi-mirror configurations. Ultimately, these advancements may contribute to the development of a novel branch of quantum technology. Additionally, the methodology is applicable to modeling light-atom interactions in realistic environments and for calculating decoherence rates in quantum computing and communication systems. Finally, the paper includes a discussion of broader implications and potential future applications. Notably, the analysis of energy conservation is conducted without relying on the controversial concept of the vacuum field. Instead, the study demonstrates that the atom-mirror problem can be resolved by considering the total energy of the complete system. This finding may help advance quantum theory by eliminating the need for the problematic concept of zero-point energy. Ultimately, this work contributes to the ongoing effort to establish a more rational and coherent foundation for quantum theory. This study introduces an optimization-based framework for fair classification on graph data by identifying and eliminating biased community structures within the underlying graphs. The approach is grounded in the theory of graph homomorphisms and the Sauer-Shelah Lemma, which defines these biased communities as non-trivial preimages of points in the target class distribution when the homomorphism map is constant on attributes. The proposed framework operates in two stages: first, it constructs a biasedness graph where nodes represent community bias, and edges denote minimal refinement via non-biased homomorphisms; second, it selects the smallest local community to eliminate using an algorithm that balances bias reduction with the preservation of predictive performance. Experimental results on both synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate that the proposed method enhances both the fairness and predictability of community-localized classifiers. This study introduces a comprehensive diagnostic approach designed to identify both fundamental and speculative asset price bubbles under conditions of rational expectations. The proposed method relies on the integrated Fisher transformation, which ensures that the conclusion of a bubble follows a stochastic time process exhibiting mean-reverting characteristics. This mathematical framework allows for the formalization of the transition out of a bubble using a wide array of statistical distributions. Furthermore, this approach facilitates the application of extensive general stochastic calculus techniques to the rational expectations bubble model. The paper validates the method by deriving the classic rational expectations bubble model based on the inverted Fisher transformation and demonstrating how the general framework can be adapted to analyze speculative bubbles within economies characterized by hyperinflation. Additionally, the discussion explores extensions of this approach for analyzing bubbles driven by irrational expectations. Overall, this work provides a versatile and robust tool for bubble analysis, surpassing the limitations of previous methods that typically relied on linearization or fixed parameters. By utilizing the inverted Fisher transformation, the study establishes a formal mechanism for modeling the end of a bubble as a stochastic time process, thereby overcoming constraints imposed by deterministic frameworks. The paper concludes by outlining potential avenues for future research. We present a straightforward formula for the time-dependent two-point correlation function of a quantum harmonic oscillator, derived using path integral methods. In this work, time discretization is achieved through a Heun scheme, and the resulting high-dimensional integral is evaluated numerically using Monte Carlo techniques guided by Langevin dynamics. Our results confirm that the path integral approach yields exact results for this system. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the Langevin method, when applied to quantum field theory, offers a viable alternative to conventional time integration schemes. Finally, we show that the Langevin method enables the simultaneous calculation of Green's functions across multiple times within the same Monte Carlo configuration. These findings pave the way for developing new Monte Carlo techniques to compute Green's functions in non-equilibrium quantum field theories. Additionally, we introduce a novel Monte Carlo method for integrating the Schrödinger equation in quantum mechanics, utilizing the same path integral framework. This approach allows for the direct computation of the wave function without the need for normalization. Our numerical tests indicate that the accuracy of the derived wave functions is comparable to that of the time-dependent variational principle applied to Gaussian states. This suggests that the path integral method holds promise for calculating real-time dynamics in non-interacting quantum field theories. As an initial application of the path integral method within quantum field theory, we examine the driven harmonic oscillator. We derive exact results for both the occupation number and the expectation value of the position operator. To achieve this, we calculate the time-dependent correlation function using the Langevin method and employ the Cayley-Hamilton theorem to determine the field configuration at multiple times simultaneously. This analytical solution serves as a benchmark for numerical tests, which show that the Langevin method produces results in excellent agreement with the exact solution. To our knowledge, these findings represent the first numerical calculations of driven harmonic oscillators based on the principle of least action. This study investigates data augmentation techniques for code-switched (CS) Arabic-English text, focusing on improving the performance of lexical substitution (LS) models. We introduce a data-driven approach that utilizes CS data to generate new training examples, thereby enhancing LS models without necessitating changes to existing architectures. Our methodology involves training a sequence-to-sequence model with attention mechanisms to produce substitutions for specific words within a target vocabulary. We evaluate this approach across various training scenarios, particularly when training data is scarce. Results demonstrate that leveraging CS data to create substituted training examples yields promising outcomes, with performance gains of up to 10 F1 points compared to models trained on original data alone. Furthermore, our findings indicate that the model effectively generates diverse lexical substitutions even for terms absent from the training corpus. Finally, we incorporate this model into a Arabic-to-Arabic text generation framework, where it acts as a post-processing step to substitute words with alternatives and restore attention to the generated text. Experimental evidence confirms that this integration significantly boosts performance, achieving up to a 16-point increase in CIDEr scores. Additionally, we provide a code-switched data augmentation framework designed to generate substitutions for out-of-vocabulary words. We demonstrate that a collection of uniform surface homeomorphisms exhibiting a uniform upper bound on their quas-isometry constants is Roelcke precompact within the homeomorphism group equipped with the uniform topology. Furthermore, we establish that, with the exception of the isometry group, the elements of such collections are Roelcke precompact in their respective homogeneous spaces. Additionally, we identify which subgroups of the homeomorphism group possess an invariant metric featuring a finite Roelcke dimension. Finally, we present examples illustrating that the Roelcke precompactness property does not invariably persist under continuous homomorphisms. To support these findings, we develop novel technical instruments with broader applicability. Specifically, we derive a characterization of the Roelcke dimension for actions on metric spaces based on the compactness of diagonal actions on the completion of the homeomorphism group under the topology of uniform convergence on compacta. We also provide a characterization of uniformly quasiconformal surface homeomorphisms as those admitting finitely representable germs under this same topology. To achieve this, we construct a novel link between the topology of uniform convergence and that of uniform convergence on compacta. Leveraging this connection, we offer an alternative approach to determining the Roelcke dimension of isometry groups for invariant metrics on surfaces. To facilitate these results, we develop an intrinsic metric on the space of surface homeomorphisms and derive a characterization of isometries for this metric. To ensure reproducibility, an implementation is available at: https://github.com/SebastianKoch/Quasisphere. Finally, we outline an effective algorithm for calculating the Roelcke precompactness of a uniform family of surface homeomorphisms with a fixed quas-isometry constant. This algorithm was applied to compute the Roelcke precompactness and, consequently, the Roelcke dimension for several significant groups acting on surfaces, including groups of finite covolume. The computational implementation can be found at: https://github.com/SebastianKoch/Quasisphere. The algorithm's output includes a basis for the space of invariant measures on the symmetric product of the manifold, which provides an alternative method for determining the Roelcke dimension. The inverse of this algorithm is also proposed, which computes the minimal dimension of such a space given the space itself. This algorithm has been utilized to determine the Roelcke dimension for specific groups with finite covolume. Relation extraction (RE) seeks to identify semantic connections between entities within a given text. Although recent advances have significantly boosted RE performance, the field still encounters two persistent challenges: (1) a substantial knowledge gap, where many entity pairs correspond to well-known relations found in knowledge graphs (KGs), yet RE models often fail to utilize this information effectively; and (2) a limited data volume, as RE datasets typically feature a scarcity of examples for certain relation types. To address these issues, we introduce a novel framework that integrates RE with knowledge graph link prediction. This framework employs a two-stage strategy: first, it performs self-supervised link prediction to enhance the model's capability in identifying common relations; second, it leverages the acquired knowledge graph information to improve performance on rare relation RE tasks. Experimental results on the WebReasoning and WebReasoning+ datasets demonstrate that our model surpasses current state-of-the-art RE methods. Furthermore, additional analysis and the release of the new dataset highlight the framework's effectiveness and potential. The code and data are accessible at https://github.com/ChenYan1996/KG-LP-RE. In summary, our findings indicate that combining RE with knowledge graph link prediction yields substantial improvements in relation extraction.

The animacy category, which groups objects based on whether they are animate or inanimate, is thought to reflect a fundamental principle in how the human brain structures visual knowledge. This study investigates the role of representational similarity analysis (RSA) in organizing the human ventral temporal cortex (VTC). We demonstrate that the animacy category is not a universal organizational principle in VTC; rather, its presence varies across subregions and correlates with an individual's behavioral animacy categorization performance. Furthermore, we introduce a unified framework for visual categorization in VTC, driven by the distinct functional roles of the posterior fusiform cortex (supporting detailed object recognition) and the anterior fusiform cortex (facilitating coarse-grained categorization). Our findings indicate that the Coarse-grained Category Representation (CCR) is a more robust functional principle than previously proposed categories, including animacy. Finally, we examined the relationship between functional principles and their anatomical substrates, revealing that the CCR is positively correlated with the extent of the fusiform cortex. Overall, this research advances our understanding of how the VTC is functionally organized and underscores the significance of the fusiform cortex in visual categorization. By integrating representational similarity analysis with region-specific neuroimaging data, we offer a framework for investigating the neural substrates of cortical functional specialization. This approach may facilitate a deeper understanding of the neural mechanisms underlying visual categorization and the development of principled methods for parcellating the cortex. Furthermore, it may aid in identifying biomarkers for cognitive disorders characterized by deficits in visual categorization. Finally, the study's open-access code and data will support future research into the neural substrates of visual categorization. This study introduces a new method for training reactive agents within multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) contexts, specifically under non-stationary conditions where the behavior of the opponent remains unknown. The primary challenge lies in reliably inferring the response to the partner's actions to achieve a shared task goal. To address this, we propose a novel intrinsic incentive of "transfer empowerment" designed to enhance the reliability of learning an implicit policy from the partner's actions. This approach enables the agent to re-act effectively to its partner's inputs, facilitating cooperative task completion. We demonstrate that the proposed algorithm, SEICT, performs robustly across various MARL scenarios, including continuous control environments and communication training. Furthermore, we establish a theoretical link between transfer empowerment and intrinsic motivation, showing that this new incentive function is a specialized form of intrinsic incentive learning. Experimental results confirm that SEICT significantly surpasses other MARL methods in achieving task objectives, even when the partner's behavior is unknown. Identifying materials from visual data is a critical challenge in robotics, particularly for tasks like construction where recognizing objects is essential. While current approaches typically rely on large datasets of examples for each material, the logistically demanding process of gathering hundreds of instances for numerous materials (such as wood, metal, and plastic) hinders practical application. This paper introduces a machine learning framework capable of identifying any material with high accuracy using only a single image per material. Our method employs a contrastive learning model trained on a comprehensive collection of internet-sourced material images, where we synthesize material appearances across diverse lighting and background conditions using a physics-based renderer. We evaluate the framework's performance in both controlled and uncontrolled environments by presenting images from various materials under novel lighting conditions, as well as by testing its ability to distinguish materials from complex, real-world objects within an uncontrolled object dataset. The results demonstrate that our approach successfully identifies wood, metal, and plastic with 100% accuracy in controlled settings and 80% accuracy in uncontrolled settings. Furthermore, the framework achieves 90% accuracy in identifying a wide variety of materials within the complex, real-world COCO dataset. These findings indicate that our framework can effectively identify materials from images captured in realistic, uncontrolled settings. We introduce a new end-to-end model for keypoint-based visual feature matching, designed to create robust 2D-2D correspondences even in textureless regions. Our approach relies on two primary components: LoFNet for local feature descriptor extraction and the LoFTransformer for processing 1D descriptors as 1D patches within a Transformer framework. This study examines the bias inherent in the Inferred Diffraction Method (IDM), a widely used algorithm for deriving vector magnetic fields from solar images captured by the Helioseismic Magnetic Imager (HMI) on the Solar Dynamics Observatory. The analysis focuses on two critical factors: the selection of the diffraction angle ($\theta$) and the precision of the line-fitting technique employed. Results indicate that bias is most pronounced in regions with low field strength, where fields are systematically overestimated. Furthermore, a line-fitting approach utilizing a robust outlier-resistant method produces magnetic field maps with reduced bias compared to standard least-squares fitting. These findings suggest that implementing a line-fitting method resistant to outliers can effectively mitigate bias in the HMI's inferred vector magnetic field data. This conclusion is supported by a direct comparison between $\theta$-maps generated using the proposed robust line-fitting method and HMI's native least-squares method, as well as an independent validation using data from the Ground-based Vacuum Ultraviolet Spectroheliograph (VSS) on the Dunn Solar Telescope (DST). Additionally, a new version of the IDM incorporating this robust line-fitting method is introduced, and a web-based version is accessible at http://www.astro.ucla.edu/~mhahn/idm/. A comprehensive description of the new IDM algorithm, including its implementation, is provided in a separate publication. This study introduces a novel demand-side management framework where consumers independently allocate and redistribute energy usage over time. To incentivize efficient scheduling, the system implements load-based instantaneous billing. To assess the effectiveness of this pricing mechanism, consumers are modeled as rational players within an aggregative game. Furthermore, the demand-side framework incorporates a smart grid supply model that accounts for renewable energy sources and supply-demand uncertainty. Finally, the performance of this framework is evaluated and compared against traditional time-of-use billing strategies. Numerical simulations demonstrate that instantaneous load billing significantly enhances the economic efficiency of both the smart grid supply-side model and the consumer aggregative game. Additionally, the proposed billing scheme improves the economic efficiency of consumers by approximately 10% compared to time-of-use policies. The results also indicate that the performance of non-renewable and renewable-based smart grid models is nearly identical. These findings suggest that consumers can achieve notable economic benefits by utilizing their local knowledge of interactions and sharing information with one another. This framework is particularly well-suited for microgrids and small-scale smart grids, where communication infrastructure is more feasible to deploy. Finally, we applied this classifier to the catalogue to identify metal-poor candidates. **Results.** Our method successfully identifies stars with [Fe/H] < -1.5, achieving a 90% detection rate and a false positive rate of 10%. The resulting sample includes 1,000 stars, with 90% confirmed as metal-poor. This approach offers a valuable tool for the community to study the properties of these ancient stars. To enhance the accuracy of computational models assessing second language (L2) complexity, it is essential to identify the underlying linguistic features these models implicitly capture. This study investigates the reliability of various corpus-based metrics for measuring morphological complexity in L2 learners. By employing a multi-method analysis that includes correlation, factor analysis, and clustering, the research evaluates the convergence of ten different morphological complexity measures. The findings reveal that syntactic complexity dominates the interpretation of most measures, while the morphological aspect is significantly represented only by the recency of first acquisition (ROF) and the degree of inflection (DoI). These results are corroborated by a discussion of the inherent properties of the measures and the analysis of specific data. Consequently, this analysis offers a novel perspective on how different measures of morphological complexity are evaluated and interpreted. Furthermore, this insight enhances our understanding of the relationship between morphological complexity and second language proficiency. Finally, the study proposes ROF and DoI as the most reliable measures of L2 morphological complexity, a conclusion that has significant implications for the design of future computational complexity measures. We introduce a method for generating low-dimensional, partially-observable hidden Markov models that are behaviorally equivalent to larger, fully-observable source models under a joint observation map. This approach enables the analysis of source model behaviors that are invisible to direct observation by inferring the underlying hidden states from composite observations. Our method is exact, leveraging observations across multiple time steps to ensure equivalence, and relies on a novel graph-based framework for identifying redundant states. We demonstrate the application of this technique in various domains, including the creation of compact HMMs from time-series data, the development of robust sensors with reduced state spaces, and the construction of robust models from noisy datasets. Furthermore, we provide empirical validation of our method's efficacy in learning HMMs from both noisy and noise-free data, as well as in creating robust HMMs from noisy training sets. Our results indicate that the proposed method can reduce model size by up to two orders of magnitude compared to existing state-of-the-art approximation techniques. The m-ar-K-Fast algorithm is an efficient, component-wise alternative to the widely used m-ar-KM algorithm. Both methods operate within the manifold framework, where data resides on a data-driven manifold embedded within a high-dimensional Euclidean space. The m-ar-KM algorithm partitions this space into multiple regions, assigning data points to the most appropriate region based on their proximity. Conversely, the m-ar-K-Fast algorithm allocates each point to a region determined by calculating the distance to specific feature vectors. This paper introduces the m-ar-K-Fast Component Analysis (m-ar-KFCA) algorithm, which is computationally efficient regarding training time and scales well with the number of regions. Experimental results demonstrate that m-ar-KFCA achieves accuracy comparable to m-ar-KM while offering a significant reduction in training time. Furthermore, m-ar-KFCA outperforms the self-organizing map (SOM) in most tested scenarios. The method's superiority over m-ar-KM in terms of training speed and scalability with respect to the number of regions is evident, making m-ar-KFCA a highly attractive algorithm for large-scale data classification and clustering tasks. Additionally, the method is adaptable to various kernel functions, enabling its application in nonlinear classification and clustering. The source code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/ahmedgaber/m-ar-KFCA. In the current display advertising market, publishers typically receive display bids from multiple ad platforms, including both real-time bidding (RTB) and direct selling channels. To prevent overspending, publishers set a budget limit for these ad sales channels. However, the risk associated with returning impressions varies across RTB and direct selling channels, yet current publisher bid strategies fail to account for this return risk when setting bids. To address this gap, we introduce a new adaptive risk-aware bidding strategy for publishers that incorporates return risk for return traffic, specifically targeting direct selling channels. We first establish a bidding model for direct selling channels that explicitly considers budget constraints and return risk. Subsequently, we propose a straightforward yet effective adaptive risk-aware bidding strategy for publishers to utilize when dealing with direct selling channels. We provide a theoretical analysis of our proposed strategy, demonstrating that it achieves asymptotic optimality for both total revenue and the expected number of satisfied impressions under specific conditions. Furthermore, we conduct empirical evaluations using real-world data, which validate the practical efficacy of our approach. Our numerical results indicate that our adaptive risk-aware bidding strategy for direct selling channels can increase a publisher's overall revenue by up to 10.5% while maintaining the desired level of return traffic. Additionally, numerical analysis reveals that our proposed strategy is highly adaptable to the differing return risks associated with return traffic in direct selling channels. Extensive experiments further show that our bidding model for direct selling channels outperforms existing bid adjustment methods that do not consider return risk. Finally, we demonstrate the applicability of our bidding model for direct selling channels to other relevant bidding scenarios. To our knowledge, this represents the first attempt to address return risk for return traffic in display advertising. Wigner negativity plays a crucial role in revealing the non-classical characteristics of quantum systems when analyzed through the lens of quantum phase-space methods. This study explores if quantum guidance waves, the Bohmian analogue of quantum mechanics, can be similarly examined via phase-space techniques, and if so, whether they exhibit analogous non-classical features. We demonstrate that quantum states serving as quantum guidance states are always Wigner-positive, yet the broader class of quantum states utilized in quantum guidance research frequently includes Wigner-negative states. Consequently, within the quantum guidance framework, Wigner negativity appears unconnected to the engagement of quantum guidance. Furthermore, we show that in quantum continuity equations where the probability density is interpreted as a measure of wave function resourcefulness, the probability density is inherently Wigner-positive, and Wigner negativity is excluded. Finally, examining the Moyal star product, we find that it is not the specific formulation of the quantum potential but rather non-commutativity that generates non-classical behaviors, including the Schrödinger cat effect and contextuality. These findings suggest that Wigner negativity is not essential to the study of quantum guidance or resourcefulness. Additionally, our results offer a pathway to resolve the longstanding debate regarding the relationship between quantum guidance and contextuality. Specifically, we demonstrate that non-contextual hidden variable models can account for the statistics of any set of von Neumann joint measurements, provided the system starts in a quantum guidance state. This implies that the quantum state itself triggers contextuality, rather than the hidden variables. Consequently, the quantum state's non-classicality is fully captured by the features of quantum hidden variable models, including non-locality. Notably, the findings of this paper are specific to quantum hidden variable models and do not extend to other interpretations of quantum mechanics. This paper introduces an enhanced delay parameter for this process, which can be significantly smaller than $T_s$ without compromising detection performance. The proposed method's feasibility is validated through simulations across various CPM schemes, including $\pi/4$-QPSK, $4\pi/M$-QPSK, and $\pi/4$-CPM with $M=8, 16, 32$. These results successfully demonstrate the practical applicability of the theory, confirming that $T_s$ is not the absolute lower limit for the delay parameter. Furthermore, the study illustrates the development of a delay parameter profile relative to the order $M$ for all specified CPM schemes. This profile indicates the potential for further delay reduction in higher-order CPMs and provides a general guideline for selecting the delay parameter in any given CPM scheme. Additionally, the paper presents a complete set of profiles for the computational complexity of the proposed detector, covering both the training and tracking phases of the phase profile estimator. Finally, a comprehensive profile of the overall detector complexity is provided, covering the entire detection process. The paper concludes that $T_s$ is not the minimum possible delay; rather, a smaller delay is achievable, as evidenced by the complexity profile. Reward learning (RL) is a prominent method for automatically acquiring rewards from demonstrations, yet it faces two primary hurdles: data inefficiency and suboptimality. The former stems from the extensive number of states and actions requiring labeling, while the latter arises because human experts often provide only a few demonstrations. To address these issues, we introduce VACER, a visually-inspired cluster-ranking approach that significantly reduces training time. Our method leverages the observation that humans naturally group similar states into clusters, allowing the reward function to be learned from representative samples of each cluster rather than every individual state. VACER employs a lightweight vision model to create these clusters and learns the reward function using a novel state-action embedding technique. We validate this approach across three diverse domains: a 2D grid world, a 3D 3DKey world, and a 3D 3DManipulation task. Our results demonstrate that the proposed method achieves state-of-the-art data efficiency and marks the first successful reward learning application on a 3D manipulation task. Furthermore, we release an open-source library to facilitate future research in this area. The source code can be accessed at https://github.com/leeyang1994/VACER. This study examines the topological characteristics of highly symmetric, frustrated Toric code models, which serve as ideal frameworks for investigating monopole dynamics in lattice gauge theories. The exceptional symmetry of the classical frustrated Toric code enables the derivation of the exact classical topological phase boundary. Furthermore, the quantum models exhibit a classical-like topological phase boundary marked by a classical-like entanglement phase transition, where the boundary is defined by a vanishing cosine cosine-Potts model partition function. These findings underscore the continued significance of the toric code as a model for exploring fundamental topological phenomena. A consistent and intuitive framework for these results emerges from the interplay between the toric code and Potts models, where the geometric line arises from the self-duality of the Potts model. This line represents the meeting point of the disordered phase of the Potts model and its associated critical phase, a phenomenon that persists in more complex models. Consequently, the Potts model provides a robust conceptual basis for analyzing the toric code's topological features, including its geometric line, within the context of frustrated systems. Additionally, we introduce a novel symmetry operator for the toric code that commutes with all stabilizers and flips the geometric line, a feature that may hold significance for understanding the toric code's topological structure. Finally, we discuss the relationship between the toric code and the toric code with a magnetic field, noting that the former can be derived from the latter in the limit of vanishing magnetic field. This connection offers a unified perspective on the topological phase boundaries of both models. Finally, we conclude by discussing the implications of these findings for the toric code's topological quantum computing applications. Overall, our results highlight the toric code's enduring value as a model for investigating basic phenomena such as topological phase boundaries and offer a unified approach to understanding the topological phase boundaries of the toric code and the toric code with a magnetic field. The geometric line, a unique feature of the frustrated toric code, provides a rich framework for exploring the topological properties of these systems, with the Potts model playing a crucial role in this understanding. The novel symmetry operator, which flips the geometric line, may hold significance for the toric code's topological quantum computing applications. In the conclusion, we discuss the implications of these findings for the toric code's topological quantum computing potential and the broader field of topological quantum information processing. This approach first clusters diverse utterances from large-scale collections into a finite set of discrete cluster labels, effectively serving as discrete hidden states. Consequently, these U-disstates capture various utterance meanings and function as a robust vocabulary for subsequent dialogue processing. Algorithmic interpretability is a critical factor in the widespread adoption of AI, yet it remains challenging to quantify. This paper introduces a cognitive learning-based model for interpretability, defining the Algorithmic Cognitive Complexity (ACC) score as the measure of score-based interpretability. The study demonstrates that the accuracy of any score-based interpretability method serves as a lower bound for this proposed model. Additionally, the influence of various parameters on ACC is analyzed, and a method for computing the score is suggested. The paper concludes by outlining future research directions. Keywords: Algorithmic interpretability, Score-based interpretability, Human learning, Algorithmic cognitive complexity.

Anomaly detection remains a critical challenge in numerous real-world applications, particularly when anomalies are rare and data is scarce. Unsupervised methods offer a promising solution in these contexts, yet most existing approaches are optimized for abundant data and remain ineffective when volumes decrease. This paper introduces TiWS-iForest, an adaptation of the Isolation Forest (iForest) algorithm designed for scenarios characterized by limited data, small datasets, and constrained computational resources. TiWS-iForest enhances iForest by implementing a five-step process: data augmentation, oversampling, data augmentation removal, oversampling removal, and retraining. The primary objective is to maximize anomaly detection accuracy across the broadest possible range of anomaly ratios. Experimental results demonstrate that TiWS-iForest achieves a substantial performance gain, reaching up to a 14% increase in the F1 score compared to the baseline iForest algorithm. The source code for TiWS-iForest is accessible at https://github.com/leopoldoalmeida/TiWS-iForest. The findings presented here were initially reported in our conference paper TiWS-iForest: Anomaly Detection with Limited Data, Small Datasets and Small Computers (TiWS'21) [1]. Subsequently, we have refined and expanded upon these results, incorporating additional experiments and further improvements. We believe these enhancements strengthen the significance of our findings. Our code is available at https://github.com/leopoldoalmeida/TiWS-iForest. TiWS'21. Anomaly detection. Limited data. This framework comprises an exponential rate function governing the arrival rate of exceedances above a specific threshold and a single parameter defining the tail behavior of the excess distribution. We demonstrate that this two-parameter reparameterization facilitates the construction of exact confidence regions for threshold selection and enhances the stability of Maximum Likelihood Estimation.
