**Context.** The existence of a metallicity spread within a single stellar population has been suggested by the presence of multiple stellar sequences in the light element abundance ratio (LEAR) diagram. However, these findings remain controversial due to significant uncertainties in stellar models and the necessity for precise abundance measurements.

**Aims.** This study aims to determine the abundances of light elements (C, N, O) for the most luminous first-generation stars in the globular cluster NGC 2808.

**Methods.** We conducted a multi-epoch spectroscopic analysis of three bright first-generation stars (V1, V2, and V3) using the UVES spectrograph on the VLT. We employed the MOSSS code to derive abundance data.

**Results.** Our analysis yielded high-precision abundance measurements for these stars. We identified a clear spread in nitrogen abundances among the three targets, with a minimum dispersion of 0.15 dex. This finding contradicts stellar evolution models that predict no such spread for single-population globular clusters.

**Conclusions.** The presence of a metallicity spread in NGC 2808, despite its classification as a single-population cluster, suggests that this phenomenon may be common among globular clusters. This supports the theory that multiple stellar populations formed within the cluster. Additionally, we observed a carbon abundance spread of 0.1 dex between V1 and V2, which aligns with theoretical predictions. Our results confirm the existence of this spread, which was previously indicated by LEAR analysis. The high precision of our abundance measurements enables the investigation of stellar mixing processes. We conclude that the observed spread in nitrogen and carbon abundances is best explained by dredge-up processes occurring during the helium flash.

**Keywords.** globular clusters: individual (NGC 2808) — abundances — stars: fundamental parameters — stars: luminosity function, mass function — stars: individual (V1, V2, V3) — supernovae: nucleosynthesis.

The investigation of single-file particle systems remains a fundamental aspect of statistical physics. In single-file diffusion, particles cannot pass one another, resulting in complex dynamics. This study examines single-file diffusion within a half-line system, where an exit window is positioned at the origin. We analyze the probability distribution and cumulative distribution of the duration required for the first exit, specifically focusing on one-particle and N-particle scenarios under both open and closed boundary conditions. Furthermore, we examine the impact of entropic repulsion on first exit times. Our findings demonstrate that the derived results align with the Central Limit Theorem. Additionally, we explore the connection between first exit time statistics and entropic forces. These findings hold significant potential for applications in both fundamental physics and biophysics. All theoretical derivations are implemented in Python and made available on GitHub. Our research findings can be accessed at https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.07009. Measurement in quantum mechanics raises the issue of how successive measurements of any observable update the state of a quantum system. We demonstrate that applying quantum Bayes' rule—which defines the updated state as the one maximizing the overlap with the state resulting from a hypothetical measurement that yielded a specific outcome—ensures consistency in state updates during sequential measurements of any observable. Furthermore, we show that this application of quantum Bayes' rule confirms the equivalence between two distinct approaches to handling sequential measurements of a given observable. The equivalence of these approaches also extends to scenarios involving sequential measurements of observables that do not pertain to the same physical quantity. Additionally, we illustrate the link between quantum Bayes' rule and the concept of least-squares estimation. Finally, we discuss the implications of these findings for understanding quantum state updates in sequential measurements, particularly regarding their relationship with the general framework of Bayesian state updates. These insights may aid in interpreting recent proposals regarding modifications to the standard quantum measurement theory. To support these conclusions, we have expanded our earlier work by including additional proofs and an appendix that details the specific assumptions underlying quantum Bayes' rule. We believe that explicitly stating these assumptions is essential for a rigorous formulation of any theory extending beyond the standard framework of quantum mechanics. In this regard, our methodology may offer a useful tool for developing future modifications to the standard measurement theory. Specifically, our approach has already been applied in recent studies proposing a generalization of quantum mechanics that incorporates a finite time resolution for measurements. In this context, our method facilitated the derivation of quantum Bayes' rule as an assumption regarding how sequential measurements update a generalized quantum state. This result is consistent with findings from an independent investigation into the same generalized measurement theory. We anticipate that our approach will prove useful in advancing further research on this subject. To facilitate these efforts, we have also expanded our earlier work by including additional examples of sequential measurements within this generalized framework. These examples illustrate the application of quantum Bayes' rule in scenarios involving sequential measurements of observables that do not correspond to the same physical quantity. Such illustrations may assist in enhancing the understanding of quantum state updates in these measurements. To support these conclusions, we have significantly expanded our earlier work by incorporating further examples of sequential measurements within this generalized framework. These examples serve to demonstrate the application of quantum Bayes' rule when handling sequential measurements using a generalized quantum state. We believe that including such examples will contribute to a deeper comprehension of quantum state updates in these measurements. To support these conclusions, we have significantly expanded our earlier work by including additional examples involving sequential measurements

This study reports initial findings regarding the Equation of State (EOS) of hot and dense QCD matter across a wide spectrum of temperatures and chemical potentials, specifically focusing on small volumes. Utilizing the framework of Finite Size Scaling, we systematically analyze finite-size corrections to bulk thermodynamic quantities, enabling the precise determination of these same quantities in the infinite-volume limit. Our approach is grounded in the Polyakov-loop Extended Wilson action, which incorporates non-local four-quark interactions. By employing the Bayesian method of Multi-Precision Analysis, we rigorously quantify uncertainties associated with both the parameters of the non-perturbatively determined QCD coupling and the continuum extrapolation of the lattice action. Furthermore, we demonstrate that Bayesian error estimation is essential for achieving a quantitative understanding of small-system QCD matter. To the best of our knowledge, this represents the first comprehensive EOS analysis for small, hot, and dense QCD matter. Our results indicate that the EOS of small systems exhibits a pronounced crossover transition, with significant finite-size corrections to the critical behavior of bulk QCD matter persisting up to radii of $R \sim 1.5$ fm. Additionally, we observe that the EOS of small systems displays a strong dependence on volume, a feature that becomes particularly evident in the presence of finite baryon chemical potentials. These findings suggest that the EOS of small systems cannot be accurately described by the bulk EOS, even when enhanced by the Hadron Resonance Gas (HRG) model. Finally, we discuss the implications of these results for future experimental investigations. In conclusion, this work establishes a foundation for future studies aimed at extracting the thermodynamic properties of small systems, thereby advancing our understanding of QCD matter under extreme conditions. This research was conducted within the framework of the Extreme QCD initiative. Specifically, the EOS of small systems was computed using the Polyakov-loop Extended Wilson action, a low-temperature effective theory of QCD, which is expected to provide a qualitatively similar result for the QCD EOS at high temperatures. This conclusion is supported by the fact that the coupling constant in the low-temperature Wilson action converges to that of the high-temperature QCD during the QCD phase transition. This paper addresses the graph symmetric problem within a network framework, focusing on distributed measurement allocation and signal estimation for networked systems that exhibit graph symmetry. These systems are characterized by cyclic time-varying dynamics, time-varying input and observation matrices, and fixed graph symmetric system matrices. The study demonstrates that for graph symmetric networks, the distributed optimal measurement allocation problem can be reformulated as a convex optimization problem. This allows each node to independently distribute its local measurements to other nodes in a distributed manner. Subsequently, a distributed algorithm utilizing distributed Kalman filtering and graph filters is developed to achieve optimal distributed measurement allocation and distributed state estimation simultaneously. The performance of the resulting distributed estimator is evaluated using a numerical example. Additionally, it is shown that the proposed algorithm serves as a special case of the recent graph symmetric optimal state estimation method presented by the authors. Finally, numerical simulations are conducted to demonstrate the application of the method in a distributed sensor target tracking scenario. In this context, node states exhibit graph symmetric cyclic time-varying dynamics, and sensor observation matrices are cyclic time-varying. The results indicate that the proposed algorithm outperforms existing distributed optimal state estimation methods in terms of estimation accuracy. Furthermore, a comparison with a centralized optimal measurement allocation method reveals that the distributed approach yields performance comparable to the centralized solution. Finally, a simulation involving a distributed network attack scenario is performed to illustrate the anti-jamming capabilities of the proposed method. In this scenario, jamming noise is added to sensor observations, and nodes execute a distributed measurement allocation attack to mitigate the impact of the noise. The outcomes confirm that the distributed attack effectively eliminates the impact of observation noise on the overall network estimation performance. Notably, the computational complexity of the proposed distributed algorithm remains low, as it only requires distributed Kalman filtering and graph filter computations. This represents a significant advantage over existing distributed optimal state estimation methods, which typically involve high computational complexity. Finally, the paper concludes by discussing the limitations of the current work and suggesting directions for future research. Specifically, it is suggested that future efforts could expand the scope of graph symmetry to include general linear time-invariant systems and linear time-varying systems, thereby broadening the applicability of the proposed method. Additionally, extending the approach to solve the general distributed optimal state estimation problem for graph symmetric networks is recommended. This would involve addressing the more complex distributed measurement allocation challenge in graph symmetric networks, which is expected to yield superior performance compared to current solutions. Finally, it is proposed to further investigate the computational complexity of the proposed algorithm

The keyless communication framework eliminates dependency on a shared secret key by utilizing public information to derive a shared random string capable of distinguishing messages. Originally developed for the binary erasure channel, this paradigm has seen significant advancement through the application of sketch and fingerprinting techniques. This paper investigates the keyless verification scheme for power-limited additive white Gaussian channel (AWGNC) encoding, comparing the achievable random string rate against a scheme based on sketching. Our findings indicate that for the specific parameters examined, the achievable rates are essentially identical. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the keyless AWGNC encoding process can be realized through a combination of convolutional coding and fingerprinting. Finally, we present an alternative construction of keyless encoding for the binary erasure channel that yields a slightly superior random string rate in certain scenarios. This new construction relies on channel output samples drawn from the Gaussian channel rather than the erasure channel. These results suggest that the performance of keyless encoding on the AWGNC is likely determined by the achievable performance on the Gaussian channel itself. Additionally, we propose that the fundamental information-theoretic properties of keyless encoding on the AWGNC remain unexplored. Ultimately, we illustrate that keyless encoding on the AWGNC can be constructed from the binary erasure channel by sampling its outputs from a Gaussian distribution. This supports the hypothesis that keyless encoding on the AWGNC is a distinct information-theoretic problem from that on the BEC. Collectively, these insights indicate that future research into keyless encoding on the AWGNC should address these specific open questions. Specifically, we recommend that subsequent investigations utilize the BEC as a foundational building block for constructing keyless encoders on the AWGNC. Furthermore, we suggest that the BEC's outputs be sampled from a Gaussian channel to enable keyless encoding on the AWGNC. Finally, we propose that the BEC's achievable random string rate and achievable randomness extraction rate serve as appropriate metrics for evaluating the performance of keyless encoders on the AWGNC. These findings aim to provide a comprehensive set of guidelines for future research in this emerging field. This study re-examines the motion of charged particles within washboard potentials, such as those experienced in Josephson junction circuits. It is demonstrated that charge dispersion leads to effective "braking," resulting in a uniform, or "drift," motion that resembles a non-dispersive regime. These findings are applicable to the study of charge and flux states in Josephson junction arrays. The discussion begins with an analysis of a single charged particle in an external electric field. By approximating the potential as a series of square wells, the system's band structure is derived. Within this framework, the single-particle Schrödinger equation is solved using WKB wave functions. This study presents a flexible local projection method for assessing the impulse response functions of structural shocks. Within this framework, variables are expressed as functions of lagged variables, shocks, and additional controls. The core advantage of this approach is its ability to eliminate the need for restrictive assumptions regarding the rank of the contemporaneous impact matrix or the dynamic multiplicative structure of impulse responses. Instead, the impulse reaction is directly estimated from the local projections. We demonstrate that the resulting estimator is consistent and asymptotically normal, and empirical analysis indicates its superiority over benchmark estimators. Furthermore, we offer new insights into the dynamics of U.S. real economies following shocks. This methodology is implemented in the \texttt{projflex} R package. Our \texttt{projflex} package serves as a functional equivalent to Jord\'a (2005)'s \texttt{seats} package (Jord\'a, 2007), which is available for MATLAB. Both approaches utilize local projections; however, while \texttt{seats} imposes a strict multiplicative structure on impulse responses, \texttt{projflex} offers a more flexible specification. Additionally, \texttt{projflex} provides an improved structural identification procedure that incorporates sign restrictions, time-varying impact matrices, and dynamic non-linearities. While \texttt{seats} relies on the `id` package for identification (Banerjee et al., 2013), \texttt{projflex} integrates its own identification \texttt{ident} package. This allows users to define time-varying impact matrices and perform sign-based identification without requiring a separate \texttt{ident} package installation. Consequently, \texttt{projflex} enables users to employ \texttt{seats} for identification while utilizing the \texttt{projflex} dynamic structure. Finally, users can easily customize the \texttt{projflex} code to adapt it to their specific requirements. We calculate the angular Casimir torque acting on a point electric charge within Landau levels. This effect emerges from the Landau diamagnetism of the vacuum and represents one of two distinct casimir-like phenomena in the Landau problem; the second is the longitudinal casimir force derived in a prior publication. Both effects stem from the finite density of states in the Landau spectrum, which contrasts with the continuous state density found in free space. Consequently, the zero-point energy and casimir forces in the Landau problem differ fundamentally from those in free space. Furthermore, these effects rely on the specific choice of Landau gauge. While the radial casimir force was previously determined, we demonstrate that the angular force is of comparable magnitude. This finding underscores the critical role of vacuum polarization in generating magnetic force fields. Additionally, we explore the potential for detecting these forces through the rotation of a charged particle using an ultrafast laser pulse. Finally, we address the issue of force balance in the presence of a third object, such as an electric dipole. This scenario introduces novel physics, as the interaction between the third object and the Landau charge is non-trivial, unlike the case involving two dipole objects in free space. We show that a static solution to the Landau problem for two dipoles is impossible, and that any time-dependent solution would involve complex dynamics. This outcome is consistent with the broader principle that all casimir forces require the system to evolve over time. The necessity of system evolution in the quantum case is more profound than in the classical case, where it arises merely from the requirement of a stress tensor traceless condition. In contrast, in the Landau problem, this condition necessitates system evolution even for the stationary states of a single charge. This further illustrates how magnetic fields fundamentally alter the vacuum. Ultimately, our findings suggest that the complete solution to the Landau problem remains an open question in quantum field theory. We conclude by discussing the implications of these results for future research. Specifically, we propose that the solution to the Landau problem is contingent upon the specific model of vacuum polarization employed. This conclusion is supported by the fact that various models of vacuum polarization yield different results. Therefore, we suggest that the most viable approach is to utilize the model of vacuum polarization that is consistent with the photon propagator in the Lorentz gauge. Using this model, we calculate the time-dependent dynamics of two dipole objects, demonstrating that the forces between them are non-trivial and that the system evolves over time. Fine-grained named entity recognition (FNE) involves identifying related entity subtypes within the same category, such as presidents, politicians, or leaders. The inherent hierarchical structure of these related subtypes suggests that representing FNE subtypes in a non-Euclidean space capable of modeling hierarchy and relationships would be highly advantageous. This paper introduces FGNET-RH, a novel framework that leverages hyperbolic space to encode FNE subtypes, thereby facilitating learning in an embedded space that captures hierarchical patterns and relational connections. By employing a hierarchical loss function, FGNET-RH enhances the modeling of the inherent structure of FNE, ensuring that similar subtypes are positioned closer together. Additionally, the refinement network within this framework improves the feature extraction capabilities of neural networks. Experimental results demonstrate that FGNET-RH surpasses current state-of-the-art methods, achieving an F1 score of 84.56% on the AGNews dataset and 85.12% on the Datasets dataset. Furthermore, ablation studies confirm the model's effectiveness and validate its proposed mechanisms. The source code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/zhongyuan1996/FGNET-RH. Keywords: fine-grained named entity recognition, hyperbolic space, non-Euclidean space, feature engineering, refinement network.

In cloud computing, the demand for Virtual Machine (VM) provisioning is growing. However, allocating resources to new VM requests can be challenging, as a full load leads to reconfigurations that disrupt running services. To address this, we introduce a novel load distribution method for handling VM reservation requests. This method is designed to minimize the rejection of new VM requests while ensuring that all accepted requests can be fulfilled. We have developed and implemented the approach within the Prepartition framework, which was previously created for VM provisioning. Our experimental results demonstrate that Prepartition reduces rejection rates by 10% to 20% compared to the existing OpenNebim cloud controller. Furthermore, we observe a 2% improvement in resource utilization over the best-performing approach among our test alternatives. Finally, we provide an analytical description of the distribution strategy, explaining the behavior of Prepartition and its interaction with VM requests. This description is supported by experimental data, allowing us to draw conclusions about the method's behavior. We also identify specific scenarios where Prepartition's performance is limited, such as when test VMs have highly disparate resource requirements. In these cases, we suggest that Prepartition could be enhanced by implementing a more intelligent distribution strategy. Additionally, we propose that further research is needed to adapt Prepartition for environments with multiple data centers. Finally, to improve the performance of other tested approaches, we recommend investigating whether their decision-making process can be made more efficient. To achieve this, we suggest that these approaches should be able to predict the arrival of new VM requests and their resource requirements. With such predictions, they could adjust their decisions in advance, potentially improving their performance. However, making these decisions would be more complex, as it would require evaluating the impact of decisions over time rather than just considering immediate effects. Consequently, this would increase the difficulty of their decision-making process. In conclusion, this paper demonstrates that Prepartition is a viable and effective distribution approach for VM reservation requests. It can be utilized to improve the performance of other tested methods and to reduce both the rejection rate and resource wastage in data centers. Ultimately, this leads to more efficient resource utilization. We also acknowledge that Prepartition has certain limitations, which we have detailed in this paper. Addressing these limitations would require further research and development. We hope that this work will inspire researchers to explore Prepartition and contribute to its continued evolution. We introduce a new category of dynamic neural networks termed Fixed Point Networks (FPNs), which are trained to reach a fixed point at the end of their processing. Unlike standard feedforward networks, FPNs maintain a persistent state throughout their computation, causing early-layer predictions to influence later ones via gradient feedback. This proposed class falls within the broader framework of unconstrained optimisation networks (ONNs), a category recently demonstrated to effectively model the dynamics of established algorithms like ADAM and SGD. We illustrate the utility of FPNs by applying them to time-series extrapolation. In this application, we leverage the inherent link between fixed points and equilibria to design FPNs that converge to an equilibrium while adhering to physical constraints. Specifically, for the van der Pol oscillator, we demonstrate that an FPN can be constructed to reach a fixed point representing a physically valid equilibrium. Our results indicate that FPNs surpass the performance of conventional neural networks on both the Lorenz attractor and the van der Pol oscillator tasks. Furthermore, we show that an FPN can be trained to accurately predict the future equilibrium of a time-varying system. Finally, we confirm that FPNs can also learn periodic solutions on both attractors. These findings suggest that FPNs offer a versatile tool for prediction that integrates the inductive biases of both static neural networks and the physical systems they aim to model. Additionally, we explore how FPNs can be utilized to construct neural ordinary differential equations (NODEs) for modeling physical systems. As an illustrative example, we present an FPN NODE that successfully predicts the future dynamics of a simulated rigid body. All code and experiments are accessible at https://github.com/DeepMind/FPN. Our findings underscore the value of FPNs as model-based approaches for prediction, a domain where such methods have historically outperformed model-free techniques. We anticipate that the ability of FPNs to embed physical inductive biases within neural networks will facilitate the development of more interpretable and generalisable models. Furthermore, we posit that further research into FPNs will deepen our understanding of NODEs and enhance our capacity to create effective neural models for physical systems. Finally, we note that FPNs can be integrated into model-based reinforcement learning, where their tendency to converge to fixed points aligns with the objective of learning policies that reach fixed points in the environment. This paper introduces novel upper and lower bounds for causal influence metrics. Since the true joint distribution $P$ is typically unknown, we consider bounds based on the set of all possible joint distributions $\mathcal{P}$ that align with a specified subgraph of a Bayesian network structure. We demonstrate that these bounds can be efficiently computed in polynomial time when $\mathcal{P}$ is linearly Gaussian. Furthermore, by integrating these results with recent advancements in learning causal structures from data, we propose algorithms to estimate the bounds of causal influence metrics directly from $\mathcal{D}$. Finally, we apply our framework to assess the impact of individual features within causal trees. Experimental results indicate that for a complex image dataset, determining whether a feature is a leaf node in the causal tree is often feasible, and we show that the mean causal influence across leaves can be effectively bounded. Additionally, we demonstrate that the tail of the distribution of causal influence values exhibits a power law decay, a pattern consistent with observations in complex systems. In summary, we present a framework for analyzing causal impact distributions that complements existing methods for causal discovery and inference. This approach is particularly valuable for high-dimensional settings where the number of variables is large, yet the number of leaves in causal trees remains relatively small. Our findings suggest that while identifying specific variables as leaves may be challenging, constraints on their causal influence can be derived, thereby providing a more comprehensive understanding of causal structures in high-dimensional data. This paper introduces a novel, attack-aware monitoring framework designed to detect stealthy attacks on the communication links of linear time-invariant systems, utilizing only the available sensor measurements. Specifically, the model accounts for communication attacks that leverage the internal system dynamics to evade traditional monitoring methods like residual analysis. The proposed method employs a bank of predictors, each linked to a single sensor, with every predictor utilizing its associated sensor's measurements to generate predictions for the entire system state. Furthermore, each predictor is intentionally blinded to the directions of the attack vectors targeting its own sensor. The system's attack vulnerability is assessed by identifying all possible attack scenarios capable of remaining undetected by this approach. Finally, the method is applied to a line-following robot case study to demonstrate its effectiveness in maintaining safe operation even during attacks. Additionally, the influence of the number of sensors on the overall system's detectability is examined. Notably, the proposed approach yields new insights into the relationship between sensor placement and system security, an aspect that has not been previously explored in existing literature. Finally, the study characterizes the inherent trade-off between measurement cost and system security, offering guidance on sensor selection for the optimal deployment of the monitoring framework. The methods are validated through numerical simulations. The code is accessible at https://github.com/abhishekkumar2000/Stealthy-Attacks-Detection. Autosummarization aims to generate concise summaries for extensive documents. While most existing approaches rely on deep learning models trained and evaluated primarily on English, there is limited research in multilingual settings. Furthermore, there is a scarcity of resources and models for Indian languages, which are predominantly low-resource. To address these gaps, we introduce GAE-ISumm, an unsupervised indium-specific framework built on the Graph-Based Summarization technique. This approach constructs an attentional graph from document sentences, where nodes represent sentences and edges denote semantic relationships. Summaries are generated by identifying the most critical sentences and arranging them into a coherent narrative. We developed this model for ten Indian languages and released the corresponding resources on GitHub. Our results demonstrate that the proposed model achieves state-of-the-art performance in unsupervised summary generation. Additionally, we observe that sentence content similarity serves as a robust feature for identifying essential sentences, a factor that significantly influences model performance. This paper introduces a new class of S-rings of Cohen type, which includes the S-ring $S_{ab}(p^m, p^{m-k})$ as a specific instance. We provide a comprehensive structural description for this new class of S-rings and utilize it to demonstrate multiple applications, such as establishing a sufficient condition under which a new class of normal $p$-complement groups emerges and generating infinite families of groups possessing the TN$_p$ property. These outcomes extend previous findings regarding normal $p$-complement groups. Additionally, we prove that every irreducible permutation representation of an S-ring of Cohen type is faithful, which further extends results concerning transitive permutation representations of finite groups. Finally, we explore various other significant properties of S-rings of Cohen type. A key result indicates that if $G$ is a finite group where every irreducible $G$-set is faithful, then $G$ qualifies as an $A$-group. Leveraging this finding, we offer a novel characterization of $A$-groups by utilizing the properties of finite groups containing normal $p$-complements. Furthermore, we demonstrate that an $A$-group $G$ possesses a normal $p$-complement if and only if its associated S-rings of Cohen type are cyclotomic. We also examine specific examples of S-rings of Cohen type, including cyclotomic and rank-two S-rings. Notably, we establish that the cyclotomic permutation representations of an $A$-group $G$ are faithful precisely when $G$ has a normal $p$-complement. **Context.** Astronomers are actively searching for dark companions orbiting the accelerating stars 55 Cancri, Groombridge 1618, 70 Virginis, 47 Ursae Majoris, and 61 Virginis.

**Aims.** The primary objective is to constrain the masses and orbital radii of potential unseen companions within a few solar masses.

**Methods.** We conducted a thorough analysis of existing data from the SIMBAD database and performed new searches to refine orbital parameters and determine the nature of dark companions.

**Results.** For 55 Cancri, we identified a dark companion with a mass of approximately 0.1 Jupiter masses orbiting at roughly 0.07 AU. For 70 Virginis, we found a companion with a mass of about 0.005 solar masses and an orbital radius of 1.5 AU. Additionally, we determined that the dark companion of 47 Ursae Majoris has a mass near 0.005 solar masses and an orbital radius of 2.5 AU.

**Conclusions.** Our findings suggest that the dark companions of 70 Virginis and 47 Ursae Majoris are brown dwarfs, while the companion of 55 Cancri is likely a planetary-mass object. Furthermore, the orbital distances of these companions are significantly smaller than those proposed by the radial velocity method. We also determined that the masses and orbital distances of the dark companions of 61 Virginis and Groombridge 1618 remain unconstrained.

The autoencoder serves as a fundamental element in machine learning, functioning by accepting an input, learning to replicate it, and effectively capturing its intrinsic features. The performance of an autoencoder is largely determined by its loss function, which quantifies the discrepancy between the input and its reconstruction. In this study, we introduce a regularized loss function for autoencoders that incorporates both Kullback-Leibler divergence and Gaussian noise. This approach enables the model to encode input data into a probabilistic representation. We evaluated our method using two datasets: MNIST and CMU PIE. Experimental results indicate that the proposed approach outperforms existing methods in terms of feature extraction capabilities. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the model can accurately classify handwritten digits from the MNIST dataset. The widespread adoption of the Internet of Things (IoT) has driven significant interest in developing smart applications, prompting researchers to propose numerous architectures and protocols to enhance security and privacy. However, these approaches often suffer from limited scalability and lack comprehensive security and privacy mechanisms. To address these shortcomings, this paper introduces a secure and private blockchain-based framework for home automation. The proposed solution employs the Radio Frequency Identification (RFID) protocol to identify home appliances and utilizes the Weighted Euclidean Distance (WED) multilateration localization algorithm to determine the distance between an appliance and the RFID reader. Furthermore, the system leverages the permissioned blockchain platform, Hyperledger Fabric, to create secure applications that ensure data integrity and maintain transparency and traceability within the network. This framework offers an additional layer of security and privacy, effectively preventing malicious actors from compromising the system. Experimental results indicate that the average error of the WED multilateration algorithm is less than 1 meter. The study concludes that the proposed framework successfully achieves the objectives of secure communication, privacy, and localization. Future work will explore integrating machine learning to improve the accuracy of home appliance localization. Additionally, the framework's performance will be evaluated under varying network conditions, including different numbers of RFID readers, transmission range, and signal strength. Finally, the design will be extended to support smart city applications. This paper is intended as a foundation for developing future smart home automation systems. To our knowledge, this work represents the first attempt to implement home automation using RFID, blockchain, and WED multilateration for appliance localization. The proposed framework is expected to serve as a reference for researchers in the field of IoT. The code for this work is available at: https://github.com/ahmedmohamed1999/Smart-Home-Gadget-Monitor. This study introduces a deep learning-based framework designed to enable low-latency, energy-efficient quantization of the L-lumped variables associated with transmission lines in planar waveguides. The primary objective is to develop a compact model for the inverse scattering matrix that supports iterative equalization. To achieve this, the paper proposes an iterative equalizer utilizing Gray-coded modulation, which is analyzed to determine the necessary model complexity. Two distinct deep learning-based approaches are introduced to iteratively approximate the inverse scattering matrix. The viability of this methodology is validated through an experimental investigation into the non-linear propagation of light within planar waveguides. The results demonstrate that the lumped-parameter model can be accurately approximated by the deep learning-based inverse scattering matrix, facilitating effective equalization. Furthermore, the study confirms that the proposed deep learning-based lumped-parameter approach outperforms both the traditional lumped-parameter and full-wave methods in terms of signal quality and computational efficiency. Finally, the feasibility of equalization under practical conditions is verified by successfully implementing the scheme on an optical link. Additionally, comparisons with state-of-the-art lumped-parameter methods reveal a significant reduction in computational complexity. These findings suggest that the proposed scheme is well-suited for deployment in future high-capacity, short-reach optical interconnects. Notably, the approach is highly adaptable, allowing for the easy extension to various modulation formats and line codes. The source code for the proposed deep learning-based lumped-parameter model is publicly accessible at \url{https://github.com/DeepLearning4Optics/Deep-Learning-Based-Lumped-Parameter-Model-For-Waveguides}. While several parameterized algorithms exist for this problem—most notably an algorithm with running time $O^*(1.614^n)$ based on the number of degree-2 vertices—we introduce a new linear-degree algorithm running in $O(n + m)$ time, where $n$ and $m$ represent the counts of vertices and edges, respectively. This result relies on a novel $n/2$-degree branching rule that complements the existing degree-2 branching approach. Additionally, we present a linear-time algorithm for generating all upward planar drawings of a specific input graph, effectively resolving an open question posed by Di Battista et al. (SGA 2010). Our algorithm is a direct adaptation of the upward planar checkers developed by Di Battista et al., enhanced with a novel upward planar edge-rotation operation. We conclude by introducing UP-SPIDER, a parameterized problem that enables the demonstration of all proposed algorithms. Specifically, UP-SPIDER features a branching rule yielding a $O^*(1.414^{sp})$ running time, where $sp$ denotes the number of spider vertices, and a fixed-parameter tractable algorithm utilizing the upward treewidth of the graph as a parameter. This study presents a new method for analyzing noisy, crowdsourced datasets, employing ensembles of deep neural networks. We demonstrate that traditional accuracy is insufficient for evaluating models trained on high-variance data and propose a complementary suite of metrics based on entropy. These metrics offer both local and global perspectives on uncertainty within the label distribution for each data point. Our approach was applied to the ImageNet dataset, specifically focusing on the 1,088 images with crowdsourced annotations. We compare our findings against the widely used "human softmax" method. The results indicate that entropy-based evaluation offers both qualitative and quantitative superior insights into the data compared to human softmax. Additionally, we investigate various ensembles of deep neural networks, demonstrating that they enhance the reliability of the labeling process. This research expands upon our prior work by providing a more general framework for uncertainty analysis in noisy, crowdsourced datasets. This work introduces a novel semiflow characterized by a transfer operator that decreases in norm. The study investigates the transfer operator's properties, defining the maximal operator on closed subsets of the space of regular Borel measures. It is demonstrated that the spectral radius of this operator aligns with the topological pressure of the zero function, thereby establishing a non-trivial cohomological equation. These findings hold significant implications for spectral theory, particularly regarding the smoothness of eigenfunctions and the regularity of invariant measures. Additionally, the associated dynamical system offers a framework for examining the regularity of solutions to certain ill-posed problems. A notable application is the development of a fractional Brownian motion model that resolves the singularity issue inherent in the classical Weierstrass model. Finally, the associated operator is linked to specific problems in signal processing.

Constructing covering arrays with strength $t=2$ and few rows is essential for applications like pairwise software testing. This paper examines the size of covering arrays derived from specific linear algebra structures, such as covering designs based on finite fields. We introduce a novel construction method for strength $2$ covering arrays that utilizes finite geometry, specifically leveraging finite linear spaces. By utilizing generalized Paley designs, we achieve arrays with a significantly smaller size compared to methods based on orthogonally symmetric matrices. Additionally, we demonstrate that our proposed design often matches or exceeds the theoretical lower bounds established by Stufken and Liu. Our results indicate that this new construction generates a wide variety of arrays that are difficult to obtain through other techniques. Furthermore, we demonstrate that applying optimization methods to these initial designs can yield even better strength $2$ covering arrays. A key advantage of this approach is its ability to escape local optima, thereby discovering arrays with fewer rows that are inaccessible to other direct search algorithms. We illustrate this capability by presenting numerous records for minimum-size covering arrays. Finally, the computational results suggest that the proposed design is highly effective for constructing strength $2$ covering arrays when the number of factor levels is a product of small primes. The source code is publicly accessible at \url{https://github.com/SebastianSchulte123/CoveringArrays}. The paper includes a demonstration video available at \url{https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=12424242424}. The video can be accessed via QR code. A direct adaptation of the quantifier iteration method fails to establish the decidability of nonlocal games involving arbitrary noisy maximally correlated states. However, significant progress is achieved when these states are restricted to the family of depolarized states, $\rho_{AB}^D(p) = (1-p)\Phi_{AB}^+ + pI/4$, where the noise $p$ is bounded by $2/3$. This family encompasses the three noisy maximally correlated states previously examined by Regev and Wittek. The proof relies on a modified quantifier iteration scheme enhanced by a quantum strategy extension lemma. This extension demonstrates that for any nonlocal game, the optimal yield can be attained using strategies composed of local qubit states and qubits shared among players. Furthermore, the approach introduces a new algorithm for computing the classical value of a nonlocal game with a noisy maximally correlated state, which runs in polynomial time relative to the game's description length. This algorithm is a generalization of the method developed by Beigi and Gohari for depolarizing states and is significant because it fulfills a conjecture by Bravyi and DiVincenzo. In this work, the classical value is approximated to an arbitrary precision with a computable error bound, achieving arbitrary precision in polynomial time. Additionally, the study presents a new example of a noisy maximally correlated state, $\rho_{AB}^{\alpha}$, for which quantifier iteration can be applied; its nested structure simplifies the analysis. For this specific state, an explicit expression for the classical value is derived, and the asymptotic quantum value is proven to be 1/2. Finally, the relationship between the classical and quantum values of a nonlocal game with a noisy maximally correlated state and its corresponding operator system is investigated. Operator systems were originally introduced to model nonlocal games with noisy maximally correlated states, and their connection to such games was further explored by Hahn and Tomamichel. This relationship is significant as it forms the basis for an alternative decision procedure. In this context, the operator system is defined as the image of the noisy maximally correlated state under a specific positive map, and the game's classical value corresponds to the optimal output of this map. Automated crash reproduction and regression testing are critical components of software testing, yet they remain underexplored in prior research. This study aims to offer practical guidance for implementing such tools within real-world development environments. We applied the Pangolin tool to a dataset of 1,000 GitHub crash reports to assess its performance on actual bugs. Our findings indicate that Pangolin successfully reproduces only a small fraction of these bugs. Additionally, we observed that Pangillin frequently generates spurious failures, which can lead to regression testing on features that are not actually flawed. To address these limitations, we propose several improvements to enhance Pangolin's effectiveness. Finally, we conducted a survey of 15 practitioners to evaluate their views on the tool's current capabilities and suggested enhancements. Based on this feedback, we implemented modifications to Pangolin and performed an ablation study to quantify the impact of these updates. Our results demonstrate that these improvements significantly boost Pangolin's capabilities. Overall, this paper provides valuable insights for developers considering the use of automated crash reproduction and regression testing tools in their software projects.

The vortex lattice in underdoped high-$T_\textrm{c}$ cuprate superconductors exhibits a complex order parameter with both d-wave d-wave symmetry and charge-4-fold anisotropy. Theoretical models predict a square-square transition driven by this charge anisotropy, alongside a re-entrant melting process. This study presents experimental confirmation of such a transition within the vortex lattice of underdoped YBa$_2$Cu$_3$O$_{6+x}$, observed via magnetic force microscopy at a fixed temperature under varying magnetic fields. The vortex lattice displays a re-entrant melting behavior, and a distinct transition from a square-pinning anisotropic grid to a nearly isotropic vortex glass grid occurs at the magnetic field $H_{hump}$. This specific field corresponds to the maximum in specific heat measured under zero-field-cooling conditions at a fixed temperature. Furthermore, the magnitude of charge carrier underdoping establishes a characteristic magnetic field scale, $H_{hump}$, which aligns with the field at which this transition takes place. These findings provide compelling evidence supporting the square-square grid transition model. Additionally, the presence of a plateau in magnetization curves at fields near $H_{hump}$ suggests the existence of metastable vortex lattice structures. Finally, the observed re-entrant melting of the vortex lattice is attributed to the competition between nearly isotropic pinning and charge anisotropy. These results offer new insights into the vortex lattice structure and its phase diagram. Ultimately, the re-entrant melting behavior and the specific anisotropy of the vortex lattice in underdoped high-$T_\textrm{c}$ cuprates can be explained by incorporating charge anisotropy into Ginzburg-Landau theory. Furthermore, the existence of a vortex lattice grid transition at $H_{hump}$ and its re-entrant melting behavior are consistent with the theoretical predictions of a phase diagram featuring a Lifshitz point. Consequently, this research provides compelling evidence for the Lifshitz point scenario regarding the vortex lattice phase diagram in high-$T_\textrm{c}$ cuprate superconductors. Finally, the specific heat peak observed at $H_{hump}$ is interpreted as a manifestation of the grid transition. We investigate magnetic ordering in a Heisenberg model featuring competing nearest- and next-nearest-neighbor interactions on triangular and kagome lattices. Our analysis, conducted via exact diagonalization for finite clusters and mean-field theory, reveals ground states including ferromagnetic, 120-degree, 60-degree, and collinear antiferromagnetic configurations. Notably, the kagome lattice exhibits a unique 3-6-60-degree ordered state absent in the 90-degree bond-ordered variant of the triangular lattice. Furthermore, we demonstrate that mean-field results for both geometries align with exact solutions on a renormalized lattice. Finally, we establish a direct connection between the derived mean-field and collinear antiferromagnetic states and those found in quantum spin ice systems. This study offers a comprehensive overview of magnetic orders on triangular and kagome lattices, facilitating a more effective comparison of phase diagrams across these related structures. Additionally, our findings are applicable to models on other comparable lattices, such as the rhombic lattice. Finally, we discuss the relationship between the collinear antiferromagnetic state and the quantum spin liquid phase in triangular lattices. This study addresses the identification of treatment effects for multiple treatments within large-scale multigroup experiments, such as large educational interventions. To achieve this, we introduce a framework that accounts for the false discovery rate (FDR) dependence among treatments. Within this framework, we establish the necessary and sufficient conditions for identifying treatment effects and propose a treatment identification procedure. Through simulations and an empirical application to the Head Start Impact Study (HSIS), we demonstrate the advantages of our proposed framework. The full replication, along with the datasets and R-package TEFDR, is accessible at https://github.com/ChenYi-ASU/TEFRDR. The package's name reflects our focus on controlling the FDR under effect size dependence, a topic we term the "feature-dependent FDR" (TEFDR). Additionally, we have developed a Python package, FDRtree, which utilizes the same approach to enable users to easily apply the TEFDR method. The Python package can be installed via pip: pip install FDRtree. The source code is available at https://github.com/ASU-DSG/FDRtree. Our findings indicate that the TEFDR method offers a straightforward and effective solution for identifying significant treatments in large-scale multigroup experiments. We anticipate this will facilitate more informed decision-making in various scientific fields, including education, medicine, and the social sciences. Furthermore, we aim to support practitioners by providing user-friendly software for implementing the TEFDR method. Practitioners can access the FDRtree package directly through the TEFDR website (https://ASU-DSG.github.io/TEFRDR/). The source code for the package is hosted on GitHub at https://github.com/ASU-DSG/FDRtree. We extend our sincere gratitude to the FDRtree developers for their dedication to creating this accessible tool for practitioners. We hope this approach will assist practitioners in identifying effective treatments and making well-informed decisions. This study examines the type-X two-Higgs-doublet model (2HDM) as a potential explanation for both the recent $g-2$ of the muon anomaly and the heavier $W$ boson mass observed by CDF. We determine the necessary conditions for the lightest CP-even scalar's contribution to satisfy both experimental results. Notably, meeting these conditions demands a lighter pseudoscalar mass, constrained by 2HDM potential parameters that also influence the $b \to s \ell \ell$ process. Consequently, we analyze the $B \to K \pi \pi$ decay, a sensitive probe for such transitions. Our findings indicate that while the heavier pseudoscalar mass can be accommodated within the 2HDM framework, a CP-even scalar mass below 1 TeV is required to resolve the $\mu (g-2)$ and $m_W$ puzzles. Furthermore, our findings regarding the $B \to K \pi \pi$ decay suggest that a future Belle II experiment could detect significant deviations from the Standard Model, offering a promising avenue for testing this model. Finally, we explore the potential of Belle II to detect additional 2HDM signatures, specifically a light pseudoscalar decaying into $\tau^+ \tau^-$. This channel offers a viable method to investigate 2HDM parameter space, allowing for a more precise determination of the heavy $W$ boson mass. Additionally, we address the necessity of including heavy CP-even scalar contributions when interpreting 2HDM parameter space. We conclude that the heavy CP-even scalar must be heavier than 1 TeV to avoid conflicting with the type-X 2HDM interpretation of the $B \to s \ell \ell$ process. This conclusion is robust across various scenarios, including those involving heavy CP-odd and CP-odd-even scalar contributions. In contrast, the type-I 2HDM, which features a tree-level contribution to the muon $g-2$, requires a heavy CP-even scalar to achieve a larger new physics effect. This results in a heavier pseudoscalar mass, leading to a smaller branching ratio for the $\tau^+ \tau^-$ channel. Therefore, the type-I 2HDM is not a viable candidate for explaining the $\mu (g-2)$ and $m_W$ anomalies through the pseudoscalar channel at Belle II. We also discuss the prospects for 2HDM signatures at the LHC and their impact on constraining the parameter space.

In software engineering, developers frequently ask inquiries to seek assistance, knowledge, or share information. Although various knowledge crowdsourcing platforms have emerged to facilitate this exchange, many posted questions are poorly formulated, hindering effective communication and responses. This paper introduces QUICKAR, a novel approach that automatically reformulates these ill-formed questions into clearer versions to improve matching with existing knowledge. QUICKAR is the inaugural method to do so by utilizing two newly identified data sources: a repository of questions and their answers, and a repository of software engineering concepts along with their usages. Evaluation results demonstrate that QUICKAR surpasses data-driven reformulation baselines and performs comparably to grammar-based baselines. Furthermore, QUICKAR exhibits significant potential for application in software development, including aiding concept location for novice engineers and enhancing question-answering systems for crowdsourced knowledge. Additionally, the datasets employed in this study are publicly accessible to support future research. The QUICKAR tool, its source code, and the dataset can be found at https://github.com/quickar/quickar. The repository also includes a pre-trained model for concept identification, which is available for use. Furthermore, existing approaches often rely on pre-processed datasets or manual annotations, which restricts their applicability to scenarios involving new corpora. We demonstrate that our DNN model surpasses all baseline methods and validate its efficacy by applying it to well-established datasets, thereby revealing insights into diverse behavioral patterns. Additionally, the proposed DNN model is being integrated into a dialogue system to explore how manipulating entrainement metrics can enhance specific system behaviors. Finally, we illustrate the broader utility of this approach in NLP and dialogue research by applying it to a corpus from a recent challenge on the prediction of social attributes. The comprehensive code for all experiments and baselines is publicly available at \url{https://github.com/DeepMind/Entrainement-DNN}. Temporal action segmentation (TAS) is a critical task in video analysis that involves identifying and segmenting action occurrences within a clip. While existing TAS methods rely heavily on extensive and costly annotation efforts, our objective is to achieve competitive performance without supervised labels. To address this, we introduce SSCAP, a Self-supervised Co-occurrence Action Analysis framework designed for the unsupervised temporal segmentation of actions. SSCAP leverages the inherent structure of video data to automatically learn task-specific representations and segmentation boundaries without any supervised examples. The core component of SSCAP is a self-supervised contrastive loss, which ensures that visual and audio features from the same temporal segment align while remaining distinct for different segments. We demonstrate that SSCAP attains competitive results on standard TAS benchmarks, surpassing several supervised state-of-the-art methods. The project can be accessed at https://github.com/Chen-YU-98/SSCAP. The source code will also be released under a permissive license. Furthermore, our method yields promising outcomes in downstream tasks, such as unsupervised video retrieval. This paper aims to inspire further research into unsupervised and self-supervised video action segmentation. Additionally, we plan to explore self-supervised learning techniques for other video analysis tasks, including object detection and semantic segmentation. This study leverages the advantages of online testing environments to enhance pedagogy. It examines the impact of integrating a software testing module into a core programming course, where students are required to develop test cases for randomly selected functions. The primary objective is to evaluate whether these exercises can effectively instill a testing mindset in novice programmers. To achieve this, an automated feedback system was implemented to assist students in creating valid function tests. A comprehensive experiment involving 120 participants across three groups was conducted to assess the efficacy of this automated mechanism. The findings indicate that providing feedback on testing tasks is highly effective for teaching beginners. Furthermore, the research demonstrates that an inquiry-based learning approach, utilizing conceptual feedback within an automated feedback system, yields superior results compared to traditional thorough feedback methods. This conclusion is supported by an analysis of the cognitive processes involved in creating software tests. Finally, the paper explores the potential of these results for software testing education and discusses the modularity and adaptability of the implemented system for application in other educational domains. Domain adaptation is a critical area within machine learning, particularly for vision and image processing. This paper introduces a new domain adaptation framework designed to function without access to the original source domain data. It is the first approach to utilize unsupervised source data, leveraging the shift in hypothesis to distinguish between source and target domains. Our method prioritizes minimizing hypothesis shift through feature alignment using domain discriminative loss and hypercircle constraint loss. The proposed framework is evaluated across six cross-domain object recognition tasks. Experimental results demonstrate that it surpasses existing state-of-the-art methods. The code is accessible at: https://github.com/abhishekkumar123456789/SSHC-DALoss.

This paper introduces a novel gas core reactor engine designed for deep space exploration. The proposed system utilizes a reactor that is inherently less complex than current reactor designs, offering specific impulse and thrust capabilities suitable for deep space missions. We demonstrate that a vacuum Brayton cycle, operating without liquid cooling, serves as an effective deep space vehicle propulsion system. This design achieves specific impulse and thrust-to-weight ratios comparable to those of the vacuum mode liquid cooling cycle, while the absence of the liquid region and the associated phase change simplifies the system and reduces engine size. Furthermore, the removal of the liquid cooling system further enhances the thrust-to-weight ratio. The study presents specific engine configurations and analyzes their performance under various operating conditions. Additionally, we illustrate how this new propulsion system can facilitate deep space missions, such as traveling from Earth to Mars in approximately three months. The paper concludes by outlining potential space missions that could be supported by this innovative deep space vehicle. Finally, the authors suggest promising areas for future research and development. This paper is intended to stimulate interest in the development of new, viable deep space propulsion systems. Keywords: Space propulsion, gas core engine, reactor engine, deep space exploration, space missions.

Neural networks are extensively utilized in the field of particle physics. This paper introduces a novel domain-informed neural network architecture designed for interaction positioning within the Cherenkov telescope CTAO. We demonstrate that this proposed approach yields superior results compared to U-net models. Additionally, we examine various hyperparameter optimization techniques, including Tree-structured Parzen Estimator (TPE), Bayesian Optimization, and Successive Halving. Finally, we analyze and compare the strengths and weaknesses of these optimization methods in the context of particle physics applications. Our findings indicate that Tree-structured Parzen Estimator (TPE) is the most effective optimization strategy. We also highlight that hyperparameter optimization is a critical component in developing optimal machine learning models for physics research. Furthermore, our results show that position reconstruction using domain-informed neural networks achieves an accuracy of approximately 1.5 cm. These outcomes underscore the necessity of optimizing machine learning models specifically for domain-related position reconstruction tasks in astroparticle physics research. The source code is accessible at: https://github.com/abdullahkaya1994/Domain_informed_neural_networks. Our approach is expected to be valuable for position reconstruction in various particle physics experiments. Additionally, we demonstrate that domain-informed neural networks achieve state-of-the-art accuracy in position reconstruction for Gravitational Wave detectors, such as LIGO. This work holds significant promise for enhancing position reconstruction accuracy in astrophysics and cosmology. Our findings suggest that domain-informed neural networks could achieve a position reconstruction accuracy of about 1.5 cm. Atmospheric retrievals serve as a critical instrument for characterizing exoplanet and brown dwarf atmospheres, yielding a comprehensive understanding of their chemical and physical properties. These retrievals depend on exoLineS, an extensive and precise exo-Atmospheric Line list (ALi) archive that includes exoMolecular Absorption Cross-Section (MACS) data for various exoMolecules. This ALi archive is essential for generating the high-quality MACS data required for atmospheric retrievals. While numerous ALi archives have been created to facilitate these retrievals, they often lack the extensive coverage and precision demanded by current retrieval practices. EXOPLINES is a meticulously curated and expanded collection of MACS data designed to support exoAtmospheric Line searches. It builds upon the foundational ALi archive established in 2014 and has since grown exponentially, incorporating data for a wide array of exoMolecules. EXOPLINES is freely accessible via the EXOPLINES website and the VizieR catalog service. The archive is structured to be easily searchable and filterable, offering a user-friendly interface for data access. Furthermore, the EXOPLINES website provides a suite of online tools to assist users in customizing retrievals and utilizing the archive. These tools include a browser-based data viewer, a retriever calculator, and a retriever simulator. The EXOPLINES team is dedicated to maintaining and expanding the archive, with a strong commitment to supporting the community. This paper outlines the EXOPLINES archive and its associated online tools, demonstrating how they enhance the efficiency of the exoAtmospheric Line search process. Additionally, the study details the specific data formats employed within the EXOPLINES archive. The EXOPLINES team is dedicated to ensuring the archive's longevity and fostering community engagement. This work serves as a foundation for the ongoing development of the EXOPLINES archive. The team acknowledges the contributions of all individuals who have joined since 2014, whose efforts have significantly expanded the archive. We also gratefully acknowledge the many users who have provided feedback, which has been instrumental in refining and improving EXOPLINES. This work is supported by the European Research Council (ERC) under the European Union's Horizon 2020 research and innovation programme (grant agreement No 756958). This research has received funding from the European Research Council (ERC) grant agreement No 756958. The EXOPLINES team

We establish the initial law governing quantum resource theories and apply it to the context of quantum coherence. Our analysis demonstrates that, under maximal free operations, the optimal rate for converting a source into target coherence is determined by the min-0 entropy of the relevant operators. Furthermore, we show that the optimality of these operations relies on the convergence properties of a generalized quantum relative entropy. Additionally, we derive an asymptotic strong converse for this specific resource transformation. These findings are anticipated to be extendable to broader scenarios involving different free operations and various quantum resource theories. **Keywords:** quantum resource theory, asymptotic theory, strong converse, min-0 entropy.

This paper introduces a new class of nonparametric estimators designed to recover functions of unobserved random variables using estimates of their moments. These moment-based approximations are generated from either a machine learning model or a structural economic model of the data-generating process. The proposed estimators are straightforward to implement, straightforward to understand, and straightforward to apply. They offer flexibility in estimating functions of interest, accommodate various sources of endogeneity, and provide an alternative to data-driven methods that directly estimate target functions from observed data. The theoretical analysis establishes consistency and the asymptotic normality of the estimators, with convergence rates that reflect the asymptotic properties of the input moments. Furthermore, simulations demonstrate that the finite-sample performance of these estimators is superior to that of data-driven approaches when estimating conditional expectations and functions. Finally, a series of empirical applications are presented to illustrate the practical utility of the proposed estimators. These include: (i) a dynamic discrete choice model of firm entry, exit, and expansion/contraction decisions; (ii) a dynamic programming model of household labor supply decisions; (iii) a model of the U.S. housing market; and (iv) a structural model of the 2008 financial crisis. In each application, the results obtained from the moment-based estimators are benchmarked against those from data-driven alternatives. Additionally, the paper provides a tutorial on how to implement these moment-based estimators within the R package `mde`. This package offers a user-friendly interface that facilitates the estimation of functions of interest and includes several examples. The tutorial is intended to serve as a resource for researchers. Finally, the code for all examples, including those in the `mde` package, is available on GitHub. This material is not intended to substitute for peer-reviewed publication.

This paper introduces a novel framework for multivariate time series analysis, characterized by heavy tails and time-varying parameters. We develop new estimators and asymptotic theory for linear functionals of this class of series, alongside optimal linear predictors that achieve the minimax rate of convergence regarding prediction error. Furthermore, we propose inferential procedures to test the significance of linear functionals within the model. The effectiveness of these methods is demonstrated through simulations and an empirical analysis of US stock returns. Keywords: Heavy tails; Markov model; Multivariate time series; Minimax estimation; Optimal prediction.

Low-density parity-check (LDPC) codes are defined by a sparse check matrix, enabling efficient decoding via message-passing algorithms. Quantum LDPC codes are defined by a check matrix that acts as the stabilizer for a stabilizer code. In the classical domain, matrix multiplication can serve as an efficient decoder for certain LDPC codes, achieving linear decoding time and constant average work per bit. This paper demonstrates the existence of a family of good quantum LDPC codes, characterized by constant rate, constant distance relative to block length, and linear size, whose check matrices can be processed in linear time. Furthermore, these check matrices can be arranged into a symmetric form suitable for use as stabilizers in distance-preserving stabilizer codes. Consequently, these codes admit efficient symmetric decoding circuits capable of correcting any error with probability below a constant threshold. To the best of our knowledge, this marks the first instance of quantum LDPC codes supporting such efficient decoding. Additionally, we establish that any family of quantum LDPC codes exhibiting constant rate and distance (or any family of good quantum codes) possesses a nontrivial encoding circuit with quadratic depth. Our findings rely on two key tools: first, a new application of the "small-set expansion" property to characterize the efficiency of message-passing decoders; second, an application of recent results on the structure of good quantum codes to characterize their encoders. Finally, we introduce a family of quantum LDPC codes that are not good but maintain constant rate and distance (with block length scaling polylogarithmically), which also admit efficient decoders. This result stems from the construction of locally expandable quantum codes by Bravyi, which are known to be good. We also present an alternative, more direct proof demonstrating that the construction in [BBB+15] yields quantum LDPC codes with constant rate and distance (and polynomial block length). Both of these results depend on the existence of classical expander graphs and are therefore considered unconditional. Furthermore, our analysis reveals that any family of quantum LDPC codes with good rate and distance (and polynomial block length) must possess a nontrivial encoding circuit with polynomial depth. Finally, we prove that any family of quantum LDPC codes with linear rate and polynomial distance (and polynomial block length) possesses a nontrivial encoding circuit with polylogarithmic depth. This result is achieved through a new application of recent results on the structure of quantum LDPC codes with large rate and distance [KSVW19]. The latter result is conditional on the Unique Games Conject

This paper investigates the distributed computation of distance-$r$ dominating groups (where $r \geq 1$) within high-girth graphs characterized by a large diameter, such as random $k$-regular graphs. We introduce a distributed algorithm capable of generating multiple distance-$r$ dominating groups simultaneously (one per round) with high probability. Specifically, for $k$-regular graphs with a high girth of at least $2r + 2$, the algorithm successfully computes $M$ distance-$r$ dominating groups in $O(\log n + r + 2\sqrt{2\ln(2n/M)})$ rounds with a success probability of at least $1 - 1/n$. Furthermore, we extend these findings to the context of distance-$r$ dominating sets. By adapting our methodology, we propose a distributed algorithm for identifying multiple minimum distance-$r$ dominating sets. For the same class of graphs, this algorithm can find $M$ minimum distance-$r$ dominating sets in $O(\log n + r + 2\sqrt{2\ln(2n/M)})$ rounds with a success probability no less than $1 - 1/n$. Additionally, we demonstrate that the proposed algorithms for multiple minimum distance-$r$ dominating groups and sets are optimal. Our results significantly enhance the likelihood of success and substantially decrease the time complexity compared to both centralized algorithms and prior distributed algorithms for this problem. Finally, we present experimental evidence supporting the practicality of our approach. In this study, we extend the concept of distance-$r$ dominating groups to the more general framework of distance-$r$ independent dominating groups. Our proposed distributed algorithm simultaneously identifies multiple minimum distance-$r$ independent dominating groups, achieving a time complexity of $O(\log n + r + 2\sqrt{2\ln(2n/M)})$ rounds with a success probability of at least $1 - 1/n$. This represents a significant improvement over existing distributed algorithms for solving the multiple minimum distance-$r$ independent dominating group problem. Furthermore, we demonstrate that our algorithm is optimal for this specific problem. Our findings also contribute to the broader field of distributed computing, where our method advances the understanding of efficient solutions for various dominating group problems in sparse high-girth graphs. Specifically, we propose a distributed algorithm for the independent distance-$r$ dominating set problem, achieving a time complexity of $O(\log n + r + 2\sqrt{2\ln(2n/M)})$ rounds with a success probability

We investigate bulk-surface correspondences within disordered higher-order topological insulators (HOTIs), exemplified by the $\mathcal{C}_{4}$-symmetric higher-order topological insulator (HOTI$_{4}$). Our findings reveal a two-level hierarchy in HOTI$_{4}$: a bulk-surface relationship linked to corner states, where bulk localization lengths equal the distance from the bulk to the corner states; and a bulk-surface-side relationship concerning surface states, which permits the existence of bulk states with localization lengths matching the distance from the surface to the side states. Furthermore, the symmetry-breaking mechanism in disordered HOTI$_{4}$ allows for the observation of bulk states, surface states, and surface-side states, while corner states are permitted only under specific conditions. These discoveries are anticipated to hold for other disordered topological systems. Finally, we address the challenges associated with numerically calculating the bulk localization length. Additionally, we note that surface and surface-side states exhibit distinct symmetries, a feature not shared by bulk states. These characteristics enable the identification of surface and surface-side states via symmetry analysis, even when their spectral densities overlap. Consequently, this approach offers a significant advantage for analyzing symmetry-protected higher-order topological insulators. Finally, we propose that these findings may extend to disordered topological systems lacking specific crystal symmetries. This contribution, prepared for CMS NOTES, outlines recent findings from the CMS experiment at the LHC regarding the search for the supersymmetric (SUSY) particle spectrum. The presented analysis synthesizes recent ATLAS and CMS CMS NOTES submissions to highlight complementary results from both colliders. Additionally, we will provide an update based on the latest CMS NOTES. This talk is co-authored with the ATLAS Collaboration.

The search for SUSY particles serves as a primary motivation for the LHC. While the Standard Model (SM) successfully describes numerous phenomena, it fails to address several critical questions, such as the origin of matter-antimatter asymmetry, the nature of dark matter, and why particles are massless. SUSY offers a promising framework to resolve these issues. Furthermore, it predicts a rich array of new particles that could be detected within the LHC's energy reach.

This presentation will detail a comprehensive search for SUSY in multilepton final states, utilizing data collected by CMS in 2016 and 2017. The investigation examines various SUSY models, including compressed regions of the parameter space, gluino-sleepion coannihilation, compressed stop coannihilation, compressed chargino-neutralino associated production, and compressed stau coannihilation. The talk will also cover a search for heavy neutralinos decaying into a Higgs boson in association with a $W$ boson, as well as Higgs decays into two heavy neutralinos. Additionally, a search for the decay of a heavy neutralino into a $Z$ boson and a stau will be presented. Finally, the neutralino dark matter scenario will be explored using the XENON1T data.

The SUSY framework extends the SM by postulating a partner for every SM particle. These partners are termed superpartners: squarks and sparticles for quarks and gluons, sleptons for leptons, and neutralinos and charginos for neutral and charged gauge bosons and Higgs particles. SUSY also introduces four additional Higgs bosons, $H$, $A$, $H^0$, and $H^\pm$, in addition to the SM Higgs boson. In the minimal supersymmetric standard model (MSSM), all superpartners share the same quantum numbers as their SM counterparts.
