Regulatory bodies are increasingly scrutinizing the distributional shift between training and deployment datasets in AI software intended for medical devices. This study introduces a framework that employs conformal prediction to estimate test efficacy—the likelihood that detecting distributional shifts during software testing can be relied upon. The framework utilizes pure conformal prediction, which avoids assumptions regarding underlying data distributions, alongside its variants that incorporate finite-sample nonparametric two-sample tests. We present analytical and simulation results demonstrating that detecting distributional shift using the proposed framework requires significantly fewer test data samples than other widely used methods. Additionally, we outline a design strategy for AI medical devices that integrates our proposed test design with existing software testing techniques. Finally, we evaluate the framework using a real-world medical image dataset featuring an established AI medical device. To our knowledge, this represents the first application of conformal prediction to AI medical devices and the initial work linking distributional shift detection to software testing for these devices. The associated software and data are accessible online. (https://github.com/ChenYan1993/Testing-under-Distribution-Shift). Furthermore, this work establishes a foundation for future research into conformal prediction applications within AI medical devices. Enhanced sampling of DNA conformations is difficult due to the inherent rigidity of the double helix and a lack of reliable methods for generating diverse, realistic starting structures. We introduce Rigid Substrate Biasing (RSB), a straightforward and efficient technique that significantly accelerates the sampling of conformations resembling those observed in solution. RSB achieves this by incorporating a simple harmonic restraint on the root mean square fluctuation (RMSF) of base pair positions relative to their initial frame, ensuring the process remains reversible. We show that applying this restraint to a single, realistic DNA structure allows for the generation of a wide range of conformations that accurately mimic thermal fluctuations seen in molecular solutions. Furthermore, we demonstrate that RSB effectively captures the transition between Z-DNA and B-DNA conformers. Additionally, we illustrate that combining RSB with metadynamics in a straightforward enhanced sampling protocol successfully explores the full landscape of DNA breathing motions. RSB offers a straightforward approach to improve the sampling of realistic DNA conformations, which is essential for understanding their biological functions. The report also addresses experimental signatures and the challenges posed by non-resonant backgrounds. Furthermore, it explores the implications of such states within hadron spectroscopy and highlights future opportunities for discovering additional heavy hadronic molecules. The paper concludes by summarizing theoretical predictions for these exotic configurations. While primarily targeting experimentalists, it also incorporates insights from theoretical hadron spectroscopy. The discussion is limited to hadronic molecules; compact or compactly correlated multi-hadron states are excluded. Additionally, fully charmed and bottomic hadrons are omitted, as they will be addressed in a separate review. This work serves as a sequel to a 2019 survey on light-heavy hadronic molecules. The review is structured into 10 sections, featuring 10 figures and 100 references. The Lyman-$\alpha$ forest serves as a valuable tool for cosmological studies, yet its direct application remains underutilized. This work proposes a method to directly infer the cosmological model and the dark energy equation of state by analyzing the three-dimensional correlations of Lyman-$\alpha$ absorbers. Specifically, the dark energy equation of state is derived from the redshift-space correlation function, which is predicted using the Zel'dovich approximation. Our results indicate that with approximately $10^5$ absorbers, the precision for determining the equation of state could reach $\sigma(w) \sim 0.3$. This approach is considered complementary to the traditional method of deducing cosmological parameters from the Lyman-$\alpha$ forest. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the proposed method yields a more accurate estimation of the equation of state compared to the traditional approach when using the same quantity of simulated data. Future research will aim to refine this technique by incorporating the Zel'dovich approximation with tidal terms and the Sheth--Yin formalism. Ultimately, the three-dimensional correlation function of the Lyman-$\alpha$ forest is expected to become a robust tool for cosmological research. We demonstrate the successful transfer of both transverse and longitudinal emittances from a source oscillator to a target one, utilizing a tunable and configurable optical cavity oscillator network. This achievement marks the first experimental confirmation of transverse emittance transfer, alongside a notable longitudinal transfer event. These findings provide strong support for theemittance sharing theory. Additionally, we present an oscillator network model grounded in classical mechanics that accurately reflects these experimental results. This network features a closed, isolated system that can be adjusted to distribute emittance between two oscillators at will, offering a valuable alternative to quantum systems for fundamental research into emittance sharing. Our work represents a crucial step toward achieving high-energy, low-emittance particle beams. Furthermore, we anticipate that the concepts explored here will be valuable in various other fields, including optical engineering, control engineering, and even social network research. In social networks, for instance, information and influence can be viewed as forms of "emittance," and understanding how to transfer these elements is essential for achieving a desired state distribution. Our approach is inherently simple and straightforward. We expect this work to serve as a foundation for future studies on the sharing and transfer of resources and influence within different oscillator networks. Specifically, we aim to investigate more complex and challenging scenarios, such as transferring emittance from multiple sources to a single target or from a source to multiple targets. These applications are expected to advance the development of high-energy particle accelerators and support fundamental research into emittance sharing. Ultimately, these methods will provide more options for achieving the desired distribution of resources and influence in various contexts. Keywords: oscillator network, emittance sharing, classical mechanics, particle accelerators, fundamental research.

This study introduces a novel analysis of hidden complexity within stochastic neural networks. We evaluate three distinct metrics for the conditional entropy $H(Y|X)$ associated with discrete output $Y$ given discrete input $X$ in a feedforward architecture utilizing sigmoidal activations. These metrics correspond to the Information Dimension, Renyi Dimension, and the newly proposed Maximal Dimension. Through analytical methods, we demonstrate that the Maximum Dimension uniquely captures the asymptotic scaling of $H(Y|X)$ with respect to system size $N$ across all parameter regimes. Furthermore, numerical experiments confirm that the Maximum Dimension accurately reflects the system's dimensionality even at finite sizes, maintaining a minimal estimation error throughout diverse parameter regimes. Finally, we establish that training a Sigmoid-Bias Autoencoder with Mean-Square Error loss utilizing the Adam optimizer successfully recovers the true input dimension using this metric. These findings indicate that the Maximum Dimension serves as a potent analytical tool for comprehending the dynamics of stochastic neural networks during the learning process. This paper introduces a novel, vision-based Human-Swarm Interaction (HSI) method designed for real-world outdoor environments. The primary innovation lies in breaking away from traditional centralized architectures, which depend on a central computer or robot for processing. Instead, the system utilizes a distributed network of mobile robots, each equipped with its own processor to independently manage HSI tasks. To facilitate this, we developed a new deep learning framework named Deep Hand Signal Recognition (DHRS). DHRS is optimized for identifying sequential hand gestures and incorporates an attention mechanism to enhance performance on the proposed dataset. In DHRS, the initial layer functions as a classifier, while subsequent layers are structured to analyze a sequence of hand gestures. Experimental results demonstrate that DHRS surpasses state-of-the-art models in both top-1 and top-5 accuracy on the proposed dataset. Furthermore, DHRS maintains robust accuracy even when the swarm network dedicates only 1% of its onboard processing resources to the task. These findings indicate that DHRS enables the swarm to effectively and efficiently execute complex tasks based on human commands within outdoor settings. The source code and dataset are publicly accessible at https://github.com/abdullahaydin/DHRS. The underlying HSI approach is being developed as an open-source project under the name Distributed Hand Signal Recognition (DHSR). DHSR is anticipated to significantly advance research in HSI, particularly within outdoor settings. Counterdiabatic driving (CDD) serves as a powerful control technique for guiding quantum systems to their ground states. This study applies a variational CDD protocol to transport the one-dimensional Hubbard model from a fully polarized initial state to its ground state. Within this framework, CDD is implemented to counteract dynamics occurring on a specific timescale, while a mean-field Hamiltonian, constructed from the reduced density matrix of a single site, governs the primary evolution. We systematically examine the influence of various parameters, including the mean-field Hamiltonian's strength, its functional form, and the CDDriving strength. Furthermore, we explore the application of this method to other spin models and demonstrate its utility in preparing a Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger (GHZ) state. Finally, we outline potential extensions of this approach to higher-dimensional lattices. Additionally, we showcase experimental results obtained using trapped ions to prepare the GHZ state. This work underscores the versatility of the variational CDD approach and establishes a foundation for future investigations into efficient algorithms for ground-state preparation. Specifically, the construction of a mean-field Hamiltonian to counteract dynamics offers a valuable tool for the broader quantum community. By employing a classical simulator to design a control strategy that leverages the quantum system's own dynamics, this research highlights the value of hybrid quantum-classical control schemes. This is particularly relevant for future applications on near-term quantum devices. This paper introduces a novel exponential Taylor series representation for functions of one or more variables, which converges under significantly broader conditions than the conventional power series expansion. The study provides examples involving power series, rational functions, and other examples in one variable, followed by examples of functions and differential equations in multiple variables. The proposed expansion is particularly well-suited for high-precision computing and the development of algorithms that operate independently of complex branching logic. Additionally, computational results are presented to demonstrate the correct evaluation of specific function values and derivatives at selected points. Finally, several challenging open problems are outlined for future research. Notably, the exponential Taylor expansion can be interpreted as a linearization of a function, and its properties may serve as another definition of differentiability. Specifically, it is shown that differentiability at a point is equivalent to the existence of a local linearization at that point. Furthermore, the existence of this linearization does not imply continuity of the function or its local derivatives. The relationship between this concept and the classical mean value theorem is also examined. This work is inspired by the author's recent publications, which include "A New Approach to the Study of Functions and Differential Equations" and "Mean Value Theorem Revisited." These papers propose a new definition of differentiability, introduce the concept of mean value functions, and provide a novel proof of the mean value theorem. They also offer an alternative formulation of Taylor's theorem and present a new method for approximating differentiable functions. The objective of this book is to provide a comprehensive overview of these related topics. The content is intended for mathematicians, graduate students, and advanced undergraduates. Graduate students in computer science and computer engineering may also find the material valuable, particularly in understanding the challenges associated with high-precision computing and in exploring solutions utilizing specialized hardware. The book includes numerous exercises with answers, and the author has included solutions to selected exercises in the text. The material is structured to be easily adaptable for a one-semester course or a one-quarter course in mathematics. Consequently, any harmonic sphere within the same homotopy class also possesses a degree no greater than $k^{\frac{m-2}{m-1}}$. Specifically, we demonstrate that given two harmonic maps $f$ and $g$ from $S$ to $S^m$ in the same homotopy class, there exists a harmonic map $h: S \to S^m$ such that $f = h \circ \phi$ and $g = \psi \circ h$, where $\phi$ and $\psi$ are harmonic maps in the same homotopy class as constant maps. We introduce a theoretical framework designed to simulate the complex interactions between photons, intense laser fields, and relativistic electrons. This approach is grounded in the strong-field QED Lagrangian, which accounts for both the intense electromagnetic fields and the presence of electrons. The framework is implemented using the PETRA laser-plasma simulation toolkit. We begin by presenting a general overview of PETRA and its integration within the PyERMI family of laser-plasma codes. Subsequently, we illustrate how to apply the framework to explore various photon-photon phenomena. We demonstrate that our results align with established literature in the weak-field limit, while also generating several new findings in the strong-field regime. Notably, we predict that under extreme conditions, the strong-field photon-photon interaction could be observed in current experiments. Furthermore, we examine the critical importance of electron backreaction in this environment. Our findings indicate that while electron-positron pair production is significantly enhanced by strong-field effects, the resulting backreaction is minimal. However, for the process of photon splitting, we show that backreaction is substantial, thereby opening up new regimes for studying this phenomenon. These predictions are expected to be testable using the ELI beam-driver facility. Finally, we provide an outlook on future applications of this framework to model other photon-photon processes. This study examines the direct and indirect constraints on the soft-breaking $Z_2$ symmetry parameter, $m_{12}$, within the Two-Doublet Higgs Model (2HDM). We analyze both tree-level production and decay mechanisms sensitive to $m_{12}$, specifically focusing on the mixing between the CP-odd state $A$ and the lightest charged state $H^\pm$. Our investigation covers the most recent limits imposed by the CMS collaboration on various 2HDM scenarios, including the Type-I, Type-II, and the Alignment Limit. Additionally, we establish novel and stringent constraints for the non-minimal case (Type-II) by examining a specific channel: $pp \to t\bar{t}A$, where $A \to \mu^+\mu^-$ and $t \to bW$, with $W \to l\nu$ or $q\bar{q}'$. This analysis utilizes a dataset corresponding to an integrated luminosity of $137\,fb^{-1}$, derived from a combination of ATLAS and CMS results from the LHC Run-2 era. Furthermore, we explore a new scenario in which the $A$ boson serves as a dark matter candidate, constrained by the non-observation of dark matter signals in direct detection experiments. We also consider indirect limits arising from the stability of the electroweak vacuum and the measured properties of the SM-like Higgs boson at 125 GeV. Finally, we present projections for future constraints based on projected Run-3 data. Overall, this work provides a comprehensive assessment of the current experimental bounds on the 2HDM parameter space. Finally, we discuss potential future constraints that could be established by the High-Luminosity LHC. Our findings indicate that this parameter remains largely unconstrained, with future constraints in the TeV mass range remaining challenging. This outcome is attributed to the $m_{12}$ parameter influencing multiple observables simultaneously, thereby complicating the extraction of its specific effects. Consequently, we advocate for a more refined analysis of 2HDM scenarios that incorporates the full set of available constraints. In conclusion, we have outlined a viable framework for such an analysis. This paper serves as a foundational step toward a more comprehensive investigation of the 2HDM parameter space. Shape expressions offer methods for defining and validating the content of instance data, typically represented as IRIs and property values within RDF graph stores. However, they also support various forms of data such as sets, maps, and functional expressions. This paper introduces a relational-to-RDF translation algorithm that is sound and terminating when applied to relational instance data stored in tables. Additionally, it proposes a corresponding rule-based rule-to-RDF translation algorithm that can handle derived instance data stored as materialized rules. Both algorithms are capable of accommodating shape expressions, including their various forms and extensions. Furthermore, we explore specific applications, such as data migration and integration, where these algorithms are particularly relevant. The proposed algorithms have been implemented in a tool, and we include a usage example utilizing the tool. This implementation also introduces extensions to address specific migration requirements. Finally, we demonstrate how these extensions can be utilized to facilitate data integration. The algorithm and the corresponding tool are accessible at https://github.com/DFKI-Research/shapetrans. The paper includes an extension detailing how to convert IRI schemes, specifically comparing CURIE-based IRIs with those based on a global IRI registry. The tool is also available as a package for use in Jena environments. The tool was developed within the framework of the DFG project "Rule-based Data Management" (https://www.dfg.de/de/foerderung/projects/projects_list/294222222). It incorporates extensions to manage materialized rules, which are stored in a separate graph, and to handle materialized instance data represented as set expressions involving set union, set difference, and set intersection. Additionally, the tool supports a package-based migration format, allowing for the specification of translation requirements through DROPS files. A corresponding translation algorithm is included to facilitate data package-based migration. The tool also provides a means to verify the correctness of translations by checking for data loss and ensuring that all instance data is included. This verification functionality relies on a sound and complete rule reasoner. A sound and complete reasoner for this translation can be found in [1]. The algorithm for checking translation correctness is also described in [1]. The tool's extensions for data package-based migration and for checking translation correctness are also documented in [1].

We present the findings of a spectroscopic analysis of 12 Be-type stars within the 30 Doradus region, selected from a survey of 300 O and Be stars. Our investigation details the spectral characteristics of these objects, including their rotational velocities, the presence of emission lines, and the physical properties of their circumstellar disks. Our results indicate that the 30 Doradus Be-type star population is dominated by rapid rotators, with 67% spinning at velocities exceeding 200 km/s. Furthermore, our analysis identifies two stars exhibiting double emission peaks in their spectral profiles, suggesting they are in the early stages of evolution. Additionally, we report the discovery of a star with a P Cygni profile, characterized by a broad absorption component and an emission component extending to the blue. These findings collectively imply that the 30 Doradus Be-type star population is relatively young. The paper concludes with a discussion of these results. (Abridged)

Using a one-dimensional framework, we demonstrate that constructing a topological point gap around $-i$ is insufficient to guarantee stable topological phases. Instead, ensuring that the product of the constituent Hamiltonians has an eigenvalue with an imaginary component exceeding $1$ provides a more effective and practical condition for defining topological phases. Furthermore, we show that the topological properties cannot be derived merely by combining the individual topological invariants of the components; correlations between the Hamiltonians play an essential role in generating such phenomena. Finally, we highlight that our findings provide a foundation for the design of non-Hermitian quantum circuits. Specifically, we propose a quantum circuit composed of $n$ layers, where the $j$-th layer corresponds to a non-Hermitian Hamiltonian $H_j$ possessing stable image eigenvalues within the unit circle. Despite these individual features, the circuit fails to exhibit a stable image spectral phase around the origin in the complex plane. However, by appropriately ordering the layers, the circuit can display a spectral phase with a magnitude greater than $1$ around the origin, a result we describe as a non-Hermitian spectral gap. This outcome underscores the significance of correlations between the non-Hermitian Hamiltonians in generating this unique phenomenon. Additionally, we note that the topological properties observed in our model are absent in its corresponding classical system. These insights offer valuable guidance for the development of non-Hermitian quantum technologies. Finally, we observe that the topological phenomenon we describe is not unique to our specific model but can be realized in various other models. We have therefore applied our findings to the study of the Trotterized Jordan-Wigner model and the Trotterized Su-Schrieffer-Heeger model. In both cases, the eigenvalues of the classical systems fall within the unit circle, and the product of the corresponding quantum Hamiltonians possesses an eigenvalue with a magnitude greater than $1$. This confirms the existence of a quantum spectral gap surrounding the origin. We anticipate that our findings will provide a useful reference for the design of non-Hermitian quantum circuits. Detecting changes in remote sensing imagery is a critical task with extensive applications in fields such as agriculture, environmental monitoring, and urban planning. However, these images are often captured across broad spectral ranges, resulting in high-dimensional data that poses significant challenges for both visualization and analysis. This study introduces a novel unsupervised deep learning approach that integrates features from multiple modalities to identify discrepancies between two co-registered hyperspectral images. By employing a multimodal fusion architecture, the method merges data from different spectral bands to generate distinct feature representations, which are then integrated to facilitate change detection. The proposed technique was validated using paired multispectral and hyperspectral satellite images, and the findings are compared against existing state-of-the-art methods. The results demonstrate that the approach effectively identifies differences between the image pairs and outperforms other leading detection algorithms. Furthermore, the method exhibits robustness in handling noisy data and successfully uncovers subtle variations between the images. Overall, this study highlights the potential of deep learning to revolutionize change detection in hyperspectral imaging, a field that has historically struggled with the high dimensionality of such data. The research also explores avenues for future enhancement, including the integration of additional spectral bands and the application to larger-scale datasets. By advancing the field of unsupervised change detection, this work paves the way for more efficient and accurate analysis of complex imaging data. The associated code can be accessed at https://github.com/abhishekkumar12345/Unsupervised-Change-Detection. Keywords: Change Detection, Hyperspectral Images, Deep Learning, Unsupervised Learning, Feature Fusion.

This study investigates the link between residual entropy and viscosity using both molecular dynamics (MD) simulations and statistical mechanical calculations. Our findings indicate that the MD results are likely influenced by the specific fluid system used, suggesting that a universal correlation is unlikely. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the logarithm of the Sherrington–Kirkpatrick model's viscosity diverges as temperature approaches zero, implying the same behavior for the Kapral–Zaleski model. Finally, we show that the viscosity of the Lennard-Jones fluid cannot be accurately described by the entropy of the corresponding hard sphere system. Overall, these results suggest that the proposed entropy–viscosity relationship lacks the generality needed for broad application. Finally, the study concludes that residual entropy alone is insufficient to characterize the glass transition. Keywords: entropy, viscosity, glass transition. We propose a cyclical cosmological framework grounded in the $\Lambda$CDM model, where each super-cycle originates from a Big Bang, evolves through cosmic acceleration, and culminates in a Big Crunch followed by a Big Bang. In this scenario, every Big Bang is preceded by a brief, intense phase of cosmic contraction known as a "Big Slurp," which initiates with a finite scale factor and a finite, elevated temperature. As this process begins, the universe's total energy becomes negative, allowing it to expand from an arbitrarily small size. We demonstrate that a Big Slurp can naturally arise from the standard Friedmann evolution under specific conditions, thereby triggering the cyclical mechanism. Furthermore, we show that if these mechanisms operate, the cumulative entropy of all super-cycles would grow indefinitely, resulting in a paradoxically infinite total entropy for the entire cyclical universe. Consequently, we argue that a one-time "Big Slurp" within an eternal cyclical $\Lambda$CDM universe is impossible. Instead, we contend that our universe must have a finite age, implying that we reside in a very early epoch of such a cyclical cosmos. Additionally, we explore the potential for our current accelerated expansion to serve as a test for this cyclical model, with results indicating that current data are highly consistent with this hypothesis. Finally, we examine how this cyclical model addresses several fundamental issues in physics and cosmology. In conclusion, we suggest that our universe may be the result of a quantum tunneling event from a state of negative total energy. This event would have occurred during a period of rapid contraction driven by a Big Slurp, which itself was triggered by a prior period of cosmic acceleration. In this sense, the cyclical $\Lambda$CDM model offers a resolution to the Big Bang theory by suggesting that the universe did not begin from a singularity. Instead, it proposes that the Big Slurp emerged from a negative total energy state, which in turn arose from a positive total energy state, thus avoiding the need to explain how negative total energy transitions into positive total energy. Ultimately, this model suggests that the Big Slurp, in turn, provides an explanation for the existence of the fine-tuning problem. Finally, we outline how this cyclical model may contribute to the ongoing search for a theory of everything. Specifically, we argue that the cyclical $\Lambda$CDM model offers a viable alternative to the Big Bang theory, as it eliminates the need for inflation, the multiverse, and other speculative concepts

Developing speech-to-text applications for IoT devices presents significant challenges, particularly in ensuring accurate transcription during continuous speech. While end-to-end neural network models offer a promising solution, their substantial size hinders deployment on resource-constrained hardware. This paper introduces an end-to-end neural network architecture designed for keyphrase spotting in low-memory environments. We demonstrate that the proposed model can be successfully trained using established state-of-the-art datasets. Furthermore, the model's performance is evaluated on IoT devices equipped with ARM Cortex-M7 microcontrollers to verify compatibility with limited computational resources. Experimental results indicate that the proposed approach achieves performance comparable to existing keyphrase spotting methods while offering notable improvements in both memory usage and inference latency. This work examines dimer models on a two-dimensional square lattice subject to non-Abelian magnetic fields, specifically analyzing their large-scale behavior in the continuum limit. We demonstrate that these systems can be mapped onto a model of massless Dirac fermions characterized by a non-Abian gauge field, accompanied by an effective charge operator. The mass term emerges from the dimer hopping amplitude and depends on the local winding number of the gauge field. We establish conditions for the massless phase and investigate the associated critical properties. Furthermore, we present numerical findings that validate our theoretical findings. Our results indicate that these systems exhibit non-Abelian properties, with a specific focus on the nematic phase, which displays a distinct symmetry breaking pattern. We also explore connections to various lattice models, including the Kosterlitz-Thouless model and XXZ spin chains. Finally, we discuss the quantum analogue of these models, which display a rich phase diagram featuring a non-Abelian critical point. This research is motivated by recent experiments involving cold atoms in optical lattices. Our findings suggest that dimer models can serve as a versatile tool for investigating topological phases of matter, including non-Abelian ones. The potential for mapping these systems to Majorana fermions and constructing Majorana-based qubits is also addressed. This study is part of a broader effort to establish a systematic link between statistical mechanics and quantum field theory, enabling the derivation of large-scale properties of quantum systems from their classical counterparts. We explicitly examine the cases of the XXZ spin chain and the Kosterlitz-Thouless model. Additionally, we show that classical dimer models can be mapped to free fermion field theories in two dimensions, where the fermion winding number corresponds to the spin-1/2 Ising model's winding number. This provides a unified framework for understanding the critical behavior of these systems. Our results suggest that these models can be utilized to construct Majorana-based quantum computers. Group lasso methods are extensively utilized for performing structured variable selection, particularly when dealing with high-dimensional data. However, the standard gasso and its variants primarily address numerical data, while gasso-hd, a method designed for high-dimensional categorical data, relies on the inefficient count vector representation. This study introduces eGasso, a novel and straightforward approach for high-dimensional categorical data that leverages the sparsity inherent in sample-specific data representations. Additionally, we propose eGasso-p, a prediction-oriented adaptation of eGasso. Both proposed methods utilize local sparsity, and to address the issue of unequal group sizes, we implement a group-wise scaling strategy. Numerical experiments demonstrate that eGasso outperforms gasso-hd in terms of both accuracy and computational efficiency. Furthermore, applied analyses using data from the Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) reveal that eGasso can identify more significant pathways and genes compared to gasso-hd. Finally, we assess eGasso-p's performance in predicting patient survival outcomes, showing an improvement over gasso-hd. The eGasso package is accessible at https://github.com/SebastianKraemer/eGasso. The source code for all examples can be found at https://github.com/SebastianKraemer/eGasso/tree/master/examples. Keywords: high-dimensional data, categorical data, group lasso, sparsity, feature selection, pathway analysis. Mathematical Subject Classification: 62J05, 62F12, 62P10.

Embedded systems are increasingly prevalent across various industries, yet they face a significant challenge in balancing security and cost-effectiveness. To address this, we introduce T-Visor, a hypervisor engineered for x86-64 architecture to manage operating systems of varying security and real-time performance levels on a single embedded platform. Leveraging hardware virtualization capabilities, T-Visor facilitates the concurrent execution of multiple OSes, each operating in a specific privilege ring (Ring 0 or Ring V) and adhering to distinct security and real-time constraints. To ensure these requirements are met, T-Visor has been optimized to minimize overhead and reallocate critical resources, such as CPU time, to the virtualized operating systems. We have conducted extensive experiments to validate the proposed architecture and its resource management strategies. The results demonstrate that T-Visor successfully balances the resources and privileges necessary to satisfy diverse security and real-time demands. Furthermore, our analysis confirms that T-Visor effectively mitigates overheads associated with virtual machine execution, thereby enhancing the performance of the embedded system. Ultimately, T-Visor represents a cost-efficient solution for embedded environments, offering a unified platform to harmonize security and real-time performance needs. This study examines a two-population chaotic chimera system characterized by uniform variability, where each population comprises 20 identical neurons linked internally and between groups via symmetric coupling strengths. We demonstrate that synchrony breaks down when the coupling between populations becomes weak, resulting in the emergence of variability-induced chimera states. These states are defined by distinct levels of irregularity in synchronization between the two populations, with the transition point shifting based on the specific type of chaos present. Furthermore, we analyze the relationship between the spectral exponents of the two populations and the coupling-induced variability, establishing the parameter ranges for these states. Additionally, we show that the boundary separating these states from full synchronization can be accurately predicted using the average synchronization index, a metric that remains insensitive to the specific variability sources. Finally, we examine the interplay between these states and those triggered by asymmetric coupling. Our findings indicate that variability-induced chimeras can be interpreted as a variant of rotating chimera states, where the rotation speed is modulated by either an external signal or an internal one arising from asymmetric coupling. In both scenarios, the rotation velocity approaches zero within specific parameter regions, giving rise to rotating chimera states with periodic variability. We also characterize the parameter regions for these states, observing that their boundaries are determined by the average synchronization index. Notably, the average synchronization index proves to be a more effective tool for characterizing periodic variability-induced chimeras than the synchronization index. Furthermore, we show that the average synchronization index can serve as a reliable metric for periodic variability-induced chimeras even under asymmetric coupling conditions. Finally, we address the stability of these states, revealing that the average synchronization index can predict the boundaries between their basins of attraction. In conclusion, this research demonstrates that chimeras exhibiting uniformly distributed variability can arise from the interaction between two populations with distinct levels of irregular synchronization, offering a new perspective on chimera states and their potential applications. Additionally, we highlight that average synchronization indices can effectively characterize these states and predict their basins of attraction. This study addresses robust regulator design for uncertain linear systems, aiming to minimize the expected cost over an infinite horizon despite parameter uncertainty. We introduce a novel model predictive control (MPC) framework that optimizes the robust value function by employing a tailored piecewise linear value function representation and defining the uncertainty set for prediction problems as the union of scaled nominal parameter sets. We demonstrate that the closed-loop system generated by our proposed MPC scheme yields a regulator whose robust value function serves as a feasible solution to the Bellman equation associated with the regulator design problem. Furthermore, we present a learning algorithm utilizing online policy search to achieve near-optimal regulator design with a sample complexity comparable to the information-theoretic lower bound. Finally, numerical experiments are conducted to validate the practical effectiveness of the proposed learning scheme. Empirical results indicate that learning robust regulators for both high- and low-dimensional systems requires a number of samples significantly fewer than the worst-case information-theoretic upper bound. Additionally, our MPC scheme outperforms existing learning schemes designed for high- and low-dimensional systems. These numerical findings suggest that learning robust controllers for high-dimensional uncertain linear systems is feasible. The source code will be made publicly available. Multi-diagrams serve as formal representations for multi-layer braids. We present a novel algebraic structure known as the higher slice braid algebra, which offers an appropriate framework for investigating these diagrams. This approach generalizes the concept of braid algebra to higher dimensions. The algebra is constructed by defining a specific set of relations among the formal multi-diagrams and subsequently forming the corresponding quotient algebra. Our work provides an initial investigation of these algebras and extends the findings presented in [17]. Specifically, we demonstrate that the multi-diagram representation is faithful and establish that the higher slice braid algebra possesses a basis, thereby confirming its status as a genuine algebra. Furthermore, we generalize the well-known correspondence between braids and linear maps to the multi-dimensional context. As a consequence, we introduce a novel method for generating braids. This paper serves as an extended abstract of our research published in [17]. Additional details can be found in our arXiv submission [6]. This work examines the asymptotic scaling of reflected tensoriality, $I_{\Lambda}$, within random tensor networks (RTNs). RTNs serve as versatile frameworks for modeling quantum many-body systems, exhibiting diverse scaling behaviors for entanglement entropy, $S$, contingent upon the underlying geometry. Specifically, when $\Lambda$ denotes a ball of linear dimension $|\partial \Lambda| \sim L$, RTNs based on quantum spin models display either area-law scaling ($S \sim L^{d-1}$) or volume-law scaling ($S \sim L^{d}$), determined by the spatial dimension $d$. In contrast, $I_{\Lambda}$ represents the information contained in the reflection of region $\Lambda$ and vanishes in pure quantum states. We demonstrate that $I_{\Lambda}$ adheres to area laws whenever $S$ does, whereas it follows volume laws in the PPT-RTNs we analyze. Furthermore, our findings reveal that the Fusalization principle—which links $I_{\Lambda}$ to the entanglement of purification—is applicable to RTNs. Finally, we establish that $I_{\Lambda}$ functions as an order parameter for the quantum phase transition occurring in these models. This conclusion is supported by numerical evidence from the Nakiucic model, which exhibits area-law scaling, and from Clifford circuits generating volume-law RTNs. These results indicate that $I_{\Lambda}$ can surpass entanglement entropy as a sensitive probe for quantum phase transitions in certain contexts. Additionally, we explore the relationship between $I_{\Lambda}$ and the entanglement deficit, showing that the former is always bounded above by the latter. These results are consistent with recent findings regarding the holographic entanglement of purification. Overall, our results suggest that $I_{\Lambda}$ can outperform entanglement entropy as a sensitive probe for quantum phase transitions in specific contexts. In numerous natural contexts, coherent structures emerge from dynamic interactions between external forces and material properties. While these patterns are often static and passive, some active forms exhibit a form of heredity by transmitting dynamic information to future states. This study mathematically explores heritable patterns within nonequivial active matter by introducing and analyzing heritable persistent homology. Using this framework, we examine the information flow in one-dimensional active matter systems that store and transmit extrinsic shape cues through heterogeneous mechanical responses and local binding. Our findings demonstrate that the system's binding heterogeneity acts as a fundamental constraint on the long-term retention of shape information, establishing both necessary and sufficient conditions for this data to persist indefinitely. Furthermore, we reveal that binding heterogeneity can induce phase transitions in the persistence of pattern information, thereby creating a novel information-based emergent property in active matter. These concepts are validated through a detailed analysis of the active nematic grooving system, an experimentally significant biological model. This study explores the visual representation of invariant sets within the three-dimensional generalized Hénon model. We demonstrate that the collection of all possible holonomies of a flat $n$-dimensional connection across closed $n$-cycles constitutes a single, unique invariant defined by the space's geometry. This discovery holds significant potential for geometric quantum gravity, as it establishes an intrinsic unitary observable for the space of holonomies. Consequently, this facilitates the construction of a decoherence functional and a $n$-holonomy, thereby advancing toward a complete formulation of the quantum gravitational path integral. Additionally, we identify several applications within the field of combinatorial geometry. For example, the number of vertices in a regular polytope can be determined by calculating the volume of a specific constant-rank lattice within a Euclidean space derived from the polytope's geometry. In two dimensions, this approach yields a method to enumerate irregular quadratic lattices based on the geometry of closed curves. Furthermore, we establish a novel identity regarding the area of closed surfaces with constant mean curvature. This identity reveals that the area functional on the space of periodic surfaces in a constant time slice can be expressed as the sum of two functionals: one dependent solely on the integral of the commutator of tangent vectors along periodic closed paths, and the other being a topological invariant of the slice. We also explore applications of this identity to the quantum theory of two-dimensional gravity. In this context, the area of a closed spacetime region bounded by a cylinder is determined by the sum of the holonomies around all cylindrical regions and the Chern-Simons invariant of the same region. We also examine a scenario where the path integral simplifies to a path sum over the homotopy class of the cylinder's base. In this specific case, the invariants associated with the geometry of the base determine the Hilbert space of the theory and the operator for the cylinder's area. We illustrate this by computing the spectrum of the operator for a toroidal spacetime where the metric is the product of a circle and a Lorentzian cylinder with a constant metric. In this scenario, the spectrum consists of a single value, representing the area of the torus as the product of the circle's and cylinder's lengths. This result aligns with the expectation that a geometric observable in quantum gravity should possess a discrete spectrum. This study introduces an independent-particle model for the tunneling duration of a spin-1/2 particle, grounded in the difference between its spin-up and spin-down probabilities derived from the Larmor clock method.

We establish a formal relationship connecting the spin-y precession rate of the incident particle to the tunneling duration across the entire transmission probability spectrum. This relationship is subsequently applied to the same system, utilizing the recently introduced analytical Larmor clock solution within a piecewise-constant potential barrier model.

Furthermore, we investigate the behavior of the tunneling duration as the barrier height approaches zero. Our findings indicate that the derived expressions for the tunneling duration align with established results in the literature. Additionally, the duration exhibits a finite value at zero barrier height, a feature that remains consistent across various other models. Finally, we demonstrate that the tunneling duration exhibits significant fluctuations as the barrier height varies. These fluctuations are driven by changes in the spin-y precession rate, which are linked to the spin-up and spin-down probabilities. Consequently, the proposed model offers a novel and independent perspective on the tunneling duration of a spin-1/2 particle. Continual learning (CL) addresses the challenge of sequentially mastering a stream of tasks without forgetting prior tasks or requiring full access to old task data during training of subsequent tasks. Our approach dynamically selects the most suitable model from the ensemble for each task by jointly learning model architecture and fusion weights. We validate our method's effectiveness through extensive experiments on the CIFAR100 and TinyImageNet datasets. The results demonstrate that our method achieves state-of-the-art performance while maintaining lower memory usage and computational costs compared to existing CL ensemble techniques. This study introduces a new hybrid control algorithm, the Probabilistic Dual Simplex Algorithm and Genetic Filter (PIDA-GF), designed for aerospace flight control systems. Unlike traditional control algorithms, this novel method is smoother and more stable. PIDA-GF combines two distinct components: a time-domain controller and a state estimator. The controller utilizes the PIDA-GF algorithm, which integrates the Speed and Simplicity (SDSA) principles into a PID controller alongside a noise rejection mechanism known as the Genetic Filter (GF). The SDSA algorithm ensures smooth transitions between states by enabling gradual, computationally stable changes in control inputs, thereby eliminating the chattering often seen in conventional PID systems. Furthermore, the GF component functions as a high-pass filter to mitigate external disturbances. On the estimator side, PIDA-GF employs an Extended Kalman Filter (EKF) paired with a Kalman Gain (K) algorithm to accurately estimate system states. Simulation results using the MATLAB/Simulink aerospace toolkit demonstrate that the proposed PIDA-GF controller outperforms standard PID and LQR controllers in terms of stability, robustness, and disturbance rejection. Additionally, the method offers superior computational efficiency, making it well-suited for integration into modern Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs). This study utilizes Hyper Suprime-Cam Wide (HSC-W) imaging to analyze the stellar populations of host galaxies associated with $10^9$ M$_\odot <$ M$_*$ $<10^{11}$ M$_\odot$ active galactic nuclei (AGN) at redshifts $0.1<z<0.6$. We constructed a dataset of 1,000 images for $z<0.6$ galaxies within this mass range using HSC-W and the Subaru Hyper Suprime-Cam Strategic Extragalactic Survey (Hyper Suprime-Cam Strategic Extragalactic Survey: Strategic) (HSC-SSC) Wide Field Camera. Leveraging this sample, we trained a machine learning model to estimate the redshifts and physical properties of these galaxies. Subsequently, we applied the model to identify and characterize the host galaxies of 100 bright AGN ($L_{\rm 5000}$ > $10^{45}$ erg s$^{-1}$) from the HSC-SSC Wide Area Survey (HSC-WAS) within the $0.1<z<0.6$ redshift interval. Our findings indicate that the AGN hosts are predominantly massive ($\langle$ M$_*$ $\rangle \sim 10^{10.5}$ M$_*$), old ($\langle$ $t_{\rm age}$ $\rangle \sim 10^{10.0}$ yr), and metal-rich ($\langle$ [Fe/H] $\rangle \sim$ +0.15 dex). Furthermore, we observed that these hosts are generally disk-dominated ($\langle$ $f_{\rm disc}$ $\rangle \sim$ 0.65) and exhibit a strong correlation between their AGN properties and host characteristics. Specifically, AGN residing in older, metal-rich, disk-dominated hosts tend to be more luminous ($\langle L_{\rm 5000} \rangle \sim 10^{45.8}$ erg s$^{-1}$) and possess higher Eddington ratios ($\langle L_{\rm Edd} \rangle \sim 0.2$). These results suggest that AGN reside in massive, evolved galaxies, with older hosts favoring higher AGN activity levels. Additionally, we demonstrate that our image-based method is capable of accurately estimating the properties of AGN host galaxies.

Recent proton-nucleus scattering experiments have detected short-range correlations (SRCs) within the nucleus. Our findings confirm the factorization of the short-range correlation wave function at low relative angular momentum ($\ell_r=0$) across all nuclei examined. Additionally, we explore the potential of high-resolution momentum distributions to reveal substructure within these correlations. These results are interpreted through the lens of a recent theoretical model that attributes SRCs to hadronic molecular states. The study incorporates a detailed error analysis, including correlations between individual data points, and provides a roadmap for future SRC measurements. Specifically, we outline requirements for extending the momentum resolution of the SRC facility to better constrain molecular model parameters. Furthermore, we identify the most promising targets for upcoming experiments that will significantly enhance our understanding of SRCs. These include light nuclei with high abundance, such as $^{12}$C, $^{16}$O, and $^{208}$Pb, which have not yet been measured. Finally, we address the impact of long-range correlations on our analysis and suggest strategies to mitigate this effect. Overall, this work aims to establish a robust framework for analyzing SRC data and to guide experimental efforts in elucidating the nature of these correlations. Amplitude variations in eclipsing binary stars are frequently linked to nonradial pulsations (NRPs), which are also a primary source of low-metallicity star variability. This study utilizes the MESA stellar evolution code to simulate a low-metallicity eclipsing binary system, which is believed to exhibit NRP activity. Our models indicate that amplitude dispersion in low-metallicity binaries arises from two main factors: (1) mode instability, and (2) mode frequency shifts caused by the third-order core-envelope interaction. The degree of NRP instability varies across different modes, and this diversity is reflected in the amplitude dispersion observed in low-metallicity binaries. Furthermore, we find that the amplitude dispersion of NRPs is primarily driven by core-envelope coupling, a mechanism that can be modeled using the third-order perturbative code, NSPA. This confirms that our modeling results are robust. This paper introduces a geometric approach to the spectral clustering of infections across networks. The study focuses on identifying network structures suitable for vaccination strategies, specifically by vaccination within a small, pre-defined region. We present a work that bridges theoretical spectral clustering with mathematical epidemiology. The objective is to divide the network into geometrically distinct communities that exhibit different interaction dynamics with a specific region. To achieve this, we utilize the Laplacian of a contact process community detection model, which is derived from the graph Laplacian used in standard spectral clustering. This model is defined as the Laplacian of a contact process at the critical infection rate. We demonstrate that the Laplacian of the contact process can be approximated by the Laplacian of an approximate contact process, which is defined on a Laplacian matrix constructed from the combinatorial Laplacian of $\mathbb{Z}^d$. However, when goals are expressed using words, semantic ambiguity can arise, leading to inefficient policies that fail to utilize relevant linguistic cues. To address this, we introduce an attention-based word embedding transformation that resolves referential ambiguity by producing dynamic, context-sensitive word representations. We validate the efficacy of our proposed method through a comprehensive experimental study, comparing it against baseline approaches on both a simple MDP and a complex robotic manipulation task. The results demonstrate that our approach outperforms existing methods in achieving high rewards and adapting to new goals. Furthermore, we validate the context-aware nature of our solution using a goal-language perturbation analysis. To the best of our knowledge, this marks the first integration of attention mechanisms into GCRL, effectively resolving referential ambiguity within such frameworks. Graphite consists of stacked layers, each composed of a hexagonal lattice of carbon atoms. In this study, we apply the renormalization group (RG) approach to investigate the stability of a many-body Fermi liquid state within Coulomb-interacting bilayer graphite. Our findings indicate that the bilayer system remains a stable Fermi liquid, with the RG flow exhibiting a marginally stable fixed point. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the bilayer system displays distinct fixed points and marginal stability, characteristic of multilayer electron systems. Additionally, we observe that the RG flow exhibits asymptotic scaling behavior, and we calculate the bilayer Green's function, revealing that it possesses poles at the Fermi energy, corresponding to the energy of real quasiparticles. Finally, we demonstrate that the bilayer system supports a gapless pseudogap state, and we observe that this gapless pseudogap state arises from the self-energy. These results are derived by solving the RG equations for the bilayer system using the RG method. Ultimately, we conclude that the RG approach is a highly effective tool for analyzing the stability of Fermi liquid states in interacting bilayer graphite. Our findings also suggest that the RG approach can be extended to analyze the stability of Fermi liquid states in interacting multilayer graphite. This study introduces a new algorithm designed to enhance the efficiency of spin measurements utilizing Ramsey sequences, specifically to optimize frequency estimation. The method dynamically adjusts the evolution time of the Ramsey fringe experiment, demonstrating rapid and precise frequency estimation within just a few iterations. Furthermore, the algorithm accounts for realistic detection noise profiles. We also examine adaptive frequency determination using pulse sequences known as chirps, showing that the proposed approach achieves significant improvements in both resolution and sensitivity compared to standard techniques. These findings are supported by simulations utilizing quantum state vectors. The research is accessible as open-source software at https://github.com/SebastianKlappert/adaptive-ramsey. Additionally, we demonstrate that adaptive Ramsey measurements can achieve rapid frequency estimation with limited qubit initialization, minimizing requirements for quantum coherence. This capability is achieved by preparing the spin in a superposition state that closely approximates the optimal state through an initial evolution period. We suggest that these findings hold significant promise for enhancing frequency estimation in general quantum systems. Finally, we outline key challenges and future directions for advancing frequency estimation through adaptive frequency measurements. Specifically, we explore how machine learning techniques could be employed to determine optimal evolution times. Furthermore, we address the question of whether adaptive Ramsey measurements can be interpreted as a form of quantum Bayesian learning. These insights may contribute to developing new quantum algorithms for frequency estimation. Overall, our work aims to stimulate further research into intelligent methods for frequency estimation using quantum systems. This is particularly relevant for near-term quantum devices, where such techniques could improve the accuracy of quantum simulations and other computational tasks. Additionally, adaptive frequency measurements could play a crucial role in quantum error correction, helping to mitigate decoherence and other errors in quantum computing. In conclusion, our findings provide a foundation for future advancements in quantum frequency estimation and error correction. By leveraging adaptive methods and intelligent algorithms, we can unlock the full potential of quantum computing and pave the way for new technological breakthroughs. We introduce a technique for quantifying the centrality of nodes in a graph by utilizing the concept of "triangle inequality exponents" defined on the graph's metric space. These exponents represent the rate at which distances scale within an $\epsilon$-neighborhood as $\epsilon$ approaches infinity. By analyzing how distances between a specific node $v$ and its neighbors increase, we can assess the centrality of $v$. We demonstrate that this method, known as Gromov centrality, effectively identifies small-world communities within real-world networks. Furthermore, we establish the existence of graphs where the Gromov centrality of a node correlates with its degree, although we also present graphs with atypical centrality distributions. Finally, we provide an algorithm to calculate the Gromov centrality of all nodes in graphs featuring polynomially bounded diameter metrics. The efficacy of this approach is validated by its ability to successfully detect small-world communities in both air transportation networks and social networks derived from Facebook and Twitter. Additionally, we illustrate the method's success in identifying small-world communities within various real-world graphs, including those representing diseases, proteins, and airports. The source code is publicly accessible at \url{https://github.com/Chetan-Chauhan1995/Gromov Centrality}. Our findings indicate that Gromov centrality effectively uncovers small-world communities in both air and social transportation networks. Furthermore, we present empirical evidence suggesting that Gromov centrality aligns with node degree in certain graphs, highlighting the method's potential for identifying highly connected nodes. We have also demonstrated the technique's success in uncovering small-world communities in various real-world networks, including those related to diseases, proteins, and airports. Finally, we have developed an algorithm to compute the Gromov centrality for all nodes in graphs featuring polynomially bounded diameter metrics. In summary, Gromov centrality serves as a versatile tool for analyzing graph structures and identifying small-world communities. We anticipate that this method will prove valuable for a broad spectrum of applications, such as network security, navigation, and graph optimization. Additionally, Gromov centrality offers a complementary approach to existing centrality measures, such as betweenness and closeness centrality, enhancing the overall toolkit available for graph analysis. We introduce a generalized gravitation model built upon the principles of Special and General Relativity, utilizing an extended Minkowski spacetime that incorporates an azimuthal coordinate to represent the angular dimension of particle orbits around a mass source. This orbit is intrinsically linked to a time coordinate, which we define as "time at the top of the orbit" rather than global time. All physical phenomena are modeled as functions of this orbit-top time. By employing polar coordinates and the metric of an Euclidean plane for the radial and azimuthal dimensions, we utilize the resulting form to describe the motion of light and massive particles. This motion is characterized by a radial component and a component aligned with the orbit-top direction. Through this framework, we derive the perihelion shift of planets, the deflection of light by the Sun, and the gravitational redshift. Furthermore, we establish the corresponding gravitational potential. These results demonstrate that our model offers an alternative description of gravitation that accounts for the same relativistic effects as General Relativity. Finally, we outline the methodology for calculating trajectories and present the specific azimuthally expanded equations of motion for both massive particles and light. These equations are designed to be solved numerically, yielding radial, velocity, and time-at-orbit-top profiles alongside azimuthal orbits. Additionally, particle velocity and the gravitational field can be derived from the computed time-at-orbit-top profiles. As a preliminary application, we present numerical simulation results for the motion of light and massive particles near the Sun. This paper serves as the first installment in a series; subsequent parts will detail further applications, including the perihelion shift of planets, solar light deflection, gravitational redshift, gravitational lensing, gravitational lensing interferometry, gravitational lensing interferometry involving massive particles, and the time delay effect. Ultimately, we aim to establish a unified framework for describing particle motion in gravitationally dominated environments, one that incorporates both classical and quantum effects. This approach would facilitate the description of particle behavior in celestial bodies, planetary systems, binary systems, galaxies, and galaxy clusters. Specifically, it would enable the study of particle motion within the gravitational fields of the Sun and other stars, the Earth and other planets, the Milky Way, the Andromeda galaxy, and the Andromeda Galaxy Center Galaxy. Additionally, it would facilitate the study of particle motion in the gravitational fields of galaxy clusters, as well as the dynamics of particles in planetary orbits, the orbits of moons and satellites, and the dynamics of electrons and other charged particles in electromagnetic fields

This study examines the construction of sparse metric embeddings featuring low treewidth, a method originally proposed by Fakcharoenphol, Halpern, Raghavendra, and P\k{a}l\'{y}i in 2008. The core strategy involves creating a sparse random metric space and subsequently identifying a low-treewidth subgraph that effectively preserves the original metric structure. While this technique has been effective for embedding graphs and simple graph metrics into polynomial treewidth, it has previously failed to yield sparse embeddings with minimal edge counts when applied to general minor-free graphs or graph metrics.

We present a novel and streamlined analysis of the embedding method. We demonstrate that metric spaces constructed from random graphs, when appropriately weighted, admit extremely sparse embeddings into graphs with low treewidth. We establish that our random metric space framework supports graphs with bounded degree and bounded curvature. Furthermore, we show that for any median graph $G$, there exists an embedding into a treewidth-$k$ weighted graph with a failure distortion of $O(\log |V(G)|)$ and edge complexity of $O(|E(G)|)$. Our metric embedding techniques also result in $O(1)$-stretch embeddings into polynomial treewidth graphs for all median graphs. Consequently, this work extends the findings of the second author and M. Misiurewicz regarding $C^0$ monotone interval maps to the setting of high-dimensional $C^1$ strongly monotone maps. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this dichotomy is prevalent in the space of all $C^1$ monotone discrete-time dynamical systems, irrespective of strong monotonicity, provided the nonlinearity is not confined to a halfspace. These findings also imply the existence of a corresponding $\prevalence$ result for generic systems, where the $\prevalence$ is defined as the limit of prevalence as the codimension of the convex hull of the image of the nonlinearity approaches zero. Our proofs integrate techniques from the theory of variational inequalities, the theory of monotone circuits, and both Baire and $\prevalence$ category methods. Variational quantum algorithms (VQAs) represent a promising approach for utilizing near-term quantum hardware to tackle difficult challenges, such as simulating quantum many-body systems. The performance of VQAs relies on the entanglement between few-qubit subsystems and their surroundings. This study introduces a novel adaptive variational quantum solver capable of dynamically detecting and maximizing the entanglement between subsystems and their environments. The algorithm determines the optimal qubit subspace excitations that trigger strong subsystem-environment entanglement, thereby enhancing VQA performance. We validate the method's effectiveness using the Hamiltonian Variational Quantum Eigensolver (HVQE) to solve the Fermi-Hubbard model on a two-dimensional square lattice. Results demonstrate that the qubit excitation-based adaptive VQA successfully identifies the optimal excitation number for maximizing subspace entanglement. Furthermore, numerical simulations indicate that this approach yields a more efficient VQA for the Fermi-Hubbard model under realistic noise conditions. Consequently, this adaptive method offers a general strategy for adaptive variational quantum algorithms to identify the optimal qubit subspace excitations required for maximizing subsystem-environment entanglement. Additionally, this technique is applicable to various VQAs, including those addressing the eigenvalue problems of general quantum systems and the variational quantum eigensolver for quantum chemistry applications. The recent NANOGrav 15-year dataset hints at a common low-frequency background, while recent LIGO-Virgo observations identify another, distinct background within the more conventional tens of Hz range. We propose that both signals can be explained by a gravitationally amplified gravitational-wave (GW) backdrop. In this framework, stochastic gravitational waves with equation of state $w=1$ are exponentially enhanced during inflation if they cross the Hubble horizon near the epoch of matter-radiation equality. This scenario offers a compelling resolution to the Hubble tension by providing a new determination of the Hubble constant, $H_0$. Furthermore, the model predicts distinct signatures in the gravitational-wave backdrop: a low-frequency component detectable by NANOGrav and other methods, and a higher-frequency component accessible to current and future gravitational-wave observatories. Specifically, the low-frequency signal exhibits a frequency dependence of $f^{2/3}$ at low frequencies, transitioning to a steeper dependence at higher frequencies, whereas a cosmological population of compact binaries follows a $f^{-2/3}$ dependence. Additionally, the model forecasts a gravitational-wave background peaking at approximately 10 Hz for LISA, a dependence that remains independent of the inflationary dynamics responsible for the stiff fluid. Consequently, the gravitationally amplified GW backdrop presents a unifying explanation for various observed gravitational-wave backgrounds and establishes a novel probe of the Hubble tension. This represents a significant advancement in our understanding of the gravitational-wave universe. Finally, we demonstrate that the gravitationally amplified GW backdrop can be generated by a simple, single-field, slow-roll inflation model. The necessary interaction between gravity and standard model fields arises from the minimal coupling of the inflaton to the standard model via the Ricci scalar. Such models are highly predictive and can be tested using the proposed probes of the GW backdrop. The Atacama Compact Array (ACA) serves as a specialized instrument for the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA), uniquely bridging a critical gap in interferometric observations by covering a wavelength range from 3.0 to 8.7 mm. This study presents the first scientific outcomes derived from the ACA, specifically a spectral survey of cometary gas emissions conducted on a single cometary target. The survey targeted the 4.6 $\mu$m bandhead of H$_2$O and the fundamental rotational transitions of H$_2$S, CS, and SO within the coma of PanSTARRS C/2015 ER61. Utilizing ALMA's exceptional sensitivity, we identified a diffuse source of CS in the coma, which we attribute to the photodissociation of CS$_2$ ice on the nucleus. Additionally, we established an upper limit for SO of 1.4 $\times$ 10$^{26}$ s$^{-1}$ at a 95% confidence level, a value comparable to the SO/CO ratio in the nucleus of 67P/Churyumov-Gerasimenko. The ACA's sensitivity also allowed for a significantly improved measurement of the CS/CO ratio in PanSTARRS C/2015 ER61, determined to be 1.1 $\pm$ 0.1 $\times$ 10$^{-4}$. This finding aligns with the previously reported 67P/Churyumov-Gerasimenko ratio of 1.2 $\pm$ 0.1 $\times$ 10$^{-4}$, suggesting that both comets share a common origin. Furthermore, the ACA's sensitivity enabled a substantially more precise determination of the CS column density in PanSTARRS C/2015 ER61, calculated as 1.1 $\pm$ 0.1 $\times$ 10$^{13}$ cm$^{-2}$. This represents a tenfold improvement over the previously reported value of 1.1 $\pm$ 1.0 $\times$ 10$^{13}$ cm$^{-2}$. These results demonstrate the ACA's capability to deliver a sensitive, high-resolution survey of cometary gas emissions, thereby facilitating a more comprehensive understanding of the physical and chemical processes occurring in cometary comas. This paper examines Tsallis holographic dark energy, where the cutoff is defined by the Hubble parameter. We treat the Hubble parameter as a dynamical field within a Tsallis field theory essence integrand. This approach yields a non-barotropic equation of state, effectively modeling dark energy as a fluid. Furthermore, the density and pressure of this Tsallis field evolve over time in a manner consistent with cosmological observations. We also provide evidence that the complex form of the Essence model satisfies the conditions for a non-singular universe. Finally, we sketch the phase portrait of the theory, showing that it possesses an unstable de Sitter point and a stable anti-de Sitter point. Multi-Objective Mixed-Integer Non-Linear Programming (MO-MINLP) problems are prevalent in numerous real-world scenarios, yet their complexity often prevents most existing solution methods from delivering results within a reasonable timeframe. This paper introduces a hybrid approach that integrates non-linear multi-criteria branch and bound (BBNCP) with the Non-dominated Sorting Genetic Algorithm II (NSGA-II). The proposed method utilizes the NSGA-II algorithm to generate an initial feasible population for the S1-check and S2-check conditions required by the bound test, which are typically difficult to obtain in non-linear contexts. Furthermore, this algorithm enhances the feasibility of incumbent solutions within the bound test. By leveraging the strengths of both techniques, the proposed method delivers high-quality results in a reasonable timeframe. The study validates its effectiveness through six numerical examples drawn from the literature, demonstrating that the method yields competitive outcomes. Additionally, numerical experiments indicate that the proposed approach significantly outperforms the standalone NLCB and NSGA-II methods. Finally, the paper applies this hybrid algorithm to a real-world problem involving the optimal design of a refrigeration system. To the best of the authors' knowledge, this work represents the first application of such a hybrid algorithm to optimize refrigeration system designs. Secure and privacy-preserving data sharing is essential for the success of the biomedical data science community. However, the high costs and intricate workflows associated with current data sharing methods create significant hurdles, particularly for researchers lacking technical expertise. To address these challenges, we propose a new architecture designed to enable privacy-preserving data sharing through the use of gateway and client software. This system incorporates a file transfer protocol (FTP) extension that allows clients to retrieve files from repositories while applying encryption, compression, and decompression directly on the cyberinfrastructure side. Additionally, custom containerized analysis environments are deployed at the gateway, allowing clients to execute analyses without needing local installation. By integrating container technologies with FTP extensions, the proposed architecture offers a flexible software deployment framework, potentially facilitating data sharing within biomedical and life science communities. Aspect-based sentiment analysis enables the extraction of user opinions regarding specific aspects within user reviews. Although existing methods have leveraged emotion words to derive sentiment polarity, emotion remains an underutilized feature in current approaches. To address this, we introduce the concept of emotion representation integration into aspect-based sentiment analysis. To learn this representation, we employ a supervised contrastive pre-training strategy that generates context-aware emotion embeddings by clustering samples with the same emotion across various views, while contrasting against differently emoted samples. Our pre-training technique surpasses models trained solely on standard text data for emotion classification and aspect-based sentiment analysis. Additionally, we present the first large-scale Chinese dataset for integrating emotion representations in aspect-based sentiment analysis, comprising 1.5 million reviews and annotations for aspects, aspect-opinion pairs, and six emotions. This study explores the identification and estimation of mediation effects within case-control designs involving a binary mediator. We establish the necessary conditions under which causal mediation effects can be derived from data collected via case-control sampling. Our primary emphasis lies on scenarios where these identification conditions are met without requiring untestable assumptions. We propose a weighted estimation method designed to achieve efficiency when analyzing such sampled data. Furthermore, we present a parametric bootstrap approach to construct confidence intervals for the causal effect of the binary mediator. Finally, a simulation study is conducted to assess the performance of the proposed estimator. Additionally, we apply this methodology to a dataset from the Breast Cancer Prevention Trial (BCPT) to estimate a biological mediation effect. To our knowledge, this represents the inaugural case-control efficiency analysis of a binary mediator. Through simulations and a real-world application, we demonstrate that our method yields an estimator that is both highly effective and computationally efficient. Notably, our approach achieves this without relying on additional assumptions. The code required to replicate the simulations and the BCPT analysis is accessible at: https://github.com/ChenchenLi1992/MediationCaseControl. Keywords: Case-control sampling, Mediation effect, Binary mediator, Bootstrap, Efficiency.

This study examines a secure, multi-user radio over Gaussian channel where an imperfect channel estimate and hardware imperfections in the multi-carrier system impact both the legitimate users and an eavesdropper. To address these issues, an intelligent reflecting surface (IIS) is introduced at the transmitter to introduce phase shifts that enhance the channel estimates for the receivers. Furthermore, random dithering is applied to these phase shifts to mitigate the impact of hardware impairments on estimation accuracy. The random dithering is evaluated based on its influence on channel estimation, with the goal of minimizing the eavesdropper's achievable information rate (AIR). Consequently, an optimization problem is formulated to reduce the total transmit power by jointly designing the precoder, channel estimator, and dithering signal. This optimization is solved using a suboptimal approach that utilizes an approximate convex formulation and an alternating optimization algorithm. Numerical results demonstrate that the proposed scheme effectively improves channel estimation quality and security, outperforming the conventional configuration free of hardware impairments. Additionally, the scheme is shown to be robust against estimation errors regarding the IS. Finally, the proposed method is compared against a configuration that employs IS but lacks the intelligent design of the IS.
