Drawing from human cognitive science, this study examines executive function, which encompasses the ability to revise and resample an individual's perception of reality by retrospectively summarizing past experiences. We formalize this concept within reinforcement learning by introducing a novel contrastive value framework. Unlike conventional value estimation methods, our approach is designed to identify and resample specific experience segments from historical data, enabling the policy to learn from counterfactual viewpoints. We provide a detailed theoretical analysis of this contrastive value function and present a new algorithm, Contrastive DQN, which is provably equivalent to the popular DQN method. Furthermore, we demonstrate that our contrastive value function and the resulting resampling mechanism can address several promising open problems in reinforcement learning. Empirical evaluations on both simple and complex tasks confirm that our method is highly effective in solving these challenges. Additionally, we illustrate the utility of this framework in two exciting applications: automated driving and robotic soccer. These case studies indicate that our method can generate coherent and interpretable behaviors that align with human intuition. Overall, we believe this work offers valuable insights and valuable tools for a wide range of applications.

The Parker Solar Probe (PSP) has successfully navigated through six heliospheric passes, reaching distances as close as 18.4 solar radii (R$_{sun}$). This study examines energy fluxes associated with inner heliosphere solar breeze streams using data from the FIELDS instrument across these six passes. Energy flux is calculated by multiplying the time-dependent electric field amplitude within each frequency channel by the frequency channel's bandwidth. Results indicate that, on average, solar breeze energy flux peaks at approximately 1.5 R$_{sun}$ across all passes, spanning frequencies from 0.1 to 100 Hz. At this peak, the PSP energy flux is roughly 10% of the total energy flux across all electromagnetic fields. Furthermore, PSP observations reveal that electric field power spectral density (PSD) in the 0.1–100 Hz range during solar breeze streams follows a power law with an average slope of $-1.0 \pm 0.2$, consistent with a Kolmogorov cascade. Additionally, the frequency at which the electric field PSD transitions from a flat profile to a $-1$ slope correlates with the total energy flux in this frequency band, suggesting that nonstationary PSP solar breeze observations may be characterized by this critical frequency. Finally, the study demonstrates that PSP energy flux is significantly lower than the total field energy flux, a discrepancy attributed to the limited frequency bandwidth of FIELDS data. Consequently, this analysis underscores the necessity of ground-based and space-based instruments with wide frequency bandwidths to accurately measure solar breeze energy flux. Additionally, it is noted that the total energy flux in solar breeze streams is roughly 0.1% of the total energy flux in the solar wind. These findings provide valuable insights for future heliospheric missions, such as the Solar and Heliospheric Observatory (SOHO), Solar Terrestrial Relations Observatory (STEREO), and Solar and Heliospheric Observatory (SOLAR), which are currently or soon will be exiting the PSP's close-approach orbits. The paper concludes with several recommendations for upcoming missions, including Solar Orbiter, Heliospheric and Interplanetary Polar Explorer (HIPER), and Interplanetary Polar Explorer (IPEX), to enhance their capabilities for measuring solar breeze energy flux. Finally, the study addresses the potential impact of PSP's changing distance from the Sun on its ability to measure solar breeze energy flux. This study investigates R-parity scissors modes within the Two-Rotors Model, which involves two rotors with opposite parity. By defining an explicit scissors mode operator, we demonstrate that the potential for an adverse R-parity scissors mode arises when the rigidities of the two rotors differ significantly. Furthermore, utilizing the moment of inertia formula derived from energy surfaces, we show that the frequency of the R-parity scissors mode is directly linked to the asymmetry in the moments of inertia between the two rotors. Finally, employing the mean-field cranking model, we examine the conditions under which an adverse parity quadrupole scissors mode might occur. Our results indicate that such a mode is more likely in systems featuring two weakly coupled rotors with distinct shapes and moments of inertia, a scenario that aligns with prior experimental findings. Additionally, we establish that the frequency of the parity quadrupole scissors mode is inversely proportional to the degree of rotors' symmetry. Finally, we explore the influence of the cranking angular momentum on the frequency of the R-parity scissors mode. We observe that at low angular momenta, the frequency remains largely unaffected by $I$, whereas at high angular momenta, the frequency exhibits a clear linear increase. These conclusions are substantiated by numerical calculations. Finally, our findings suggest that nuclei with near-spherical shapes, such as those in the region around $N=82$, are particularly promising candidates for the existence of adverse parity quadrupole scissors modes. This is because the small moment of inertia in near-spherical systems results in a greater disparity between the rotational frequencies of the two rotors, thereby increasing the likelihood of adverse parity scissors modes. Consequently, the impact of rotors with different moments of inertia on the R-parity scissors mode is especially significant in near-spherical nuclei. To our knowledge, this represents the first theoretical investigation into the possibility of adverse parity quadrupole scissors modes. Our findings may stimulate further experimental research on the characteristics of parity quadrupole scissors modes. Specifically, future experiments should prioritize nuclei with two rotors of markedly different moments of inertia, such as those with near-spherical shapes. This study introduces the cell-mean-based neural network (CMNN) method for solving both hyperbolic and parabolic partial differential equations. The approach approximates the cell-mean-based flux within the finite volume method using a deep neural network. Results indicate that the proposed CMNN-FL method achieves high-order convergence in both space and time, surpassing conventional neural network approaches like the residual-based neural network (NNR) and the finite element-based neural network (FE-NN). Numerical experiments demonstrate the method's robustness across hyperbolic problems, including the linear advection equation, Burgers' equation, and the shallow water system. Furthermore, the CMNN-FL approach successfully addresses a class of nonlinear reaction-diffusion equations featuring steep gradients and discontinuities where NNR and FE-NN methods fail. The analysis reveals that the CMNN-based framework enhances stability and accuracy for both hyperbolic and diffusion-dominated problems. Additionally, the proposed CMNN method exhibits superior performance compared to the finite volume-based physics-informed neural network (CV-PINN) for hyperbolic equations and outperforms FE-NN for diffusion-dominated equations. Finally, the study confirms that the CMNN method is highly scalable and effective for solving large-scale problems. Keywords: hyperbolic equations; diffusion dominated equations; finite volume method; deep neural network; computational efficiency.

The ALICE experiment is dedicated to investigating the Quark-Gluon Plasma generated in heavy-ion collisions, as well as hadronization mechanisms and the jets they produce, via p+p, He+He+He, and p+Ar collisions, in addition to those involving heavy ions. The ALICE upgrade has been fully implemented, with data collection currently underway during a brief running period. However, the experiment faces a significant gap between its present capabilities and its future scientific goals. To bridge this divide, a comprehensive enhancement plan has been formulated, which is now being evaluated by ALICE working groups and the broader community. This initiative aims to investigate the physics of small and medium colliding systems, probe the internal structure of nuclei and their response to ultra-relativistic collisions, and significantly expand the exploration of the heavy-ion physics program, which will be revitalized in the post-Run 3 era. This contribution outlines the proposed advancements for the ALICE experiment. Specifically, it details the evolution of the experiment's scientific goals and the necessary detector upgrades to achieve them, including a new central tracking system, upgraded electromagnetic calorimeters and muon spectrometers, and new or upgraded devices for forward and vertex experiments. Furthermore, new data collection scenarios are proposed for the post-Run 3 period, featuring high-multiplicity Pb+Pb collisions alongside lower-energy p+p collisions at $\sqrt{s}=23$ GeV. Finally, the text addresses the necessary efforts to ensure the post-Run 3 ALICE experiment remains competitive within the broader LHC context. The discussion concludes with a summary of the challenges and opportunities awaiting the experiment. This document was prepared for the 2022 ALICE Upgrade and Beyond conference. The Unruh effect predicts that uniform acceleration generates entanglement between frequency modes within future and past light cones, even though these modes are a priori uncorrelated. This study demonstrates that the entanglement is characterized by a singular $2\times 2$ density matrix in the annihilation operators associated with the combined future and past light cones of the accelerated frame. We show that the Unruh effect can be detected through the Berry phase accumulated by a spin system weakly coupled to a scalar quantum field within these specific future and past light cones. Furthermore, the phase acquired by the local spin system exhibits characteristics of the Unruh effect, such as $\pi$-phase shifts for resonant frequencies and suppressed scattering for off-resonant frequencies. Finally, we propose an experimental setup utilizing ultracold atoms in optical cavities to observe this phenomenon. Our findings indicate that the Unruh effect can be measured via the Berry phase of the local spin system coupled to the quantum field, offering a more accessible means to detect acceleration-induced entanglement between future and past light cones. Additionally, the proposed scheme allows for the detection of future and past light cone entanglement at arbitrarily small accelerations, a regime where traditional methods like mirror interferometry fail. This research holds significant potential for advancing quantum gravity, as it enables the study of quantum field entanglement in curved spacetime and the investigation of quantum systems interacting with the quantum field under time curvature. Specifically, our findings suggest that entangling future and past light cones is essential for understanding quantum systems interacting with the quantum field in curved spacetime, a concept closely linked to the Unruh phenomenon in accelerated frames. Consequently, our results may facilitate the direct observation of quantum entanglement in curved spacetime, thereby advancing our understanding of the relationship between gravity and quantum mechanics. Finally, the proposed scheme may contribute to directly testing the equivalence principle in quantum mechanics. In this context, the Unruh phenomenon in curved spacetime can be viewed as a "time-like" acceleration, whereas gravity in quantum mechanics manifests as entanglement between spatial modes within the quantum field. Thus, the proposed scheme may enable the direct observation of quantum entanglement in curved spacetime, providing a means to test the equivalence principle within quantum mechanics. This could help resolve the conflict between quantum mechanics and general relativity, as well as the problem of time in quantum gravity. Extracting incident details from multilingual social media requires not only understanding incident detection and classification but also the extraction of associated data. While these tasks have been extensively researched in the English language, there is a notable lack of study on non-English languages. To address this gap, we introduce a novel dataset and propose incident extraction as a new challenge across multiple languages. Our analysis reveals significant variations in mentioning patterns, specifically regarding the distance between an incident and its mentioning entity, as well as the diversity of expressing entities. We present MEE, a new dataset comprising over 1.5 million posts in 11 different languages, annotated for entity linking and mention extraction. Furthermore, we explore and validate various entity linking strategies and mention extraction models tailored for multilingual settings. This dataset and resource will be made publicly available at https://github.com/Chenchenchenchen/MEE. The experimental findings and associated resources will also be shared with the research community. We hope the MEE dataset will support future research in incident extraction and entity linking. The concept of a vector bundle extends to any globally defined mathematical object. We utilize this generalization to establish a positivity result for characteristic forms applied to generic subvarieties within abelian varieties. This finding enhances a theorem by Mumford regarding varieties characterized by specific index properties. Furthermore, our methodology yields a push-forward formula for algebraic K-theory under generic morphisms. As an application, we confirm a conjecture proposed by Atiyah and Bott in the context of modular varieties. Additionally, we demonstrate the sharpness of the Mumford index theorem and offer a streamlined proof of the Lazarsfeld conjecture concerning big line bundles on surfaces. We also address the existence of non-constant holomorphic maps from projective spaces to projective varieties equipped with ample canonical bundles. To achieve these results, we introduce the notion of twisted equivariant K-theory and develop an appropriate Todd class formula. This framework not only provides a generalized Grothendieck-Riemann-Roch theorem but also generates novel formulas for research in algebraic geometry. Specifically, we derive a rationality formula for equivariant K-theory rings involving rational torus actions and rational gerbes. Furthermore, we derive rationality formulas for equivariant K-theory rings relative to finite group actions on projective spaces and weighted projective spaces. These formulas offer a unified approach to the rationality of equivariant elliptic genera and the rationality of the Euler characteristics of moduli spaces of sheaves on projective spaces. Additionally, we present a rationality formula for the equivariant K-theory ring of flag varieties under the action of a reductive Lie group. This advances the work of Grojnowski and establishes a link to the recently formulated equivariant K-theory of the affine Grassmannian. Finally, we propose a conjecture regarding a rationality formula for the K-theory of a smooth variety fibered by projective spaces. This addresses a question raised by Atiyah and provides a comprehensive answer to a conjecture by Atiyah and Bott concerning the rationality of the Hirzebruch-Petersson integrand. Furthermore, this formulation clarifies the recent work of Atiyah and Pandharipande on Gromov-Witten invariants associated with projective space fibrations. Our approach to the rationality formula also yields a rationality formula for the K-theory of projective spaces. This advances the recent work of Atiyah and Pandharipande on the Gopakumar-Vafa invariants of Calabi-Yau threefolds

In this regime, the stellar breeze—thermal material ejected from the donor star—may significantly influence both the spectral and timing properties of the X-ray emission. This study investigates the impact of such a stellar breeze on the X-ray spectral-timing characteristics of Cyg X-1 during its hard state. We employed the continuum spectral model pexbr combined with the timing model raqpet to simulate the contributions of this breeze. Our results indicate that a moderate breeze, defined as one with a mass of approximately 10 Earth masses, can alter the spectral shape of the accretion flow by roughly 10% and generate measurable changes in the power spectral density (PSD) at low frequencies. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the breeze can produce a "red noise" component in the PSD, a feature that has been observed in the hard state of Cyg X-1. Consequently, we propose that the donor star's breeze likely plays a significant role in shaping the spectral and timing properties of accretion flows around black holes. This finding underscores the necessity of including the donor star's mass loss in future modeling efforts aimed at understanding the spectral and timing behavior of black hole accretion flows. Additionally, we discuss the potential effects of the breeze on the spectral-timing properties of other low-mass X-ray binaries. Our findings suggest that the donor star's breeze can explain the red noise component present in the low-frequency PSD of these systems. The study examines the impact of an ether-like, or vector-coupling term, on a gauge theory at high temperatures. While this term is known to induce a first-order deconfinement transition in pure $SU(N_c)$ gauge theories, its presence in matter-containing gauge theories has not been previously explored. Drawing an analogy with the Schrodinger-Ising model, the authors predict that this vector-coupling term likewise triggers first-order deconfinement and deHosos transitions within these theories at finite temperatures. This prediction is supported by an analysis of the perturbative partition function, which reveals a first-order phase transition when the theory includes matter in the fundamental representation. Furthermore, the anticipated crossover behavior observed in QCD at a chemical potential of $\mu = m_{\pi}$ is also accounted for. Finally, the implications of these findings for Quantum Computing are briefly discussed. This represents a significant advancement in our understanding of quantum thermodynamics. We introduce a joint syntactic and meaning parsing framework that produces a single, unified parse tree for both tasks. This study examines post-merger outflows generated by magnetized neutrino-cooled disks, which may serve as the origin for short gamma-ray bursts (sGRBs) and/or kilonovae. We analyze a sequence of three-dimensional, general-relativistic, neutrino-coupled, two-temperature magnetohydrodynamic simulations of binary neutron star (BNS) mergers. Our findings indicate that a self-consistent outflow can be established if the total angular momentum is sufficiently high, resulting in a compact disk. The jet-driven post-merger outflow is characterized by a dense, hot, and magnetized gas. We demonstrate that outflows can be initiated by a single ejecta mass as small as $10^{-3} M_{\odot}$, provided the specific angular momentum is adequate. The resulting outflows are generally dense and hot, with temperatures ranging from $\sim 10^{8}$ to $10^{9}$ K. We also explore the potential for neutrino-driven post-merger outflows. Our results suggest that the outflows arising from these BNS mergers could be the source of sGRBs and/or kilonovae. Furthermore, we show that the outflows are likely to be neutron-rich, with a mass fraction of $Y_e \lesssim 0.1$, and that neutrino fluxes are insufficient to significantly alter the electron fraction. Finally, we discuss the implications of our findings for future multi-messenger observations. For instance, we predict that outflows from this scenario could be detected by the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) as early as 10 days post-merger, with a luminosity of $\sim 10^{40}$ erg/s. Additionally, we suggest that the outflows may be detectable by the Square Kilometer Array (SKA) as a fast radio burst (FRB) approximately 10 days after the merger. Our predictions regarding the spectral characteristics of the FRB are $f \sim 100$ MHz, with a duration of $\sim 10$ ms and a luminosity of $\sim 10^{40}$ erg/s. Finally, we propose that the post-merger outflows could be observed by the Cherenkov Telescope Array (CTA) as a very high-energy gamma-ray burst (VHGRB) with a luminosity of $\sim 10^{41}$ erg/s. We utilize public imaging data from the Hyper Suprime-Cam Subaru Strategic Program (HSC-SSP) to analyze 10,500 early-type galaxies (ETGs) situated between redshifts of 0.03 and 0.25. Our analysis examines 12 distinct tidal features, including tidal tails, bridges, and accretion streams, to determine their flux fractions relative to the galaxies' total light. We observe that tidal feature flux fractions diminish as stellar mass decreases and increase with cosmic epoch. Notably, the most prominent features, such as tails and streams, are predominantly found in the most massive ETGs and are significantly more common in the earlier epochs of the universe. We estimate the rates of major and minor mergers for these systems using a novel method that accounts for tidal feature visibility windows. This approach reveals that major and minor mergers involving ETGs are more frequent than previously indicated by dynamical studies. Furthermore, we find that major mergers are more prevalent than minor mergers for ETGs with stellar masses exceeding $10^{11} M_{\odot}$. Finally, we demonstrate that the fraction of ETGs exhibiting tidal features declines with increasing stellar mass, a trend that aligns with hierarchical galaxy assembly models. These findings collectively suggest that massive galaxies are less likely to experience mergers at the current epoch compared to their less massive counterparts. These results are consistent with the predictions of the IllustrisTNG cosmological hydrodynamical simulation. We conclude that HSC-SSP imaging offers a highly effective means of detecting and characterizing tidal features around ETGs, thereby providing critical insights into galaxy evolution. Our findings also reinforce the hypothesis that the most massive galaxies in the universe are dynamically relaxed. This study is the first in a series to be based on HSC-SSP imaging. Subsequent papers will explore the relationships between tidal features and ETG properties, the origins of these features, and the impact of merging on the star formation history of galaxies. The datasets used in this research are accessible via the Data Archive for the HSC-SSP Survey. The source code for tidal feature detection and flux fraction calculation is available at https://github.com/akimura123/HSC-SSP_TidalFeatures. Additionally, the tidal feature catalog can be downloaded from the HSC-SSP Survey Data Archive. This study introduces a novel gravitational framework, the Azimuthally Symmetric Theory of Gravitation (ASTG), which extends the well-established Tolman-Olinto solution in general relativity. ASTG posits that the gravitational field originating from a rotating, azimuthally symmetric mass distribution generates a bipolar outflow. This phenomenon is interpreted as a form of anti-gravity, where the gravitational field acts as a repellent force perpendicular to the equatorial plane. The mechanism relies on space curvature that flips sign above and below the equatorial plane, thereby producing a bipolar outflow. The gravitational field is described by two potentials: a Newtonian-like mass potential and a vortex potential that dictates the direction of the bipolar outflow. The bipolar nature of this repellent effect is demonstrated through its application to the bipolar outflows observed in young stellar objects (YSOs) and active galactic nuclei (AGNs). In ASTG, the required space curvature is achieved by the gravitationally bound motion of a mass within a spiral trajectory. The paper provides the solution for an axisymmetric mass distribution with finite thickness and outlines the solution for a infinite thin disk. Additionally, the solution is extended to handle bipolar outflows that are not azimuthally symmetric. Finally, the paper discusses the implications of this repellent gravitational effect for YSOs and AGNs. The ASTG represents a significant advancement over the Tolman-Olinto solution because it can explain bipolar outflows, a phenomenon for which the original theory offers no explanation. This capability arises from the bipolar characteristic of the repellent gravitational effect, which is governed by a vortex potential. The vortex potential is derived from the angular momentum of a spiral motion, and its inherent bipolar nature is responsible for the bipolar gravitational effect. Furthermore, the paper proposes that the spiral gravitation bond between a central star and surrounding molecular clouds is the mechanism driving this repellent effect. In contrast to the attractive bipolar effect associated with star formation, the repellent effect is linked to star disintegration. These conclusions are supported by the analysis of the $\rho$ Oph A cloud, a region containing both YSOs and AGNs. The paper concludes that ASTG is a viable alternative to the black hole theory, which currently faces significant challenges. The ASTG can be found at https://www.researchgate.net/publication/341100532_Bipolar_outflows_as_a_repellent_gravitational_phenomenon_Azimuthally_Symmetric_Theory_of_Gravitation_II. This study introduces the most comprehensive simultaneous and delayed optical search to date for well-defined Fast Radio Bursts (FRBs), specifically targeting 11 previously unidentified repeating FRBs. We detected no optical emission within 100 seconds before or after the radio bursts, nor any optical afterglow within 10 days post-detection. For each FRB, we establish 95% confidence upper limits on optical flux and radio-optical luminosity ratios at the burst peak, which are at least 100 times more stringent than prior constraints. Our findings indicate that if repeating FRBs originate from magnetars, their optical emission must be at least $10^4$ times fainter than their radio bursts. We further discuss the implications of these results for potential future optical follow-up strategies. We introduce an approach that enables observing language models through visual states, specifically by connecting them to external visual memory. This method leverages autoencoder networks to create a continuous, low-dimensional space for model visual states, allowing models to interact with this environment via visual controls. Our experiments on simple tasks demonstrate the efficacy of this approach for multi-modal applications. Furthermore, by extending this framework to multi-time-step generation, we uncover novel ways to study and analyze existing mono-modal generation models. For instance, we show the utility of visual controls in enhancing multi-modal few-shot learning and address the challenge of generating complex text via simple image commands. Additionally, this work marks the first application of continuous latent state models to natural language processing. Overall, we argue that incorporating continuous visual states opens significant avenues for multimodal learning and provides a new framework for analyzing models that utilize continuous inputs. The brightness of charged particle beams is a critical parameter in particle physics and accelerator technology. Brightness is defined as the product of per-charge density and the normalized emittance. This parameter is particularly valuable for applications involving high per-charge currents, such as particle physics accelerators, electron optics, and electron beam technology. Because brightness combines two emittance components, it remains constant during emittance exchange. We introduce a new method for emittance and brightness measurement that utilizes an electrostatic scanner. This technique enables emittance determination without relying on external beam pick-ups. Additionally, we present a comprehensive emittance analysis method that utilizes brightness scans. This approach offers broad applicability and demonstrates robustness. We validate the method through simulations and brightness measurements, demonstrating its accuracy. Furthermore, we outline a potential implementation plan for the future. This proposed scanner could be integrated into the HZDR accelerator complex, including the ELBE source line. We illustrate the scanner's potential utility by showing how it could enhance emittance analysis at HZDR ELBE. Our findings indicate that the scanner can improve overall brightness analysis accuracy from 10% to below 1%. Our results confirm that the scanner is capable of measuring both brightness and emittance. This capability is especially relevant for next-generation beamline experiments, such as the proposed ELBE Free Electron Laser (ELBE-FEL). This paper introduces AskewSGD, a novel algorithm designed to train deep neural networks using quantized weights. We begin by deriving a new class of layer-restricted cross-entropy loss functions, which can be approximated via a layer-restricted cross-entropy (LCCR) loss. Subsequently, we demonstrate that minimizing the LCCR loss for consecutive layers within a QSGN neural network is equivalent to minimizing the cross-entropy loss by applying an asymmetrical annealed interval restriction to the subsequent layer's weight matrix. Furthermore, we establish that the QSGN neural network layer involved in this restriction operates within a specific region of its weight space, characterized by an asymmetrical distribution of quantized weights. Finally, we illustrate that the proposed annealed interval restriction technique can be readily integrated into existing Adam optimization methods for quantized neural networks. Experimental results confirm that AskewSGD achieves high classification accuracy for image datasets such as CIFAR10 and CIFAR60. Additionally, we show that the annealed interval restriction can be effectively combined with other quantization strategies, including those utilizing stochastic quantization and post-training quantization. Table-based fact verification involves verifying claims within the context of tables, where both the claims and the tables are represented as tables, and verification relies on data extracted from them. A significant challenge in this domain is identifying the necessary information to verify a given claim. We introduce "disassembly," a novel strategy that breaks down both the query table and the claim into fundamental components to facilitate verification. Our method involves transforming tables into "information tables" and decomposing claims into "information statements." To validate information statements using information tables, we design various reasoning tasks. Experiments conducted on the TableQA and TABFact datasets demonstrate that our approach outperforms existing baselines. Furthermore, analysis reveals that our disassembly approach effectively localizes the critical data required for verifying factual claims. Generative adversarial networks (GANs) are powerful tools for synthesizing realistic images, yet learning the joint image-label space remains difficult due to limited labeled image data. This paper introduces a conditional GAN framework that learns the joint space by conditioning the generator on image attributes within an embedded label space rather than in the original input space. Our method employs a shared network to generate both images and their corresponding labels simultaneously. We assess performance using the Fréchet Inception Distance and demonstrate our framework's ability to produce images paired with accurate label pairs. Furthermore, we show that the proposed approach facilitates the learning of semantically meaningful directions within the latent space of the conditional GAN. Finally, we apply this method to generate images of specific fruit types accompanied by accurate descriptions of their color, peel texture, and seed count. Experimental results confirm that the model successfully generates semantically rich images with proper color, texture, and seed counts, as well as images with controlled attributes, such as varying the number of seeds. Additionally, the generated images exhibit high fidelity and diversity. Code is available at: https://github.com/ashishkumar1996/HiCGAN. Bayesian model comparison frequently employs evidence as the deciding metric. However, calculating this evidence via marginal likelihood integration is often computationally prohibitive, and Monte Carlo estimates can exhibit high variance, rendering them unreliable. Nested Sampling addresses this by transforming a multidimensional integral into a sum, where the stochastic component converges more rapidly, thus enhancing the reliability of estimates for the evidence necessary for model selection. This study compares different step selector algorithms within the Nested Sampling framework, specifically the standard dynamic nested sampling algorithm alongside two novel selectors: the quantile nested sampling algorithm and the nested sample density estimator. By analyzing simulated datasets, the performance of these methods is evaluated based on computational efficiency and accuracy in determining the evidence difference. The findings indicate that the density estimator outperforms the other approaches, offering superior accuracy and efficiency. This suggests that standard dynamic nested sampling may be overly complex and inefficient for simple model selection tasks, and that the quantile nested sampling algorithm holds promise for future applications. The source code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/JamesBuckley1994/step_selectors. Furthermore, the authors propose that dynamic nested sampling should be utilized solely when a prior predictive check confirms the absence of non-identifiability among model parameters. Finally, the paper concludes that, in general, model selection relying solely on evidence is insufficient; therefore, the nested sampling likelihood ratio algorithm is presented as a more effective alternative. This algorithm utilizes an approximate posterior distribution to assess whether models are not only equally likely but also more useful. Its performance is demonstrated using a dataset regarding the causes of the 1988 collapse of the M5 Bridge in the UK. The objective of distance labeling in undirected graphs is to assign label sets $S(v)$ to each vertex $v$ such that the intersection of these sets identifies pairs of vertices with a specified distance. While this is unfeasible for arbitrary graphs due to label size constraints, it is achievable with sublinear labels in dense graphs or in specific sparse structures like tree decompositions. However, for sparse graphs, an infinite label structure is required, as traditional sublinear bounds apply only to the maximum label size. This paper introduces a finite-label scheme for planar graphs that maintains robustness against vertex failures. Specifically, for a graph $G$ with $n$ vertices, we assign a collection of $O(n)$ subsets to vertices, ensuring that for any two vertices $u$ and $v$ at distance $k$, there are at least $k-2$ vertices $w_1, \dots, w_{k-2}$ on a shortest path between them such that a subset shared by both $u$ and $v$ also contains a subset assigned to each $w_i$. This framework enables a nearly optimal algorithm for the All-Pairs Shortest Paths problem, demonstrating resilience against a polynomial number of vertex failures. Furthermore, it facilitates a $k$-Shortest Paths algorithm that outputs a single shortest path in $O(n)$ time and the remaining $k-1$ paths in $O(kn)$ time. The proposed scheme also advances research into various graph distance problems. Additionally, we extend the model to handle distance between vertex pairs and demonstrate an $O(n^2)$-time algorithm for 2-SAPSP on planar graphs with unit edge weights. This approach also yields a $k$-SPSP algorithm with a runtime of $O(kn^2)$, representing an improvement over the previous best runtime of $O(k^2n^2)$. Finally, our model serves as a foundation for a distance oracle that answers queries in $O(1)$ time while using $O(n^2)$ space and supporting the deletion of a polynomial number of vertices. This oracle can be adapted to manage edge deletions and insertions. Notably, when vertex deletions are restricted to a polynomial number, the space complexity can be reduced to $O(n)$. All these methods are applicable to unit-weight graphs. This study examines time- and frequency-domain two-particle correlations within a driven, dissipative Bose-Hubbard model, utilizing both symmetry-adapted-adapted contraction (SACC) and stochastic quantum state purification (SQSP) to analyze the system's dynamics. The model involves $N$ bosons in a ring of $L$ sites, characterized by coherent tunneling and boson loss and gain at a single site. At steady state, the system exhibits two distinct phases: a superfluid phase with uniform particle distribution at low interaction strengths, and a phase transition to a Mott insulator with integer particle occupation at high interactions. In the dissipative setting, the spectrum of the Liouvillian governing the system's dynamics displays three distinct regimes based on the ratio of interaction strength to the boson chemical potential. The low-interaction regime corresponds to a hydrodynamic regime where the spectrum is dominated by the real and imaginary components of a single pole. At finite system sizes, this regime features a single excitation with a frequency scaling inversely with $L$. In the large $L$ limit, the two-particle correlation function in this regime converges to the steady-state spatial correlation function of a translation-invariant system, which is dominated by a single-particle mode. In the high-interaction regime, the two-particle correlation function is governed by a real, time-independent term. Finally, an intermediate interaction regime exists where the two-particle correlation function is dominated by a single excitation, but unlike the low-interaction case, this excitation lacks a well-defined frequency in the large $L$ limit. These findings are derived using the aforementioned numerical techniques, which enable the simulation of dynamics over extended time scales and the accurate calculation of the Liouvillian spectrum. SQSP is also demonstrated to efficiently compute the time evolution of non-equilibrium observables. Furthermore, the computational costs of SACC and SQSP are compared, showing that SACC scales more efficiently with system size. These methods are expected to be applicable to a broad range of quantum many-body systems. Supplementary material includes additional numerical results and a detailed comparison of the computational costs associated with SACC and SQSP. This paper investigates the solvability of divergence-form elliptic equations defined on the distributional current tensor field $q$ within $L^2(\mathbb{R}^n; \mathbb{C}^N)$. Since a tensor is divergence-free precisely when it represents the curl of a 1-cocurrent, the primary challenge involves establishing $L^p$ estimates for current forms. We establish that solvability holds if and only if specific "non-resonance" conditions are met, with an additional requirement for $n=2$. These findings are applied to second-order elliptic equations in divergence form involving $L^2(\mathbb{R}^n; \mathbb{C}^N)$ currents. Notably, in the case $n=2$, we demonstrate solvability without any non-resonance constraints. This result relies on a sharp estimate for the Green operator linked to the operator $\mathrm{d}\delta + \delta \mathrm{d}$ acting on $L^2(2)$-forms on $\mathbb{R}^n$, which we derived using a variant of the Hodge-Dirac method. This approach yields optimal spectral bounds for said operator, thereby confirming a conjecture proposed by A. Kiselev and S. Volberg. Furthermore, our methodology enables the proof of solvability for a broad class of elliptic equations in divergence form, encompassing various "nonstandard" scenarios. These include equations with non-diagonal symbols, those featuring a non-zero trace symbol, and systems of second-order elliptic equations in divergence form, provided certain non-resonance conditions are satisfied. Our primary tool is a novel estimate concerning the solvability of the Beltrami-Laplace operator $\mathrm{d}\delta + \delta \mathrm{d}$ on $L^2(k)$-forms over $\mathbb{R}^n$. This estimate is derived via a Fourier-analytic variant of the Hodge-Dirac method, which also establishes non-endpoint $L^p$ estimates for the Helmholtz-Weyl projectors on $\mathbb{R}^n$. Although deep neural networks have achieved significant advancements, they remain susceptible to out-of-distribution (OOD) inputs, which can result in severe errors. To address this, we introduce a Bayesian framework utilizing distributional Gaussian processes (DGPs) to enhance OOD detection. This method employs a Gaussian process on a manifold to model the relationship between inputs and the distribution of outputs generated by a deep neural network. By integrating an appropriate distance metric, we identify regions of similar data to establish confidence bounds for OOD detection. Furthermore, we propose a novel distance metric for distributional values and introduce the DGS (Distributional Gaussian Stratum) concept to increase model flexibility. Our approach is validated for OOD detection across various real-world datasets, including MNIST, FashionMNIST, and CIFAR10. Experimental results demonstrate that our method surpasses existing state-of-the-art techniques. Additionally, ablation studies confirm the efficacy of both the distance metric and the DGS in improving detection performance. Periodically driven quantum systems are prone to heating, a phenomenon known as thermalization, which prevents the emergence of non-thermal phases. This study demonstrates that heating can be halted within an open system by engineering a dissipative drive that extracts Floquet-generated excitations. The proposed protocol prevents thermalization by inducing Bose condensation of scalar field amplitudes representing these excitation modes. The proposed method is exemplified using a driven Rabi model featuring dissipative decay, where amplitude scrambling is avoided within its integrable sector. Consequently, the system remains stationary in a scar-like state, a finding that extends to broader classes of quantum models. These results suggest that scar-like states, which defy thermalization, can be discovered by analyzing open quantum systems. Furthermore, the mechanism of Bose condensation of scalar amplitudes may prove valuable for stabilizing non-thermal phases in periodically driven systems. The study includes experimental data confirming that dissipation eliminates heating in a two-level system. Additionally, numerical simulations indicate that amplitude condensation effectively prevents heating in a driven lasing optical-lattice system. These outcomes highlight the utility of open quantum systems in investigating quantum phases of matter that exist beyond thermal equilibrium. The model systems examined can be implemented using current experimental techniques. Furthermore, the concept of lasing into a quantum many-body system may enable the creation of novel quantum phases of matter. The proposed approach to dissipatively engineering non-thermal phases is supported by the observation that dissipation-driven localization of bosons in an optical lattice is feasible. Ultimately, the findings suggest that the interplay between Floquet heating and Bose condensation can be harnessed to design non-thermal quantum phases of matter. The paper concludes by outlining potential applications, including the realization of non-thermal phases of matter. We introduce a statistical time-domain analysis designed to characterize the performance of optical clock networks, addressing scenarios where the underlying noise is non-periodic and non-Gaussian. This approach is particularly relevant for analyzing individual clocks and tightly coupled, short-term networks. By utilizing a time-domain representation, we enable the characterization of arbitrary correlation noise structures and non-Gaussian noise properties. We demonstrate this analysis through a case study of an optical clock network network, comparing it directly with standard time-domain methods. The study highlights that the proposed analysis offers superior sensitivity for both comparison and coherent coupling networks. Furthermore, we show that the analysis capabilities derived from optical clock networks can be generalized to any system of time-domain instruments. Finally, we discuss the application of this generalized analysis in the context of time-domain instrument characterization. **Keywords:** optical clock, time-domain analysis, stability, comparison, coherent coupling, optical network. **Abbreviations:** AFQ: All-Fiber Q-switch; ALM: Atomic Laboratory of Metrology; ALPO: Atomic Laboratory of Physics Optics; FROG: Frequency Domain Optical Grid; LLO: Local Optical Clock; TDO: Time Domain Output; TOY: Time of Flight; AFQ: All-Fiber Q-switch. **Acknowledgments:** The authors thank the Italian National Research Council (CNR) for funding this research. This study introduces a fog-assisted software-defined networking (SDN) architecture integrated with fog computing to enhance service reliability, ensure fault prevention, and optimize resource efficiency for service function chains (SFCs). Relying on the adaptability of service restoration strategies, the proposal is segmented into two phases: an offline failure prevention phase and an online failure restoration phase. To mitigate failures during the offline phase, an evolutionary algorithm is employed to jointly optimize the provisioning of SFCs and their deployment within the integrated fog architecture. The objective is to minimize the number of failed network services, services disrupted by failures, and infrastructure costs. The system is designed to remain operational during failures by utilizing service migration and rerouting, which are triggered by the failure of one or more network service function (NSF) virtual machines (VMs). In the online phase, when a NSF VM fails, the architecture facilitates the migration of the NSF to a new VM. Subsequently, in the migration phase, failure recovery is achieved through service rerouting. This process involves reconfiguring flow rules to restore service connectivity and, if necessary, adjusting the flow rate to meet service quality of experience (QoE) requirements. To validate the architecture's efficiency, an analytical model is developed to assess QoE. Finally, numerical results are presented to demonstrate the architecture's performance. These results are compared against two baseline schemes: (i) a baseline that performs only service migration without rerouting, and (ii) an architecture that executes both failure prevention and QoE-based QoS-aware rerouting. The numerical findings indicate that the proposed architecture outperforms the baselines in terms of the count of failed services, services experiencing service interruption, and total cost. Furthermore, it achieves a 20% reduction in failed services and services with service interruption compared to the second baseline. Additionally, the architecture saves up to 30% in total cost relative to the first baseline and 20% compared to the second baseline. These outcomes underscore the architecture's superiority in terms of failure recovery, prevention, and energy-efficient QoE-based resource management. The numerical results also confirm that the architecture performs better than the baselines when rerouting is required. However, rerouting incurs higher costs than migration alone, particularly when the number of failed VMs is low. Conversely, when the number of failed VMs is high, rerouting results in lower costs than migration because it prevents service interruption. Consequently, the choice of optimization strategies becomes pivotal in determining which specific subset of parameters is selected. This study investigates the gradients produced by various objective functions to uncover insights into these learned functions. We apply a conceptual framework termed "gradient surgery" to isolate and analyze gradient contributions from distinct hypothesized components within neural networks. By integrating gradient surgery with objective functions designed to measure these contributions, we validate our hypotheses through numerical experiments on both synthetic tasks and real-world datasets. Furthermore, we explore potential extensions of this approach to gain deeper insights into neural network optimization. Finally, the accompanying code and experiments are made publicly available. We introduce a new holographic error correction code, the Hyper-INVARiant MERA (HIMERA), which approximates Holographic Hyperbolic Tiling Errors (HHTEs) using a neural network. This model achieves lower cost than HHTEs by incorporating higher-order connections. By utilizing the Holographic Error Correction (HEC) method, we demonstrate that the minimum distance of HIMERA scales exponentially with its code length, thereby ensuring a constant rate. Furthermore, we prove that HIMERA meets the product code criteria, establishing it as an approximate codeword. Additionally, we establish an upper bound on the local entanglement entropy for points in the hyperbolic plane, which is crucial for analyzing the complexity of HHTEs. Our findings suggest that HIMERA, as an approximate neural network, can effectively address the primary challenges of HHTEs, including the need for larger bond dimensions, increased circuit depth, and the absence of an explicit boundary. Consequently, HIMERA offers a viable alternative to HHTEs for modeling quantum many-body systems in the presence of a power-law external field. Finally, we outline several directions for future research regarding HIMERA. This work was conducted within the Holographic Quantum Matter (HQM) initiative. The Galactic Center exhibits a complex structure of highly ionized gas, characterized by numerous filaments that have been extensively studied. While several works have analyzed their radial density profiles, morphological properties, and dynamics, the spatial distribution of these filaments remains largely unexplored. This study focuses on the spacing between filaments, aiming to determine if they are randomly distributed or if their arrangement follows a different pattern. To achieve this, we employ the Pair Correlation Function (PCF) and the Structure Function (SF). Our analysis reveals that the SF displays a logarithmic slope of approximately 2 at scales below 100 pc, a feature also observed in the radial density profiles of individual filaments. We attribute this behavior to the hierarchical nature of the filaments, noting that the SF exhibits a break at a scale of roughly 100 pc. Additionally, the PCF shows a power-law increase at small scales, though the transition to a linear regime occurs at a larger scale compared to the SF. These findings are consistent with the radial density profiles, further supporting the conclusion that the filaments surrounding the Galactic Center are not randomly distributed. Furthermore, the PCF indicates a weak preference for the clustering of filaments. Finally, we compare our results with other studies and discuss the implications of the observed spacing between filaments. Our conclusions suggest that the filaments are likely the result of a combination of both large and small scale processes. This study investigates the optimal Conservation Voltage Decrease (CVD) problem within integrated primary-secondary distribution systems featuring distributed generation. Since secondary feeders are the main source of significant voltage deviations in these systems, addressing CVD issues at both primary and secondary levels is crucial for maximizing voltage deviations and load reductions. To address this, the paper introduces a distributed optimization algorithm capable of handling network topology changes, generation fluctuations, and varying load conditions in real-time. This approach utilizes local and low-bandwidth communication between distribution transformers (DTs) and secondary-side DG units to iteratively adjust secondary switch configurations and reduction strategies, thereby minimizing total decreased active power from distributed generators. Simulation results using a test system with 14 primary and 10 secondary feeders demonstrate that the proposed algorithm effectively mitigates excessive voltages and lowers active power losses. Furthermore, a comparative analysis indicates that the proposed method achieves performance comparable to centralized approaches while significantly reducing computational complexity. Finally, the algorithm's robustness regarding network topology changes and stochastic generation and loads is verified through comparative studies. Numerical simulations confirm that the proposed approach yields superior results compared to existing literature. Finally, the communication overhead of the algorithm is evaluated to demonstrate its lightweight nature. This study investigates a delay-tolerant advisory framework employing nonstochastic bandits. In this context, an advisor offers recommendations to a learner, who subsequently pulls an arm that incurs a delay-specific loss. Crucially, the delay associated with each pulled arm is stochastic, arm-dependent, and independent of both the learner and the advisor. Under these conditions, we introduce a new team algorithm designed to minimize the expected weighted sum of two regrets: one reflecting the learner's delay sensitivity and the other representing the advisor's expertise. We demonstrate that this approach achieves an optimal trade-off between these two delays, even when the learner possesses only a prior estimate of the pull delay distribution. Furthermore, we apply this method to two decision-making scenarios: one modeling a human-in-the-loop system where a learner prioritizes minimizing the number of suboptimal arms tested, and another addressing AI safety, where an advisor prioritizes minimizing the exploration of potentially dangerous arms. In both applications, our method outperforms existing techniques. Additionally, we extend this approach to settings where multiple learners with heterogeneous delay preferences operate alongside a single advisor. Extensive experiments confirm that the proposed approach secures optimal delays for all participants. Our code is accessible at https://github.com/ChenchenWang1996/Bandits_Advisors_Delays. Text-generation models are typically trained to continue a prompt, which often results in outputs that deviate significantly from human conversation. To address this, we introduce a new framework that leverages conversational rules to direct the model's attention toward a specific subset of the training data for response generation. This system is evaluated across various tasks, including open-domain conversation, dialogue state tracking, and summarization. Our results demonstrate that utilizing a model equipped with these conversational rules consistently matches or surpasses the average human performance on these tasks, without requiring any further fine-tuning of the base model. Additionally, our repository features a novel transformer architecture called "The Alchemist," which integrates concepts from the LEATHER framework to enhance standard transformer performance. This paper reviews recent lattice QCD findings regarding finite-temperature and finite-density hadronic matter. It highlights new results on the quark-hadron phase transition, the pseudo-critical temperature, the screening mass, and the interaction strength of light mesons at non-zero temperature, along with the pseudo-critical behavior under isospin chemical potential. Furthermore, the discussion examines results on heavy quark thermodynamics, the quarkonium phase diagram, and the screening mass and thermal width of the heavy meson $D$ at non-zero temperature. The review also addresses significant advancements in finite-density QCD, including findings from $2+1$-flavor systems with isospin chemical potential, the proposed pseudo-critical phase diagram, and the investigation of the first-order phase transition and polyakov loop behavior at isospin chemical potential within the chiral limit. Additionally, the quark mass dependence of the chiral phase transition is explored. This study introduces a novel, multi-fidelity surrogate modeling approach designed to estimate stochastic load time histories for offshore wind turbines. The method employs a model hierarchy that begins with a fast, low-fidelity physics-based code and a more accurate but computationally expensive numerical simulation. To analyze the non-stationary stochastic response, the stress data is segmented into local stationary segments, which are then modeled using a chained Gaussian Process (chained-GP) framework. This framework is specifically selected for its ability to capture non-stationarity in offshore structural responses. By utilizing the chained-GP framework, the study demonstrates the effectiveness of the proposed approach in generating probabilistic characterizations of the offshore wind-turbine system under varying sea-state conditions. The results indicate that the proposed surrogate model achieves a 99.9% reduction in computational time compared to high-fidelity simulations while maintaining a very low predictive variance. Furthermore, the framework is shown to be highly effective in propagating the uncertainty inherent in the surrogate model to the final probabilistic outputs. Finally, the study confirms that the surrogate model can reliably estimate the statistical properties of the stress time history, including the mean, standard deviation, and the 95th percentile. These findings are derived from a case study involving a 5.0 MW semi-submersible wind turbine situated in deep water. The methodology is expected to be of significant value to researchers developing probabilistic structural models for offshore wind-turbine systems. Additionally, the approach is anticipated to greatly benefit the offshore wind-turbine industry by enabling the rapid assessment of the impact of various design and operational parameters on probabilistic stress estimates. This capability is essential for advancing the development of next-generation offshore wind-turbine systems. To facilitate future probabilistic modeling efforts, the chained-GP framework and the proposed surrogate modeling method have been implemented in an open-source Python library. The library is available at https://github.com/akshaykumar1992/chained-GP. A detailed description of the library and its capabilities can be found in our prior work [1]. Social media platforms have become integral to daily social interactions, with over 50% of global internet users now active on these networks. This paper investigates the Izmir Earthquake event from 2005, analyzing data collected from the Twitter platform. The collected dataset was categorized into four distinct groups: disaster-related, hashtag-related, rumor-related, and non-related tweets. Subsequently, sentiment analysis was performed on the first three categories to determine the emotional tone of the event. Finally, an examination of the influence of highly active users was conducted. The event data was gathered using the event-specific hashtag #IZMIR2005. The findings indicate that sentiment analysis is a valuable tool for monitoring the progression of natural disasters. The source code for this research can be accessed at https://github.com/ozgurkayacik/twitterdataexamination. Furthermore, the study was conducted in a manner that ensures reproducibility, with all tweets accessible via the provided hashtag. Additionally, the most active users were identified through their follower counts. While the primary focus was on sentiment analysis, future research could explore other event features, such as geolocation. This work represents an initial step toward developing advanced sentiment analysis for natural disasters. The gathered tweet data is now available for further research applications. This research was carried out as a final project for the Social Network Analysis course within the Computer Engineering department at Dokuz Eylul University. We investigate generalized abelian Baumslag-Solitar groups originally introduced by Geoghegan and Lück, specifically analyzing their $R_\infty$ invariants through the examination of nilpotent quotients. Our analysis yields both affirmative and negative findings regarding these quotients. Notably, we demonstrate that an infinite family of these nilpotent quotients possesses property $R_\infty$. Furthermore, our proof relies on an explicit formula for the nilpotent lower central series of these groups, which we establish to be supercommutative. We anticipate that this formula will find applications in other mathematical contexts. Additionally, our methodology involves an extension of the Munkholm-Davidek method, which was previously utilized to study the property for one-parameter families of nilpotent groups. This work serves as a component of the author's thesis, which addresses the $R_\infty$ property across a broad spectrum of algebraic structures. This study introduces a new method for reconstructing time-resolved data, utilizing techniques from optimal control theory. The approach involves optimizing a trajectory parameter vector to maximize the discrepancy between observed data and data generated by a model utilizing the current estimate. This optimization result then updates the reconstruction estimate. The proposed algorithm is demonstrated through two examples: recovering a time-varying magnetic field from magnetization transfer recovery data, and reconstructing time-resolved magnetic resonance fingerprinting data. In both cases, the algorithm is shown to outperform an iterative T2-weighted image reconstruction method. Additionally, the method is expected to offer superior noise robustness, a hypothesis tested here by adding Gaussian noise to the magnetic resonance fingerprinting data. Finally, the paper concludes with a discussion of the method's general applicability. Notably, the demonstration code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/erikvoss/robust-inversion. This work is based on the author's thesis, available at https://www.diva-portal.org/smash/get/diva2:1220000/FULLTEXT01.pdf. The research was conducted while the author was a PhD candidate at KTH Royal Institute of Technology, Stockholm, Sweden. The thesis title was subsequently changed to reflect the focus on robust inversion of time-resolved data via forward-optimization in a trajectory basis. Additionally, the author acknowledges the reviewers for their insightful comments, which have been incorporated into this paper. This paper introduces SceNDD, a situation-based naturalistic driving dataset designed to facilitate research into automated driving scenarios. Compiled from the German Naturalistic Driving Study (NDS), the dataset encompasses 1,000 driving episodes across three primary scene types: urban, rural, and motorway. For each episode, we provide pre-recorded video streams from seven camera angles, along with contextual metadata including the driving task, maneuver, and a sequence of events. We have established four benchmark tasks to support two primary research directions: understanding human driving behavior and developing context-aware driving applications. To enhance usability, we offer two interactive exploratory tools for rapid dataset investigation and the ability to construct custom driving episodes. The dataset is freely accessible at www.scedata.de. Furthermore, we intend to make the episode annotations publicly available to enable the training of machine learning models for situation recognition. This initiative aims to provide a comprehensive, standardized benchmark for evaluating context-aware driving applications and to foster new research focused on situational awareness and context understanding. To facilitate this, we will release the annotation data in two formats: the original episode annotations and a unified annotation scheme. Both formats will be made available through the open-source platform GitLab. We anticipate that these resources will foster research into advanced context understanding and enhance the usability of context-aware driving applications. To support this goal, we will also provide open-source code for the interactive exploratory tools and the unified annotation scheme. Finally, we will host a workshop to demonstrate the dataset's potential and encourage contributions from the community. We examine the quantum information measure known as reflected friction within interface conformal field models, which arise from stacking two conformal field models at criticality. This measure is defined by the overlap between the conformal field theory and a specific reference state. We calculate the reflected entropy for these interfaces and identify the conditions under which it converges to the mutual information found in standard conformal field models, effectively recovering that mutual information. Furthermore, we investigate the reflected entropy across several simple yet non-trivial cases, including a kink model, surface Landau-Ginzburg models, and electron-hole interfaces. In every scenario, the reflected entropy remains analytic and exhibits symmetry with respect to the two conformal data involved. We also derive an explicit formula for the reflected entropy in a particularly simple model featuring non-analytic behavior and demonstrate the recovery of the entanglement entropy of an interval in two-dimensional conformal field theory, entanglement entropy on a sphere in three-dimensional conformal field theory, and the entanglement entropy of a half-line between two regions in two-dimensional conformal field theory. Additionally, we analyze the reflected entropy and correlation functions in the electron-hole model, observing that the reflected entropy diverges when correlation functions diverge. Finally, we explore the monotonicity of reflected entropy under thermal operations for this class of models and establish the strong subadditivity property for reflected entropy in both quantum and classical systems. Finally, we compute the reflected entropy for a spherical region in a four-dimensional free fermion model and compare our findings with the recent replica wormhole method. This comparison indicates that the replica wormhore approach fails to capture the complete reflected entropy for this specific model. We also address the issue of divergences in the replica wormhole contribution to the reflected entropy. Our findings suggest that the divergences in the replica wormhole contribution to the reflected entropy are regularized by the nonlocality of the electron-hole model. Finally, we establish a lower bound for reflected entropy in electron-hole models and subsequently extend this result to more general cases. In conclusion, we demonstrate that the reflected entropy of a half-interval in two-dimensional conformal field theory is regularized by the non-analyticity of this entropy. This study examines the stability of $\mathrm{G}_2$-instantons within nearly $\mathrm{G}_2$ geometries, specifically focusing on the moduli space of these instances on the $\mathrm{G}_2$-instanton manifold $S^3 \times \mathbb{R}^3$. The findings indicate that, consistent with the $\mathrm{G}_2$-instanton scenario, the moduli space comprises an isolated point representing the trivial connection. Furthermore, a finite number of additional isolated points arise, representing non-trivial flat connections. The primary innovation of this research lies in the explicit identification of these non-trivial flat connections. The methodology employed is also applicable to analyzing $\mathrm{G}_2$-instantons in more general nearly $\mathrm{G}_2$ geometries. Ultimately, the results demonstrate that the assumption of normality, typically imposed on the underlying $\mathrm{G}_2$-structure, is unnecessary for establishing the stability of instanton connections. This conclusion extends to generalised Calabi--Yau $G_2$-instantons. The techniques utilized are expected to be valuable for investigating instantons in broader geometric contexts. The strategies applied here successfully generalize the concept of the moduli space of instantons on asymptotically locally Euclidean manifolds to settings involving non-calibrating geometries. This paper introduces a C code creator grounded in a shallow embedding of the C programming language within ACL2. Unlike many existing tools that utilize an abstract interface for code generation, this tool produces code directly from a specific C implementation, resulting in what is termed a shallow embedding. The primary advantage of this approach is its ability to generate provable code; because the source code is identical to the one used for formal verification, there is no need for a separate "proof-friendly" variant typically required when using a shallow embedding. In contrast, deep embeddings used in other code creators often necessitate adjustments to standard source code to facilitate formal proofs. The tool produces ACL2 representations of C programs that are sufficiently high-level to be amenable to formal analysis. To demonstrate practical utility, the paper includes examples of formal analyses conducted in ACL2 on the generated code. Furthermore, an extended version of this tool, which incorporates support for dynamic memory management, is available online. The authors intend to explore potential applications of this work in the future. Keywords: ACL2, C programming language, code creation, formal verification, formal analysis, formal analysis tools, provable programs.

This study utilizes the relationship between Hurwitz zeta functions and fractional parts to derive a specific formula for odd zeta values, ensuring all terms are explicitly defined. Consequently, we present a streamlined proof of Ramanujan's formula for Riemann zeta values at positive odd integers. Furthermore, we examine the connection between the fractional part of $\pi^2 n^2 / (2\zeta(2))$ and the fractional part of $2\pi^2 n^2 / (\pi^2 - \lambda_0)$, where $\lambda_0$ denotes the first eigenvalue of the Laplacian on a random hyperbolic triangle group. We calculate the probability distributions for these fractional parts within the interval $[0,1)$ and provide numerical data regarding the first few moments of the corresponding random variables. Additionally, we offer a geometric interpretation for the value of $\zeta(5)$. Finally, we outline a potential link between these fractional parts and the vanishing of the Riemann $\xi$-function.

We investigate $J/\psi$ angular distributions for the processes $e^{+}e^{-} \to J/\psi+\eta_c,\chi_{cJ}$ ($J=1,2,3$) at center-of-mass energies near 10.6 GeV, incorporating corrections up to the order of $v^2$ in the heavy-quark velocity and $\alpha_s$ in the strong coupling. Our analysis of the longitudinal polarization fraction reveals significant deviations from the non-relativistic QCD (NRQCD) leading-order (LO) and $v^2$ corrections within the NRQCD next-to-leading order (NLO) approximations. Furthermore, we examine the effects of the topological spin structure on these distributions, finding that the LO and NLO $\alpha_s$ corrections to the longitudinal fraction are negligible at $\sqrt{s} \approx 10.6$ GeV. In contrast, the corrected LO (CLO) approximation, which includes an $\alpha_s$ correction, yields a longitudinal polarization fraction exceeding 90% at the same energy. Additionally, we provide the first explicit expressions for the forward-backward asymmetry and transverse polarization fractions at NLO $\alpha_s$ within the CLO approximation, demonstrating that these quantities are sensitive to the next-to-leading-order term. Finally, we compare our findings with existing experimental data. Our results indicate that the relativistic QCD NLO (RQCD NLO) approximation offers the best description of the $J/\psi$ angular distributions at $\sqrt{s} \approx 10.6$ GeV for the $e^{+}e^{-} \to J/\psi+\eta_c,\chi_{c1,3}$ processes. However, for the $e^{+}e^{-} \to J/\psi+\chi_{c2}$ channel, the RQCD NLO and NLO $\alpha_s$ corrections are small, rendering the LO NRQCD (NRQCD LO) approximation sufficient to describe the $J/\psi$ angular distribution. These conclusions are derived from the combined analysis of the forward-backward asymmetry, longitudinal and transverse polarization fractions, and the recent BESIII measurement of the transverse polarization fraction at $\sqrt{s} \approx 10.6$ GeV. Although the Signal messaging application enforces the creation of a PIN during onboarding, there is a lack of research into how users perceive and comprehend this security measure. This study employs a mixed-methods design to investigate user perceptions of Signal PINs. Our findings reveal that 40% of Signal users either lack a clear understanding of the PIN's purpose or are uncertain about its contribution to their communication security. Furthermore, among those who do understand, there is a significant divide in their attitudes: while some view the PIN as a valuable security feature, others consider it an unnecessary hurdle that impedes their messaging experience without offering tangible benefits. These results highlight a substantial gap between the technical design intentions of Signal PINs and how the user community interprets and values them. To foster more informed decisions regarding the use of such security mechanisms, we propose the need for additional user education and more accessible communication from security tool providers. Finally, we offer a series of recommendations for researchers and practitioners involved in the design and implementation of security features. Specifically, we recommend conducting user studies to evaluate perceptions of features like PINs prior to their widespread adoption, ensuring that there is a sufficient base of users who are both aware of and supportive of the feature before it becomes standard. Additionally, providers should establish clear, consistent guidelines to facilitate user education and ensure that security features are understood and utilized as intended. By aligning the design intentions of these features with the perspectives of their users, we can create messaging applications that are not only secure but also enjoyable to use. This paper is the inaugural entry in a series that will explore the views and experiences of users regarding various security mechanisms found in Signal. The rapid advancement of solar power generation has necessated its careful study and precise simulation. However, accurately modeling solar-spectrum absorption is complicated by underlying physical processes that create highly structured, non-smooth spectra, rendering traditional numerical methods often inaccurate. We introduce an analytical approach to precisely calculate the precise-solar-integration problem, which involves integrating precise-solar-absorption functions across the solar-spectrum range. This solution utilizes Gaussian quadrature and identifies the roots of specially tailored orthogonal polynomials, thereby enabling high-precision calculations with minimal computational cost. Furthermore, we provide a Python library containing our analytical solutions, offering both standalone access to the precise-solar-integration algorithm and the capability to reproduce our findings. This work serves as a comprehensive guide for effectively integrating precise-solar-absorption functions. Our developed library is accessible at https://github.com/leopoldo-oliveira/solar-gaussian. Additionally, we have created a jupyter-notebook tutorial to assist users in utilizing the library for their own precise-solar-integration needs. The tutorial is available at https://github.com/leopolaro/solar-gaussian. We demonstrate that the solar-weighted Gaussian quadrature algorithm yields high-precision results when computing the precise-solar-integration of precise-solar-absorption functions. This method is highly effective for precise-solar-integration across the entire solar-spectrum, particularly when dealing with non-smooth spectral functions. We provide detailed examples of high-precision calculations for the precise-solar-integration of precise-solar-absorption spectra featuring sharp spectral lines, step functions, and delta functions. Our findings indicate that the solar-weighted Gaussian quadrature algorithm is both accurate and highly efficient for these computations. We conclude that solar-weighted Gaussian quadrature is the ideal approach for solving the precise-solar-integration problem. We anticipate that this method will be widely adopted in future research to enable high-precision calculations of solar-absorption spectra. The curvature information provided by the generalized Gauss-Newton (gGN) matrix is vital for comprehending and enhancing numerous optimization-based learning algorithms. However, its size, scaling with the square of the input dimension, renders it impractical for large-scale applications. This study introduces a low-rank approximation of the gGN matrix that addresses these challenges. We demonstrate that this approximation yields a curvature-based local model with equivalent convergence guarantees as the original gGN approach. Furthermore, the proposed approximation is adaptable to various data-centric learning tasks involving input data and structural priors. By integrating curvature awareness with structural priors, our method enhances the understanding of optimization and learning processes in high-dimensional contexts. The effectiveness of our low-rank gGN framework is validated through numerical experiments and empirical evaluations on few-shot learning and few-sample reinforcement learning tasks. Our learning framework is accessible at https://github.com/SebastianSchauer1992/ViViT. Additionally, our source code for the numerical experiments can be found at https://github.com/SebastianSchauer1992/curvature_access. The source code for empirical experiments is available at https://github.com/SebastianSchauer1992/few-shot-learning and https://github.com/SebastianSchauer1992/Reinforcement-Learning. Sebastian Schauer is a Ph.D. candidate at the University of Bonn, Germany. His research focuses on statistical learning theory, particularly deep learning, with an emphasis on stochastic and iterative methods. He is particularly interested in analyzing these methods regarding their computational complexity, memory usage, and convergence properties.
