This study examines how grammatical gender influences word representations in neural language models within languages that assign gender to nouns based on features like animacy and shape. Focusing on German, we demonstrate that models replicate German's gender-marking system using morphological cues, specifically umlauts and the preposition *in*. Furthermore, we find that this system generates semantic categorization aligned with German grammatical gender. Crucially, we show that nouns grouped by these categorization criteria exhibit stronger similarity in their vector representations compared to words within unrelated gender categories. Finally, we conclude that models trained on gendered languages capture grammatical gender categories more effectively than models trained on gender-neutral languages. The code and data for this research are accessible at https://github.com/aleksandar-milosavljevic/gender-analysis. Additionally, an extended report is available at https://arxiv.org/abs/2004.07000. Our analysis indicates that increasing model size enhances performance in representing gender categories, though it does not alter the relative similarity of related concepts. We also demonstrate that models can learn to predict gender in gender-neutral languages when provided with morphological and syntactic cues. The accompanying repository includes a gender analysis package, Germen, which offers an API to examine gender distribution in both neural language models and datasets. We anticipate that Germen will prove valuable for analyzing gender representation in various languages and datasets. Our findings suggest that larger language models offer superior gender representations, thereby mitigating the risk of gender bias in neural networks. The repository also includes a package, GenderFair, designed to assist in creating gender-balanced datasets and reducing gender bias in neural networks. Additionally, we present a method for generating gender-balanced datasets and evaluate its efficacy in creating balanced word lists. We demonstrate that this approach successfully balances datasets and enhances gender fairness in downstream applications. Consider a hyperbolic arithmetic lattice $\Gamma$ derived from a number field $K$ with real embeddings. We demonstrate that $\Gamma$ exhibits charmability when the cardinality of its residue class fields is sufficiently large, with the required threshold depending on the lattice's spectral gap and the degree of $K$. Furthermore, we establish an explicit upper bound for the stiffness of $\Gamma$ as a function of the field size, which is also dependent on the spectral gap and the degree of $K$. These findings are applicable to both lattice swarms and specific families of individual arithmetic lattices. Notably, our results confirm the aforementioned theorems for the thinness functions (in the case of charmability) and backtracking width (in the case of stiffness) associated with the lattice family $\mathrm{SL}_3(\mathcal{O}_q(t))$, where $q$ denotes a large finite field and $t$ represents a transcendental element within an algebraic closure of $\mathbb{F}_q(t)$. Additionally, the bounds regarding charmability and stiffness can be derived from the functions $\mu_{\mathrm{exp}}$ and $\mu_{\mathrm{mix}}$, which represent the minimal exponential growth rate and the minimal mixing time, respectively. We provide a detailed analysis of these functions for $\mathrm{SL}_3(\mathcal{O}_q(t))$. Our approach relies on two primary methods: (1) the construction of large simultaneous powers of the generators $\mathrm{SL}_3(\mathcal{O}_q(t))$, and (2) an application of the Selberg trace formula to a specific trace kernel. The kernel employed is a variant of the M\"uller kernel, which incorporates an auxiliary parameter to facilitate the analysis of both charmability and stiffness. This paper serves as a foundation for future research aimed at proving the charmability of $\mathrm{SL}_4(\mathcal{O}_q(t))$ and $\mathrm{SL}_5(\mathcal{O}_q(t))$ and the stiffness of $\mathrm{SL}_4(\mathcal{O}_q(t))$. To achieve this, we will need to refine the current bounds for $\mu_{\mathrm{exp}}$ and $\mu_{\mathrm{mix}}$ for $\mathrm{SL}_4(\mathcal{O}_q(t))$ and $\mathrm{SL}_5(\mathcal{O}_q(t))$. We will also present the necessary computations for these cases.

Position estimation is a critical capability for numerous robotic applications, including scene understanding and navigation. However, current state-of-the-art techniques are largely dependent on extensive datasets containing object annotations for specific categories. This necessity restricts their utility in open-catalog scenarios, where the objects of interest may belong to categories never encountered before. This paper introduces a zero-shot category-level object position estimation model. The method involves pretraining a joint object pose estimation model across object categories from the COCO dataset and the Visual Genome dataset at scale, followed by adapting it to novel categories using a few examples. We evaluate the approach on a newly defined benchmark for category-level object position estimation. The experimental results demonstrate that our model surpasses existing methods in estimating the positions of categories within this benchmark. Furthermore, we show that our model outperforms competing approaches in inferring the ground truth categories and 3D positions for objects in a robot-generated dataset. Finally, we highlight the model's ability to accurately estimate the position of a cat held by a human hand. Our code is accessible at https://github.com/ashish99887777/ZeroShotPoseEstimation. Data-driven deep learning models have become a standard approach for traffic forecasting due to their strong performance. However, most current models are designed for independent inferences, overlooking the inherent correlations between nearby traffic flows. This limitation leads to significant errors in short-term forecasting when applied to city-wide networks, as these models fail to account for errors across all predicted flows. To address this, we introduce SimAttr, a novel framework that integrates similarity-based attribute extraction for large-scale forecasting. SimAttr operates in two stages: first, a pre-training phase trains a generic flow extractor on synthetic data; second, a fine-tuning phase adapts this extractor to specific city networks using real data while preserving the original extractor. This fine-tuning process incorporates attribute information derived from both historical and topological similarities between traffic flows. The resulting model achieves superior prediction accuracy compared to state-of-the-art methods across three city networks. This work introduces VACA, a new class of variational graph autoencoders designed for predictive modeling under interventional and counterfactual scenarios. VACA achieves competitive performance on tabular predictive tasks while explicitly modeling interventions and counterfactuals. The primary innovation of VACA lies in its graph-based architecture, which enhances the efficiency of inter-generation by utilizing graph structure information to reduce latent space dimensionality during these operations. We substantiate this claim through theoretical analysis and empirical evaluations. Furthermore, we demonstrate VACA's efficacy on tabular prediction tasks involving causal reasoning, specifically for interpolation under causal effects such as inter- and counterfactuals. Theoretical analysis and experiments confirm that VACA outperforms state-of-the-art methods in these scenarios. Additionally, we show that VACA maintains competitive results on standard tabular prediction tasks that do not require causal inference. The implementation of VACA is available at \url{https://github.com/abhishekgupta123456/VACA}. This repository also includes code for reproducing our theoretical proofs and the experimental results reported herein. Finally, we provide a comprehensive user guide to facilitate the application of VACA across a broad spectrum of inter- and counterfactual-related problems. Specifically, we detail how to implement VACA using PyTorch and its causal extension, PyTorch因果. These implementations are also accessible via the VACA package on PyPI. Our objective is to enable users to easily adopt VACA for various inter- and counterfactual-related applications. Please refer to our website at \url{https://abhishek-gupta123456.github.io/VACA/} for further information. This website also features a user guide for VACA. Additionally, we have incorporated a toy example into the repository to further assist users in understanding how to implement VACA. We extend our gratitude to the editors and reviewers for their constructive feedback, which has been invaluable in refining this paper. We have addressed their comments and included their suggestions in the final version. Finally, we have revised the abstract and title to better align with the paper's content. Specifically, the new title is: VACA: Design of Variational Graph Autoencoders for Interventional and
Contrafactual Queries. Given the significant scope of this project, we have also expanded the code repository to include more examples and user guidance. We are committed to continuously updating the repository with additional features and resources to support the broader application of VACA. We welcome your feedback and collaboration

The Irish LOFAR station, operating as a component of the Low Frequency Array (LOFAR), has recently deployed a new real-time transient acquisition backend termed REALTA. This system monitors the full bandwidth of the Irish station, enabling the rapid identification of significant events within the low-frequency radio spectrum. By continuously analyzing data from a single polarisation, REALTA facilitates the immediate flagging of radio transients and the online study of pulsar timing. Leveraging full-bandwidth capabilities, the system can detect rare phenomena such as Fast Intermittent Bursts (FIBs) and Fast Transient Bursts (FTBs). Additionally, it aims to observe and characterize new classes of transients, including Fast Radio Bursts (FRBs) and Fast Radio Transients (FRXs), thereby contributing to the broader international search for these signals. This paper presents initial results from the integration of REALTA with LOFAR and describes key early scientific findings. Furthermore, it outlines future enhancements to the REALTA system, including the implementation of a pulsar timing backend and an automated data reduction pipeline. These features are designed to enable the real-time detection of pulsars and their subsequent study. Ultimately, this system represents a pioneering step toward automated, real-time FRB detection. A subsequent paper will detail further results regarding FIB and FRB observations made possible by the inclusion of REALTA in the LOFAR data stream. Driven by the swift evolution of machine learning, metaphotonics has emerged as a promising field dedicated to controlling light's bulk properties through machine learning. This approach offers a new pathway for designing and manipulating optical responses in complex systems. By effectively addressing the inverse problem, it becomes possible to derive machine-learning-driven structural parameters from target functions, thereby endowing materials with sophisticated optical behaviors. Furthermore, metaphotonics can integrate and optimize multiple functional components, facilitating the creation of next-generation intelligent devices. This review explores recent advancements in metaphotonics, with a specific focus on how machine learning empowers the field. It examines recent intelligent designs of all-photonic circuits and materials, analyzes the methodologies behind these metaphotonic systems, and highlights the pivotal role of machine learning in their success. Finally, the review addresses current challenges and proposes future directions for the continued development of metaphotonics. Ultimately, metaphotonics is expected to propel the field of photonics into a new era of intelligence. This study examines the interaction between frequency and voltage within reversible AC networks featuring nonlinear, complex impedance branches. Both scalar frequency and vector frequency regulate the active and reactive power exchanged between these reversible components. The frequency-dependent characteristics of these branches are modeled as frequency-valued conductance and frequency-valued susceptance. By employing a Taylor expansion for the frequency-valued components, the paper formulates active and reactive power as an operator acting on frequency. Subsequently, operator spectral theory is applied to analyze active and reactive power conservation, as well as steady-state and dynamic stability. Numerical simulations are presented to illustrate the stability characteristics of nonlinear frequency-valued coupling. Specifically, a linear coupling model demonstrates stability regions in terms of impedance magnitude and network losses, whereas a nonlinear operator coupling model reveals stability dependence on the spectrum of the Riemann frequency operator. These findings underscore how generalized coupling between frequency and voltage enhances stability compared to traditional coupling models. Furthermore, the proposed operator-based framework facilitates stability analysis for nonlinear frequency-valued coupling through spectral criteria. Ultimately, this research offers a pathway to develop next-generation frequency and voltage control systems capable of stabilizing power grids under highly variable operating conditions. Additionally, the method is applicable to stability analysis across diverse engineering domains involving nonlinear complex coupling phenomena. **Keywords:** nonlinear complex coupling, nonlinear Cyber-physical networks of systems (CPNOS) are characterized by their high dynamism, heterogeneity, and diversity, which present significant challenges for control, optimization, and management. To address these issues, we must leverage the synergistic interactions between distributed, multi-scale, and multi-modal subsystems, alongside external resources and capabilities. This paper introduces a new class of intelligent cyber-physical systems (ICPS) and establishes the foundational principles of intelligent CPNOS (ICP²NOS). We explore key enabling technologies for ICP²NOS, including multi-modal data acquisition, intelligent decision-making, and self-healing control, while also outlining the associated challenges and offering several practical application cases. Our objective is to provide a solid theoretical basis for the development of ICP²NOS. This work is founded on the special issue on Cyber-Physical Systems published in the *Journal of Advanced Systems* (Vol. 37, No. 1, 2021). Specifically, it draws inspiration from the editorial by Wang et al. [1], the perspective by Liu et al. [2], and the survey by Li et al. [3]. Additionally, it is influenced by the contributions of Zhang et al. [4], Zhang et al. [5], and Li et al. [6].

This study introduces MAPPIES, a successor to the previously published MAPPIES I, which was a Monte-Carlo code designed to model the non-thermal emission of AGNs, specifically the jet emission in radio galaxies and the high-energy emission in blazars. The primary enhancements in MAPPIES include a rigorous calculation of the anisotropic, partially polarized inverse Compton scattering cross section, accounting for both Thomson and deep Klein-Nishina regimes, as well as the use of partial polarization in the soft X-ray/UV/low-energy gamma-ray range. Additionally, a low-resolution spectral model for the seed photon field has been added. We applied this updated model to analyze the soft X-ray/UV excess observed in the spectra of blazar 3C 279. By utilizing polarization data from the Swift Polarimeter (POLAR-BE) and spectral data from Swift/XRT, we determined that the soft X-ray/UV excess in 3C 279's spectrum can be explained by the jet emission resulting from inverse Compton scattering of seed photons originating from the accretion disk or broad emission lines. Furthermore, we derived constraints on the magnetic field strength within the BLR region of 3C 279, finding it to be approximately $10^{-3}$ G. Finally, we compared the predicted polarization degree and electric vector position angle (EVPA) from our model with Swift/XRT polarization measurements from the Swift Polarimeter (POLAR2), noting that the observed EVPA in 3C 279 exhibits a 180° shift relative to the predicted value. These findings suggest that the BLR region is a promising candidate for hosting a compact emission zone in the X-ray/UV band. Finally, we conclude that the MAPPIES code is a valuable tool for studying the non-thermal emission of AGNs, including the jet emission in radio galaxies and the gamma-ray emission in blazars. The code is publicly accessible at https://sourceforge.net/projects/mappies/. The MAPPIES source code is also available upon request from the corresponding author. We examine the extension of real analytic functions to the complex domain, a process essential for interpreting real-valued landscape models within complex spaces. This approach is particularly pertinent for global optimization using complex evolution strategies, which require learning complex weights and biases. Our primary contribution involves generalizing interval under-approximations of real functions to methods that bound their complex extensions. We apply these techniques to function landscapes, specifically examining the complex under-approximation of finite algebraic expressions. Furthermore, we present a preliminary application of complex under-approximation to optimization, specifically the evolution of complex artificial neural networks. We present a quantum detector designed to distinguish between two a priori pure states that are not equally weighted. This operational task holds significance for quantum cryptography and sensing. Our primary finding is that a nontrivial distinction between these two states can be achieved with a single measurement. We optimize the state discrimination strategy by employing a positive-valued linear combination of the two states. We analyze the optimal detection protocol across two frameworks: general quantum measurements (POVMs) and projective measurements. Furthermore, we extend these findings to the scenario involving the discrimination of n a priori pure states exhibiting a specific symmetry. Finally, we examine how measurement errors impact the detection process. Additionally, we explore applications in quantum sensing, proposing a method to determine the orientation of an unknown qubit by preparing it in one of two nearly identical orientations. This is achieved by repeatedly measuring the state using our optimized detector. We evaluate the protocol's performance through convergence analysis and numerical simulations. Our results demonstrate that the average orientation error can be reduced to the fundamental limit imposed by quantum mechanics. Light field imaging has garnered significant attention due to its capacity to capture extra spatial and temporal data through multiple sub-apertures. This additional information enables real-time rendering of realistic 3D scenes via synthetic light field image (LFII) generation, a process essential for applications like augmented reality and virtual reality. However, the high dimensionality of LFDs results in substantial file sizes, making compression a critical challenge. Although recent learning-based methods offer promising compression ratios, they often fail to maintain high fidelity, particularly in textured regions. To address this, we introduce a novel LFII compression framework utilizing deep learning. Our approach leverages a deep neural network (DNN) to synthesize additional sub-aperture images from existing ones, thereby expanding the LFII dimension and improving compression. Unlike previous methods that rely on generic models, our parallax-aware model specifically targets reconstruction errors in textured areas by utilizing sub-aperture image patches as inputs. This model is integrated into a pruned practical compression system that incorporates a distortion metric to enhance reconstruction fidelity. Experimental results demonstrate that our method outperforms state-of-the-art techniques in fidelity, achieving up to a 1.1% PSNR improvement. Furthermore, our approach is computationally efficient for deployment on embedded devices, requiring only 1.2 ms for inference on an NVIDIA Jetson TX2. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first practical, learning-based system designed for synthesize-aware LFII compression. The associated code will be made publicly available. The origin of protoplanetary disks within prestellar cores remains a fundamental mystery in star and planet formation. This study investigates the link between the internal structure of prestellar cores and the formation of these disks. By applying a high-resolution magneto-hydrodynamical simulation to the collapse of a prestellar core, we generated a self-consistent system featuring both a protostar and a protoplanetary disk. Our results indicate that the disk originates from the fragmentation of the collapsing core's inner region, driven by the self-gravity of the gas. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the collapse of a prestellar core naturally produces a gas disk with a surface density profile closely resembling observed protoplanetary disks, characterized by an outer region of $10^{-3}\,\mathrm{g\,cm^{-2}}$ and an inner region of $10^{-1}\,\mathrm{g\,cm^{-2}}$ at $1\,\mathrm{au}$. We also show that the disk's surface density is regulated by the balance between self-gravity and the magnetic pressure of the ambient medium. Finally, we argue that this mechanism offers a viable explanation for the formation of protoplanetary disks. Atmospheric dispersion correctors (ADCs) are instruments designed to eliminate atmospheric dispersion, a phenomenon where the atmosphere acts like a prism, causing light of different wavelengths to refract by varying amounts. This paper serves as the second installment in a series detailing at-sky measurements of this effect; the accompanying paper will describe the measurements and analyze them against model predictions. This work specifically focuses on the modeling of atmospheric conditions and the development of the AirMass and RayAtmosphere software used to simulate these conditions. We introduce a novel method for characterizing at-sky measurements of atmospheric dispersion, utilizing a combination of prisms and a wavelength-dependent mask to measure extinction across a broad field of view. This approach surpasses the precision of point-based measurements, such as those from refractometers, and is applicable to any optical system. Furthermore, we have developed a software suite to model these conditions and compare them with on-sky measurements. This suite includes: (1) a ray-tracing model for prisms and other optical elements, (2) a model for the atmosphere, and (3) a method for simulating detector images. These tools facilitate a comprehensive understanding of the measurement process and enable accurate predictions of at-sky performance. This model has been validated using a dispersion corrector for the Large Binocular Telescope. The expansion of federated learning (FL) has sparked extensive research into addressing challenges like data imbalance and fairness issues. To mitigate these problems, many solutions rely on reweighting techniques, such as adjusting server-level weights based on dataset sizes. However, these methods often require knowledge of the true data distribution, a requirement that conflicts with the fundamental privacy-preserving nature of FL. To overcome this limitation, we propose a novel approach that integrates differential privacy (DP) with federated learning. Our proposed DP-FL framework employs a two-stage training strategy: first, a global model is trained on the server using aggregated client models; subsequently, clients utilize this global model as initialization for further local training. This architecture effectively mitigates bias caused by varying data distributions while maintaining privacy guarantees. Experimental results demonstrate that DP-FL outperforms existing rebalancing methods in FL scenarios. Furthermore, ablation studies indicate that DP-FL achieves a favorable trade-off between bias reduction and privacy preservation. Additionally, we observe that increasing the number of participating clients in FL training enhances model performance and strengthens privacy guarantees. Finally, we extend the DP-FL framework to handle class imbalance within federated environments, evaluating it against two alternative methods that remove the necessity of global model sharing. The classification results confirm the superiority of our proposed framework over these alternatives. Finally, we address the integration of differential privacy with FL through a theoretical analysis of the resulting bias-variance trade-off. This analysis elucidates the underlying mechanisms of the bias-variance relationship and establishes a quantitative connection between FL parameters, privacy levels, and bias. We introduce a supersymmetric minimal $U(1)_X$ model at the TeV scale featuring a right-handed neutrino that acts as dark energy. This framework incorporates two right-handed neutrino superfields, $N$ and $\bar{N}$, which transform as singlets under the Standard Model gauge group but are essential for model construction. Their vacuum expectation values spontaneously break the $U(1)_X$ symmetry, generating masses for right-handed neutrinos and accommodating the observed dark energy density. The model predicts a heavy $Z'$ boson with a mass near 5 TeV and a $Z'$-mediated flavor violation between the second and third generations that can be detected by the LHC. Furthermore, the model allows for dark matter candidates including right-handed muons, taus, and squarks, with their weak interaction cross sections enhanced by the relatively low $Z'$ mass. Finally, we examine the constraints imposed by LHC data and determine that the $U(1)_X$ symmetry breaking scale must exceed approximately 10 TeV. Additionally, R-parity must be violated at energies above roughly 100 TeV to ensure the dark matter density remains consistent with observational limits. These theoretical constraints can be tested through LHC flavor violation measurements and dark matter relic density observations. Finally, we address the model's implications for neutrino masses and mixing. Specifically, the $U(1)_X$ breaking scale sets an upper limit on neutrino masses, while the $Z'$-mediated flavor violation in the lepton sector must remain below experimental sensitivity. We also explore the model's predictions for neutrino oscillation data and the necessity of additional beyond-standard-model contributions to the lepton mixing matrix. Finally, we discuss the model's implications for baryon asymmetry generation. In this scenario, $R$-parity is not a necessary symmetry, and the $Z'$-mediated flavor violation between the first and second generations must also remain undetected by the LHC. Consequently, the $U(1)_X$ breaking scale must be higher than approximately 10 TeV, and the dark matter lifetime must exceed roughly 100 TeV. These constraints are testable through LHC flavor violation measurements and dark matter relic density observations. Overall, this model offers a viable alternative to the super symmetric dark matter paradigm. The charging phase duration is optimized to maximize the average energy harvested by information-bearing users during the data transmission phase. Furthermore, unsupervised deep learning algorithms are leveraged to determine the optimal IRS phase shifts during the information transmission phase, aiming to further enhance throughput. Specifically, a K-means clustering algorithm is employed to identify user groups, followed by the application of a Variational Autoencoder (VAE) to optimize the phase shifts for maximizing total throughput. Simulation results confirm the efficacy of the proposed approach. Notably, the work introduces a novel throughput maximization strategy for wireless powered networks by integrating interference, marking it as the first study to explore throughput in such environments with interference. Additionally, this is the initial research to utilize an IRS-driven interference source for throughput enhancement. Finally, the proposed method represents the first application of unsupervised learning to optimize IRS phase shifts in wireless powered networks. We investigate the coexistence of neutrino leptogenesis and dark matter production within a unified framework, incorporating right-handed neutrinos and a dark sector. In this model, the decay of heavy particles in the early universe generates both leptonic asymmetry and dark matter simultaneously. Specifically, we analyze a simple $\mathcal{Z}_2$-symmetric scalar field model that extends the Standard Model. This approach ensures the stability of dark matter candidates while allowing the simultaneous production of the required leptonic asymmetry and dark matter density. We present the parameter space where successful high-scale leptogenesis and dark matter generation occur concurrently, demonstrating that the dark sector significantly influences the viability of leptogenesis. Furthermore, we explore the possibility of detecting dark matter through its annihilation into heavy neutral gauge bosons, emphasizing that the model can simultaneously account for dark matter, neutrino masses, and cosmological leptonic asymmetry. We also examine the potential for neutrino experiments to constrain the parameter space, which could subsequently inform dark matter searches. Finally, we discuss how future experimental results in these areas could help determine the nature of dark matter and the mechanisms behind leptonic asymmetry. Finally, we conclude that the interplay between leptogenesis and dark matter offers a promising avenue for understanding fundamental physical phenomena. Future efforts must therefore address both the origin of leptonic asymmetry and dark matter to achieve a complete understanding. We introduce a new machine learning-driven control framework designed for robots operating in dynamic environments with limited and noisy data. This approach addresses scenarios where information is fragmented across disparate sources, such as sensor logs, human experts, or historical records. We formalize this as data-driven control with side information (DDCWI) and demonstrate its versatility by successfully training a fixed humanoid robot to walk, swing, fly, and reach on a dynamic platform using only 20 minutes of data. The proposed framework integrates two novel components: (1) a library of controllers derived from existing human motion data, and (2) a reinforcement learning algorithm that selects the most appropriate controller based on real-time environmental conditions. Our results indicate that DDCWI can construct a robust controller library from noisy data and effectively learn to switch between these controllers, enabling the creation of versatile robots. This method holds significant promise for advancing autonomous systems in real-world settings characterized by data scarcity and noise. Relation networks have recently demonstrated significant potential for image recognition and generation tasks. Building on this, we introduce a new triplet-based unpaired image-to-image GAN designed for face attribute manipulation. In this framework, the relation network functions as a feature extractor that automatically acquires discriminative features for a specific attribute through adversarial training. During this process, the relation network either receives pre-trained weights or is trained in an unsupervised manner. For image generation, we employ a pre-trained relation network alongside a style transfer approach. Experimental results validate the efficacy of our proposed Relation GAN across various attributes, including age, gender, glasses, and indoor/outdoor settings. The network successfully performs face aging, gender transformation, glasses addition/removal, and background shifts while preserving identity, achieving visual outputs that closely resemble the target. Furthermore, we demonstrate enhanced stability in pre-trained relation network training and improved quality in random image generation. Additionally, we explore face set generation by extending the relation network with a latent vector generator. To our knowledge, this represents the first application of relation networks within the GAN domain. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/ChenYi-1996/RelationGAN. We introduce a twin-field quantum key exchange (TFQKE) protocol that operates without requiring phase locking between twin fields. In this approach, when users share a local reference frame, they can generate a secure key by randomly selecting between two methods: either measuring the twin-field NOON state or the twin-field single-photon state at the receiver's node. This method ensures that the secret key's security relies solely on the coherence of optical twin-photon states, while the contribution from the far-field probe photon is negligible. Consequently, the need to stabilize the paths of far-field probe photons is eliminated. Furthermore, the framework remains secure against collective noise, making it suitable for deployment on existing free-space optical links. Numerical simulations indicate that under atmospheric turbulence, the system can achieve a secure key rate of approximately $10^4$ bits per second with 100 mW twin-field optical power over transmission distances ranging from 10 to 100 km. Additionally, the system maintains a secure key rate of about $10^3$ bits per second at distances between 1 and 100 km. These findings suggest that TFQKE could serve as a viable candidate for satellite-based quantum communication networks. To support these conclusions, we have also provided the simulation code. Specifically, the first part of the code calculates the secure key rate for TFQKE without phase locking under collective noise, while the second part computes the rate when phase locking is applied. The results confirm that the secure key rate achieved without phase locking is nearly identical to that achieved with phase locking. The provided code is available at \url{https://github.com/zhongqiangwang/TFQKE}. Finally, we have included supplementary materials to demonstrate the security of the TFQKE protocol without phase locking against collective noise, as well as to calculate the secure key rate for various optical power levels and transmission distances. Although current object detectors are trained on extensive datasets, they fail to generalize to new categories due to the high cost of annotating bounding boxes. To address this, we introduce a method utilizing pseudo bounding-box labels, where each image is marked as either containing the target class (1) or not (0). Our approach employs a straightforward yet effective strategy: training standard object detectors on images with this binary label. To mitigate the issue of label imbalance, we implement a novel training protocol that alternates between the difficult standard training regime and an easier one using pseudo labels, thereby enhancing generalization to novel categories. Experimental results demonstrate that our method surpasses previous approaches on the CUB-200, Visual Genome, and WSI datasets, while also outperforming standard training on the source datasets. The young stellar object S1 in the Rho Ophiuchus cluster is a massive binary located at the center of a complex nebula, featuring both ionized and molecular components. This study utilizes new optical and near-infrared spectroscopy to analyze the gas structures surrounding S1. We identify three distinct regions: an ionized zone extending 10 arcseconds from the star, a cold atomic hydrogen region 20 arcseconds away, and a cold molecular region situated 30 arcseconds out. The boundaries between these zones align with the Strömgren radius and the radius where the hydrogen number density drops to $n(H) = 10^3$ cm$^{-3}$. Additionally, we detect a 10 arcsecond-wide transition zone between the ionized and cold atomic areas, characterized by PDR emission from H$\alpha$, [FeII] 1.644 $\mu$m, and Paschen-$\alpha$. The size of this PDR region correlates with the H$\alpha$ emission radius, suggesting it is driven by the ionizing flux rather than the radiation field. Finally, we observe a 10 arcsecond-wide molecular layer between the cold atomic and molecular regions, which appears to be illuminated by the PDR. These findings support the hypothesis that PDRs can sustain molecular emission even when exposed to relatively weak ultraviolet radiation fields. Overall, this system demonstrates a sequential transition from ionized gas to cold atomic gas, and finally to molecular gas, driven by the decreasing intensity of radiation and ionizing flux with distance from the star. This structure is consistent with theoretical models of PDRs. Furthermore, the radial extent of the molecular layer is approximately 10 arcseconds, which aligns with the predicted size of the molecular region based on the radius of molecular outflows. This suggests that PDRs may play a role in shaping the molecular region around massive young stellar objects. These results provide a new perspective on the interaction between PDRs and molecular gas. Finally, the paper discusses the implications of these findings for our understanding of PDRs and their role in star formation. The rapid proliferation of transformer-based language models has significantly transformed natural language processing (NLP). This survey examines the application of these architectures to various NLP tasks focused on veracity, including fake news identification, fact-checking, and misinformation detection. We analyze transformer variants, sub-architectures, pre-training methods, and their specific impacts on the target domains. Furthermore, we explore how pre-trained transformers facilitate few-shot and zero-shot learning for veracity tasks, while also addressing associated challenges and proposing potential future research directions. We aim to provide a comprehensive overview of transformer usage in veracity tasks, offer critical insights, and inspire continued investigation and novel research within this field. The accompanying Python package, Transformers in Veracity, organizes and visualizes survey data to assist researchers in efficiently grasping the current research landscape. Our analysis indicates that transformer models are highly effective for real-world veracity tasks, with performance comparable to task-specific models. Additionally, few-shot and zero-shot learning approaches utilizing pre-trained transformers demonstrate strong capabilities in identifying veracity in unseen contexts. This survey serves as a foundational reference for the field, highlighting the transformative potential of pre-trained transformers in veracity research. Most current mortality prediction approaches rely on model-based techniques, including non-parametric methods like kernel smoothing and parametric models such as the Li and Lee (2005) model. While these methods have proven highly effective, their primary objective has been to determine the optimal functional form for time-varying loadings. This study introduces a novel factor model featuring time-invariant loadings to predict mortality rates. We evaluate this new approach against established methods using simulated data and apply various model-selection criteria to real-world data to forecast mortality between 2019 and 2030. The analysis covers life expectancies for individuals aged 60 and 80 at the start of the prediction period, across both sexes in the United States and South Korea. Our results indicate that the proposed factor model with time-invariant loadings is particularly well-suited for predicting mortality rates over short-term horizons. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this model can accurately identify abrupt mortality shifts, such as those caused by the COVID-19 pandemic. Finally, we provide estimates regarding future life expectancy. The project's R code is accessible at https://github.com/taehyuk-lee/Mortality-Prediction-Using-Factor-Models. Additionally, an extended version of this paper is available in the journal *Demographic Research*. This manuscript corresponds to a translation of the same work originally published in Korean under the title "사망률 예측을 위한 인자 모형: 시간변화적 인자하중이냐, 시간불변적 인자하중이냐?" in the journal *Korean Demographic Association Bulletin*. The Korean original was published in 2021, with this translation released in 2022. The English version incorporates several minor enhancements to the original Korean publication. Keywords: Factor model, mortality prediction, time-varying loadings, time-invariant loadings, model selection, life expectancy.

Neural Architecture Search (NAS) offers a promising method for automatically designing neural networks for specific tasks. However, the Interleave Search strategy, which parallelizes training and sampling multiple architectures to reduce computational costs, often suffers from inter-architecture interference that degrades performance. This paper provides the first detailed investigation into the causes of interference within the Interleave Search paradigm. Our findings indicate that the primary source of interference is the fluctuation of gradients caused by data batch sampling variance. Consequently, we introduce a novel algorithm called Interference Reduction via Data Augmentation (IRDA), which mitigates this interference by applying specific augmentations to the interleaved training data. Experimental results demonstrate that Interleave Search with IRDA achieves comparable accuracy to sequential search while maintaining significantly higher efficiency. The code for this work is available at https://github.com/ChenYixuan1999/IRDA. Time series data is prevalent across numerous fields, and with the advancement of data collection and computational capabilities, analyzing and modeling these data have become essential. However, the rapid growth of available modeling techniques often complicates the selection of the most appropriate model for a specific application. This challenge is particularly acute in the financial sector, where numerous models exist for pricing derivatives and for forecasting and modeling implied volatility. While theoretical methods can be used to derive features from time series to compare models, such an approach is often inefficient. We propose an alternative method that computes features from time series to facilitate the comparison and selection of suitable models. This approach is especially valuable when dealing with multivariate and high-frequency financial time series. The technique is implemented in the R package "theft," which provides examples of time series features and models. This tutorial introduces the package and its features, aiming to assist financial analysts, data scientists, and modelers in making informed decisions regarding time series modeling. The intended decision-making process regarding models and models+features is demonstrated using the Yahoo! stock dataset. The article is designed to be accessible to readers with only basic knowledge of financial time series modeling. Furthermore, the associated R scripts are available in the "theft" package under the "scripts" folder. We hope this tutorial inspires financial analysts and modelers to explore the extensive suite of features offered by the "theft" package to enhance their own decision-making processes. Additionally, we welcome the community to contribute further features to the package to aid their own analyses. The paper includes an appendix listing the features from the "theft" package that were not covered in this tutorial. This tutorial serves as a foundation for the book "Statistical Arbitrage and Market-Making with R," which will be published by Packt Publishing. The book will expand upon this work, covering additional features and models from the "theft" package, as well as introducing new features and models. The book will provide a more comprehensive explanation of the theft package's features and the various techniques employed to select the most suitable ones. This paper introduces the notion of CAT(0) boundaries, defined as quasi-isometry invariant quotients of the directed set of positive-rank geodesic rays, and demonstrates that not all CAT(0) spaces possess this property. Furthermore, we prove that a CAT(0) space is geodesically complete precisely when it possesses a CAT(0) boundary, providing examples where this boundary arises naturally. We also examine the properties of these boundaries in relation to maximal abelian subgroups (tori) and identify solvable groups that lack tori by analyzing their CAT(0) boundaries. Additionally, we investigate the existence and structural characteristics of CAT(0) isotropic groups. The study of these boundaries is particularly significant for spaces that are not proper, as certain sequences of closed subspaces fail to converge to any single subspace. We derive negative results from this perspective, notably showing that the CAT(0) boundary of a product of trees is improper. The paper concludes with an extensive exploration of the subspaces within CAT(0) boundaries.

This study introduces a novel statistical framework for evaluating translator quality and reliability. We model the translation process as a reparameterized Bayesian probit model. Within this model, a translator's quality corresponds to the probability of producing a correct translation, while their reliability reflects the consistency of their performance across different correct source sentences. We derive closed-form analytical expressions for the posterior distributions of translators parameters, facilitating efficient computation. Additionally, we propose a decision rule to classify translators as either reliable or unreliable. A simulation study was conducted to determine the values of hyper-parameters that optimize both reliability and the accuracy of our decision rule. Finally, we applied this model to real-world data to estimate the quality and reliability of two professional translators. Our results demonstrate that the model offers a robust approach for characterizing translator performance. Furthermore, we show that our methodology can assist translation service providers in identifying the most suitable translators for specific projects. We present an exact universal sum rule governing energy deposition in scattering systems, formulated through sum principles linked to the eigenvalues of a specifically defined non-Hermitian matrix. This work extends and applies the principles of stationary phase and oscillation to a class of matrices characterized by these eigenvalues and their associated eigenvectors. The methodology for calculating these parameters is detailed, with an analysis of the sum rule's structure and implications for random wavefunction scattering. Furthermore, we demonstrate the rule's validity by applying it to both two-dimensional and three-dimensional scattering scenarios. Additionally, we explore the connection between this derived sum rule and the moment sum rules previously established by Brody and Brody. The findings are broadly applicable to quantum scattering involving short-wavelength waves, such as electrons and atoms. Specifically, the proposed mathematical framework is relevant to quantum transport phenomena, including electron scattering in mesoscopic devices and atom scattering off surfaces. Moreover, the approach extends to other scattering contexts, such as photon scattering in the context of radiative transfer. Finally, we outline a potential generalization of the sum rule to broader classes of scattering problems. The paper concludes with an application to the study of surface wave propagation across two-dimensional interfaces. This final section is based on joint research conducted by the second author with J. B. Keller. The resulting sum rule for surface wavefront propagation is derived from the moment sum rules and offers a new perspective on the dynamics of the surface wave S-matrix. Notably, the sum rule derived in this work is universally applicable to any two-dimensional interface between two three-dimensional media, regardless of the specific nature of the waves involved. Consequently, the methodology and findings presented herein have wide-ranging implications for surface wave propagation studies. The work is broadly significant for scattering theory, as it provides new insights into the universal properties of scattering systems. Moreover, the approach is applicable to systems exhibiting Anderson localization, where it can be utilized to analyze the statistical distribution of localization lengths. Finally, the proposed sum rule is relevant to the study of quantum chaos, where it can provide new insights into the universal statistical properties of quantum scattering systems. The paper is comprehensive, featuring detailed derivations and an abundance of new results. Additionally, it includes several new and significant conjectures regarding the fundamental nature of Anderson localization and the universal statistical properties of quantum scattering systems. Overall, the work represents a significant contribution to the field of scattering theory. Pruning techniques aim to enhance the efficiency of deep neural networks by eliminating redundant components. This study investigates the sifting and preservation of convolutional network characteristics within fully connected architectures. By analyzing the structural distinctions between these network types, we demonstrate that unique features can be preserved during the pruning process. This capability allows us to isolate convolutional networks embedded inside larger fully connected models that exhibit superior generalization performance. Consequently, this approach offers a novel, structurally sound method for identifying and extracting high-performing subnetworks. Extensive experiments validate the effectiveness of our proposed fully connected network pruning strategy, which successfully recovers convolutional networks with minimal performance degradation. The code for this work can be found at: https://github.com/ChenYan1992/FC-Pruning. Furthermore, additional code and experimental results are available at: https://github.com/chenyan1992/Winning-Lot-Ticket-FC-Pruning. We anticipate that this work will inspire further research into the relationship between fully connected and convolutional networks. Specifically, future studies should explore the underlying reasons why convolutional networks can be embedded in fully connected networks with only slight performance loss, thereby deepening our understanding of network characteristics and redundancy. Additionally, extending this pruning method to other network structures, such as residual networks, is expected to yield significant improvements in efficiency. Multidimensional scaling (MDS) is a well-established technique for visualizing high-dimensional data, with t-SNE being a prominent and widely used variant. However, traditional MDS and t-SNE rely on Euclidean distance, which is inappropriate for spherical data where angular metrics are necessary. To address this, we introduce spherical t-SNE (t-SNE), which replaces Euclidean distance with angular distance, alongside two novel t-SNE variants that incorporate Fisher information to define the similarity function. We evaluate these methods across three vision tasks: visualizing dataset samples, comparing the visual similarity of representations, and interpreting visual features. Our results demonstrate that t-SNE effectively visualizes spherical data, with versions that leverage Fisher information outperforming others in visualizing dataset samples and interpreting visual features. Furthermore, t-SNE successfully uncovers the visual structure of existing image segmentation models, revealing that ViT-based architectures tend to overfit more than ConvNets. Overall, our findings indicate that t-SNE is highly effective for visualizing spherical data, and our proposed Fisher-based variants hold significant potential for vision tasks. The CMS experiment at the LHC has measured the elliptic flow ($v_2$) of electrons originating from the semi-leptonic decays of charm hadrons during Pb-Pb collisions at $\sqrt{s_{\rm NN}}$ = 5.02 TeV. This analysis utilized a sample of approximately 600k minimum bias events from the Run 1. The study selected electrons with transverse momenta between 15 and 80 GeV/$c$ and pseudorapidities within $\left| \eta \right| < 2.4$. To determine the $v_2$, the CMS collaboration applied the two-subevent method, comparing the azimuthal angle distribution of electrons against the average of the event plane reconstructed using tracks from two distinct pseudorapidities separated by $\Delta\eta > 2.0$. The resulting $v_2$ values for these electrons are compared with predictions derived from hydrodynamic models and a transport framework incorporating initial geometry fluctuations. Furthermore, the findings are discussed in relation to the $v_2$ observed in charged hadrons. These results indicate that electrons from charm hadrons are produced with significant hydrodynamic flow, reflecting the collective behavior of the quark-gluon plasma formed in heavy-ion collisions. Notably, the $v_2$ of electrons from charm hadrons exceeds that of light hadrons at low $p_{\rm T}$, a trend also present in the data for charged hadrons. These observations support the hypothesis that heavy quarks experience the same medium as light quarks and may be produced later in time than light quarks. The necessity to categorize data has expanded significantly, particularly within the financial and financial services sectors. This paper introduces a method to jointly adaptably categorize data using formal concept analysis and Dempster-Shafer theory. The algorithm operates by defining a context and generating a hierarchy of formal concepts, where the categorization process involves formally computing the belief of each concept based on the empirical evidence in the context. The algorithm's functionality was tested using a dataset of 1,000 US stocks from 2007 to 2018, which was divided into two subsets of 500 stocks each. The results indicate that the proposed method achieves a 90% accuracy rate. Furthermore, the method is shown to be more efficient than the data categorization approach suggested by the European Securities and Markets Authority. Finally, the paper outlines the method's potential applications in the financial services industry. Overall, the study demonstrates that the combination of formal concept analysis and Dempster-Shafer theory is highly effective for categorization tasks. This paper investigates multitasking allocation under time-critical constraints, where agents possess skills across multiple tasks and can execute them concurrently. We examine two distinct scenarios: the first allows agents to utilize shared processing resources, while the second mandates that all agents share a global processing unit for every task. Our primary goal is to assign processing to these agents to minimize the maximum completion time across all tasks. We first demonstrate that computing optimal solutions for both scenarios is NP-hard. Subsequently, we design approximation algorithms for each case and establish that these algorithms are essentially optimal. Additionally, we explore non-preemptive settings in both contexts, proving that 2-approximation algorithms exist and are tight. Finally, we analyze a specific instance type where task durations are uniform for each agent, showing that optimal allocation can be computed in polynomial time. Throughout the study, we incorporate both preemptive and non-preemptive models. Notably, our algorithms for the shared processing context are task non-preemptive, whereas in the global processing context, we focus on agent non-preemptive allocations. We also provide a comprehensive analysis of the preemptive case. Our primary focus remains on multitasking allocation with shared processing, where global processing allocation serves as a comparative baseline. We begin by reviewing related literature and formally defining the problems. We then present hardness of approximation results, followed by the development and analysis of our approximation algorithms. The paper concludes with a discussion of open problems.
Keywords: Multitasking Allocation, Shared Processing, Preemptive, Non-preemptive.

The Internet of Things (IoT) represents a rapidly expanding ecosystem of interconnected devices that communicate across various networks, enabling the collection and processing of vast amounts of data. As the number of devices grows, so does the complexity of managing and maintaining them. However, keeping these devices up-to-date poses significant challenges, particularly regarding the reliability of over-the-air firmware updates. This paper presents an extensive performance analysis of firmware update reliability across the Contiki-NG/Contiki-NG-WideHole, the communication layer of the Contiki-OS/NG, deployed on the EmberZ1 Pro/EmberZ1 Pro-ZB communication board within large-scale LoRaWAN/LoRaWAN-Passive networks. This hardware is utilized in the Smart City/Smart City-Passive deployment framework. The study examines the efficacy of various firmware update strategies, including different update windows, scheduling policies, and mechanisms for handling update failures. Our findings indicate that a sequential scheduling approach, combined with a dedicated window specifically for executing update failures, ensures the most reliable and dependable delivery of firmware updates. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the LoRaWAN-Passive/LoRaWAN-Passive deployment offers the most effective balance between system efficiency and reliability. Finally, our results confirm that the proposed strategies can achieve a 99% success rate in firmware updates, with an average time-to-success of approximately 10 minutes. This paper serves as a foundational resource for future research and development in the area of reliable over-the-air firmware updates. Additionally, the Contiki-NG/Contiki-NG-WideHole network layer and the Contiki-OS/NG/EmberZ1 Pro/EmberZ1 Pro-ZB communication board are available as open-source resources to support further research and development in this domain. The LoRaWAN-Passive/LoRaWAN-Passive deployment framework will also be made available as an open-source resource in the near future. All referenced open-source resources can be accessed at: https://github.com/SmartCity-Passive/SmartCity-Passive. Interactive graph search is a prevalent method for efficiently locating target nodes within large graphs through yes/no questioning. This study addresses the challenge of co-localizing $k$ target nodes using a limited search budget of $T$ queries, where $k$ is known but the specific target locations are unknown. We evaluate the performance of existing algorithms across graphs with varying topologies and sizes, and introduce a novel algorithm grounded in the concept of graph separation distance, demonstrating its superior efficacy. Furthermore, we present the first analysis of the problem's computational complexity, revealing that it is NP-hard even when $k=2$. Finally, we explore the connection to graph separation and propose the concept of optimal interactive $k$-separation, which is proven to be NP-hard. Experimental results validate the practical utility of this theory. Our algorithm is accessible at \url{https://github.com/Chenchenchenchen/BLISMT}. Additionally, we have made our data and code available at \url{https://github.com/Chenchenchenchen/BLISSearchData}. Our code can be accessed via: \texttt{git clone --depth 1 https://github.com/Chenchenchenchen/BLISSearchData}. The search data utilized in this project is sourced from Chenchen Chen's repository under the above link. We utilized this code to conduct the experiments presented in the paper. The BLISSearchData repository contains precomputed data for several datasets, including random graphs, small-world networks, and social networks, which can be directly loaded into our code. For the remaining datasets, such as those in papers [1-4], users are required to load the data themselves. The repository provides a readme file with instructions on how to access these other datasets. We offer guidance to assist users in accessing the required data.

Quantum classifiers hold potential for handling large-scale datasets, yet their susceptibility to adversarial attacks remains a critical vulnerability. This study investigates such attacks on quantum classifiers, demonstrating that adversarial examples generated via customized methods can be transformed into a universal set of instances and normalization vectors producible by a shared generator. These universal elements successfully deceive various single- and multi-layer quantum classifiers across diverse datasets, including MNIST, FashionMNIST, CIFAR10, and CIFAR100. Furthermore, these instances generalize to unseen classifiers that were not part of the original training process. The findings underscore the importance of developing robust quantum classifiers and highlight the need for further research into defense mechanisms against adversarial threats. Additionally, we examine the relationship between input normalization vectors and adversarial success, revealing that certain normalization strategies can significantly diminish attack effectiveness. Our results also indicate that the NISQ era is approaching a point where it may become challenging to reliably distinguish between adversarial and natural perturbations. Finally, we explore the possibility of generating universal adversarial instances that remain effective against quantum classifiers employing fully supervised, semi-supervised, and unsupervised learning techniques. These contributions aim to advance the field of quantum machine learning and foster more resilient models against adversarial attacks. This paper investigates Steklov eigenvalues within two-dimensional smooth domains that are closely resembling circles. We demonstrate that the multiplicity of these Steklov eigenvalues is bounded by a constant that depends solely on the Steklov spectrum and the degree of proximity to a circular shape. Furthermore, we establish that each Steklov eigenvalue, accompanied by its corresponding eigenfunction, exhibits significant regularity, including a nearly constant number of zeros and turning points, and fluctuates slowly over time. These findings are notably applicable to the evolution of Steklov eigenvalues and eigenfunctions driven by the mean curvature flow. Consequently, our results yield novel, non-asymptotic insights into the long-term behavior of two-dimensional Steklov eigenfunctions, as well as their multiplicity and interlacing properties. Additionally, the paper features distinct contributions to the general theory of Steklov eigenvalues, namely a sharp multiplicity bound and a new proof of the interlacing inequality. Our methodology also relies on a new isoperimetric inequality tailored to weighted Dirichlet energies and weighted Laplacians, a tool that may find broader utility in other areas of analysis. Finally, the paper includes a numerical section dedicated to validating the derived theorems and exploring their practical implications. Our computational findings indicate that the multiplicity bound is sharp and offer a more precise estimate for the exponent governing the slenderness of nearly round domains. In the context of the mean curvature flow, the computed eigenfunctions display complex dynamics, characterized by irregular oscillations and sudden transitions between different multiplicity regimes. This behavior contrasts with the smooth evolution of eigenvalues and suggests the existence of nontrivial resonances within the associated linearized problem. While these phenomena are well-documented in the literature, they remain challenging to analyze and understand. We conclude by outlining several promising avenues for future research. Specifically, we intend to extend these results to higher dimensions and to settings involving anisotropic surface energies. Extending the results to higher dimensions would provide a new perspective on the evolution of Steklov eigenvalues and their long-term behavior. Generalizing the results to anisotropic surface energies would offer new insights into the relationship between geometry and spectral theory. Extending the results to other types of surface evolution would deepen our understanding of the dynamics of Steklov eigenvalues and eigenfunctions. Finally, extending the results to higher codimension would provide a new framework for analyzing the stability of minimal submanifolds. Conformance checking is a key element of process mining, focusing on identifying deviations between actual process executions and modeled processes. Traditionally, this field has concentrated on analyzing complete traces. However, the growing need to verify conformance for trace fragments—such as partial process executions, trace subfragments, or trace extensions—has emerged as a critical research area. While several methods for conformance verification of trace fragments now exist, they often depend on specific algorithms for trace alignment, including prefix, suffix, or infix alignments. Despite these options, no single method is universally superior across all scenarios. For instance, infix alignments may be computationally inefficient for certain fragment types, whereas post-fix alignments might be more efficient. This paper introduces a novel conformance verification approach based on postfix alignments, which offers a general framework applicable to any fragment alignment algorithm. Furthermore, we demonstrate through a case study that our method can be more efficient than existing techniques when verifying conformance using postfix alignments. Ultimately, our method represents the first step toward a general, algorithm-independent solution for verifying the conformance of trace fragments. The proposed approach is available as an open-source software tool. Source code and documentation can be accessed at: https://github.com/Advanced-Process-Mining/pmining-postfix. Accurate radio coverage maps are essential for planning and optimizing cellular networks. Traditional modeling methods rely on ray-tracing and link budget calculations derived from the Friis equation, which are computationally intensive and unsuitable for real-time applications. In contrast, deep neural networks offer a solution by learning the complex relationship between a transmitter's position and received signal strength from measured data. However, this data-driven approach demands vast amounts of data, and standard architectures like Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) struggle to generalize effectively to new locations outside the training set. To address these challenges, we propose a novel Cellular Network Radio Transmission Model based on hierarchical feature extraction through Heterogeneous Deep Convolutional Neural Networks (H-DCNNs). Our model achieves high generalization capabilities, significantly outperforming existing DCNN variants in predicting signal strength at unseen locations. Furthermore, the model is lightweight, enabling deployment on cellular network User Equipment (UE) devices. Validation using the OpenCellular platform confirms that our approach surpasses state-of-the-art methods in both hierarchical feature extraction performance and computational efficiency. As a result, our H-DCNN model is ideal for integration into cellular devices to facilitate real-time signal strength prediction. The source code is accessible at: https://github.com/DeepCellular/RadioML-2020_Cellular_Network_Radio_Transmission_Modeling. This work was presented at the 22nd International Conference on Information Fusion (ICIF 2020). Additional details can be found at: https://ief.iai.csic.es/radioml/. The project website is: https://deepcellular.github.io/. For inquiries, contact: deepcellular@csic.es. Our contributions include: 1) A new, more general and accurate cellular radio transmission model utilizing hierarchical DCNNs with H-DCNNs for superior feature extraction; 2) An open-source RadioML framework for cellular network radio coverage modeling, available at https://github.com/DeepCellular/RadioML. Our framework supports various applications, such as device-to-device communication, in future releases. 3) An R-package for benchmarking and evaluating cellular radio coverage models, accessible via: install.packages("DeepCellular", repos = "https://deepcellular.r-universe.dev/"). The package is also available at: https://github.com/DeepCellular/RadioML. 4) An R-package for benchmarking and evaluating Deep Cellular Networks, available at: https://github.com/DeepCell

This study introduces a straightforward, compact, and verifiable semantics for temporal planning languages, which extends the established classical planning semantics with support for timing constraints. We demonstrate that this semantics can be validated using an existing proof obligation framework for language definitions, a process that has been successfully completed and formally verified through the ProverDet2 tool. Leveraging the same tool, we developed and formally verified a procedure to eliminate choice points from temporal planning problems, thereby reducing them to standard classical planning problems with explicitly defined start and goal states. Finally, we provide and verify the soundness of our proposed semantics using the formally verified descriptions of both classical and temporal planning problems generated by our verified transformation procedure. All definitions, proofs, and verified experiments are encapsulated within the formally verified language definition repository, LDEP, which serves as the foundational repository for this work. Furthermore, we outline several directions for future research. Specifically, we aim to extend our verification methodology to incorporate resource constraints, a verification framework for procedural specifications, and a comprehensive verification of the HIRO temporal planner. These future efforts will continue to rely on LDEP as the primary repository for formal definitions and verified experiments. Additionally, we intend to formalize and verify various well-known results from AI, operations research, and applied mathematics, as these areas share similar characteristics with temporal planning. Finally, we plan to develop a general framework for problem transformation and verification, which will also be based on LDEP. This framework will facilitate the formalization and verification of various problem transformations and enable the systematic generation and verification of new transformations. By providing a robust foundation for reasoning about problem transformations, we aim to enhance the understanding and effectiveness of temporal planning. This work was conducted as part of the author's PhD thesis, which was completed under the supervision of Prof. Dr. Bernhard Beckert and Dr. Ralf Zimmermann. The thesis is available at http://www.bbeckert.de/theses/beckert_thesis.pdf. Power system expansion models are widely used to assess the responsiveness of power systems to policy shifts, such as carbon pricing and renewable subsidies. However, the accuracy of these models in predicting system-level outcomes remains uncertain. This study examines the internal model structure and the resulting responsiveness of two power system expansion models, together with two distinct models representing low- and high-resolution sectors. We demonstrate that a model's responsiveness is determined by its structure, rather than by parameters like computational power or run-time. Specifically, structural characteristics such as the number of variables, the count of internal markets, and the nature of the objective function drive this phenomenon. Our findings indicate that sophisticated models can be constructed with variable-specific tuning to achieve a system-level responsiveness that matches that of complex models. This insight is valuable for resource allocation when utilizing power system expansion models. We conclude by discussing the implications of this research for the model community. This article is dedicated to Prof. Dr.-Ing. Reinhard Madlener, a pioneer in energy systems analysis, on the occasion of his 70th birthday. His work has inspired a generation of researchers to engage with energy system models. We are confident that the lessons learned from our research will be of interest to him. Reinhard's unwavering commitment to the field, his dedication to his colleagues, and his profound understanding of the power systems necessary for a prosperous future have inspired us. We are honored to dedicate this work to him. Reinhard passed away in 2021. We extend our deepest condolences to his family, friends, and colleagues. We remain confident that he continues to watch over the power systems that will secure a better future.

This study establishes the global existence of classical solutions for both the Vlasov-Poisson and ionic Vlasov-Poisson systems within bounded regions. Regarding boundary conditions, we apply specular reflection to the Vlasov equation, while imposing either homogeneous Dirichlet or Neumann conditions on the Poisson equation. Under these conditions, we demonstrate the global well-posedness of the system solutions. Furthermore, we derive a potential estimate for the ionic Vlasov-Poisson system under homogeneous Dirichlet boundary conditions. This derivation utilizes a novel technique to secure the necessary $L^\infty$ estimate for the electric field. Consequently, by employing a bootstrap argument, we achieve global well-posedness for the ionic Vlasov-Poisson system. Additionally, we secure the global well-posedness for the periodic case. In this specific scenario, we utilize existing methods from unbounded settings and successfully prove the existence of a classical solution. Notably, we do not impose smallness conditions on the initial data. To our knowledge, this represents the first global well-posedness result for ionic Vlasov-Poisson systems with homogeneous Dirichlet boundary conditions. We also provide a comprehensive summary of all potential estimates. Finally, we explore the connection between our findings and those of other researchers. Our work extends the global well-posedness of the Vlasov-Poisson system to include cases with homogeneous boundary conditions. Moreover, we provide the initial global well-posedness result for the ionic Vlasov-Poisson system in a bounded domain. In this context, global well-posedness relies on specific smallness conditions regarding the initial data. We examine the necessary smallness requirements for the particle density and potential, with or without ion density, to ensure the electric field remains small. We explicitly outline the necessary and sufficient conditions for the ion density. Additionally, we demonstrate the global well-posedness of the Vlasov-Poisson system with homogeneous Dirichlet boundary conditions for ionized plasma by applying our theorems. However, this result necessitates a stricter smallness condition on the initial potential. We conclude by addressing several open questions.
