Despite being a staple of software maintenance, concept location remains a labor-intensive and time-consuming task. Although various techniques have been proposed to assist developers in finding concepts within large systems, they often depend on manual input, limiting their practical utility. This paper introduces STRICT, a novel keyword identification method that leverages information retrieval to automatically extract search terms from code. STRICT constructs a text document from the source code of a specific method, treating the code structure as its index. By applying a text search algorithm to this index, STRICT generates ranked code elements relevant to the searched concept. Evaluated on the Big-Bench dataset, STRICT achieved a precision of 0.61 and a recall of 0.49 in identifying relevant code elements. Furthermore, an empirical study with 12 industrial developers revealed that STRICT is more precise than a baseline approach, with 66.7% of participants finding it easier to locate concepts using the tool. These findings suggest that leveraging external information can enhance concept location accuracy and usability. The STRICT tool is accessible at https://github.com/ChenYi2000/strict.

Colloidal gels, formed by weakly aggregated colloids, are widely utilized across various scientific and industrial fields. Their structure is typically anisotropic, resulting in direction-dependent rheological properties. This study introduces a new method for controlling gel architecture and rheology by applying ultrasonic vibrations during assembly. Specifically, we examine a model system of weakly interacting, highly concentrated polystyrene spheres. By imposing a standing acoustic wave, we promote the formation of a crystal-like structure within the gel. This "rheo-acoustic" assembly enables precise control over the internal structure and mechanical properties. Furthermore, we demonstrate that strong ultrasonic vibrations can induce a gel-to-liquid transition by disrupting the ultrasonic gel's structure. These findings offer new insights into the assembly and structural dynamics of colloidal gels, alongside significant technological applications. For instance, our ultrasonic gel could facilitate the creation of new materials with switchable mechanical properties and advanced acoustic devices. Additionally, rheo-acoustic gelling may enhance the production of pharmaceuticals and food products, allowing for the generation of anisotropic materials and reducing energy consumption during assembly. Finally, we show that mechanical stress can alter the crystal structure of the ultrasonic gel, leading to complex, non-linear mechanical properties. This contrasts with gels assembled under quiescent conditions, which exhibit linear mechanical behavior. We attribute this non-linear response to the competition between acoustic and mechanical forces acting on the gel structure. This discovery expands the range of materials displaying non-linear mechanical properties and may inspire new materials for energy absorption and vibration damping. Our results also provide a means to control the anisotropy of the elastic modulus in colloidal gels. We demonstrate that the modulus is significantly lower in the direction of the ultrasonic wave compared to the perpendicular direction, with an aspect ratio of up to 100. This non-hydrostatic elastic modulus is attributed to the anisotropic structure of the ultrasonic gel. We further show that this anisotropy can be erased by applying a small shear stress, revealing complex linear mechanical properties. This ability to control the degree of elastic modulus anisotropy may enable the development of new materials with switchable elastic properties. In summary, this work presents a novel approach to controlling the structure and rheological properties of colloidal gels. We anticipate that these findings will advance the fundamental understanding of colloidal gels and open new avenues for technological applications. Classification serves as a fundamental operation for enabling large-scale information retrieval and processing. However, traditional classification methods struggle to identify the semantic meaning of entities within STEM documents, often resulting in misclassification. To address this, we introduce a new mathematical entity linking technique designed to enhance STEM classification. This task involves gathering knowledge graph data from an external source and annotating mathematical symbols in documents by creating links to the knowledge graph. By utilizing this method, we can effectively capture the semantic meaning of entities in STEM documents, thereby improving classification accuracy. We have created a new dataset, MathQA, to support research in this area. MathQA comprises mathematical question-answer pairs extracted from exam documents, featuring both symbolic and latent meanings. Additionally, we provide a novel entity linking algorithm, MathEntityLinker, which successfully maps mathematical symbols in STEM documents to the MathQA knowledge graph. Our proposed math meaning-enhanced approach, MEEMath, achieved state-of-the-art performance in document-level mathematical question classification, yielding a 10.5% increase in F1-score compared to the best baseline. We have made the MathQA dataset publicly available to support further research in mathematical entity linking. The dataset and code can be accessed at https://github.com/MyungjaeLee/MathQA. Our source code is also available on arXiv at https://arxiv.org/abs/2101.01041. The results demonstrate that our approach significantly enhances STEM document classification performance. Stable Marriage and Collaborative Filtering algorithms rely on specific rules and preferences to determine optimal pairings. This paper examines the first such rule in the Stable Marriage context: the consideration-by-number rule. We analyze its impact on both classic and online versions of the problem. Regarding classic stable matching, we demonstrate that for any consideration number $k$, there exists a preference structure where the rule results in only $O(k)$ matches, rendering it ineffective. Consequently, we introduce the online stable matching problem and prove that considering number $k$ yields a competitive ratio of $1/(k+1)$ compared to the optimal offline solution. Furthermore, we present a specific matching process that achieves a competitive ratio of $\ln(n)/n$ over the optimal offline solution. Finally, we apply the concept of number $k$ to the collaborative filtering task of finding the best user-item pairs. In this application, we present an algorithm with a competitive ratio of $1/(k+1)$ relative to the best offline algorithm when selecting $k$ proposals per user. Additionally, we establish a lower bound of $1/2e$ for the ratio achievable by any online algorithm that chooses a non-empty set of matches of size at most $k$ for each user. Our proposed algorithm for this scenario achieves a competitive ratio of $\ln(e)/e$, which approximates this lower bound. We conclude by outlining several open questions for future research. This study examines dissipation-range fluid turbulence by modeling it as a system of interacting, randomly distributed charged particles within a self-consistent electrostatic field. The primary focus is on the evolution of electrostatic potential energy, $W$, relative to total kinetic energy, $T$. Analysis reveals that when $W$ approaches $T$, the system generates a self-consistent electrostatic field capable of dissipating and smoothing out random velocity fluctuations. Consequently, the velocity distribution becomes anisotropic, forming a thin shell in velocity space characterized by a narrow dissipation range. This dissipation mechanism is driven by electrostatic energy. Furthermore, when kinetic energy is replaced by heat conductivity in the governing equation, the resulting thermal disturbance also drives velocity fluctuations toward anisotropy within a dissipation range, with fluctuations in the field variable aligned with the large-scale gradient direction. These findings offer a theoretical basis for explaining the observed dissipation range in the solar wind. A comprehensive comparison of these results with prior observations and theoretical models will be presented in our upcoming paper. Finally, the implications of these discoveries for understanding the physics of the dissipation range are explored. While the primary focus remains on the solar wind, the associated theoretical framework is also applicable to other high-frequency plasma environments. Additionally, the associated computational model is suitable for simulating other high-frequency, collisionless, dissipative fluid turbulence phenomena. Designers frequently resolve issues through discussion, yet capturing the relevant information within this dialogue remains a significant challenge. This study addresses the issue of consistently and accurately identifying relevant information from design discussion dialogues by establishing a vocabulary and set of rules for conclusion stability. This research is driven by the need to automatically extract relevant data from design discussions to construct digital repositories. Since dialogue extraction methods often yield inconsistent results, we propose a vocabulary and rule set grounded in a qualitative analysis of current findings. We demonstrate how this framework ensures result consistency and illustrate its application in generating task-specific vocabulary and rule sets. Furthermore, we validate its effectiveness by demonstrating how these frameworks facilitate the accurate and consistent extraction of digital design repositories. Finally, we reflect on the framework's strengths and limitations and suggest directions for future research. This paper is intended as a readable introduction to our work, which is based on the findings presented in [1]. Given that this is a conclusion paper for a special issue, we invite readers to consult the original publication for a more comprehensive presentation of our results.

This paper presents H-STREAM, a new big data processing engine designed for handling, computing, and querying massive streams of events. This study investigates the production of top and bottom partners at the LHC and future high-energy colliders. Through a comprehensive analysis of the full phase space, we examine the characteristics of these processes in both proton-proton and electron-positron environments. Our results indicate that at the LHC, these production mechanisms achieve their peak cross-sections at lower parton momentum fractions and higher center-of-mass energies. Furthermore, our findings demonstrate that the kinematic signatures of these scenarios are most pronounced at lower momentum fractions and elevated collision energies. Additionally, we observe that our results remain consistent with previous literature at higher momentum fractions. These insights are crucial for designing experimental searches and interpreting data in the near future. Finally, we present our findings in a didactic manner, aiming to assist newcomers to the field in grasping the fundamental concepts of single top and bottom partner production. Our work is intended to serve as an educational resource for students and researchers entering the field. Knowledge Base Neural Machine Translation (KB-NMT) represents a bi-directional task involving two distinct domains: natural language sentences and a knowledge base modeled as a graph. In this environment, KB-NMT systems must manage three types of elements when processing KB terms: term definition, term substitution, and copy generation. While previous studies have primarily prioritized term insertion, this research identifies copy generation as the most critical operation for effective KB-NMT. To address this, we introduce a new algorithm designed to control copy system operations, thereby enhancing performance across all KB ST elements. Additionally, we propose novel loss functions to regulate copy systems during both training and testing phases. Experimental results demonstrate that our method surpasses existing state-of-the-art approaches, achieving MTE scores of 0.50 for P, 0.45 for PRec, and 0.47 for F. Furthermore, we find that loss functions applied during the testing phase yield superior performance compared to those applied during the training phase. Finally, our approach successfully resolves the conflict between inverse parallelism and copy generation, issues that often hinder traditional KB-NMT systems. We introduce a straightforward and transparent approach to assessing scientific papers that serves as an effective alternative to citation-based metrics for early career evaluations. Our method relies exclusively on CDR scores—a normalized variant of impact factors—published by major conferences and journals. By compiling a large dataset of CDR scores from over 3,000 venues covering approximately 100 conferences and journals, we developed a new tool named Venue Analytics. This system calculates a paper's quality score by integrating the scores of its citing venues and, where available, the venues of its co-authors. We validated this model using data from more than 10 million papers and demonstrated that it outperforms both H-indices and hardware-related factors in predicting future individual publication success. Furthermore, when applied to Computer Vision researchers, Venue Analytics yields gender bias results comparable to those of DeNisi et al. (2021), who analyzed citations directly. The system is accessible at https://venueanalytics.org. While not a substitute for peer review, Venue Analytics can assist researchers in making informed decisions regarding conference and journal submissions. We anticipate this tool will facilitate deeper discussions on metrics and contribute to the broader effort to reduce bias and enhance transparency within scientific communities. Venue Analytics is open-source and available on GitHub at https://github.com/venueanalytics/venueanalytics. Additional details and documentation can be found at https://venueanalytics.org/docs. This study examines the application of deep learning in control systems, specifically addressing the challenge of verifying the robustness of neural networks (NNs) against adversarial attacks. We introduce a novel validation framework based on a new loss function designed to test the resilience of neural controllers within closed-loop systems against these attacks. Since this loss function is non-differentiable, we employ evolutionary strategies to efficiently compute the worst-case perturbation required by the verifier. The proposed method's effectiveness is demonstrated through case studies involving a neural network controller for a self-driving car and a neural network optimizer for a seven-segment display controller. Ultimately, our findings indicate that the verification method produces results that are both logical and consistent with established literature.

We introduce a new deep learning framework designed for reconstructing large-scale, high-resolution, and dynamic video streams captured by moving platforms, such as drones and robots. Our strategy relies on breaking videos into patches and utilizing the visual correlations between overlapping regions to fill in missing data. The proposed method consists of three core components: 1) A patch tracking module that leverages visual correlations among adjacent patches to create a dense, patch-level trajectory for each frame; 2) A tensor loop completion module that leverages correlations across multiple frames and modalities to reconstruct entire patches; and 3) A blending frame generation module that smooths patch-level reconstructions by exploiting inter-patch visual correlations within specific frames. Extensive experiments on public datasets demonstrate the method's effectiveness in reconstructing video streams with complex camera movements and rapidly changing content. The code is accessible at https://github.com/ChenchenLi1999/Patch-Tracking. Furthermore, our results show a substantial improvement in automatic content recovery compared to current state-of-the-art techniques. Specifically, on the Mip-NeRF 360 dataset, our approach yields an 18.4% increase in PSNR and a 10.2% increase in SSIM relative to the original method. On the NeRF Synthetic dataset, the gains are even more pronounced, with an 80.4% PSNR improvement and a 72.1% SSIM increase. On the Mip-NeRF dataset, our method achieves a 20.4% PSNR gain and a 13.6% SSIM gain over the original. Additionally, we recover 95.5% of video streams from the Mip-NeRF-KITTI dataset, compared to 84.4% recovered by the original approach. Finally, we successfully recover 95.5% of video streams from the NeRF Wild dataset, representing a 91.1% recovery rate compared to what the original method could achieve. These findings confirm that our approach significantly outperforms existing state-of-the-art solutions in automatic video stream recovery. Additionally, we demonstrate that our method is computationally efficient, requiring only 1.5 seconds to reconstruct video streams on a Tesla V100 GPU. This efficiency enables real-time video stream reconstruction during data collection, a capability that other current methods lack. In summary, our work presents a novel and effective solution for video stream reconstruction, offering significant advantages in both performance and computational efficiency over existing alternatives.

This paper introduces a novel iterative algorithm designed to find the size of the maximum independent set in general graphs, particularly for inputs with small degrees. The method constructs a sequence of iterative normalizations for the graph and determines the maximum independent set size based on this sequence. We establish a complexity bound for the algorithm and demonstrate its convergence within a quadratic number of steps. Furthermore, we present a direct application to the coloring problem, proving that the algorithm can color graphs with degree $d$ using no more than $d^2+d+1$ colors. This result improves upon Broersma's bound of $2d^2-2d+1$ and complements Zaremba's bound of $(\frac{d+1}{2})^2$. Additionally, the algorithm is shown to achieve the weaker but still significant color count of $d^2+d+1$. Finally, we examine the coloring problem specifically for squares of trees. In this context, the algorithm either produces a tree coloring or a bipartite coloring, depending on the specific input tree. We also provide an upper bound for the algorithm's performance on tree squares, which compares favorably with other known bounds. Notably, this approach yields a direct proof of the conjecture by Faudree and Lehel regarding the maximum chromatic number of tree squares. The paper concludes with an outline of an algorithm that refines our upper bound on the algorithm's performance. Finally, we address the problem of identifying induced minors of bounded size in general graphs and propose an upper bound for this quantity, which surpasses all other known upper bounds. We also consider the case of tree powers. For this scenario, we present an upper bound that improves upon one existing bound and complement another known upper bound. However, for the case of tree powers, we are unable to determine the algorithm's performance. We conclude by outlining an upper bound for the algorithm's performance on tree powers, which is comparable to other known upper bounds. Furthermore, the algorithm provides an upper bound for the number of colors required to properly color tree powers, matching the count achievable for squares. This study investigates the thermodynamic characteristics of electrically modulated monolayer graphene. The electric displacement vector is calculated using the self-consistent framework within the tight-binding model. Furthermore, the electric conductivity and specific heat capacity are examined across various temperatures and chemical potentials. Ultimately, these theoretical findings are compared against available experimental data. This work is essential for understanding the fundamental properties of two-dimensional materials. Additionally, the models developed could facilitate the design of energy-efficient electronic devices. **Keywords:** tight-binding, electric conductivity, electric modulus, thermal conductivity, specific heat capacity.

We report a 14-year continuous radio observation of the binary system CR Draconis, which revealed two distinct phases of electron-cyclotron maser emission from the active star. The initial phase, detected between 2004 and 2006, was characterized by high-intensity, low-frequency radiation. Approximately eight years later, a second phase of low-frequency emission was identified, exhibiting a significantly longer duration. The persistent nature of the low-frequency emission suggests a stable population of electrons within the star's corona. Furthermore, the temporal behavior of the low-frequency radiation indicates that the electron population is likely confined to the star's polar regions. These findings provide critical insights into the mechanisms driving non-thermal radio emission from flare stars. Additionally, the observed radio flux from CR Draconis may contribute to the unresolved radio background detected from M-type stars in the nearby Taurus-Auriga molecular cloud. The identification of this second phase of low-frequency emission marks the first such detection from an M-type star, underscoring the significance of low-frequency observations for studying stellar activity. Future research should prioritize the investigation of other M-type stars to further explore the characteristics of this low-frequency emission. Humans perceive images that have undergone severe transformations, such as those found in the PALETTE dataset, more effectively than machines do. While current machine learning models often struggle with these distortions, achieving the opposite result—where humans fail to see what machines do—is surprisingly easy. This observation raises critical questions about the fundamental differences between human and machine perception. The present study aims to accelerate our understanding of these disparities by examining how models respond to transformations that are typically easy or difficult for humans to process. Our findings reveal that humans and machines are often challenged by completely different transformations. To address this, we introduce the concept of "human-AI confusion," which quantifies the extent of this divergence across a spectrum of transformations. This new metric demonstrates that certain approaches, like those utilizing generative models, are more robust against human-AI confusion than others, such as those relying on image compression. Furthermore, our results indicate that understanding and leveraging human-AI confusion can enhance the robustness of machine learning models against out-of-distribution data. Finally, we explore the implications of these results for the relationship between humans and machines.

We examine the spin-$1/2$ trimer antiferromagnet (TFA) on a two-dimensional square lattice by mapping it onto a quantum cluster model and employing cluster Monte Carlo simulations. Our analysis focuses on the impact of intercluster interactions, which are represented by the strength of coupling between nearest-neighbor $S=3/2$ triflers. These triflers are defined as effective spins within the TFA, derived from the local ground state of a three-spin cluster. Our findings indicate that the TFA exhibits significant magnetic frustration, resulting in a ground state characterized by short-range antiferromagnetic correlations and a lack of long-range order. Furthermore, the strength of the most dominant intercluster interaction is governed by the specific pattern of these short-range correlations. Finally, we demonstrate that the TFA displays distinct crossover behaviors, transitioning from a 1D regime, where interactions between adjacent triflers dominate, to a 2D regime, where interactions between triflers separated by a single trimer are significant. This evolution is driven by the strength of the TFA's second strongest intercluster interaction. Consequently, the TFA experiences a series of crossover transitions from 1D to 2D, with the number of these transitions determined by the ratio between the two dominant intercluster interactions. Our results suggest that the TFA could be effectively modeled as a trimer version of the trimer Heisenberg model. Additionally, we show that the TFA possesses a non-zero energy gap, with the magnitude of this gap modulated by the strength of the intercluster interactions. Finally, we discuss the potential for the TFA to exhibit a variety of exotic phases, including gapless phases, phases with short-range order, and phases with long-range order. These phases are identified by analyzing the behavior of the correlation length and the structure factor of the trimerization order parameter. Specifically, the 1D and 2D regimes correspond to long and short correlation lengths, respectively, while the trimerization order parameter vanishes in the 1D regime but remains finite in the 2D regime. The number of phase transitions from 1D to 2D is determined by the ratio between the two dominant intercluster interactions. Furthermore, the 1D and 2D regimes correspond to the trimerization and ferromagnetic orders, respectively, of the trimer Heisenberg model. Pretrained language models have achieved significant success across various NLP tasks, yet they remain difficult to adapt for zero-shot learning due to the lack of task examples during training. This study introduces an approach that combines dynamic dataset assembly with dynamic prompt assembly to enable zero-shot learning without any modification to the underlying language model. First, we introduce dynamic dataset assembly, which constructs training instances from a collection of datasets to train the model on specific tasks without altering its weights. Second, we develop dynamic prompt assembly, which generates static prompts for each target task during zero-shot inference to facilitate direct weight transfer from the example-based training phase. We evaluate this method for zero-shot learning across three standard benchmarks: image classification (65 categories), text classification (115 categories), and question answering (104 questions). The method requires no weight tuning and successfully enables GPT2 to perform zero-shot learning without prior exposure. Furthermore, we demonstrate how the approach allows completely unseen tasks to leverage weight patterns from related tasks for zero-shot learning. Our method proves effective in zero-shot learning scenarios, particularly when dealing with limited training data. Additionally, we provide empirical evidence indicating that the proposed method can identify weight updates most beneficial for target tasks by analyzing the relationships among datasets, dataset assemblies, prompts, and prompt assemblies. This paper examines the implications of recent LHC findings on a third-order electroweak phase transition (EWPT) within the $Z_3$-invariant Next-to-Minimal Supersymmetric Standard Model (NMSSM). We analyze the constraints imposed by LHC data on the model's parameter space to explore the viability of a first-order EWPT and the associated scale. Furthermore, we investigate the stability of dark matter against these LHC results, considering both first- and third-order EWPTs. Finally, we assess the prospects for detecting gravitational waves generated by this first-order EWPT. Our findings indicate that, under these LHC constraints, the range of parameters allowing for a first-order EWPT is highly restricted, rendering the generation of a detectable gravitational wave signal highly improbable. Additionally, we observe that detecting dark matter through the EWPT mechanism is challenging, particularly when accounting for the latest LHC limits. To maximize the potential for observing dark matter via NMSSM, we recommend focusing on parameter regions situated far from the parameter space favored by LHC data. Finally, we note that while the sensitivity of current gravitational wave observatories is insufficient to probe parameter regions yielding a third-order EWPT, future observatories may be able to do so. These conclusions remain robust even if we assume future experimental advancements. (arXiv:1905.07706v1 [hep-ph]) Keywords: NMSSM, Electroweak Phase Transition, Dark Matter, Gravitational Waves. We introduce a new diagnostic tool designed to evaluate the robustness of submillimeter redshifts, offering an alternative to the traditional Sudoku test. This method is grounded in Bayesian statistics and maintains the same fundamental principles as the original approach. By utilizing this instrument, we can effectively identify the most reliable redshifts for future spectroscopic confirmation, thereby optimizing the use of scarce (sub)mm telescope time. We demonstrate the instrument's capabilities through a test case involving a sample of 100 galaxies at $z\sim2.5$. Furthermore, we show that redshifts selected with this method result in a sample with significantly higher reliability and fewer misidentified objects compared to those chosen by other techniques. We also provide a user-friendly online interface for the tool, which is publicly accessible at http://www.highzsudoku.net. This interface includes a demonstration sample and a tutorial to guide users on applying the instrument to their own datasets. We conclude that High-z Sudoku represents a valuable resource for (sub)mm astronomers, particularly those engaged in redshift survey projects. By ensuring the selection of galaxies with robust redshifts, this tool will ultimately enhance the efficiency of (sub)mm redshift surveys. Additionally, we have released a Python package, also named High-z Sudoku, which implements this instrument; it is available on GitHub at https://github.com/alejandro-fernandez-sanchez/High-z-Sudoku. The package includes the source code for the Bayesian calculations, an implementation of the method, and a sample dataset for testing purposes. The package can be easily installed via pip using the command: `pip install High-z-Sudoku`. We demonstrate that the results produced by our implementation are consistent with those from the online interface. We anticipate that High-z Sudoku will prove to be a highly effective tool for (sub)mm astronomers aiming to verify the redshifts of galaxies they discover. We believe that adopting this tool will significantly improve the efficiency of upcoming submillimeter redshift surveys. Our goal is for the community to adopt High-z Sudoku, as its widespread use will substantially enhance the effectiveness of upcoming redshift surveys. This study presents numerical simulations of the dynamics within the $S=1/2$ Heisenberg antiferromagnet on a triangular lattice using quantum Monte Carlo methods. We investigate dynamics on timescales ($\tau$) ranging from the instantaneous limit to the $\beta$-correlation limit, covering approximately two orders of magnitude, by modeling a single classical spin interacting with its environment on a lattice of quantum spins. Our results reveal clear signatures of the low-temperature 120$^{\circ}$-ordered state, characterized by a Kosterlitz-Thouless transition as the environment's temperature varies. Additionally, we identify potential indicators of the recently proposed $120^{\circ}$-ordered quantum spin liquid phase. Finally, we offer the first numerical evidence of a quantum critical point occurring along a specific line in the parameter space, which separates regions where 120$^{\circ}$ order and quantum spin liquid behavior dominate. These findings are interpreted within the framework of the quantum Monte Carlo renormalization group scheme. Overall, our work demonstrates effective techniques for simulating classical spin systems with a quantum environment and provides a pathway to detect symmetry-breaking phases and quantum critical points in novel materials. Furthermore, the study offers insights into the nature of quantum spin liquid phases and their experimental detectability. These conclusions are supported by a comparison with the results of a related mean-field theory. Finally, we address the necessity of including temporal fluctuations in the environment to accurately capture dynamics near the quantum critical point. This work is based on the doctoral thesis of J. A. M. P. L. de Groot. Additional details can be found in the full thesis, which is accessible at https://dare.uva.nl/record/1720074. Antiferromagnets are crucial for both fundamental research and technological applications, yet their complex internal structures and interactions often hinder the design of practical devices. This study examines the magnetic properties of Cr2Al, a recently discovered, high-temperature antiferromagnetic metal, using a combination of first-principles calculations and neutron powder diffraction. The results reveal a novel type of in-plane antiferromagnetic arrangement that cannot be explained by the Heisenberg model, indicating strong contributions from higher-order exchange interactions. Furthermore, the analysis demonstrates that modifying the lattice parameters can effectively switch the magnetic state. These findings provide a foundation for developing new antiferromagnets and offer valuable insights for creating spintronic technologies. Additionally, the detailed first-principles results are expected to advance the understanding of magnetic correlations in other transition metal compounds. Finally, this work illustrates how integrating computational methods with experimental techniques can efficiently and accurately determine the ground state of complex magnetic materials. All data and computational resources are publicly accessible.

Semantic grounding involves determining the mapping between natural language and internal representations. Recent progress in training semantic interpreters has enabled languages to be mapped onto minimal neural embeddings. However, these learned mappings often fail to generalize effectively to unseen vocabulary or concepts outside of training data, particularly when transfer targets consist of structures significantly different from internal representations. This paper proposes an approach to train semantic interpreters that enhances transferability to minimal, naturalistic representations. Our method involves replacing small, artificial internal interpretable units with larger, more naturalistic ones, thereby reducing the dependency of learned mappings on specific tiny units. We evaluate our method on word sorting and object tracking tasks, demonstrating that this approach substantially improves generalization to novel training sets and transfers more robustly to larger, naturalistic representations. Our code is available at https://github.com/alexander-pfau/semantic-interpreters-semantic-data. Additionally, we introduce a new paper template for the 2022 ICML Machine Learning for Symbolic Reasoning and Learning (MSSL) workshop, accessible at https://github.com/ICML-2022-MSSL/paper_template. The upcoming Electron-Ion Collider (EIC) will investigate the internal structure of protons and nuclei, as well as the formation of hadrons and jets from quarks and gluons. To achieve this, the EIC's detector must track forward light hadrons with exceptional precision and robustness. This paper outlines the advancements made in the design, fabrication, and testing of the silicon tracker for the EIC forward region (EFT), which utilizes planar CO2-based silicon sensors. These sensors are engineered to deliver a pixel transverse position resolution of 3 micrometers. The process of bonding these sensors to flexible printed-circuit boards (fPCBs) featuring on-sensor readout has been successfully completed. A 2x2 EFT module incorporating four EIC-style sensors with on-sensor readout has been installed between layers of two 3D-printed cylindrical plastic scintillator hodoscopes. Testing results from these modules within the prototype magnetic field have confirmed the anticipated performance metrics. Furthermore, this work details the current status of the EFT readout system, the integration of new sensor and fPCB production, and the ongoing development of sensor bonding techniques. The target completion date for the EIC silicon tracker is the second half of 2023. Additionally, the paper addresses the development of a novel silicon sensor technology for the Muon Collider, which involves a two-stage process: first, designing and testing sensors with superior performance compared to the EFT, and second, developing and implementing an advanced bonding method that enables on-sensor readout. This technology is also being considered for the High-Luminosity LHC upgrade. The goal is to deliver a fully functional, high-performance readout system for the EIC tracker by the end of 2022. Keywords: Electron Ion Collider, Silicon Tracker, Planar CO2 Sensors, On-sensor Readout, Muon Collider.

This paper establishes the free boson representation of the Dunkl intertwining operator within one dimension. Utilizing this formulation, we derive several representations of key objects, including the Chiral Operator, CHL Operator, and CHQ operator, all expressed through the free boson representation of the Dunkl intertwining operator. Furthermore, we demonstrate the conversion of representations between the free boson representation and the ordinary representation for the Minkowski space, $q$-deformed Minkowski space, and $q$-sphere. Additionally, we examine the invariance of the free boson representation of the $SO(2,1)$ and $U_q(2,1)$ intertwining operators under the action of the $SL_q(2,\mathbb{R})$ group. Finally, we outline the implications of these findings for the $q$-deformed Virasoro algebra. We present ALMA observations of the H30$\alpha$ recombination line in the low-metallicity galaxy NGC 5253, a system known for intense star formation. These observations reveal a compact, central HII region spanning approximately 100 pc, with an ionized gas mass of roughly 10$^7$ solar masses and an ionizing photon production rate of about 10$^{51}$ s$^{-1}$. We conducted a comprehensive analysis of the H30$\alpha$ line using various radiative transfer models, including the radiative transfer code RADMC-3D and the statistical models PyKE and MAPPINGS. Our findings indicate that the observed line emission is primarily driven by the central core, which is in the optically thick regime. Consequently, we determined that the ionized gas within this core has a density of approximately 10$^4$ cm$^{-3}$, with an electron temperature around 10,000 K. By utilizing the derived core properties, we applied PyKE and MAPPINGS to model the H30$\alpha$ emission, confirming that the core is the dominant source. Our results suggest that the MAPPINGS model aligns best with the observations, indicating a gas density of roughly 10$^4$ cm$^{-3}$ and a temperature near 10,000 K. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the H30$\alpha$ line is a highly effective probe for characterizing the physical properties of ionized gas in low-metallicity environments. Finally, we compare these measurements with those derived from the H$\alpha$ line, confirming that the H30$\alpha$ line serves as a reliable tool for characterizing the physical properties of star-forming regions. This study underscores the value of recombination lines with high critical densities for characterizing the physical properties of star-forming regions. This study introduces a novel observer for a specific class of partial functional differential equations (PFDEs), with the goal of estimating dynamic infection parameters within time-varying epidemic processes. These parameters are modeled as solutions to a specific system of ordinary differential equations (ODEs). The proposed observer offers two primary advantages: first, it relies on accessible infection data for its design; second, it adheres to a separation principle. Additionally, we provide rigorous mathematical proofs regarding the stability of both the observer error dynamics and the overall closed-loop system. Finally, a numerical simulation demonstrates the observer's effectiveness. This efficient observer is applicable to a broad range of processes, including those with additive time delays. Furthermore, it serves as a foundational tool for designing control measures to mitigate the spread of infectious diseases. Integrating temporal information into knowledge graphs enables a broader and more precise representation of real-world entities and events. This data is typically structured as temporal knowledge graphs (TKGs), a format that has recently spurred research into applying machine learning to TKGs for tasks such as link prediction. However, TKGs often suffer from sparsity, and the complexity of tracking entity temporal states makes link prediction difficult. This paper introduces the use of static models for link prediction within temporal knowledge graphs. We propose two approaches: (1) employing a static model for link prediction on a TKG, and (2 adapting a static model to leverage temporal information during the process. Experimental results demonstrate that temporal models can enhance accuracy by approximately 1% over static models on a TKG. Furthermore, we find that static models are better suited for predicting links with longer lifespans, whereas models that explicitly model temporal state changes excel at link prediction for shorter lifespans. Finally, we observe that the temporal modeling component of static models is primarily responsible for the performance gains seen in our experiments. The code for the models and data is accessible at https://github.com/ashishkumar2001/TKG-LinkPrediction. This work investigates how geometric parameters influence the stability and performance of Kerr-lens mode-locked (KL-MC) oscillators. A key parameter introduced is the effective cavity aperture, which quantifies the spatial truncation of the cavity mode by the Kerr lens. We demonstrate that when effective lensing is strong and the Kerr lens surges to the extent of over-focusing, the fundamental longitudinal mode becomes unstable, giving way to quasi-CW or multi-pulse lateral mode-locking. Furthermore, reducing the effective cavity aperture leads to the formation of deeper, narrower potential wells and enhances the peak power of generated pulses. Numerical simulations indicate that peak power can reach up to 100 MW/cm² when the effective cavity aperture is approximately 10% of its standard value. Additionally, we examined multi-pulse lateral mode-locking, observing that the number of lateral pulses increases with effective lensing strength but diminishes as the effective cavity aperture shrinks. These findings offer a comprehensive framework for designing high-peak-power ultrafast KL-MC oscillators. Additionally, the parameters studied can aid in diagnosing multi-pulse lateral mode-locking events and guiding strategies to mitigate them. A Python-based design tool for KL-MC oscillators, incorporating these geometric parameters, is available at https://github.com/zhongyuanwang1990/KL_MC_design_tool. Its source code can be requested from the corresponding author. Finally, we outline a pathway for future experimental validation of these results. The optical absorption of silicon films is enhanced using three-dimensional photonic band gap (3D-PBG) materials as back reflectors. By substituting the conventional metallic back reflector with a 3D-PBG structure, a substantial improvement in light absorption is achieved. This performance gain stems from two primary factors: the elimination of unabsorbed light being re-reflected out of the device and the scattering of unabsorbed light within the 3D-PBG unit cells. To assess this enhancement, the absorption characteristics of silicon films with varying thicknesses were compared against those using conventional metallic reflectors. Numerical simulations were conducted across a broad spectrum ranging from 300 nm to 2000 nm. The results indicate that for a silicon film thickness of 300 nm, the maximum absorption reaches 99.9% within the 3D-PBG configuration, a stark contrast to near-zero absorption observed with a conventional metal reflector at the same thickness. Furthermore, a significant increase in absorption is noted across the entire spectral range when 3D-PBG back reflectors are employed. These findings suggest that 3D-PBG back reflectors offer a promising solution for achieving high absorption in thin-film and thin-film-like photonic devices. Additionally, this 3D-PBG configuration is applicable to silicon photonic platforms, enabling the development of efficient silicon-based photodetectors and solar cells. The potential for manufacturing these 3D-PBG back reflectors via standard silicon foundry processes is currently under investigation. Ultimately, this research paves the way for the creation of thin-film and thin-film-like photonic devices with superior absorption capabilities. Keywords: 3D-PBG back reflector, thin-film, thin-film-like, high absorption.

Graph representation learning has gained significant traction recently, yet most existing methods are tailored for dense networks, leaving sparse networks underrepresented. This domain is challenging because the limited number of edges results in scarce information and high node sparsity, which hinders accurate learning of the underlying network structure. This paper introduces an efficient and interpretable approach to generate node representations specifically for sparse networks. We achieve this by integrating the geometric properties of high-dimensional manifolds with the structural characteristics of the Nodal Entropy Model. To our knowledge, this marks the first time such a model has been applied to this problem, leveraging information theory to enhance the algorithm's interpretability. We validate our proposed algorithm, Sparse Spectral Node Embedding (SSNE), across various real-world datasets, demonstrating that it outperforms current state-of-the-art methods. Furthermore, our method surpasses the second-best approach by a substantial margin in sparse networks, while maintaining competitive performance in moderately dense ones. We also show that SSNE effectively identifies communities within the network. To support future research, we have made our code and data accessible at https://github.com/ahmedhassan12345/SSNE. We introduce a novel method for constructing atomic vapor cells utilizing micro-fabricated deep silicon etching. This approach enables the fabrication of compact cells with exceptional optical and mechanical durability. By applying the technique to an optimized etch pattern, we achieved a cell with a minimal absorption cross-section of 1.4 mm² featuring an etalon effect. Leveraging the high mechanical strength of silicon, we demonstrated that micro-vapour cells can operate at pressures exceeding 10 bar. Furthermore, we established that deep silicon etching is a viable method for manufacturing integrated optical instruments suitable for applications in quantum information science. These quantum atomic devices could be embedded within silicon photonic integrated circuits, thereby facilitating miniaturized optical and atomic field sensors. Such technology holds significant promise for advancing space-based quantum communication systems. Additionally, we illustrate how these robust micro-vapour cells can be embedded within monolithic structures, paving the way for fully integrated optical systems. This paper introduces a model designed to forecast nonlinear distortion distortion products in dual-polarization quadrature amplitude modulation (DP-QAM) optical transmission systems. By utilizing the nonlinear coefficients derived from back-to-back back-to-front (BBOF) characterization experiments, the model accurately predicts system performance across various fiber lengths. Additionally, it estimates the depletion of amplified spontaneous emission (ASE) noise within unmodulated polarization multiplexed channels under different power allocations. The findings indicate that this model is applicable to a wide range of formats, including dual-polarization quadrature phase-shift keying (DP-QPSK), DP-8QAM, and DP-16QAM. Furthermore, the results demonstrate that nonlinear distortion products are more prevalent in BBOF configurations than in real-world transmission systems, particularly under low launch power conditions. Consequently, a power threshold exists below which the depletion of ASE noise within modulated channels becomes negligible. Beyond modeling nonlinear distortion products, this approach also facilitates the quantification of digital backpropagation (DBP) benefits in practical transmission environments. Ultimately, this model serves as a valuable tool for designing and analyzing complex formats in optical transmission systems. Detecting wildfires in real-time is crucial for preventing property damage and loss of life. Deep learning-based computer vision has become increasingly popular in this domain, yet it faces significant hurdles when applied to infrared (IR) and visible (VIS) satellite imagery. Specifically, the often sparse and noisy IR data generated by current sensors makes it difficult to train robust deep learning models. To overcome these challenges, we introduce a deep learning architecture that integrates IR and VIS imagery using the novel FIRe-GAN (Fused Infrared and visible Earth Observation imagery GAN) model. By incorporating VIS data, the model enhances and regularizes the information available to deep learning algorithms, thereby boosting performance. We evaluated FIRe-GAN across various wildfire detection tasks, including fire pixel segmentation, fire detection, and smoke detection. Our results demonstrate that combining IR and VIS data with the FIRe-GAN approach yields superior outcomes compared to other state-of-the-art methods. Furthermore, we offer a comprehensive analysis of the model's behavior regarding different input data characteristics. Our findings indicate that FIRe-GAN is highly effective for fire and smoke pixel segmentation, though it performs less reliably in fire and smoke detection tasks. This study presents a data collection methodology designed to identify indicators of depression in social media posts. The approach involves interviewing participants to learn their online habits, gathering consented user accounts, and labeling those users' posts regarding the users' mental states. We applied this framework to gather data on depression signs, which was then used to train and evaluate classification models. The analysis involved interviewing 20 college students from two distinct age groups (18–25 and 26–35) to understand their online activities, subsequently gathering 3,000 posts from 60 selected users and annotating them for depression status. Finally, we developed two classifiers—an Naive Bayes algorithm and a Support Vector Machine (SVM) with a linear kernel—and assessed their performance using various text preprocessing techniques. Results indicate that SVMs outperform Naive Bayes models, achieving an average accuracy of 80.5% across different preprocessing configurations. Furthermore, the post-processing stage demonstrated an 8% accuracy improvement by filtering out incoherent sentences from the posts. These findings suggest that SVMs are highly effective for detecting depression cues in social media text, offering valuable applications for mental health professionals. This research holds significant potential for aiding mental health services, including suicide prevention initiatives. Additionally, the study confirms that social media posts contain discernible signs of depression, providing a foundation for future research into additional mental health conditions. This study investigates the influence of coupling between isoscalar monopole and quadrupole excitations on the properties of the Isoscalar Giant Monopole Resonance (ISGMR) in $^{24}$Mg and $^{28}$Si. Theoretical calculations were performed using the relativistic RPA framework, incorporating an effective interaction that includes a newly derived isoscalar scalar-quadrupole channel. This scalar-quadrupole interaction, which couples the monopole and quadrupole modes, was constructed based on the effective scalar-isoscalar interaction used in previous ISGMR research. The results indicate that including the scalar-quadrupole channel causes a slight reduction in the ISGMR energy for $^{24}$Mg and a marginal increase for $^{28}$Si. Furthermore, this interaction enhances the energy-weighted sum rule of the ISGMR by 1.5% in $^{24}$Mg and 2.1% in $^{28}$Si. These findings align well with experimental data. Overall, the effects of the monopole-quadrupole coupling on ISGMR characteristics are more pronounced in $^{28}$Si than in $^{24}$Mg. These results provide essential insights for future research on giant resonances. Additionally, the derived effective scalar-quadrupole channel interaction can be utilized to investigate other nuclear phenomena, such as pairing vibrations and collective excitations. This work is dedicated to the memory of Professor Jie Meng. Keywords: Isoscalar giant monopole resonance; Isoscalar monopole-quadrupole interaction; Relativistic RPA. This study addresses the finite-time Bellman insurance problem, introducing a novel probabilistic framework for learning both the value function and the optimal control. The value function is expressed as a conditional expectation dependent on a sufficient statistic of the control up to the current time. Leveraging the universal approximation capabilities of deep neural networks (NNs), we employ a recurrent architecture to model the value function using this efficient control summary. By applying the Bellman equation, the network is trained via the least-squares method. Control optimization is achieved through the implicit differentiation of the learned value function with respect to the sufficient statistic of the control. This approach, termed Deep Bellman insurance, is demonstrated through numerical examples involving two insurance claim models. The proposed method is computationally efficient, easy to implement, and demonstrates robust performance across a wide range of parameters. Furthermore, the method is adaptable to various insurance claim models and can be readily extended to address more complex optimization challenges. Notably, the approach remains applicable to infinite-horizon problems. Additionally, the technique is versatile and can be utilized in contexts beyond insurance, such as general optimal control and economics. Finally, the paper concludes with a discussion of potential future research directions. This work serves as a contribution to the field of optimal control, specifically focusing on the Bellman equation. It is anticipated to be valuable for researchers in this domain, including those in economics and engineering. The paper is also expected to interest the broader deep learning community, as it introduces a new, distinct approach for solving control problems. This offers an alternative to the widely used deep reinforcement learning (DRL) methods. Crucially, unlike DRL, which requires extensive computational resources and time, Deep Bellman insurance is shown to be computationally efficient. This is demonstrated through extensive numerical experiments, including those utilizing high-dimensional inputs. The resulting efficiency is expected to be highly attractive to practitioners in industry and academia. Finally, the paper is relevant to the scientific community, as it presents a new approach that complements existing methods and opens avenues for further research and innovation. This is evidenced by the inclusion of detailed mathematical proofs and discussions of the method's theoretical underpinnings. Sequential recommenders are prevalent in real-world scenarios due to their ability to capture user behavior patterns and deliver personalized items. However, a critical challenge remains: how to effectively predict a user's intent based on their recent history. To address this, we propose a sequential recommender system that explicitly models purpose topics within its latent space. By employing non-negative matrix factorization, the model decomposes user interactions into a set of latent purpose topics. It then constructs user purpose profiles by calculating the user's profile distribution across these topics, while item purpose profiles are represented by their distributions across the same topics. Finally, the model estimates user-item interactions by measuring the compatibility between their purpose profiles. Extensive experiments on two real-world datasets demonstrate that our approach outperforms several state-of-the-art sequential recommender systems. Furthermore, analysis of our model and its parameters reveals that the latent purpose topics align with real-world purposes, offering interpretability to both researchers and practitioners. The reducible double confluent Heun equation features a symmetric source composed of two quadrupoles and two dipoles arranged in a specific configuration. This configuration can be continuously deformed into an arrangement of six dipoles with maintained dipole-phase symmetry, a configuration known to generate the reducible double confluent Heun equation through a specific Jordan block source. Both deformed sources arise from a single master source upon continuous evaluation of a single complex parameter. This newly identified continuous symmetric unfolding of the source is highly relevant for applications involving monodromy data and scattering matrices. Additionally, we examine a specific discrete unfolding of this master source, which yields a novel master equation capable of describing a wide range of double confluent Heun equations. This discrete unfolding was previously identified by one of the authors as a method to generate all solvable instances of the double confluent Heun equation. In this work, we provide a direct derivation of the discrete unfolding and demonstrate its application to various solvable cases of the double confluent Heun equation. Furthermore, the discrete master equation possesses a constant source consisting of two dipoles with opposite phases, representing a generalization of a previously known two-dipole source. We also present a unified approach to the solvable cases based on the continuous unfolding of the symmetric source. Finally, we discuss the relationship between the discrete and continuous unfoldments. These findings are supported by several conjectures regarding the general symmetric unfolding of the double confluent Heun equation. Notably, we show that the symmetric five-point equation is a special case of the master equation, thereby disproving a recent conjecture. Additionally, we conjecture that all symmetric unfoldings of the five-point equation are captured by our discrete and continuous unfoldments. Our results are closely linked to the symmetric five-point equation and the symmetric five-point equation with one dipole, which are also discussed. We further conjecture that the discrete and continuous unfoldments of the five-point equation are derived from the discrete and continuous unfoldments of the double confluent Heun equation, respectively. Finally, we address the double confluent Heun equation with a single quadrupole, a case not covered by our derived unfoldments, and discuss its properties. In conclusion, we propose a conjecture regarding the symmetric unfoldings of the double confluent Heun equation. Specifically, we conjecture that the reducible, dipole-only case is described by the discrete unfoldments of the five-point equation, while the quadrupole-only case is covered by the discrete unfoldments

We derive fundamental limits for the estimation error under various sampling conditions and propose a variational approach that leverages both the low-rank and groupwise sparsity structures of the signal. Our theoretical findings regarding the performance of this estimator match the information-theoretic lower bounds up to logarithmic factors. We introduce an intrinsic topological framework for octupole-ordered systems that does not rely on crystal symmetries. Through an order-parameter-based analysis of eight sublattice sites, we construct a topological model defined by an inherent topological quantum number. Furthermore, we demonstrate the construction of various octupole- and charge-quadrupole-type topological phases by circumventing crystal symmetries. Our findings expand the topological classification of octupole-ordered systems and provide insights into the development of intrinsic topological models. We anticipate that the proposed classification and intrinsic topological model will be applicable to a broad category of octupole-ordered systems. Specifically, we illustrate the intrinsic topological characteristics of a generic octupole-ordered system, where the energy spectrum exhibits a four-way degeneracy at the crossing point. These features are also observed in the charge-quadrupole ordered state of the $k$-agreed $t$-$J$ model. Our results offer a comprehensive understanding of intrinsic topological phases in octupole-ordered systems and their potential applications in the design of novel quantum materials. Additionally, we establish a classification scheme for octupole-ordered systems based on their quasicrystalline properties. We believe our findings will facilitate further investigations into the quasicrystalline characteristics of octupole orders and their potential applications in quasicrystalline materials. Finally, we show that the quasicrystalline nature of octupole ordering allows for the presence of intrinsic topological phases in quasicrystalline systems, a topic that has not been previously explored. This study introduces a two-stage deep learning approach for categorizing COVID-19-related tweets into specific topics. In the first stage, BERT models are trained to extract domain-specific features from the tweets. These aggregated features subsequently serve as input for a second model, which is trained to perform the final classification task. The methodology was evaluated using the Kaggle dataset containing tweets from May 2020, which span four distinct topics: general COVID19 issues, masks, vaccines, and general health. The results demonstrate that the proposed feature-categorization technique achieves high accuracy in classifying tweets within this domain. Furthermore, an ablation study confirms that the BERT-based feature extraction model is essential for the success of the overall two-stage approach. The paper concludes by discussing the method's advantages and outlining potential future research directions. This technique is particularly well-suited for social media analysis where the goal is to categorize unstructured text into a fixed set of predefined topics. By leveraging pre-trained BERT models to capture contextual features, the initial model achieves superior accuracy compared to using BERT solely for the final classification stage. Additionally, the study addresses a significant challenge in social media analysis: the scarcity of labeled data, which often hinders the training of effective deep learning models. The research begins by detailing the dataset and preprocessing procedures, followed by an explanation of the two-stage categorization technique and its evaluation within the specified context. Finally, the paper provides insights into the findings and their implications. Through the successful implementation of the suggested research, the authors aim to offer valuable resources for the COVID-19 community, which can be utilized for further analysis of social media data. Ultimately, this work seeks to contribute to the broader effort of combating the COVID-19 pandemic. The source code is publicly available at: https://github.com/raufhassan12345/Two-Stage-COVID19-Topic-Categorization. Future research will explore applying this technique to other domains, such as news categorization and customer feedback analysis. Additionally, the authors plan to investigate the impact of increasing the number of topics on the performance of the two-stage model. Finally, the source code will be made public to enable other researchers to replicate the findings and conduct similar analyses. The authors extend their gratitude to the Kaggle community for providing the dataset. Over the past few decades, increasing evidence has highlighted connections between eco-evolutionary dynamics and ecosystem dynamics, driven by the fact that evolution can occur rapidly. This review examines the mechanisms behind these interactions, with a specific focus on the roles of timescales and rate modulators. It begins by outlining the key components of eco-evolutionary dynamics and establishing a conceptual framework for timescale analysis. The discussion then explores how genetic variation, the strength of ecological selection, and phenotypic expression influence evolutionary rates. Furthermore, it addresses how life-history traits, mutation rates, and mutation spectra serve as modulators of mutation supply, alongside the impacts of sexual reproduction and outcrossing. Finally, the review synthesizes these factors to analyze eco-evolutionary dynamics across various organismal lineages. The intended audience includes evolutionary biologists, ecologists, geneticists, and genetic engineers. Theoretically, the paper demonstrates how a mechanistic understanding of timescales and rate modulators can guide mathematical modeling and experimental design. Practically, it elucidates the factors driving evolution from both historical and contemporary perspectives, while also considering the implications for engineering organisms with altered evolutionary trajectories. Overall, this work provides a comprehensive perspective on eco-evolutionary dynamics, timescales, and rate modulators, aiming to inspire future research. Additionally, the associated data, materials, and code are publicly accessible. Specifically, all figures, including the conceptual framework, are available as supplementary material at https://doi.org/10.6084/m9.figshare.12312002. The review was prepared using LaTeX and Overleaf, with all diagrams generated in Adobe Illustrator. The framework figure was developed using the TikZ package. While deep learning models are notoriously vulnerable to adversarial attacks, recent self-supervised methods (SSP) offer a potential alternative to traditional supervised approaches (SSP). This study investigates the resilience of speech self-supervised pretraining (SSP) against such attacks. Our findings indicate that SSP models are generally less susceptible to adversarial threats than SSP models, with the degree of robustness directly correlating with the extent of self-supervised pretraining. Furthermore, attacks targeting SSP with self-supervised pretraining involve perturbation magnitudes that are $10\times$ smaller than those required for SSP, demonstrating superior robustness. Additionally, we observe that adversarial examples generated for Speech Embeddings (SE) fail to transfer effectively to SSP models, suggesting that se represents a more secure alternative for deploying deep learning in safety-critical environments. Finally, we explore various defense mechanisms and identify the most effective strategies for mitigating adversarial risks. The accompanying code repository will be made publicly available. **Keywords:** Adversarial attacks, Self-supervised learning, Speech recognition, Deep learning, Safety-critical systems.

The E-value serves as a metric for quantifying sensitivity to missing data within a Bayesian framework. It represents the minimum factor by which the proportion of missing data must increase to alter a specific finding. This study outlines methodologies for calculating E-values to assess sensitivity in three contexts: missing completely at random, missing at random, and missing not at random. To demonstrate these approaches, the sensitivity of a log odds ratio estimating a vaccine's protective efficacy against disease was analyzed. Furthermore, an implementation utilizing R and JAGS is provided in the form of an open-source package. The study also extends these methods to handle multiple missingness mechanisms and scenarios involving no information priors. Ultimately, the E-value offers a versatile and straightforward tool for sensitivity analysis in missing data problems. The accompanying R package, EVALSE, is available on CRAN. Keywords: Bayesian inference, missing data, missingness mechanism, sensitivity analysis. Mathematics Subject Classification: 62F15.

These classifications demonstrate that the Laurent extension possesses a complete set of $q$-Weyl operators, a complete set of quantum angular momentum operators, complete sets of step-ladder operators, and complete sets of quantum rotation operators. The convergence of the Internet of Vehicles (IoV) and Machine Learning (ML) holds immense promise for enhancing traffic management, improving road safety, and optimizing traffic flow. However, the widespread adoption of ML in IoV applications is hindered by significant privacy risks, as data collection and processing often occur in untrusted environments. To address these challenges, this study employs a systematic literature review to investigate the integration of blockchain and federated learning within the IoV domain. The research aims to identify, analyze, and evaluate existing blockchain-enabled federated learning frameworks specifically for IoV. Furthermore, the study seeks to assess the current state of the art, uncover potential gaps, and offer recommendations for future research in this field. By synthesizing insights from 30 selected papers, this review provides a comprehensive overview of blockchain-assisted federated learning applications in IoV, establishing a robust foundation for subsequent scholarly efforts. Additionally, it outlines a recommended roadmap for advancing blockchain-enabled federated learning in connected vehicles. This roadmap emphasizes in-vehicle distributed learning, decentralized traffic signal control, and privacy-preserving applications, with a specific focus on vehicular ad-hoc networks (V2X) and IoV scenarios. Ultimately, the findings suggest that blockchain-assisted federated learning is poised to significantly transform traffic management, road safety, and traffic optimization services. Furthermore, the review demonstrates that blockchain-enhanced federated learning can effectively mitigate privacy and data leakage concerns in IoV, while also offering guidance for future research directions. This guidance underscores the necessity of developing cost-effective, privacy-preserving, and distributed learning solutions that are tailored to the unique characteristics of IoV environments. Additionally, it is recommended to explore emerging technologies such as edge computing, fog computing, and cloud computing to further refine and expand blockchain-assisted federated learning frameworks for IoV. Finally, the study addresses the challenge of resource-constrained IoV nodes, proposing that lightweight federated learning algorithms be integrated with blockchain to ensure efficient distributed learning. The large millikelvin system situated inside Room 3B1 at the end of a 120-foot underground tunnel within the Main Experiment Hall of Fermilab is optimized for quantum computing applications. This study examines a collection of 95 crypto-related projects from Python PyPI that employ .py files for key material. Our findings indicate that these files are predominantly located in directories such as "crypto", "secret", or "key", and their dimensions are generally minute, typically comprising less than 100 lines of code. Historical texts present significant challenges for natural language processing due to substantial shifts in language over time, including phonological, morphological, syntactic, and lexical variations, as well as a higher propensity for orthographic inconsistencies. These issues are particularly acute in Old Norse, the ancestral language of Icelandic and Norwegian, which has been extensively studied in historical linguistics and computationally analyzed through automatic tagging and parsing. Given that the vast majority of Old Norse texts have survived within syntactically annotated frameworks, such as the *Egils saga* and *Njáls saga* from the 13th century, leveraging these resources to enhance Tag-of-Possession (TOP) models represents a promising avenue for further research. This study demonstrates that augmentating a contemporary Swedish model with historical corpora yields a statistically significant improvement in TOP tagging accuracy. Additionally, we explore set-valued prediction as a technique to enhance the reliability of generated tags. Our results indicate that this approach not only delivers confidence scores for individual tags but also substantially reduces the count of tags assigned with low confidence. Consequently, set-valued prediction emerges as a more robust alternative to the traditional word-by-word tagging strategy. Our computational experiments confirm that this method delivers a statistically significant improvement in tagging correctness. Furthermore, we illustrate that the set-valued approach facilitates the detection of tags that are highly probable given the available evidence, thereby enhancing the overall interpretability of the tagging process. Finally, we show that this interpretability can be utilized to identify potential orthographic errors in historical documents. These findings underscore the value of integrating historical corpora into modern NLP workflows to achieve both quantitative and qualitative advancements. Additionally, our work underscores the potential of applying contemporary, data-driven language models to historical datasets to address longstanding linguistic challenges. This paper presents non-continuous integrability as a framework capable of handling functions with discontinuities across any dimension, applicable to both single and multi-variable scenarios. A function falls within this theory if it adheres to a continuity condition on intervals and satisfies the multi-dimensional Henstock-Kurzweal integral (as defined by Fitzpatrick, 1981; Maitin-Shepard, 1991; and Fiore, 1993). This approach resolves the inconsistency between integrability rules and the continuity discontinuity principle, an issue that has plagued various theories since the inception of the Daniell-Schwarz theory in 1907. Furthermore, the Daniel-Schwarz framework is extended to discontinuous functions via the development of the non-continuous Henstock-Kurzweal integral. Key properties—including the fundamental theorem of calculus, Riemann integrability implications, and absolute integrability implications—remain valid. Additionally, the change of variables formula is derived, and the concept of mixed integrability is proposed to address current limitations. The work concludes with an extensive list of unresolved questions. Finally, the paper presents novel theorems and theorems reformulated from historical sources to honor historical contributions to the field. Specifically, M. Riesz's 1909 theorem regarding the equivalence between non-continuous and continuous integrability is generalized to higher dimensions, and a new proof is offered. Furthermore, a novel definition of the Riemann integral is introduced, which generalizes the Riemann-Whitney integral. This new definition retains all fundamental properties of the classical Riemann integral while enabling the integration of a broader class of functions. Finally, a significant advancement in the theory of functions of bounded variation is presented. Building upon Lebesgue's 1906 work, Bounded Variation is generalized to arbitrary dimensions, thereby addressing the problem of Borel's Indivisibles. This achievement marks a substantial contribution to the theory of Multi-Dimensional Functions of Bounded Variation. Overall, this work represents a substantial advancement in the field, with implications for mathematics, physics, and engineering. It successfully integrates multi-dimensional analysis with the historical foundations established by the founders of the discipline. This paper introduces a new approach to automatically transform urban requirements into a formal specification language. We argue that partially automating this process enhances the manageability of large, intricate requirements, which often involve numerous conflicts and redundancies. Our method is designed to be used by non-experts through a requirement engineering approach that integrates the formal specification phase into the development of requirement engineering assistants. This study introduces a novel quantum error correction approach for superconducting qubits utilizing hidden inverses, termed the Hidden Inverses Protocol (HIP). The framework demonstrates robustness against both coherent and incoherent errors, with HIP effectively identifying and reversing deviations caused by both error types. Furthermore, the system achieves high-fidelity performance by minimizing the retrieval time of the residual operator representing the inverse of the hidden inverse error. Quantum kinetic analysis indicates that, under specific conditions, the method can reduce logical error rates by several orders of magnitude. Additionally, simulations show that incorporating an auxiliary ancilla with a distinct transition frequency enhances performance by lowering the overlap between the auxiliary and system density matrices. These findings suggest that the proposed scheme holds significant potential for the development of fault-tolerant quantum computing systems. Finally, the paper outlines potential applications of HIP in the context of the variational quantum algorithm, which is a promising avenue for future research. Given the method's promising outcomes, it is expected to inspire further investigations into quantum error correction. Finally, the work concludes with several suggestions for enhancing the efficiency of HIP. Keywords: quantum error correction, hidden inverses protocol, fault tolerance, variational quantum algorithm. Enhancing pre-trained vision-language models (VLPs) is crucial for improving their performance on downstream tasks. This paper introduces VT-CLIP, a method that boosts VLP capabilities by incorporating visual-directed text features, which are derived from the interaction between VLPs and image-text contrastive learning (VT-CLIP). Our findings indicate that VT-CLIP improves VLPs in two key ways: first, it aligns text features more closely with visual inputs, thereby strengthening the visual-textual embedding space; second, it refines the visual encoder by introducing additional regularizations. Extensive experiments on image classification and visual question answering demonstrate that our approach significantly outperforms current state-of-the-art techniques, achieving improvements of 3.5% and 2.1% on ImageNet and VQA v2, respectively. The code is accessible at https://github.com/ruixiangwang/VT-CLIP. Furthermore, we provide a novel image classification benchmark comprising 1,000 categories drawn from various fine-grained datasets.
