This study explores the proton recoil polarization observable within the framework of Deeply Virtual Compton Scattering (DVCS). We demonstrate that, at leading twist, the polarization vector aligns exclusively along the z-axis, and its magnitude relies solely on the hadronic Generalized Parton Distributions (GPDs) $H$ and $E$. Consequently, measuring this polarization offers a distinct DVCS observable that allows for the separate extraction of $H$ and $E$. Furthermore, we illustrate that the maximum magnitude of this observable is achievable at the CLAS12 experiment. Our findings are particularly relevant for future precision dvcs measurements aimed at investigating the connection between the quark charge radius and the spatial distribution of the Dirac form factor. Additionally, we have made the code used to compute this observable publicly available. Our results will be applied to analyze the experimental dvcs data from the Jefferson Lab Hall-B. Finally, we will present the calculated values of this observable for the nucleon at HADEX experiments within the CLAS12 detector. The associated code can be downloaded from our GitHub repository. The rapid evolution of computing, communications, and information technology has driven significant social and economic shifts. The term "Post-Internet" signifies a new era of social and economic change, marked by a new paradigm of "Augmented Synthetic Intelligence" (ASI). ASI blends human and machine capabilities to generate superior outcomes in knowledge creation and conversion. This period is characterized by a new form of human-machine collaboration that integrates augmented intelligence into a new value system. Fundamental changes in knowledge production and diffusion have sparked a social revolution, giving rise to "Augmented Synthetic Intelligence Societies." This paper explores the implications of this transition for society and institutions, with a specific focus on education. It proposes "Augmented Synthetic Intelligence Education" (ASIE) as a new educational paradigm designed to cultivate the cognitive, social, and emotional skills necessary for ASI-driven value systems. A potential model for achieving ASIE is "Multi-Intelligence Education" (MIE), which leverages the strengths of both human and artificial intelligence intelligences. Finally, the article outlines key research and development initiatives required to advance ASIE. These initiatives center on three primary themes: (1) the cognitive, social, and emotional skills essential for ASI value systems; (2) learning and instructional design grounded in constructivist and socio-cultural theories; and (3) the design and development of intelligent learning environments. These components are collectively referred to as "Intelligence Ecosystems." The authors argue that establishing such ecosystems is crucial for the successful realization of Augmented Synthetic Intelligence Education. We present findings from a numerical study of one-dimensional correlated bosons under spin-orbit coupling (SOC) within an optical lattice. Our finite-size scaling analysis reveals that the thermal evolution of this system involves two distinct phase transitions as the ratio of SOC strength to hopping increases. The initial transition, identified as a superfluid-solid phase transition, is driven by quantum criticality of the Kosterlitz-Thouless type in the low-coupling regime. This is followed by a second transition at a higher SOC strength, which is primarily a thermal Berezinskii-Kosterlitz-Thouless transition occurring in a solid phase with soft correlations. We also examine a third transition at even higher SOC values, which appears to be primarily a Bose glass phase driven by coupling to the zero-point energy of the optical lattice. Finally, we discuss the implications of these findings for experimental setups. These results are derived from a model of Bose-Hubbard-like correlated fermions with SOC in an optical lattice, a system proposed as a platform to explore the interplay between bosonization and the Kondo effect. Our study highlights the complex phase diagram of SOC-linked bosons in an optical lattice and the diverse critical behaviors it exhibits. The paper begins with an introduction to the model and its motivation, followed by a detailed analysis of the phase diagram, and concludes with a discussion of the broader implications of these findings. Keywords: Spin-orbit coupling, Bose-Hubbard model, Kondo effect, Kosterlitz-Thouless criticality, Bose glass. PACS: 05.30.Jp, 71.10.Fy, 71.10.Pc, 74.20.-z, 74.25.-n.

Rooted graphs, where edges have designated sources and targets, are realized by finite abelian groups $G$ through root-preserving homomorphisms. This paper investigates the degenerations between such groups. Specifically, given two graphs $F$ and $H$ realized by abelian groups $G$ and $H$, respectively, a degeneration from $G$ to $H$ exists if there is a $G$-cover $\pi: \widetilde{X} \to X$ over any realization $\phi: \widetilde{X} \to F$ of $G$ and $\psi: X \to H$ of $H$, provided that $\pi$ commutes with $\phi$ and $\psi$. We demonstrate that finite abelian groups admitting realizations other than their multiplicity do not admit degenerations to the circle. Furthermore, for any two realizations $F$ and $H$, an explicit criterion is established to determine whether a degeneration from $G$ to $H$ occurs. Additionally, we characterize all nontrivial degenerations of the torus and compute the number of degenerations for finite abelian groups when edge multiplicity is irrelevant. These findings rely on an explicit characterization of realizations and multiplicity-free realizations of finite abelian groups, as well as a characterization of all (and specifically nontrivial) degenerations of the torus. As an application, we introduce a new invariant: the number of multiplicity-free realizations of a finite abelian group, which we denote as $C(G)$. We establish that $C(G)$ equals the number of subgroups of $G$ and derive a recursive formula for calculating it. This study examines low-dimensional AdS spaces derived from massive Type IIA string theory. Specifically, it analyzes 3D, 2D, and 1D solutions located at the minima of massive Type IIA scalar potentials. These solutions correspond to supersymmetric or supersymmetric-like anti-de Sitter geometries, alongside non-supersymmetric vacua found in specific moduli directions. The analysis focuses on identifying the AdS/CFT duals of these solutions and exploring novel applications within low-dimensional gauge theories. Notably, the non-supusymmetric vacua suggest that confinement in these theories can be modeled without the necessity of a string tension scale. Additionally, the study investigates non-supersymmetric 3D solutions to uncover new instabilities within the AdS$_3$ vacuum. Finally, the paper explores the existence of new 3D supersymmetric solutions that are not anti-de Sitter geometries. Throughout, the focus remains on the properties of the dual field theories, including their moduli spaces and symmetry structures. The paper concludes with a summary of these findings and suggestions for future research. A comprehensive list of relevant references is also provided. Keywords: String theories in various dimensions, supersymmetric gauge theories, string vacua, and low-dimensional string theory.

Recent advancements in Gaussian process modeling have spurred the creation of numerous kernels that incorporate mathematical functions to capture new patterns within data. However, many of these proposed kernels suffer from poor scalability, making them impractical for real-world applications. This study demonstrates a method for constructing scalable, flexible Gaussian process kernels from basic mathematical expressions. We introduce the scalable Gaussian Gaussian convolution kernel, which matches the performance of Gaussian processes with locational Gaussian processes while reducing computational complexity. Furthermore, we outline a general framework for convolving two Gaussian processes, enabling the accurate and efficient modeling of complex data patterns. Finally, we introduce the polynomial Gaussian convolution kernel, showing that it can successfully detect and link multiple data modes. Our results indicate that these efficient and scalable Gaussian process kernels outperform state-of-the-art alternatives. Beam-induced background remains a critical challenge for detectors at muon colliders, prompting an investigation into mitigation strategies. This work examines the impact of various approaches to diminish background generation and accumulation on machine components. The simulations were conducted using the 6TeV collider design by the Muon Collider Design Initiative (MCDI), which was adapted for this study. A custom code, built upon the public GEANT4 toolkit, was employed to model background deposits within the machine. Our findings indicate that rotating the interaction point between bursts can reduce background levels by an order of magnitude, while implementing a machine interlock system to halt the machine upon reaching specific background thresholds on components can achieve a hundred-fold reduction. Additionally, we demonstrated that colliding beams with opposite helicity can significantly lower background deposition in the final focus region, and directing the spin of the incoming beams away from this region offers further benefits. These outcomes were derived from a "worst-case" scenario regarding existing knowledge of component material properties. Consequently, these results highlight the necessity of conducting materials research to identify components with reduced susceptibility to background-induced effects. Furthermore, the study underscores the continued relevance of final focus and machine interlock region studies for the ultimate collider design. We conclude by outlining several open questions concerning background effects and the strategies to address them. Finally, we present a novel concept for mitigating beam-induced emittance growth, which may prove particularly significant for the collider's final stage. This paper serves as a foundation for the upcoming Beam-Induced Effects and Mitigation Workshop scheduled for late 2022. The discussions presented here are intended to stimulate dialogue on beam-induced effects and their mitigation, thereby guiding future research in this domain. We also aim to provide the initial impetus for a dedicated final focus region materials study. The strategies proposed herein are not mutually exclusive and can be integrated to achieve even greater reductions in background-induced effects. We anticipate that the outcomes of this study will inform the selection of components and the design of the final machine region. Ultimately, we believe that the final focus region will be the primary driver of the overall machine design. We also present a preliminary analysis of the final focus region, including an investigation into the effects of a final focus region surrounded by a toroidal magnetic field. This analysis will serve as the basis for the upcoming Final Focus Region and Materials Study. Additionally, we have demonstrated the feasibility of using the toroidal field to cancel the beam polarization depolarization caused by the torus, thereby preserving the reduction in beam-induced noise along the final focus region achieved

We introduce Spartan, a regularization technique that facilitates the learning of sparse models by framing sparsity as a transportation cost minimization problem with an entropy regularization term. This approach yields a differentiable objective function suitable for end-to-end training. Theoretically, we demonstrate that the optimal solution produced by Spartan possesses $\alpha$-sparsity, where $\alpha$ depends on the differentiator's parameters, and that the training process converges to this sparsity. Empirical results across various computer vision tasks indicate that Spartan achieves superior sparsity and model performance compared to current methods. Furthermore, we find that combining Spartan with gradient clipping enables the creation of robust models against adversarial attacks. Additional experiments on model compression show that Spartan significantly reduces model size while maintaining strong accuracy. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/DeepMind/Spartan. Our implementation supports TensorFlow, PyTorch, and PyTorch Lightining. Spartan is compatible with convolutional networks, residual networks, point-wise MLPs, and multi-layer perceptrons with or without batch normalization. It functions as a regularizer for any differentiable objective and can be applied to any input-output pair. We have provided a Jupyter notebook example for training a sparse MNIST classifier using Spartan. Future work will explore extensions for sequence modeling and graph neural networks. We welcome collaborations on applying Spartan to novel domains. For inquiries, please contact us at {alexey.g.,alexey.k.,paul.f}.google.com. The Pauli exclusion principle is a fundamental concept in quantum mechanics that dictates the behavior of fermions by preventing multiple identical particles from occupying the same quantum state. In this work, we investigate the unexpected emergence of Pauli obstruction in Bose gases, where bosons can typically condense into a single quantum state. We demonstrate that a weak attractive interaction between bosons can create an effective repulsion, causing a significant depletion of low-momentum states within the condensate. Utilizing large-density expansions for both the energy and momentum distribution of the weakly interacting Bose gas, we identify the precise threshold for the strength of the attractive interaction. Below this critical value, the conventional superfluid-to-superfluid phase transition is replaced by a unique superfluid-to-supersolid phase transition. Furthermore, we have derived an accurate analytical expression for the transition point using the large-density expansion, with numerical Monte Carlo simulations confirming its validity. Additionally, we show that this Pauli-obstruction-driven supersolid phase persists in systems of finite size. Our findings provide a novel pathway to achieve supersolids within experimentally accessible parameter ranges. Finally, our results offer valuable insights for understanding other quantum systems, such as the attractive Hubbard model, where weak attraction is known to induce strong correlations and repulsion among quasi-particles. We anticipate that the techniques employed here will be instrumental in uncovering the origins of repulsion and superrepulsion in various quantum systems. Test smells are suboptimal patterns in test code that hinder testing activities. Although numerous studies have explored these suboptimal patterns from a development perspective, their severity from a user standpoint remains largely unexamined. This paper investigates the severity of test smells through the lens of software developers. It details the methodology and findings of an empirical study where 30 developers from industry and academia evaluated 20 test smells from the literature for severity. The results indicate that test code refactoring, parallel test execution, and test code design were perceived as the most severe problems. Furthermore, while developers acknowledged that test smells pose significant challenges, they often doubted their own ability to resolve them. Finally, the study examines how factors such as experience, role, and gender influence perceptions of test severity. The research contributes to the field by providing an in-depth analysis of developer evaluations regarding the severity of test smells. Additionally, it offers a novel approach to empirically assess test code quality by directly engaging developers in the assessment process. We examine the nonconvex brushing process integro-differential equation (BPIDE) within the context of the LASSO framework, where the brush function is defined as $b(z) = \frac{z}{\sqrt{1 + z^2}}$. This function exhibits non-convexity, non-differentiability at $z = 0$, and approaches but never reaches $\pm 1$ as $|z|$ increases. Consequently, it invalidates the differentiation under the integral sign used in prior analyses. To address this invalid differentiation and enable valid convergence analysis, we develop alternative bounding techniques. These methods not only accommodate a broader class of brush functions but also extend applicability to non-differentiable ones. Our analysis demonstrates that the LASSO objective utilizing this specific brush function attains a global minimum. Furthermore, we explore applications in the deconvolution of $f(x) = \frac{1}{2} e^{-\frac{1}{2} x^2} * g(x)$, where $g(x)$ is a periodic square wave. We derive a closed-form solution for this operation and numerically compare it against other brush function approaches. Finally, we present numerical results comparing solutions obtained with and without brush functions. This work is grounded in the paper "A Brushing Process Integro-Differential Equation with Applications" by J. L. Arroyo, J. M. Sanz, and J. A. Tenreiro, to be published in the Proceedings of the 2022 International Conference on Mathematical Methods for Industrial Applications of Spline Techniques (Búzios, Brazil). Additional details can be found at https://arxiv.org/abs/2202.03001. Our code is available at https://github.com/jlmarroyo/NonconvexBrushingProcess. This study introduces the Tiramisu model, a novel method for estimating inter-beat intervals (IBI) that demonstrates superior accuracy compared to existing models. We demonstrate that IBI data adheres to a long-range correlated (LRC) structure, characterized by the fluctuation of signal amplitudes over time. While various fractal dimension models have been developed to capture the scaling properties of LRC data, we propose that these models can be integrated into a unified architecture to enhance estimation performance. Specifically, we employ a multi-task learning (MTL) approach to fuse multiple estimators. To address the limitations of current MTL methods, we introduce Tiramisu, a new framework that combines a shared base estimator with several specialized sub-estimators. This structure utilizes a MTL strategy to estimate distinct features of IBI data, thereby improving overall performance. Furthermore, we show that the proposed MTL model can be effectively implemented using both recurrent neural networks (RNN) and convolutional neural networks (CNN). Extensive experiments conducted on the MIT-BIH Atrial Fibillation (MIT-BIH A-FIB) dataset confirm that Tiramisu significantly outperforms existing models in IBI estimation. Additionally, our approach exhibits robustness against noise, outperforming current MTL methods. The source code is publicly available at \url{https://github.com/abhishekkumar1992/Tiramisu}. Finally, we provide a comprehensive analysis of various hyperparameters to offer practical guidance for future MTL applications. Our approach is highly effective for IBI estimation, and we believe Tiramisu will serve as a valuable resource for the field. We hope this work inspires further research into advanced MTL techniques for biomedical signal analysis. Our goal is to develop more precise and reliable models for health monitoring and disease prediction. We look forward to contributing to the advancement of AI-driven healthcare solutions. The Randomized Riemannian Conjugate Gradient (RRCG) algorithm is a highly efficient approach for computing a singular value decomposition (SVD) on a tensor. By employing a sweep strategy, RRCG achieves rapid convergence, typically requiring only 1 to 3 passes to obtain an accurate low-rank approximation. However, when aiming for greater accuracy, additional passes are necessary, which can result in excessive time consumption. To address this limitation, we introduce the Randomized Riemannian Conjugate Gradient in Any Number of Passes (RRCNAP) algorithm. This method allows users to specify the desired number of passes, enabling a flexible trade-off between computational time and approximation accuracy. We provide theoretical analysis to establish a lower bound on the achievable accuracy for any given pass count. Furthermore, numerical experiments demonstrate that RRCNAP is more efficient than existing state-of-the-art algorithms for low-rank approximations that require 5 or more passes. The Python implementation of RRCNAP is available at https://github.com/ChenchenLi1993/RRCNAP. In addition to its speed, RRCNAP is memory efficient, making it particularly suitable for large-scale problems. Finally, we illustrate the application of RRCNAP in image inpainting. The supporting code can be found at https://github.com/ChenchenLi1993/RRCNAP/tree/master/RRCNAP_for_Image_Inpainting. Our implementation is also incorporated into the Python package TensorTools, accessible at https://github.com/ChenchenLi1993/TensorTools. The package includes examples for computing singular value approximations, image inpainting, and solving large-scale linear systems. Specifically, the image inpainting example is located at https://github.com/ChenchenLi1993/TensorTools/tree/master/examples/image_inpainting. Embedding static graphs has garnered substantial interest, driven by the capacity to capture pairwise node interactions and enabling the application of efficient, well-established machine learning techniques to network data. However, many real-world networks are temporal and experience continuous evolution, making static graph embedding insufficient for such scenarios. This survey examines methods for embedding evolving graphs, with a specific focus on temporal networks. We present and organize existing approaches based on their primary characteristics, including network model, representation, algorithms, applications, and challenges. Furthermore, we explore how embedding evolving graphs differs from both static and network science perspectives. Finally, we identify key challenges and promising directions for future research in this field. We anticipate that this survey will inspire researchers from diverse backgrounds to deepen their understanding of evolving graph embedding and advance the field. Our survey can be accessed at https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.01006. Additionally, the accompanying website, https://www.researchgate.net/publication/341075640_A_Survey_on_Embedding_Evolving_Graphs, offers supplementary materials, such as code for reproducing experiments from several surveyed papers. The ground state of $^7$H is characterized as a narrow resonance utilizing the $^3$H + 4n cluster configuration. In the present study, we extend the three-body model previously employed for the $^5$H ($^3$H+2n) ground state to incorporate the $^7$H system by adding neutron pair excitations to the $^3$H+4n excitation. The calculated energy splitting resulting from neutron pair excitations aligns with the energy width, suggesting that the wave function of the $^7$H ground state is predominantly composed of configurations involving neutron pair excitations relative to the $^3$H+2n core. Furthermore, the calculated matter radius of $^7$H matches experimental data, while the matter radius of the $^7$h excited state exceeds that of the ground state, indicating that the ground state exhibits a more compact structure. These findings support the conclusion that the ground state of $^7$H possesses a diffuse spatial structure. Additionally, the calculated matter root mean square (rms) radius of the $^7$H ground state is comparable to that of the neutron-rich mirror nucleus $^7$Li. Finally, the calculated matter rms radius of the $^7$h excited state is significantly larger than that of the ground state, implying that this excited state is primarily characterized by a very diffuse spatial structure. These results suggest that the $^7$H ground state and the $^7$h excited state may serve as valuable candidates for studying neutron skins in nuclear physics. Moreover, the proposed cluster model for $^7$H is expected to facilitate further investigations into its properties, including the potential existence of a narrow zero-width ground state resonance. This conclusion is reinforced by the observation that the calculated energy splitting due to the four neutron excitations accounts for nearly the entire energy width, indicating that the $^7$H ground state is mainly formed by configurations with extended spatial structures. Consequently, the $^7$H ground state is characterized by a very narrow width and a very long lifetime. The proposed cluster model for $^7$H offers a viable explanation for the experimental observation of the $^7$h state and its associated properties, such as its very small matter radius and large matter width. This conclusion is further supported by the finding that the calculated energy splitting due to the four neutron excitations explains nearly the entire energy width, demonstrating that the $^7$H ground state exhibits a very narrow width

This paper investigates a specific case of the Nirenberg problem on the standard sphere: determining the existence of a conformal factor $u \in C^{\infty}(\mathbb{S}^{n})$ satisfying $\frac{k u}{(1+u)^{2}}=A$ on $\mathbb{S}^{n}$, where $A$ is a given function. The study imposes the constraint that $A$ equals $\frac{k u_{0}}{(1+u_{0})^{2}}$ on a subset $\Omega \subsetneq \mathbb{S}^{n}$ and is defined as $0$ on the remainder of the sphere. Here, $u_{0}$ represents any smooth function on $\mathbb{S}^{n}$ such that $\int_{\mathbb{S}^{n}}\frac{du_{0}}{(1+u_{0})^{2}}=0$. We establish that if $\Omega$ possesses a non-empty interior, then for sufficiently large values of $k$, no positive solution exists. Furthermore, we extend this finding to domains $\Omega$ situated on half-spheres, provided that $A$ satisfies specific symmetry conditions relative to $\Omega$. These findings contribute to the broader understanding of solvability in conformal geometry under mixed boundary conditions. Additionally, the paper examines related problems involving Neumann boundary conditions. In this context, we demonstrate that if $A$ exhibits a positive minimum within an open subset $\Omega \subsetneq \mathbb{S}^{n}$ and satisfies $\frac{\partial u}{\partial \nu}=0$ on $\partial \Omega$, then $u$ must be constant. This result contrasts sharply with the solvability findings of Chen and Lin (2008) regarding similar problems. Finally, the work includes an appendix that provides an alternative perspective on Li's work concerning the Nirenberg problem on the standard sphere. Through the appendix, we derive a novel Poincaré-type inequality applicable to domains with non-constant mean curvature. This inequality holds significant interest in spectral geometry, as it facilitates the analysis of eigenvalues for Dirichlet and Neumann problems on such domains. Specifically, it yields a positive lower bound for the first non-trivial eigenvalue of the Laplacian on a half-sphere when considering functions odd with respect to a specific coordinate. Neural networks excel at extracting features from data, yet identifying appropriate feature metrics remains a challenging task. Recently, optimal transport theory has been applied to learn these metrics, but most existing approaches rely on fixed feature representations, hindering the models' expressiveness. This paper introduces a new method that integrates deep neural networks into the process of constructing transporters. By allowing neural networks to learn deep optimal representations via Sinkhorn divergences, our approach overcomes the limitations of shallow structures and explicitly captures complex feature relationships. We validate the efficacy of Sinkhorn Divergences in representing optimal metrics across three key applications: image classification, transfer learning, and transfer source selection. Furthermore, we provide theoretical insights into the convergence behavior of our proposed algorithm. The code is accessible at https://github.com/ChenchenLi1997/SinkDivergences. Additionally, our datasets for image classification and transfer learning can be found at https://github.com/ChenchenLi1997/Image-Datasets. This study employs a simulation-based approach to evaluate how partnerships between local tracing teams and digital contact tracing applications influence the efficacy of COVID-19 transmission control through contact tracing in England. We constructed a discrete-event simulation of England's contact tracing system, integrating a digital app, where infected individuals utilize the app with a probability of 70%. The results indicate that when 70% of people use the app, the tracing system reduces transmission by 35% (with a 95% confidence interval of 28% to 42%). Furthermore, increasing app adoption to 90% or ensuring that every case is processed by the tracing system within 48 hours results in a transmission reduction exceeding 50%. These findings were corroborated by transmission data from the COVID-19 Infection Survey in England. Additionally, we analyzed how variations in key parameters, such as the latent period and the distribution of infectious periods, impact outcomes. Ultimately, this research demonstrates the critical role of the digital contact tracing application in achieving significant transmission reductions via contact tracing, while also outlining the necessary app usage levels and operational efficiencies to secure a transmission reduction greater than 50%. This insight is vital for informing future decisions regarding the scale and scope of COVID-19 contact tracing efforts. To support these conclusions, we have made our code accessible through a GitHub repository. Finally, the study underscores the value of integrating data from sources like the COVID-19 Infection Survey into mathematical models, as this data was utilized to validate the simulation outcomes. Such validation strengthens the credibility of transmission reduction estimates, which are essential for evaluating the effectiveness of various interventions aimed at controlling the pandemic. Furthermore, the research highlights the potential of utilizing large-scale surveys to inform decisions on government policies, such as the extent of COVID-19 transmission control measures. Specifically, the transmission reductions predicted by the model align with the easing of restrictions observed in England during the autumn of 2020. This consistency underscores the utility of mathematical models in providing evidence-based guidance for policy decisions aimed at mitigating the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic. Additionally, the transmission reduction estimates generated by the model can guide decisions on the scale and scope of COVID-19 transmission control interventions. Additionally, we analyze the color-magnitude diagram and investigate the distribution of member stars within the color-magnitude diagram (CMD) and color-color diagram (CCD). We further assess the cluster's dynamical state by calculating its relaxation time and examining the distribution of members in the CMD, CCD, and CCD-CCD spaces. Given that $G$ possesses a finite expected degree and almost sure Betti numbers that grow at most exponentially, we demonstrate a phase transition for the voyages within the Gaussian cooling schedule. Specifically, when $G$ is sparse, we establish an upper bound for the Betti numbers of the voyages as a function of the cooling schedule. Additionally, we provide an exact characterization for one-dimensional graphs, encompassing all cases of finite expected degree. Our approach relies on a fundamental lemma that links voyags to thermodynamic ground states. Furthermore, we prove that Gaussian cooling effectively eliminates large loops in the resulting homology. This finding is particularly significant for graphs exhibiting polynomial growth. We further examine various extensions of this finding. Our findings are applicable to the analysis of persistent homology in point clouds generated by a Gaussian mixture model under Gaussian cooling. Our method involves training a neural network to identify the moving camera within the image and estimating its location. Recent years have seen a surge in research on reinforced constrained reinforcement learning (CRL), which involves learning policies under constraints defined by cumulative rewards from auxiliary objectives. This paper introduces a novel framework called Reverse Constrained RL (RCRL), aiming to identify the simplest policy that satisfies constraints with the highest possible relaxation. Specifically, it seeks the maximum allowable reduction in the cost of auxiliary objectives while ensuring the primary objective remains optimal. Formally, CRL and RCRL are shown to be mathematically equivalent, allowing standard CRL algorithms to solve RCRL issues. However, we demonstrate that applying conventional CRL to RCRL often results in suboptimal policies. To address this, we propose a new algorithm named RCRL-Q, derived by reversing the search direction of the Lagrangian used in existing CRL methods. Since RCRL-Q requires solving linear programs, we further develop a policy iteration method, PAPIQ, to enhance efficiency. Numerical experiments confirm that RCRL-Q outperforms standard CRL approaches in terms of optimality and computational speed. Furthermore, we illustrate how RCRL can encourage energy-efficient behaviors in reinforcement learning scenarios. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/tae-kyu-lee/rcrl. Our findings suggest that RCRL-Q serves as a valuable tool for discovering simpler, more interpretable policies. Additionally, we anticipate that optimizing for policy simplicity could open new research avenues, such as maximizing the number of states or transitions in learning tasks. Ultimately, this work aims to promote the exploration of learning for simple systems and facilitate simple decision-making processes. The code is available at https://github.com/tae-kyu-lee/rcrl. Our results indicate that RCRL-Q is effective for identifying simpler policies. Finally, RCRL offers a means to promote learning for energy-efficient systems, and we envision that prioritizing simpler systems will open new research opportunities, including solving Markov decision processes with fewer states and transitions. A vertex divider for a graph $G$ with $n$ vertices and positive integers $k_1, \dots, k_m$ (where $\sum_{i=1}^m k_i = k$) consists of a set of $m$ vertices $\{v_1, \dots, v_m\}$ within $G$ and $m$ paths $P_1, \dots, P_m$ originating at these vertices, satisfying $|\bigcap_{i=1}^m P_i| \leq 1$, such that removing the union of these paths leaves $G$ with treewidth at most $k - \min_{i=1}^m k_i$. This concept was recently introduced by Marx, Shaffer, and Srinivasan [SODA'22] to facilitate a nearly linear-time algorithm for the Vertex Cover problem on treewidth $k$ graphs, running in $O(n \cdot 2^{O(k)})$ time. Their randomized algorithm constructs such dividers with $m = O(k^2)$. In this work, we demonstrate that it is possible to achieve a linear number of dividers, $m = O(k)$, with a space usage of $O(nk)$. Our approach builds upon recent advancements in treewidth decomposition techniques, specifically the $O(nk)$-sized treewidth decomposition by Marx and Maheshwararao [STACS'21] and the compact treewidth decomposition by Marx and Shaffer [SODA'22]. By applying the latter, we can represent the vertex dividers compactly using $O(nk)$ space. This improvement yields a faster algorithm for Vertex Cover, operating within $O(nk)$ space and executing in $O(n \cdot 2^k)$ time. Furthermore, our findings have broader implications for other graph problems defined on treewidth decompositions. We illustrate this by presenting a generic, space-efficient framework for vertex deletion problems, which, when combined with our optimized vertex divider construction, produces space-efficient algorithms for Independent Set and Dominating Set. These problems are represented via $O(nk)$-sized treewidth decompositions, utilizing the same $O(nk)$ space as our vertex divider solution. Grouping methods are essential for analyzing networks, particularly when dealing with heterogeneous or inferred data. In the context of directed networks, existing approaches often rely on undirected grouping techniques, which can lead to unintended outcomes. We examine the implications of applying current methods to directed networks and propose two research directions to address these issues. First, we develop a mathematical framework for directed networks to clarify the consequences of using methodological weight functions to balance homophily across different network types. Second, we explore applications in inferred networks by creating a statistical model that defines appropriate weight functions and introduces the INFERED package to facilitate this analysis. We validate the proposed methodology through simulations and case studies. Additionally, we present a new application leveraging inferred social ties to investigate gender homophily in professional networks. These methodological advancements offer a pathway toward resolving the challenges associated with directed, inferred, and heterogeneous networks. Our framework provides a reference for the mathematical and statistical properties of weighting schemes, enabling researchers to make informed decisions regarding network grouping. Furthermore, the open-source INFERED package allows users to apply these methods to their own networks.

**Keywords:** Heterogeneous networks, inferred networks, gender homophily, trust networks, reciprocity, methodological weights, mathematical framework.

This study introduces a method for estimating and certifying the potential errors of a machine learning model, specifically the Collocation Network, which solves the Navier-Stokes equations. The proposed approach, termed the Collocation Network Mistake Estimator, utilizes a measure of the residual of the Navier-Stokes equations to calculate an $L^{\infty}$-type error bound for the solution. By integrating the concept of the certificate tree, the method identifies and quantifies the error contribution of each training data point. Furthermore, it applies the Morris method to assess the sensitivity of the solution to individual input parameters. The study's findings are illustrated through numerical examples involving flow around a cylinder and a NACA0012 airfoil. These results demonstrate that the error bounds are sharp and that both training parameters and problem dimensions significantly influence the solution's accuracy. Ultimately, this technique offers a valuable means for assessing and communicating the uncertainty inherent in machine learning outcomes. Additionally, it serves as a complementary approach to the Collocation Network Uncertainty Quantification method, which employs Bayesian neural networks. Together, these methods provide a comprehensive strategy for quantifying errors in machine learning applications. Finally, the research highlights the necessity of employing robust machine learning algorithms, such as the Adam optimizer, to ensure reliable and accurate solutions. We present a theoretical analysis of tunneling spectroscopy within the Kondo regime for a Majorana box, focusing on how ohmic dissipation influences the tunneling density of states. Our research examines the impact of an external magnetic field and evaluates the stability of the Majorana zero mode. Our primary finding indicates that the Majorana Andreev peak can be differentiated from other peaks by employing resistive tunneling electrodes. Consequently, we suggest that resistive tunneling electrodes offer a promising method for experimentally verifying Majorana modes. Furthermore, our simulations demonstrate that increasing the external magnetic field causes the Majorana Andreev peak to diminish. Finally, we conclude that the tunneling electrodes proposed in this study are feasible for experimental implementation. This approach not only facilitates the detection of Majorana modes but also aids in distinguishing them from other potential zero-energy peaks. Our findings provide a robust theoretical basis for the rigorous identification of Majorana modes, thereby advancing the field of topological quantum computing. Additionally, our work establishes a new framework for investigating the Majorana box, a system that has not yet been explored experimentally. Linear contextual bandits with diverse action sets are extensively researched, with the least squares estimator being a widely used and popular approach. Although the standard theoretical guarantee for this method is $O(\log T)$, recent advancements have leveraged structured sparsity to achieve faster rates, specifically $O(\log |{\cal S}| \log T)$, where $|{\cal S}|$ denotes the maximum number of features in the action set. This paper revisits and extends the non-sparsity framework to a more general setting. We establish a nearly tight bound of $O(\log T \cdot \log\log\log T)$, demonstrating that structured assumptions offer only marginal improvements in estimation and highlighting the necessity of sparsity for achieving faster convergence rates. Furthermore, we examine the impact of this approach on hypothesis testing, proving that it enables highly accurate confidence intervals and p-values, even when applied to existing methods designed for sparse models. Finally, we validate our findings through experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets. Our results indicate that for practical values of $T$ and $|{\cal S}|$, the performance gap between structured and non-structured models is negligible, while the computational advantages of unstructured models provide a significant edge. Additionally, we find that existing p-value calculations are prone to severe errors, underscoring the critical importance of our proposed inference techniques. While the orbital Hall effect in gapless graphene lacks a measurable Hall response due to vanishing net charge and valley-resolved velocities, opening a gap in graphene enables an alternative manifestation of this effect. This paper demonstrates that the valley and charge currents associated with the valley Hall effect can be equivalently expressed as domainite and charge orbital Hall currents, respectively. Consequently, the non-zero conductivity observed in gapless graphene serves as a conductivity domainite (CD) effect. Furthermore, we show that the CD effect and the orbital Hall effect (OHE) become dominant in gapped graphene, thereby refuting prior claims that the orbital Hall effect is absent in this system. In contrast to the CD effect, the OHE in gapped graphene manifests as an orbital Hall conductivity. We illustrate the experimental signatures of both the CD effect and the OHE, with the latter potentially detectable via an orbital magnetization response in the transverse direction using the Hall pick-up method. Additionally, we identify that the OHE in gapped graphene can be interpreted as a manifestation of the valley Hall effect, an interpretation that does not apply to the CD effect. Finally, we explore how to enhance the OHE in gapped graphene by analyzing the influence of electron-electron interactions, spin-orbit coupling, and electron-phonon interactions. Although interactions can amplify the OHE, it is more effective to open a large gap through sublattice asymmetry. Furthermore, we observe that electron-phonon interactions can be viewed as a manifestation of the valley Hall effect, whereas the CD effect and the OHE do not arise in this scenario. These findings offer a novel perspective on Hall effects in condensed matter physics and may stimulate new experimental investigations. **Keywords:** orbital Hall effect, conductivity domainite effect, valley Hall effect, graphene. **PACS numbers:** 72.15.Rn, 72.25.Mn, 72.25.Bh, 72.25.Lk. **Author contributions:** YL and YW proposed the research concept and wrote the paper; YL performed the numerical calculations. Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) are machine learning models specifically designed to process tabular data represented as graphs. While prior research has largely focused on how data within single nodes or edges influences graph contamination, the impact of node features across an entire graph remains under-explored. This study investigates that gap by demonstrating a reinforcement learning approach where data contamination occurs in response to specific features across all nodes within a graph. Furthermore, we analyze how graph size and feature dimensionality affect learning, revealing that the algorithm's sensitivity to data varies according to these structural properties. Our findings indicate that the proposed method can significantly impair GNNs by introducing features that mislead the model. Consequently, this highlights the critical need for future research into the sensitivity of GNNs regarding the features used to represent graph nodes. To facilitate this, all code for our experiments is made available at https://github.com/SebastianKlauer/RL-GNN. Additionally, we present a series of benchmark tests designed to evaluate the robustness of various GNN models against data contamination strategies. These benchmarks are accessible via our repository and are intended for use by the broader community to assess the effectiveness of existing GNN architectures. Specifically, the repository includes tests for GraphSAGE, GIN, and GCN models. We conclude that these benchmarks provide a valuable tool for assessing GNN resilience to data contamination, thereby advancing the field's understanding of these models' vulnerabilities. By promoting a more robust and secure GNN model, the community can foster greater trust in graph-based machine learning applications. Our contributions are threefold: (i) we demonstrate a novel, feature-driven data contamination strategy for graph-based RL models; (ii) we provide a series of benchmarks assessing a GNN model's susceptibility to this attack; and (iii) we offer insights into the benefits of our attack, which will help promote more robust and secure GNN models. This work serves as a catalyst for the community to develop more robust and secure GNN models. The benchmarks presented here can be utilized to evaluate the robustness of existing GNN architectures against the proposed attack, and the resulting insights will guide the community in creating more secure models. Specifically, we provide benchmark tests for GraphSAGE, GIN, and GCN models. These benchmarks can be used to assess the susceptibility of GNN models to the presented attack, and the insights derived will help promote more robust and secure GNN models in the future.

Catalogue matching serves as a critical method for assigning physical properties to colour-magnitude diagram (CMD) sources, thereby enabling the investigation of various stellar population characteristics. This process involves aligning sources from a sample catalogue with two stellar catalogues, Gaia DR2 and Gaia EDR3, utilizing a suite of observables derived from astrometry and photometry. By employing a machine learning approach, we can identify the most effective observables for catalogue matching and subsequently refine the methodology to enhance the reliability of matching outcomes. Our analysis of catalogues with varying resolutions and coverage reveals that while a broad selection of astrometric observables is essential for matching samples with high proper motion, rich in high-quality Gaia data, this is less so for samples characterized by limited astrometry but abundant precise photometry. Consequently, we developed an improved matching technique that leverages a wide array of additional photometric data to significantly boost the reliability of matching results for samples where astrometry is sparse. We demonstrate this approach by matching the Gaia EDR3 data to two external catalogues: the M31-100 catalogue, which comprises 100 years of M31 proper motion data, and the Gaia-CMC catalogue, which contains 20 years of proper motion data for MWC stars. In both scenarios, we show that incorporating supplementary photometric data leads to a substantial increase in the number of matches, with a corresponding significant reduction in the rate of false matches. Furthermore, we provide an assessment of the impact of these additional matches on the derived properties of the two M31 and MWC samples. Ultimately, this strategy offers a robust solution for enhancing catalogue matching when samples lack sufficient Gaia astrometry, a common limitation for many ground-based surveys. The code utilized in this study is publicly accessible at https://github.com/astro-ml/astro-ml. Ontologies serve as formal, explicit specifications of categories within a particular domain, where concepts are linked through various relationships. While visualization tools for ontologies offer both conceptual and technical benefits, existing solutions primarily focus on non-overlapping subontontologies and do not adequately address associations between concepts from different subontontologies. Furthermore, due to the ontology explosion phenomenon, many systems struggle to visualize subontontologies exceeding 100 to 200 concepts. This paper introduces OntoPlot, a new visualization method designed to display the non-hierarchical associations found in large ontologies containing hundreds or even thousands of concepts. The study presents findings from a survey of OntoPlot's usage across various ontologies and identifies key challenges and future research directions. Ultimately, this work aims to advance ontology visualization by enhancing the scalability of existing tools. The OntoPlot source code is accessible at https://github.com/ChenYingjie/OntoPlot. Additionally, a web-based version is available at https://chennyj.github.io/OntoPlot/, and the authors invite further contributions to this tool.

We introduce a new approach that leverages CycleGAN to train an end-to-end automatic speech recognition (AE-ASR) model without retraining. This method enables recognition across two acoustic domains by incorporating an inter-domain loss into both adversarial and Asr-identity losses. Additionally, we demonstrate that integrating a feature-level speaker verification loss further improves performance. Extensive experiments conducted on the WSJ-96 dataset reveal a 10% enhancement in CER relative to the baseline AE-ASR system that utilizes only standard ASR losses. Additionally, we observe a notable improvement in E2E-ASR models that integrate speaker verification losses. Our code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/ashish-agarwal123/CycleGAN-E2E-ASR. To our knowledge, this represents the first application of CycleGAN in the context of end-to-asr speech recognition. Furthermore, this is the inaugural study to explore the impact of inter-domain losses within the CycleGan framework for ASR applications. Finally, we aim to facilitate future research by releasing our code to the community, thereby providing a foundational starting point for developing AC-ASR across diverse acoustic environments. We anticipate that this approach will significantly enhance automatic speech recognition performance in varying acoustic domains. Our code can be accessed at https://github.com/ashish-agarwal123/CycleGAN-E2E-ASR. To our knowledge, this serves as the first instance of applying CycleGan in the context of end-to-asr speech recognition. Standard deep neural networks (DNNs) excel at mapping inputs to outputs but offer no mechanism for controlling system dynamics. Conversely, control-theoretic methods can manage system dynamics but struggle with complex input-output mappings. This paper introduces a novel deep active prediction framework that integrates DNNs with model predictive control (MPC) to unify perception and motion planning. By utilizing a DNN to forecast the system's future state based on current dynamics and recent history, MPC generates an open-loop control signal to achieve a desired future state. The framework's name stems from the prediction component, which actively leverages both system dynamics and its own past predictions. We validate this approach on a two-wheeled robot navigating a simulated corridor. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method surpasses MPC in terms of prediction accuracy. Furthermore, we evaluate the framework's ability to predict the robot's trajectory around corners and under occlusions. Our results indicate that, unlike standard MPC, the proposed framework effectively anticipates the robot's path even when its presence is partially obscured. The code is accessible at https://github.com/ashishgarg123/DAPP. Additionally, we have released a simulated dataset of a two-wheeled robot navigating a corridor occluded by a person. This dataset supports a wide range of applications, including object detection, tracking, segmentation, trajectory prediction, and next frame prediction. Automated Essay Scoring (AES) represents a longstanding challenge that intersects both education and natural language processing. This study introduces a framework that integrates multiple transformer-based language models to address two core AES tasks: predicting essay quality and detecting plagiarism. We benchmark various state-of-the-art transformer models, including BERT, RoBERTa, and ALBERT, to evaluate their performance in automatically analyzing student essays. Furthermore, we compare these results against other methods and pre-trained language models to determine the optimal architecture for effectively evaluating student performance. Our findings indicate that the best performance is achieved by fine-tuning a BERT model that incorporates additional features, such as character n-grams, alongside the text. Additionally, experiments conducted on real-world datasets containing actual essays demonstrate that the proposed multi-model framework achieves an accuracy of 80.11% for quality prediction and 80.15% for plagiarism detection. These outcomes confirm that integrating different transformer-based models can effectively address automated essay scoring challenges. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/abhishekgupta1001/AES. Keywords: Automated Essay Scoring, Quality Assessment, Transformer-based Language Models, Plagiarism Detection.

Domain adaptation is essential for addressing the false positive problem in large-scale pedestrian detection, yet it remains largely ignored in current auto-labeling pipelines for supervised deep learning models. This occurs because existing frameworks typically transfer pre-trained object detectors from supervised domains to unsupervised domains without implementing any adaptation mechanism to reduce false positives. To address this, we introduce Box Re-Ranking, a domain-adaptive technique that mitigates false positives in deep learning models without requiring additional unsupervised training. Our approach employs a novel multi-domain re-ranking method to efficiently identify high-confidence pedestrian boxes within the output of a supervised object detector. Furthermore, a robust selection method is developed to integrate these boxes into the training dataset. Extensive experiments on multiple real-world datasets demonstrate that our method achieves state-of-the-art performance across various domain-adaptation scenarios. The proposed approach holds significant potential for large-scale pedestrian detection applications. The code is accessible at: https://github.com/MyungJinKoo/Box-Re-Ranking. We introduce a two-stage deep learning framework designed to enhance the quality of mono music recordings. The initial stage employs a generator network to increase the audio's brightness, which is subsequently integrated with a vocoder to boost the music's overall clarity. This approach is versatile and capable of performing various music improvement tasks, such as music enhancement and interpolation. Experimental results demonstrate that our method surpasses several state-of-the-art enhancement techniques on the Music Enhancement benchmark. Additionally, we show that the model is effective in the field of music interpolation. To support future research, the Audio Super Intelligence (ASI) platform has been developed to deploy these deep learning models, with the ASI server now serving as a baseline for music enhancement services. The system's user-friendly interface and the availability of pre-trained models on the platform aim to facilitate music quality improvement for both academic and industrial applications. The source code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/ai4s/Server.git. This paper was submitted to the MMSP 2019 conference. The full version is available at https://arxiv.org/abs/1909.00019. Finally, by utilizing the FauxThrow score, we automatically generate new animations that surpass those created by existing state-of-the-art methods. These results are achieved without relying on high-resolution motion capture data, thereby maintaining data privacy. Although Neural Machine Translation (NMT) has advanced significantly, it frequently fails to maintain accurate grammatical structure, a shortcoming that directly correlates with degraded translation quality. To address this, we introduce a top-down tree-structured decoding framework that leverages an explicit syntactic parser to guide the NMT decoder. This approach employs a shared decoder structure for both translation and dependency parsing, integrated with a tree-augmented LSTM that utilizes syntactic links to capture grammatical relationships. By combining syntax-informed decoding with syntax-aware fine-tuning, the model achieves superior performance in both translation and dependency parsing tasks. Experimental results demonstrate that our model surpasses previous methods by effectively integrating syntactic knowledge into the translation process. Furthermore, our top-performing system has secured first place in the TED Multimedia Summit Neural Machine Translation challenge. The Binding Energy Assessment Platform (BEAP) hosts a database of binding energy distributions designed for the astrophysical and astrochemical communities. These distributions, derived from quantum chemical calculations, cover various ice species interacting with small molecular and atomic gas particles. Accessing BEAP is streamlined through a user-friendly web interface, and new data entries are continuously being added in collaboration with researchers. This platform aims to facilitate the assessment of molecule-ice binding energy distributions, thereby enhancing the accuracy of astrochemical models. BEAP's online presence is established at https://www.sci-fisica.unige.it/bepap. The initiative is led by a core team from the University of Geneva, including Andrea Pagliaroli, Andrea Mappian, Andrea Mura, and Andrea Galli, with ongoing contributions from other scientists. Future developments will focus on expanding the database with new binding energy distributions. Additionally, the team intends to integrate a novel method for calculating binding energy distributions using the Periodic Density Functional Theory (P-DFT) approach, which will allow for the study of larger ice matrices. This method will be implemented via a university-wide high-performance computing facility at the University of Geneva, known as the High-Performance Computing Laboratory (HCL), which is part of the larger Scientific Computing Laboratory (SCl). The P-DFT method was developed by Andrea Galli, and its application to compute binding energy distributions for ice species is currently being carried out by Andrea Pagliaroli. To further improve usability, BEAP will implement a novel feature enabling the download of binding energy distributions in common formats, such as JSON. This functionality will be developed by Andrea Pagliaroli, who is also responsible for maintaining the BEAP web interface. Pagliaroli will also continue to populate the database with new quantum chemical results. The development team will actively engage with the astrophysical and astrochemical communities to gather feedback and refine the platform's features. The study begins by establishing a mathematical framework for a multiplicative stochastic process constrained by a logarithmic stochastic trajectory. It outlines the system's characteristics, deriving formulas for key metrics such as the mean, variance, and variance gap, which gap plots display power-law scaling. Subsequently, synthetic datasets generated from this model are analyzed to validate the model and distinguish it from other significant stochastic processes. Specifically, the analysis demonstrates that these new data can be effectively represented by a Pólya Urn process, whereas they cannot be accurately modeled using a Multiplicative Noise process. Furthermore, it is observed that the stochastic trajectories of the analyzed data align with the theoretical bounds of the proposed mathematical model. Overall, these findings suggest that the mathematical model proposed herein offers greater flexibility than the two comparative processes when characterizing and analyzing multiplicative stochastic data. The paper concludes by discussing potential applications of this model in fields such as neuroscience, network science, and machine learning. The code utilized for the analysis is available at: https://github.com/rahul-agarwal-17/PolyaUrnProcess. Additionally, the authors note that the terms "gap" and "fitted" are employed here in a descriptive capacity rather than as statistically rigorous terms. The term "gap" refers to the difference between the upper and lower bounds of a theoretical growth curve, while "fitted" indicates that the growth parameters of this theoretical curve were optimized to best match the data. While acknowledging that "gap" is a standard statistical term, it is used here to avoid alternatives like "space" or "width," which may carry different connotations. Similarly, "fitted" is used to signify that the theoretical growth curve's parameters were tuned to optimally align with the data, despite the more common statistical association of "fitting" with least squares regression. These choices aim to maintain clarity and avoid confusion. Finally, the authors apologize for any inconvenience caused by these linguistic choices. (End of note)

We introduce a random Clifford algorithm designed to evaluate expected values with low-depth quantum circuits under the "shallow" assumption, which requires that significant contributions arise from circuit expectations involving few qubits. Our method involves sampling expectation values of k-qubit observables (where k is small) across the circuit, weighting these by $(1/2)^k$, and aggregating the results into a weighted sum. We demonstrate that the algorithm's output converges to the correct value with high probability, and we establish bounds on the necessary number of samples. Additionally, numerical experiments on randomly generated circuits indicate that the algorithm performs well even when the shallow assumption is violated. This approach is particularly well-suited for implementation on noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) hardware, as it employs low-depth circuits and simple observables, thereby effectively mitigating noise-related errors. Furthermore, our algorithm is expected to enhance the accuracy of variational quantum eigensolver (VQE) algorithms in scenarios satisfying the shallow hypothesis. Finally, we apply this method to estimate kinetic and potential energy expectation values using low-depth random Clifford circuits for the hydrogen molecule, observing satisfactory results. These findings suggest that the algorithm can improve energy estimation precision for molecules where low-depth random Clifford circuits yield high-quality approximate eigenstates. Ensuring robustness is essential for Natural Language Processing, especially text classification. Although ensemble methods have proven effective for classification tasks, they depend on generating diverse samples from the original input. This paper introduces Sibyl, a novel approach that ensures robustness in classification by leveraging classification models with inherent sample variation. Sibyl demonstrates that Sibylvariant modifications, which fall into four categories, yield robust classification results when used with neural network classifiers. These modifications include embedding perturbations (SibylEmbed), sequential word reordering (SibylOrder), sequential character reordering (SibylOrderChar), and word replacement (SibylSub). Experimental results on the RobustBERTChallenge 2021 benchmark task SibylMod show that Sibylvariant methods achieve performance comparable to state-of-the-art ensemble techniques. Furthermore, Sibyl exhibits superior performance on the RobustEvalChallenge 2021 task SibylEval across both BERT and Transformer-based models. This confirms Sibyl's effectiveness in improving model robustness while offering the advantage of significantly lower computational costs. Meta-learning has recently gained significant traction for its capacity to rapidly adapt to novel situations by learning from a diverse array of examples. Although numerous methods have been developed to train models in this manner, their underlying mechanisms remain largely opaque. This paper introduces a method that demonstrates how meta-learning facilitates the transformation of input data into a representation space where linear algorithms suffice for adaptation. We illustrate that even seemingly complex meta-learning procedures, when applied to linear models, can be shown to induce a representation learning process that allows for fast adaptation within the original input space. Furthermore, we present experimental results comparing meta-learning against standard learning, confirming that these theoretical predictions hold true in practice. The code supporting this work is available at https://github.com/epeli/demo-meta. Our findings suggest that meta-learning does not necessitate the learning of unique representations for each task but rather contributes to learning general representations that enable swift adaptation. Consequently, this implies that meta-learning offers no inherent advantage over standard learning when applied to deep neural networks trained with stochastic gradient descent (SGD). This result is particularly salient given the widespread interest in meta-learning as a solution to generalization challenges in SGD. We conclude by outlining several open questions for future research. Specifically, we demonstrate that our theoretical insights rely on assumptions that may not always be valid, indicating that further investigation is required. Additionally, we show that while our theoretical framework explains how meta-learning operates in limited scenarios, it fails to account for its functionality in more complex settings. Finally, we suggest that future research should explore how to design meta-learning approaches that are less dependent on complex regularization methods, such as data augmentation. These conclusions are derived from the specific example employed in this work. While other examples exist in the literature, they often lack a clear theoretical explanation for their behavior. We anticipate that addressing these limitations will lead to more robust and reliable meta-learning methods in the future. In summary, our work provides a novel perspective on meta-learning that may help clarify its function and guide further research in the field. We hope this study will contribute to a deeper understanding of meta-learning and inspire new avenues of inquiry. Our results indicate that meta-learning does not offer any inherent benefit over standard learning when applied to deep neural networks trained with SGD, and we conclude by suggesting that future research should explore how to develop meta-learning methods that are less reliant on complex regularization techniques, such as data augmentation. Building upon the success of neural machine translation, numerous models have been created to enhance performance, yet they often demand substantial computational power. To address this, researchers have explored two primary strategies: reducing model size and narrowing the gap between compressed and original performance. This paper presents a comparative analysis of quantization and distillation methods aimed at achieving small model sizes while maintaining minimal accuracy loss. We evaluated these techniques using English-to-Italian and English-to-French language pairs. The results indicate that for English-to-Italian translation, distillation yields better outcomes than quantization. However, the opposite holds true for English-to-French, where quantization outperforms distillation. Ultimately, our findings demonstrate that both quantization and distillation are effective approaches for creating high-performing machine translation models. We introduce a new density defined on oriented d-graphs, which serves as the product of a generalized Euler characteristic and a modified lagrangian density applicable to any combinatorial d-graph. This density adheres to several properties relevant to the general theory of dynamical systems, including a property related to the d-Alexander duality of periodic dynamical systems. Given its distinct characteristics, we propose that this density be termed the "illogical lagrangian density" of a hypergraph. Furthermore, we outline several additional properties of this density that are pertinent to topological field theory. Specifically, we demonstrate that the integral of this density across any d-complex embedded within a hypergraph remains independent of the specific embedding, provided the cohomology classes of the complex with respect to the density's coefficients are fixed. Additionally, we illustrate that the integral over any combinatorial d-sphere within a hypergraph, when the cohomology classes of its elements relative to the density are trivial, equals the Euler characteristic of the graph. This finding supports aspects of the generalized Poincaré lemma. These results contribute to the formulation of the principle of general invariance for the "illogical lagrangian density" of a hypergraph and the principle of general duality for the dynamical systems described by the corresponding hypergraph equation. Finally, we provide a representation of the principle of general invariance for the principle of general duality. In conclusion, we suggest that the term "general duality" should be replaced with "Poincaré duality." Deep learning-based segmentation models typically require extensive labeled datasets, which are often time-consuming and costly to create. This paper introduces a novel approach designed to reduce the amount of training data needed for segmenting lung fields in chest X-rays to treat pneumonia. We successfully applied this method to a real-world dataset of 2,000 clinical pneumonia cases. Our proposed strategy involves training the model using a combination of three distinct image augmentation techniques. We evaluated the impact of various parameter settings for these methods and determined that the optimal configuration involves three rounds of training. The training utilized a Cascaded R-Fully Convolutional Network (R-FCN) architecture, which was adapted from an object detection model originally developed for the COCO dataset. The final configuration yielded an Intersection over Union (IoU) score of 0.81, representing a 9% improvement over the baseline and an 8% gain compared to the best-performing single data augmentation technique. Furthermore, we demonstrated that the model maintains robustness by achieving an IoU of 0.77 on a separate test dataset. These findings indicate that the proposed image augmentation strategy effectively enhances the model's performance and generalization capabilities. Consequently, this approach is highly promising for developing segmentation models in clinical settings where labeled data is scarce. Our method is available at https://github.com/abhishekkumar123456789/lung_pneumonia_segmentation. Additionally, we have made the associated code, model weights, and sample outputs accessible for review. We welcome your feedback and suggestions. Thank you. Although recent advancements in Vision-and-Language Models (VLMs) have significantly improved image captioning, they often generate repetitive and uninteresting descriptions. To address this, we introduce Prompt 'n' Cap, a non-iterative, prompt-based approach designed to produce diverse and engaging image captions. Our method employs prompt generation to create a library of open-ended prompts, which are then utilized in conjunction with prompt embedding to produce varied outputs. Furthermore, these prompts enable the system to describe images from multiple perspectives. Extensive evaluations on COCO, Referring-Expression, and SCUT-RefExpr datasets demonstrate that our non-iterative method outperforms existing state-of-the-art approaches. Additionally, reference expression matching reveals that our method can generate references to new expressions not present in the training data, indicating a high degree of controllability in the produced descriptions. Finally, human assessments confirm that our approach generates more diverse and interesting captions compared to current VLMs. The code is accessible at https://github.com/lyx1515/Controllable-Image-Captions.

The concept of harm is both intuitive and ubiquitous, yet its definition remains contentious. While some scholars define it through negative consequences, others propose it as a distinct causal relation independent of consequences. This paper argues that the latter definition is necessary and outlines one such account. Furthermore, I demonstrate how this account effectively addresses various problematic scenarios, including castration, birth control, and abortion. Finally, I evaluate an alternative formulation and illustrate how it fails to handle certain problematic cases. Although the interaction between harm and consent is significant, it falls outside the scope of this paper. The goal is to establish a foundational framework for harm upon which future research can build to incorporate consent. By focusing on the interaction between harm and causation, this approach provides a tractable starting point for the broader and more complex issue of harm and consent. Ultimately, this work aims to offer a manageable initial step toward a comprehensive theory of harm and its various problematic interactions. Specifically, the paper presents definitional examinations of harm, its causal structure, and its relationship with consequences. The analysis begins by reviewing relevant existing literature. Subsequently, Section 3 introduces an intuitive account of harm based on preemption theory, which is then formalized in Section 4. Section 5 demonstrates the efficacy of this formalization by addressing problematic cases involving birth control and castration. This paper introduces MMLSpark, a new open-source distributed machine learning and deep learning library that offers adaptable and scalable alternatives to both R's `mlpackages` and Apache Spark's `MLlib`. Backed by the R community and integrated with R, RStudio, and Python, MMLSpark is designed to be easy to use, accessible, and straightforward. The system includes unified, scalable, and easy-to-implement implementations of 35+ algorithms, such as linear models, generalized linear models, decision trees, random forests, gradient boosting machines, k-nearest neighbors, logistic regression, naive Bayes, support vector machines, principal component analysis, clustering, and factor analysis. These algorithms are optimized for execution across distributed Apache Spark clusters. Additionally, MMLSpark features new implementations for decision trees, random forests, and k-nearest neighbors within R that support out-of-core processing, enabling analysis of datasets exceeding available RAM. Furthermore, the package introduces a new deep learning algorithm module for Spark, which includes neural networks, deep belief networks, autoencoders, and recurrent neural networks. This module ensures consistent algorithm execution across all MMLSpark modules and supports decision model export to Python. The paper also presents performance benchmarking results comparing Spark and R implementations of ten algorithms, including linear regression, random forests, and support vector machines. Finally, a comparison of performance and functionality between the existing R `mlpackages` package and the new R MMLSpark implementation is provided. This work was presented at the R User Conference 2017 in Vienna, Austria. The source code is available at https://github.com/Microsoft/SparkR.

Voice translation involves converting speech from one language into another language via spoken word(s). Current state-of-the-art methods typically depend on extensive bilingual data, making zero-shot voice translation a relatively underexplored area. This study addresses zero-shot voice translation by leveraging class-conditional latent variables of voice characteristics within a sequence-to-sequence framework. We introduce an auxiliary classification task to learn these voice traits and utilize the resulting class-conditional generative model for zero-shot voice translation. Furthermore, we incorporate voice characteristics into the attention mechanism to enhance the voice change aspect of the task. Experiments conducted on the VoxCeleb and Librispeech datasets demonstrate that our model achieves reasonable performance in zero-shot voice translation, yielding results that are both intelligible and distinct in voice quality. Additionally, our results are supported by comprehensive evaluations using various automatic metrics. Finally, an extensive ablation study was conducted to analyze the model's contributions regarding speech intelligibility and voice change. The code for this model is available at: https://github.com/ashishkumar12345/ZeroShotVoiceTranslation. This work was presented at the 60th Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (Volume 1: Long Papers).</thinking>
