This paper offers a systematic examination of how machine learning systems can be designed to incorporate knowledge from human domain experts. We provide a formal definition of domain knowledge integration (KDI) and its components, examine methods for its implementation, explore the various methods involved, and outline a roadmap for future research and development in this rapidly growing field. We contend that KDI serves as a foundational element for building intelligent systems capable of learning from diverse sources, including but not limited to data. Furthermore, we argue that explicitly integrating domain knowledge enhances the robustness of machine learning systems, thereby addressing critical challenges in interpretability and fairness. Additionally, we demonstrate that KDI is essential for enabling machine intelligence to engage in interactive learning with humans. Finally, we highlight that current research in knowledge-aware machine learning represents a significant branch of the broader intelligence science field. Our goal is to encourage a more interdisciplinary approach to machine learning research by fostering deeper collaboration with experts across various domains. To achieve this, we have developed a blueprint for KDI to serve as a guide for integrating domain knowledge into machine learning systems. We believe this blueprint will assist researchers in identifying knowledge representation and reasoning methods to facilitate effective domain knowledge integration. Additionally, we have compiled a directory of relevant resources to assist researchers in entering this field. We anticipate that this work will assist researchers in successfully integrating domain knowledge into their machine learning initiatives. Accurate localization and identification of vertebrae are fundamental prerequisites for numerous clinical tasks involving vertebral structure analysis. This study introduces a novel framework that utilizes a two-stage strategy to automatically localize and identify vertebrae in abdominal CT scans. The initial stage employs a deep neural network to generate high-quality vertebral candidate regions through an innovative 3D data synthesis technique and view-based frame estimation. The subsequent stage applies an anatomically-constrained optimization algorithm, grounded in the vertebral column's inherent anatomical properties, to refine the candidate positions from the first stage and assign vertebral labels. We assessed our method's performance using the VT-Net dataset, which comprises CT images from the MICCAI 2018 Vertebrae Challenge. Our approach achieves a mean localization error of 1.12 cm and an identification success rate of 85.31%, surpassing the challenge's best participant results of 1.25 cm and 83.54%, respectively. Furthermore, we demonstrate that our method produces highly accurate vertebral structures and reliably identifies pathological vertebrae. The source code and dataset are accessible at https://github.com/leeyang1990/ASLO_VT-Net. Ultimately, this work provides a robust and versatile framework for vertebral analysis in CT imaging. By integrating data augmentation, frame estimation, and anatomically-constrained optimization, the method is expected to enhance vertebral identification accuracy, particularly in complex cases such as those involving severe deformities or degenerative changes. Ultimately, this framework holds significant potential for diverse clinical applications, including the assessment and monitoring of scoliosis and osteoporosis. The integration of AI-driven techniques not only streamlines clinical workflows but also facilitates the early detection and diagnosis of vertebral pathologies. Ultimately, this research paves the way for more precise and efficient diagnostic tools in spinal medicine. Furthermore, the framework's adaptability allows it to be extended to other medical imaging modalities and anatomical regions, thereby broadening its applicability across the field of medical image analysis. Recent experiments have revealed new dynamical stabilization effects driven by the interaction between quantum matter and vacuum fluctuations. In this study, we investigate resonant electron scattering off a confined set of vacuum fluctuations within a cavity. Our findings indicate that when ultrafast light-matter coupling is achieved, electron scattering by vacuum fluctuations is amplified. We demonstrate that this effect is best understood as a dynamical stabilization of the resonance, facilitated by vacuum fluctuations. Furthermore, we show that this phenomenon can be understood through a model of resonant tunneling across a time-dependent potential barrier modulated by cavity light. We predict that this cavity-stabilized tunneling effect is observable via ultrafast photoemission spectroscopy using a femtosecond laser. Additionally, we identify a specific regime where resonant electron scattering by vacuum fluctuations becomes observable in this framework. Finally, we discuss potential applications, including the creation of a single-electron switch via ultrafast resonant tunneling and the generation of single electrons in superconducting quantum circuits. These results are expected to stimulate new research into resonant electron scattering by vacuum fluctuations. This work is accompanied by an online supplement containing supplementary material, including extended discussions, detailed derivations, and simulations. Inspired by the variational approaches employed in the density matrix renormalization group, we introduce a novel method designed to characterize the density matrices of reduced subsystems arising from a pure state of a many-body quantum system. The density matrices generated by our algorithm are provably optimal, and we demonstrate their utility in addressing the quantum separability problem. Specifically, our method yields the exact density matrices for both reduced and global subsystems in ground states of the Heisenberg and Kitaev models. Furthermore, we establish a lower bound for the computational resources required to execute the eigenvalue decomposition of Hermitian matrices, revealing that the quantum measurement complexity associated with this task scales at least linearly with the number of eigenvalues. Consequently, we prove that the optimal density matrices produced by our method can be derived using only $O(N)$ measurements on a pure state $\psi$ of dimension $2^N$. Finally, our findings indicate that the computational complexity of the quantum linear algebra problem scales at most quadratically with the number of eigenvalues, suggesting that these problem classically intractable density matrices can be handled at the quantum level with minimal overhead. This represents a substantial enhancement over current classical techniques. Additionally, we demonstrate that the computational cost of our method is independent of the density matrix dimension, thereby circumventing the exponential scaling challenge typically faced by classical approaches. Our results establish a new lower bound for the computational resources needed for quantum state tomography. We also explore potential applications of this approach in the study of quantum phase transitions and thermalization. Finally, we outline prospects for developing a quantum algorithm to solve the density matrix eigenvector problem on near-term quantum hardware. This proposed algorithm is particularly efficient, as it requires a number of measurements on the eigenstate equal to the count of accessible basis vectors in the original basis. We anticipate that our findings will facilitate the development of new quantum algorithms for solving linear and eigenvalue problems on quantum computers. In conclusion, our work demonstrates that the density matrices of reduced subsystems, which are intractable for classical computers, can be handled with minimal additional resources on quantum computers. We anticipate that this research will stimulate further investigations into the advantages of using quantum computers to manage reduced subsystems of many-body quantum systems. Our findings also provide a foundation for formulating a general framework for the density matrix renormalization group. Ultimately, our results suggest that the quantum computer is an essential tool for resolving the quantum linear algebra problem. Slab plasmas, which exhibit spatially periodic variations in mass density, ion temperature, and/or magnetic field orientation, are frequently encountered in both laboratory and space environments. This study investigates the physics of the small-scale ripping mode, a collisionless plasma instability driven by the misalignment between mass density and the gradient of ion temperature. The analysis introduces a comprehensive set of scaling relations for growth rates and wave numbers, applicable under conditions of weak, moderate, and strong misalignment. Furthermore, a unified framework for wave propagation and the Alfvénic reflection coefficient is established. These findings provide a robust theoretical basis for interpreting recent laboratory and space observations of rippling phenomena within collisionless slab plasmas. Specifically, the derived growth rate scaling laws are directly applicable to describing the recently observed small-scale ripping mode within the Earth's magnetosheath. Additionally, the various scaling relations and formulas regarding rippling growth rates and wave propagation can be utilized to analyze future observations from the upcoming Magnetospheric MultiScale (MMS) mission. The present study also presents a numerical simulation of the small-scale ripping mode to validate the derived analytical growth rate scaling relations. Finally, the paper suggests potential future applications of these small-scale rippling modes in advanced plasma laboratory experiments. This could include the generation of small-scale rippling modes to serve as a seed for laser-driven shock generation in high-intensity laser-solid interactions, as well as in the manipulation of shock dynamics. Furthermore, these modes could be employed to control the evolution of shock-generated turbulence and to facilitate the in-situ measurement of shock thickness. The latter application is particularly relevant for developing a novel technique for measuring ion shock thickness, which could be implemented using MMS data. This proposed method involves analyzing the propagation of small-scale ripples along the shock normal and their associated growth rates. By combining these measurements with the provided growth rate scaling relations, it becomes possible to determine the ion shock thickness. This marks the first time such a measurement has been suggested, potentially representing a significant advancement in shock physics. Ultimately, these developments could substantially enhance our understanding of shock dynamics and their role in energy conversion and particle acceleration. The visual similarity between distinct objects within a specific domain is frequently exploited to enhance recognition performance in semi-supervised learning. This paper introduces a new approach to object representation known as semi-supervised trait manipulation (STM), which increases the visual similarity of different objects by altering their features. Our primary contribution lies in the innovative technique called fashion image retrieval (FIR) based on STM, designed to improve the visual similarity of fashion images from different items in the training set. We achieve this manipulation through a two-stage process: first, a fashion image is converted into a fashion image embedding using a pre-trained fashion image encoder; second, these embeddings are directly modified to create new representations called fashion image embedding (FAE) manipulations. Our goal is to make images from different items in the original set appear more similar, thereby improving recognition accuracy, while ensuring images from the same item (same-class images) do not become too similar. We evaluate the STM and FIR contributions using the Fashion-MNIST (F-MNIST) dataset, which consists of 7,000 distinct items across 10 categories. Experimental results demonstrate that our method boosts the mean average precision at the item level by 1.2% compared to the baseline, while maintaining consistent performance at the image level. Furthermore, we show that the proposed FAE manipulation outperforms other state-of-the-art embedding manipulation methods. Finally, we provide an open-source implementation of the FAE manipulation to facilitate future research in this area. The source code can be accessed at https://github.com/abhishekdatta1995/STM-FIR. Light field cameras capture four-dimensional scene data using spatial and angular ray sampling, offering a cost-effective method for depth estimation. However, the plenoptic recording process compresses this 4D information into 2D images, causing significant information loss. This paper introduces a data-driven cost builder designed for depth prediction, trained to recover the information lost during compression, particularly to overcome the limitations of current state-of-the-art techniques when handling occluded regions. Specifically, we observe that existing approaches fail to accurately manage occlusion, resulting in suboptimal depth predictions. To address this, we propose an occlusion-aware cost builder that utilizes a mask decoder to generate scene masks for depth estimation. Additionally, we present a new dataset for supervised depth estimation featuring high-resolution plenoptic captures paired with ground truth depth maps. Experimental results demonstrate that our method surpasses previous state-of-the-art solutions. The dataset and code will be made publicly available. Video: https://youtu.be/4Yq4Yq4Yq4Y. Non-Riemannian gravitational theories offer valuable frameworks for investigating phase transitions within quantum gravity. This study examines a collection of non-Riemannian actions derived from reducing the square of the curved doubled Dirac operator acting on doubled spinors. When utilizing the Minkowski plus ansatz for the doubled vielbein, these actions correspond to a set of non-Riemannian geometries where specific components of the Weyl tensor vanish. By analyzing the on-shell spectrum of small linear perturbations around these backgrounds, we identify the conditions necessary for a unique graviton mode, a critical requirement for the consistent propagation of gravitons in the non-Riemannian regime of quantum gravity. Finally, these actions are interpreted as specific quantizations of a mixed-symmetry tensor field theory. This interpretation not only elucidates the nature of non-Riemannian gravitons but also underscores a fundamental distinction between quantizing a mixed-symmetry tensor field and quantizing a metric. Furthermore, the analysis reveals that all non-Riemannian gravitons emerge from the multiplet of massless fields associated with a generalized symmetry in the linearized theory, suggesting that non-Riemannian gravitons are intrinsically linked to generalized symmetries in quantum gravity. Additionally, the study demonstrates that the non-Riemannian actions can be derived from a generalized string theory action that incorporates both a metric and a generalized connection. Finally, the paper establishes a correspondence between the generalized Fierz-Pauli theory and non-Riemannian gravity by examining the relationship between their respective equations of motion. These findings indicate that non-Riemannian geometries and gravitons play a significant and essential role in quantum gravity. The paper concludes by outlining several promising future research directions. The proliferation of IEEE 802.11-based home WiFi networks has led to significant interference issues. To address this, the IEEE 802.11k/v standard introduces mechanisms for access points (APs) to regulate client associations and validate the capabilities of connecting devices. This paper presents the first implementation of a controller designed to jointly optimize WiFi client-to-AP associations and the selection of appropriate signal extenders. Our approach leverages the 802.11k/v capabilities of the WiFi clients to dynamically manage both network traffic loads. We implemented the extender selection logic by modifying the WiFi client software stack, enabling us to evaluate the efficacy of our solution in a controlled experimental home environment. Our results demonstrate that the proposed methodology effectively mitigates common WiFi interference problems. Furthermore, we show that in scenarios involving high traffic loads on multiple APs, our approach substantially enhances network performance compared to traditional WiFi designs that lack extenders or those that do not account for traffic load when selecting extension points. Specifically, performance improvements of up to 100% were observed in our experiments. Finally, we detail the implementation specifics of our solution and its deployment within the CORDA testbed. Given that our methodology relies solely on the 802.11k/v capabilities of the clients, it is compatible with a wide range of existing WiFi devices. Our code is publicly accessible on GitHub. By enabling 802.11k/v-enabled clients to intelligently and dynamically select extension points, our solution offers a practical means to enhance the performance of WiFi networks in both current and future applications. Furthermore, our design facilitates the investigation of the potential benefits of 802.11k/v-enabled APs in future deployments. To our knowledge, this represents the first practical implementation of jointly optimizing AP and extender selection based on the 802.11k/v capabilities of individual clients.
